articles.title: Critical Apache Tomcat Flaw Lets Remote Attackers Join Trusted Server Clusters Without Authentication
articles.description:
The Apache Software Foundation has disclosed a critical flaw in Apache Tomcat that allows a remote attacker to join a trusted server cluster without authentication. Tracked as CVE-2026-133325, the flaw affects clusters that use TLS 1.3 with a pre-shared key. Apache published the advisory on November 19, 2026, and credited researcher Mike Read with finding […]

The post Critical Apache Tomcat Flaw Lets Remote Attackers Join Trusted Server Clusters Without Authentication appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The Apache Software Foundation has disclosed a critical flaw in Apache Tomcat that allows a remote attacker to join a trusted server cluster without authentication. Tracked as CVE-2026-133325, the flaw affects clusters that use TLS 1.3 with a pre-shared key.

Apache published the advisory on November 19, 2026, and credited researcher Mike Read with finding the issue.

The Apache Tomcat 11 security advisory identifies versions 11.0.28 and 11.0.29 as affected. Apache also lists Tomcat 10.1.62 and 9.0.124. Running one of those versions does not by itself mean a server is exposed.

The flaw requires the affected cluster encryption setup, and a remote attacker needs network access to the service that handles communication between cluster members. A public Tomcat website does not necessarily expose that service.

Tomcat Cluster Authentication Failed

Apache Tribes handles communication between servers in a Tomcat cluster. Those servers can share session data so that a user can stay signed in when another server takes over. A pre-shared key is a secret configured on trusted members in advance.

In the affected TLS 1.3 setup, Tomcat did not verify the identity of the server at the other end of the connection. The connection could be encrypted without proving that the server was allowed to join.

Cyber Security News previously covered flaws in Tomcat’s EncryptInterceptor, an older component used to protect cluster traffic. The new advisory concerns a different failure: Tomcat accepted a cluster member it had not authenticated. Apache’s advisory does not report active exploitation or say that joining a cluster gives an attacker remote code execution.

Apache recommends switching cluster communication to TLS 1.2 while keeping the pre-shared key enabled. This change applies to traffic between Tomcat servers, not the HTTPS connections used by website visitors. The fixed versions are 11.0.30, 10.1.63, and 9.0.125 for their respective branches. Apache listed them as pending release in its Tomcat 11, Tomcat 10, and Tomcat 9 security notices.

Administrators should check the running version and cluster settings on every member, restrict cluster ports to approved servers, and review available logs for unexpected membership changes. After applying the workaround or updating, confirm that every expected member reconnects and that session replication still works where enabled. A website can still respond while its servers are no longer sharing session data.

The earlier CISA warning about an exploited Tomcat encryption flaw concerned CVE-2026-34486. That warning does not establish exploitation of CVE-2026-133325, and the two flaws should be tracked separately.

articles.title: Hackers Use 355 Domains to Spread Fake GTA 6 PC Launchers Delivering Malware
articles.description:
A malware campaign called CyberLeek is using more than 355 domains and subdomains to promote fake Grand Theft Auto VI PC launchers. The sites offer what they claim is a leaked or early Windows release of GTA 6. Instead of a playable game, the download delivers a ZIP archive containing a malicious program disguised as […]

The post Hackers Use 355 Domains to Spread Fake GTA 6 PC Launchers Delivering Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A malware campaign called CyberLeek is using more than 355 domains and subdomains to promote fake Grand Theft Auto VI PC launchers.

The sites offer what they claim is a leaked or early Windows release of GTA 6. Instead of a playable game, the download delivers a ZIP archive containing a malicious program disguised as an installer.

The campaign takes advantage of a familiar search: players looking for a GTA 6 PC release before they can get one through an official store.

Earlier reporting on fake GTA 6 downloads documented a separate operation that bundled password stealers, remote-access malware and file-destroying code with a fake game installer. Those findings do not establish what CyberLeek’s launcher does after it runs.

Researchers at the Vecert Foundation identified the malware distribution network and traced its activity to mid-October 2026, with notable spikes in November.

The count comes from domain and certificate records. It reflects the size of the infrastructure the researchers linked to CyberLeek, not the number of people infected or the number of distinct malware samples.

Hackers Use 355 Domains to Spread Fake GTA 6 PC Launchers

One site examined by researchers advertised a playable GTA 6 port for Windows 10 and 11. It used search-friendly text and page markup that presented the supposed launcher as a software download.

A prominent button promised a direct file with “no ad wall,” making the page look like a convenient alternative to the pop-ups and redirects users might expect from an unofficial download site.

The download button did not always lead to the same file location. Researchers found that the page could send visitors to changing links on public hosting platforms, with a local ZIP archive available as a fallback.

That distinction matters for defenders: blocking one download URL may leave the original landing page reachable and other download paths available.

CyberLeek also used multiple domain endings and subdomains while keeping the same branding. This gave the campaign several places to send visitors if a site was blocked.

The approach echoes gaming search poisoning campaigns that use credible-looking pages to reach people searching for game tools or popular software. A high search ranking does not verify who published a file or what it contains.

The reported infection step is running the program inside the archive. Visiting the page or finding the ZIP in a Downloads folder does not, on its own, show that the installer ran.

Fake GTA 6 demo

In a separate case involving a fake GTA 6 demo, analysts identified Vidar, a program that steals passwords and browser sessions. Vecert did not name a specific malware family for CyberLeek or confirm what data the fake launcher collected.

Security teams can search DNS and web proxy logs for the reported hosts, then compare any matches with endpoint records for archive downloads and installer launches.

A generic script name or installer filename is not enough to establish a compromise. A recorded launch after a visit to a reported domain gives responders a stronger lead and a reason to check the device for unusual processes and network connections.

Players who downloaded the ZIP but did not run it should delete it without opening the installer. Anyone who ran the program should disconnect the device from the network and have it checked.

Since password and session theft can put accounts at risk even after the download is removed, use a clean device to change important passwords and revoke active sessions if compromise is suspected.

For future releases, check the publisher’s official channels or a trusted storefront rather than a site promising an early build.

articles.title: Hackers Turn Legitimate VPN Software Into a Stealthy Tool for Spying on Government Networks
articles.description:
Hackers have rebuilt the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge to keep a quiet route into compromised networks. The modified Windows program, branded internally as NtMonitor VPN, can link an external network to a victim’s local network while leaving fewer of the traces defenders expect from a standard SoftEther installation. Researchers link the tool to Webworm, a […]

The post Hackers Turn Legitimate VPN Software Into a Stealthy Tool for Spying on Government Networks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers have rebuilt the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge to keep a quiet route into compromised networks. The modified Windows program, branded internally as NtMonitor VPN, can link an external network to a victim’s local network while leaving fewer of the traces defenders expect from a standard SoftEther installation.

Researchers link the tool to Webworm, a China-aligned espionage group with a history of targeting government organizations, particularly in Europe.

The distinction is that the bridge helps operators stay connected after a breach; the report does not show how they broke in. Nor does it name agencies newly affected by this build or establish what data, if any, was taken through it.

Earlier coverage of Webworm’s GraphWorm documented a separate backdoor that used Microsoft OneDrive for communications. NtMonitor serves a different purpose: it gives operators a network route rather than a built-in command shell.

Researchers from Rapid7 identified the modified VPN tool and attributed it to Webworm with moderate confidence in a November 19 report.

They compared a public 64-bit Windows sample with the matching SoftEther source release, version 4.44, build 9807, and found no added command-execution backdoor.

At the time of analysis, only one antivirus vendor on VirusTotal flagged the sample, even though it had been publicly available since January.

Hackers Turn Legitimate VPN Software Into a Stealthy Tool

A VPN bridge connects networks rather than simply giving one user remote access. Every configuration Rapid7 examined linked a remote network to the local one.

That can make the Windows host running the bridge a route to other systems on its network. The risk comes from an existing feature being used without authorization, not from a newly disclosed SoftEther vulnerability.

Earlier reporting on Flax Typhoon’s SoftEther use illustrates how another group used the same open-source project to retain access after a breach.

The public sample described itself as “Network Monitor Software” from “Network Systems Solutions Inc.” and listed netcapa.exe as its original filename.

The disguise was inconsistent: some internal strings used NtMonitor branding, but the service entry point still referenced SEVPNBRIDGE, and several registry paths retained the SoftEther Project name.

The build also packaged a normally separate resource archive inside the program and stored its settings in an encrypted file. Together, those changes meant an installation could look unfamiliar even to a team that knew what stock SoftEther leaves behind.

The network traffic changed, too. Rapid7 found web request paths that resembled routine update traffic and a different marker in the opening exchange between VPN peers.

That made signatures written for standard SoftEther traffic less useful. A separate case involving modified WireGuard also involved a rebuilt VPN tool, but that version ran embedded code. Rapid7 found no comparable execution feature in NtMonitor; the bridge itself was enough to maintain access.

How Government Defenders Can Detect Unauthorized VPN Bridges

Rapid7 found that configurations not considered likely tests pointed to addresses in AS20473, a hosting network associated with The Constant Company and Vultr.

That overlap with past Webworm activity supported the attribution, but the network number alone is not evidence of compromise. ESET’s earlier Webworm research documented targeting in Belgium, Italy, Poland, Serbia, and Spain.

Those countries describe earlier activity, not a confirmed victim list for NtMonitor. For defenders, the best starting point is an inventory of approved VPN services, the hosts allowed to run them, and the remote networks they are supposed to reach.

Investigate unexpected Windows services, firewall rule changes, and connections to unapproved peers together. Earlier reporting on malware in isolated government networks illustrates why investigators should check which systems a compromised host could reach, not just identify the first machine that raised an alert.

If a bridge is unauthorized, preserve its executable, configuration, and connection logs before removing it so responders can reconstruct where it led.

articles.description:
A heap buffer overflow in OpenSSL’s Base64 encoding function can corrupt application memory when the library processes very large inputs. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-121481, was published on November 18, 2026, with a critical CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8. That score describes the potential severity, but it does not mean every service that uses OpenSSL […]

The post OpenSSL Hit by Critical 9.8 Heap Buffer Overflow Vulnerability in Base64 Encoding Function appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A heap buffer overflow in OpenSSL’s Base64 encoding function can corrupt application memory when the library processes very large inputs. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-121481, was published on November 18, 2026, with a critical CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8.

That score describes the potential severity, but it does not mean every service that uses OpenSSL is remotely exposed.

The flaw affects EVP_EncodeBlock(), which converts binary data into printable text. Base64 produces four output bytes for every three input bytes, with padding for a partial group. The application supplies the buffer that holds the result.

For very large inputs, OpenSSL’s calculation of the encoded length can exceed the range of the integer used to store it. That calculation error can cause the encoder to write beyond the end of the supplied buffer. The write can corrupt nearby memory or crash the application.

OpenSSL Heap Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

This differs from the OpenSSL flaw that could leak server memory: the Base64 bug writes outside a buffer, while the earlier DTLS flaw read data outside one.

The key question for security teams is whether an application passes large amounts of untrusted data to the affected encoder. A server’s use of OpenSSL for encrypted connections does not, by itself, answer that question.

Teams should check where their applications call the function and which size limits apply before encoding begins. The CVE version record lists OpenSSL 4.0.0 through 4.0.3 and OpenSSL 4.1.0 as affected, with 4.0.4 and 4.1.1 marking the upper bounds of those ranges.

Those version numbers do not, by themselves, confirm that a fixed package is available from a particular vendor. As with earlier OpenSSL memory corruption fixes, check the release or package notes for the branch you run.

Ubuntu’s security tracker assigns the issue Medium priority and lists its main openssl packages as needing evaluation. It also marks the nodejs package in Ubuntu 22.04 LTS as vulnerable.

Ubuntu notes that this package embeds its own copy of OpenSSL, so checking only the system library can miss software that bundles it.

Inventory OpenSSL copies in system packages, containers, and application bundles. Prioritize applications that Base64-encode data supplied by users or external services.

Until a vendor-confirmed update is available, enforce application-level input limits before encoding. After updating, restart or redeploy affected workloads and verify that they are running the updated build.

For developers, the OpenSSL encoding documentation explains that callers must reserve space for the encoded data and a final zero byte that marks the end of the string. Review that calculation alongside input limits. For large files, consider an encoding interface that processes data in chunks rather than passing the whole file to one call.

articles.title: BYOD Ransomware Hackers Play Audio Ransom Messages on Computers Across Hospitals and Universities
articles.description:
Staff at the University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center reported hearing ransom messages from their computers during an October 26 cyberattack. Two weeks later, a recording from Vanderbilt University captured a voice announcing, “You have been compromised by BYOD.” The messages took the ransom demand out of a private note and made the incident […]

The post BYOD Ransomware Hackers Play Audio Ransom Messages on Computers Across Hospitals and Universities appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Staff at the University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center reported hearing ransom messages from their computers during an October 26 cyberattack.

Two weeks later, a recording from Vanderbilt University captured a voice announcing, “You have been compromised by BYOD.” The messages took the ransom demand out of a private note and made the incident visible to people far beyond the IT team.

The disruptions were real, even where the hackers’ claims remain unverified. New Mexico’s only Level 1 trauma center diverted ambulances for two hours, and more than 30 clinics canceled appointments and outpatient surgeries.

On November 9, Vanderbilt told students, faculty and staff to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi while it investigated.

Researchers at TrendAI noted the reported ransomware activity in their analysis of the BYOD campaign, which claimed at least nine organizations between October 5 and November 9, 2026.

The researchers did not have a public malware sample to examine. Their findings draw on victim statements, public reporting and claims by the group, so the report separates confirmed disruptions from unverified accounts of encryption and data theft.

BYOD Ransomware Hackers Play Audio Ransom Messages on Computers

At UNM, employees reported that the audio claimed patient, student and employee data had been stolen. BYOD later claimed it compromised 36,000 systems, including Microsoft Entra and two Oracle databases.

UNM said the incident affected some end-user devices but did not reach core systems or servers. As the Ascension hospital ransomware incident also showed, ambulance diversion is an operational consequence, not a measure of how far attackers reached.

The Vanderbilt campus device shutdown came as the university warned users about unfamiliar applications, unexpected login approval requests and unusual file or permission changes.

Campus Wi-Fi returned that evening, with other services restored in phases. BYOD claimed it encrypted databases and stole more than one million Social Security numbers, but Vanderbilt had not confirmed the group’s involvement, encryption or data theft in the reporting reviewed by TrendAI.

The audio tells investigators less than it might seem. It shows that a message played on affected computers, but it does not establish how the group delivered it, whether the same method was used at both sites, or whether attackers controlled a central directory.

Its clearest effect was public pressure: staff and students could hear and record the demand before either institution had finished assessing the incident.

Credential compromise

Michigan State University offers a separate clue about account security. It reported a possible credential compromise and required university password resets in early October, before BYOD listed it on November 1.

The university said it had no evidence that its central Active Directory was compromised or that other data was accessed, altered or stolen. The group’s claim about 1.3 million current and former students therefore remains unverified.

Unexpected login prompts deserve attention even when endpoint tools find no malware. Separate reporting on cloud account takeover tactics shows how repeated approval requests can precede unauthorized access.

TrendAI recommends checking identity, endpoint and cloud logs together, then reviewing what a suspected account accessed before its password was reset, including shared files and administrative settings.

For hospitals, the response plan should also cover what happens when staff cannot use their computers. TrendAI advises testing offline backups and rehearsing downtime procedures that do not depend on the network.

The company also recommends giving patients, students and staff a trusted way to report unsolicited messages from anyone claiming to hold their data.

That preparation matters before the first ransom message plays, because restoring computers and containing public pressure are two different jobs.

articles.title: Hackers Use AI-Powered ARTEX Framework to Automate Cyberattacks Without Relying on Zero-Day Exploits
articles.description:
Attackers are using an AI-driven testing tool called ARTEX to break into company networks. It needs no secret software flaws to do this. Instead, it hunts for ordinary mistakes such as exposed apps, weak passwords and loose permissions, and it keeps working at them far longer than a human would. ARTEX is an open-source framework […]

The post Hackers Use AI-Powered ARTEX Framework to Automate Cyberattacks Without Relying on Zero-Day Exploits appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers are using an AI-driven testing tool called ARTEX to break into company networks. It needs no secret software flaws to do this.

Instead, it hunts for ordinary mistakes such as exposed apps, weak passwords and loose permissions, and it keeps working at them far longer than a human would.

ARTEX is an open-source framework that connects a large language model (LLM) to a set of hacking tools. It was built for authorized security testing, but criminals and state-linked groups now use it.

The FBI warned that hackers have used it since at least August 2026 and, in some cases, reached privileged access in under three hours.

Researchers at TrustedSec noted that ARTEX works like a familiar scanner with an AI brain attached. The framework gives a model tools to inspect a target and act on what it finds. Each result feeds the next decision, so the tool can follow a lead without waiting for a person.

Hackers Use AI-Powered ARTEX Framework

The attack flow is not new. According to TrustedSec, attackers still find assets with subfinder, check web services with httpx, map services with Nmap, run nuclei templates and use ffuf to find hidden content.

What changes is the work after that first scan. The model picks an action, the framework runs it, and the output becomes the next input.

It may adjust a request with curl, write a small script or check an exposed file. A secret it finds becomes a new question: is it valid, and what can it reach?

Microsoft showed the tool paired with Nmap, curl, Python HTTP clients and Playwright. It tracked Storm-3358 using ARTEX to scan internet-facing systems and exploit flaws like anonymous file upload and SSRF.

Mandiant also logged rapid AWS permission probing. Other groups have used it to automate Active Directory attacks and move sideways inside networks.

The real shift is cost. Many firms have custom apps, old APIs and forgotten subdomains that nobody tests closely. Attackers used to skip these because one exploit for a common product hits thousands of targets, while a custom app pays off once.

TrustedSec called limited attacker attention an economic assumption, not a control. An AI agent can spend hours on every odd response for little money.

The tool also has weak points. It can burn many tokens on a false lead, and repeating a wrong guess does not make it right. Broad scanning and fast retries also create noise that defenders can spot.

Backdoored Copies and Sandbox Escapes

ARTEX is risky even for people who run it legitimately. The tool holds model API keys, target data and captured sessions, so it becomes a rich target itself.

TrustedSec described a third-party ARTEX copy that pointed users to backdoored Docker images. The changed login handler allowed unauthenticated command execution inside the container. The finding covers those copies only.

It does not show that the original ARTEX source held a backdoor. The WorkOS case shows the other side of the problem. The company said an ARTEX agent used by a researcher running benchmark tests reached a real internal tool.

Reports say the agent escaped a sandbox and pulled sales and support records. The tool had a public API, a predictable development credential and no rate limits.

WorkOS has not shown a true container flaw. An agent with internet access can leave its intended scope without breaking out of anything.

Defenders can act on several points:

  1. Move one exposed employee tool or management API behind an identity-aware proxy, private access service or VPN, then confirm the original server cannot be reached directly.
  2. Set limits in the WAF and application controls for path enumeration, repeated exploit probes and bulk record retrieval.
  3. Trim the permissions of public web apps so one flaw does not open the wider network.
  4. Test whether the team can link odd API use to an account and revoke access while retrieval is still running.

User-agent blocking helps only against default setups, since an operator can change the string. Anyone testing ARTEX should use a disposable VM, temporary credentials and a lab network whose outbound policy denies unrelated destinations.

Scope rules should be enforced by the network, not by a prompt. Security teams should also watch for frameworks exposed on public servers, because open consoles give attackers a free starting point.

The original developer pulled the public code in October after reports of abuse, but forks keep circulating. Defenders should not wait for a zero-day alert, because these intrusions rely on gaps that already exist.

articles.title: Signal Restricts Screenshots to protect User Privacy from AI assistants
articles.description:
Signal is restricting screenshots on iOS 27 and some Android devices to stop built-in AI assistants from reading private chats through screen capture. The encrypted messaging app is targeting Apple’s Siri AI and assistants such as Google Gemini. On Android, the block turns on when Signal detects an assistant trying to read the screen. The […]

The post Signal Restricts Screenshots to protect User Privacy from AI assistants appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Signal is restricting screenshots on iOS 27 and some Android devices to stop built-in AI assistants from reading private chats through screen capture.

The encrypted messaging app is targeting Apple’s Siri AI and assistants such as Google Gemini. On Android, the block turns on when Signal detects an assistant trying to read the screen.

The change addresses what happens after a message arrives. End-to-end encryption protects messages as they travel between devices, but Signal must show readable text when someone opens a chat.

An assistant that can read the screen does not have to break that encryption to see the message. It can capture the same text the recipient sees.

On iOS 27, Signal’s “Block Siri AI” setting prevents Siri from scanning Signal content and blocks screenshots inside the app and in the App Switcher.

On Android, Signal automatically turns on “Screen security” when it detects an assistant seeking screen access. Signal says detection varies across Android versions, so the protection does not work the same way on every phone.

The move follows Signal’s 2025 decision to block screenshots by default in its Windows 11 desktop app to keep chats out of Microsoft Recall’s searchable history. Other developers took a different route. As Cyber Security News reported, Brave blocked Microsoft Recall while preserving regular screenshots.

Signal Restricts Screenshots

Apple says Siri’s onscreen awareness lets it answer questions or act on what users are viewing. Google’s Gemini help page says some screen actions upload visible content to give the assistant context.

That does not mean either assistant routinely records every Signal chat. The risk is that once an assistant captures a message, Signal cannot control how that copy is handled.

Users can turn off the protection in Signal’s privacy settings to take screenshots again, but doing so can also expose messages from other people in the chat. The Electronic Frontier Foundation points to a separate option on iOS 27.2: open Settings → Siri → Excluded Apps and add Signal to block Siri’s access, including on-screen awareness.

Screenshot blocking does not cover every route to private data. Signal says it cannot offer the same protection on macOS and warns that an assistant may still reach content already saved on a device.

In related coverage, Meta’s Muse read Signal message text through Android notifications and Mac permissions without breaking Signal’s encryption.

Signal is asking Apple, Google and Microsoft to give developers a clear way to opt out of AI access to screens, files and notifications without disabling ordinary features such as screenshots. It also wants better documentation about what assistants can read and where that data goes.

The distinction matters for anyone sharing sensitive information. A screenshot block can close one route into a private chat, but it cannot decide what a phone shows in a notification or what permissions another app receives. Those controls sit with the operating system, which is why Signal is pressing platform makers for stronger limits.

Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that a critical Java vulnerability affects Idira Privilege Threat Analytics, Remote Access Connector, and on-premises HTML5 Gateway products. Tracked as CVE-2026-114938, the flaw could let a remote attacker run code without signing in when specific hardware and software conditions are met. The company’s security advisory, published November 20, assigns the […]

The post Palo Alto Confirms Java Vulnerability Impacts Privilege Threat Analytics and Remote Access Connector appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that a critical Java vulnerability affects Idira Privilege Threat Analytics, Remote Access Connector, and on-premises HTML5 Gateway products. Tracked as CVE-2026-114938, the flaw could let a remote attacker run code without signing in when specific hardware and software conditions are met.

The company’s security advisory, published November 20, assigns the issue a CVSS score of 9.2 and moderate response urgency. Palo Alto Networks says it is not aware of malicious exploitation and continues to review its wider product range and cloud services.

The flaw sits in the optimized Base64 decoder inside HotSpot, the Java Virtual Machine used by affected Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM, and OpenJDK releases.

Base64 converts binary data into text for storage or transfer. Specially crafted input can make the decoder write beyond its assigned heap memory, creating a possible path to remote code execution.

This memory error falls under CWE-787, an out-of-bounds write. In simple terms, the decoder can overwrite memory outside the space reserved for its output. Such writes can damage data, crash software, or allow unwanted code to run.

Palo Alto Confirms Critical Java Flaw

Successful exploitation requires an affected Java release running on an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support. The accelerated Base64 decoder must be enabled, and the application must pass untrusted input to it. Palo Alto says no special product configuration is required, but these underlying conditions still apply.

Cyber Security News previously covered the issue in its Java4Shell vulnerability report, explaining why the affected Java runtime and processor features matter when assessing exposure.

Privilege Threat Analytics 15.2 releases before 15.2.3 are affected. Customers should install version 15.2.3 or later. Those running the 14.6 branch should upgrade to 14.6.4 or move to 15.2.3 or later. All releases in the 15.0 branch are affected, and customers should upgrade to 15.2.3 or later.

Remote Access Connector versions before 1.1.1002202 require an update to that release or later. The separate Remote Access Connector CLI needs version 1.1.3701 or later.

Palo Alto released fixes for affected 15.2.2 and 15.0.3 installations, with no known workaround, while managing updates for ADEM Infrastructure, Prisma Access-MSP, Prisma AIRS, Idira EPM SaaS, Idira Remote Access, and hosted HTML5 Gateway, requiring no customer action.

PAN-OS-based firewalls, Panorama, WF-500-B, and PAN-DB private cloud appliances are not affected. This separates the Java issue from earlier Palo Alto PAN-OS code execution vulnerabilities.

Customers remain responsible for updating custom Java applications, third-party tools, and integration components in their environments. Fixing a listed Palo Alto product does not remove that separate responsibility. The vendor directs customers to follow each software provider’s security guidance while its broader product review continues.

articles.title: ClamAV Patches 10 High-Severity Vulnerabilities That Could Let Attackers Crash Antivirus Scanners
articles.description:
ClamAV has released versions 1.5.5 and 1.4.7 to fix 10 security flaws that could let attackers crash antivirus scanners, trap scan workers in endless loops, or drain system resources using crafted files. Published on November 18, 2026, the updates also address memory errors that could expose process data or corrupt memory during scanning. The fixes […]

The post ClamAV Patches 10 High-Severity Vulnerabilities That Could Let Attackers Crash Antivirus Scanners appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
ClamAV has released versions 1.5.5 and 1.4.7 to fix 10 security flaws that could let attackers crash antivirus scanners, trap scan workers in endless loops, or drain system resources using crafted files.

Published on November 18, 2026, the updates also address memory errors that could expose process data or corrupt memory during scanning. The fixes cover email handling, document parsing, archive extraction, and executable unpacking. Both releases patch all 10 CVEs.

However, the official ClamAV release notice does not provide CVSS scores or label every flaw as high severity. It also does not report active exploitation, so the documented risks should not be confused with confirmed attacks.

CVE-2026-76422 affects the bridge between Rust and C logging code. Attacker-controlled text could be treated as a C format string rather than plain data, causing a crash, memory disclosure, or memory corruption. The flaw dates back to version 0.105.0.

CVE-2026-76411 affects URL processing when ClamAV scans crafted emails with full-hash phishing database entries loaded. Incorrect length tracking could write beyond a stack buffer. This condition matters because the vulnerable path depends on those database entries being present.

Three other flaws affect packed files and compressed content. CVE-2026-76415 could make the yC unpacker read beyond a heap buffer after an offset calculation underflows.

ClamAV Fixes 10 High-Severity Flaws

CVE-2026-76421 could cause an out-of-bounds heap write while handling LZX data in CHM archives. CVE-2026-76430 could trigger similar writes during UPX decompression and Windows executable rebuilding.

These fixes follow earlier ClamAV parser vulnerabilities that disrupted antivirus scanning. The recurring concern is that security software must inspect untrusted files, making errors in its file readers a direct threat to scanning availability.

Several patched bugs can stop useful scanning without relying on a memory overwrite. CVE-2026-76414 allows cyclic directory data inside a CHM file to trigger an endless scan loop. CVE-2026-76416 affects InstallShield archives, where invalid file counts and offsets could keep a scan worker occupied.

Two issues affect OLE2 documents. CVE-2026-76417 could exhaust the process stack through deeply nested document properties. CVE-2026-76515 could cause excessive CPU use while following directory chains. The stack exhaustion flaw reaches back to ClamAV 0.71, showing how long some affected code has remained in use.

Separately, CVE-2026-76516 could let crafted XAR archives exhaust temporary storage because extraction writes occurred before file-count and scan-size limits were enforced. The patch moves those checks ahead of writes.

Cyber Security News previously covered an OLE2 parsing flaw that could crash ClamAV. The latest OLE2 bugs are separate issues involving stack depth and directory traversal, not that earlier decryption error.

Administrators should install ClamAV 1.5.5 or the 1.4.7 long-term support release from the official downloads page. Updating malware signatures alone does not replace the engine fixes. ClamAV states that both the engine and virus database must stay current.

The releases also restore ClamAV submissions, improve OpenSSL 4 support, and update Rust dependencies. Alpine and Debian container images are offered through Docker Hub. However, ClamAV warns that updated images may appear later than release files.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Misconfigured Temenos Banking Platform to Deploy Web Shells Without Passwords
articles.description:
Hackers gained administrator access to an internet-facing Temenos Quantum Fabric deployment without a password and used the banking platform’s own tools to install malicious Java components. The campaign, dubbed BankWeaver, turned a service that should have been private into a route to the application server and its connected systems. Investigators confirmed one compromise at a […]

The post Hackers Exploit Misconfigured Temenos Banking Platform to Deploy Web Shells Without Passwords appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers gained administrator access to an internet-facing Temenos Quantum Fabric deployment without a password and used the banking platform’s own tools to install malicious Java components.

The campaign, dubbed BankWeaver, turned a service that should have been private into a route to the application server and its connected systems. Investigators confirmed one compromise at a financial services institution.

Six other banks across Asia, the Middle East, Europe, and the Americas appeared to have the same configuration and internet exposure. Investigators did not confirm that any of those six banks were compromised.

The suspected exposure matters because Quantum Fabric, formerly Kony Fabric, links customer-facing web and mobile apps to identity systems, payment services, databases, and customer records.

Researchers from Forescout’s Vedere Labs identified the malware while investigating the breach in early September. In its November 19 report, Forescout named the two components FabricShell and FabricShadow.

One let the attackers run commands and query databases; the other gathered information about the server and sent it out of the network.

Hackers Exploit Misconfigured Temenos Banking Platform

Forescout traced the intrusion to a Fabric authentication service that issued privileged tokens but was configured to accept anonymous access.

A token is a digital credential that tells a service what its holder is allowed to do. Here, a token meant for anonymous application access was accepted across an administrative trust boundary. The attackers gained administrator privileges without supplying valid login credentials.

With those privileges, the attackers abused Fabric’s support for custom Java integrations. The platform loaded the malicious code as part of its normal service framework, giving it access to the application’s network and database connections.

Earlier reporting on VMware vCenter web shells describes a separate campaign in which attackers also planted backdoors in enterprise infrastructure.

FabricShell was registered as a Fabric service. It could run operating system commands, return their output, and submit database queries.

Forescout found hardcoded PostgreSQL connection details tied to another victim, raising the possibility of both reading and modifying data.

That capability is not proof that customer records were stolen. Separate reporting on Lazarus IIS web shells shows how similar tools can combine server control with database access.

FabricShadow ran before the application processed data requests. It collected details such as the hostname, network interfaces, Java version, and service account, then saved a local copy and sent the findings to remote infrastructure.

Forescout identified more than 30 IP addresses used during the campaign and said the operators routed activity through compromised devices and victim servers.

Access configuration

Temenos attributed the behavior to the access configuration, according to Forescout. The vendor released updates and guidance to make the service private and advised customers to restrict internet access to Spotlight and Fabric’s administrative and authentication services.

Closing that route prevents the same exposure from being abused again, but it does not remove an implant already installed.

Defenders should check for unexpected Java package registrations, service imports, and application publishing events. Java or Tomcat launching shells, downloaders, or network utilities is another signal worth investigating alongside outbound traffic and application logs.

Earlier NSA web shell guidance likewise stresses checking both internal and internet-facing servers for persistent backdoors.

Where investigators find signs of compromise, Forescout recommends preserving logs, memory, and suspicious packages before cleanup, revoking active sessions, rotating exposed credentials, and rebuilding affected nodes from known-good images.

The key check before restoring service is whether anonymous access is confined to its intended public workflow and can no longer yield administrative privileges.

articles.description:
Transport for London (TfL) has warned that around 265,000 Oyster photocard account holders may have had personal information exposed following suspicious activity on its photocard website. The transport authority detected the incident on November 16, 2026, and took the system offline to limit access. According to TfL’s incident notice, the potentially compromised information includes email […]

The post Hackers Breach TfL Oyster Photocard Accounts, Exposing Personal Data of 265,000 Customers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Transport for London (TfL) has warned that around 265,000 Oyster photocard account holders may have had personal information exposed following suspicious activity on its photocard website. The transport authority detected the incident on November 16, 2026, and took the system offline to limit access.

According to TfL’s incident notice, the potentially compromised information includes email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses, dates of birth, and security questions and answers. TfL emailed customers believed to be affected on November 18 and asked account holders to check their spam and junk folders.

TfL’s current assessment indicates that passwords, bank details, payment card information, and customer journey records were not compromised. Photographs and copies of supporting documents were also excluded from the information believed to have been exposed.

The authority separately stated that names and dates of birth belonging to children with Zip Oyster cards were not compromised. That distinction is important because the affected account holders’ information includes dates of birth. At the same time, the notice specifically excludes those children’s details.

Hackers Breach TfL Oyster Photocard Accounts

TfL said the incident affected only its Oyster photocard website. Its other websites and services were not affected, according to the TfL’s incident notice. Customers who did not receive the November 18 warning email are not currently believed to have been affected.

The exposure of security questions and answers deserves particular attention. Unlike a password, an answer based on personal history may be reused across several services. TfL has advised customers to change matching passwords or security answers used on other accounts.

The notice does not identify the attackers, explain how they gained access, or name a software flaw. There is therefore no confirmed basis for describing the incident as ransomware, phishing, or an attack involving a specific hacking group.

Cyber Security News previously covered TfL’s 2024 network breach, which affected internal systems and disrupted customer services. However, the current notice provides no evidence linking the November 2026 incident to that earlier attack.

Exposed contact details could also help criminals create convincing account-recovery messages. Cyber Security News’ coverage of phishing and impersonation tactics shows how attackers use trusted identities to persuade people to grant account access. That reporting does not establish how this TfL incident began.

Existing Oyster photocards remain valid for travel. Customers who need to renew a photocard or ask about journey history can contact TfL on 0343 222 1234. Calls may carry charges.

Customers holding a 60+ London Oyster photocard can continue using their cards even if an annual address check is due. TfL said it will contact them to complete that process.

Affected customers will receive another email when the photocard website returns. TfL will then ask them to change their password and security question and answer.

Anyone contacted by someone claiming to possess their data should report it through Action Fraud. TfL says it is monitoring for further impact and will provide updates when available. Customers should remain alert while recovery work continues.

articles.title: Hackers Actively Scan LiteLLM AI Servers for Critical Flaws Enabling RCE Attacks
articles.description:
Attackers are now scanning the internet for exposed LiteLLM servers. They want to chain two flaws that give them remote code execution (RCE) without a login. The scans target a test endpoint in the LiteLLM AI gateway and abuse a weak spot in the Starlette web framework that it relies on. LiteLLM sits between apps […]

The post Hackers Actively Scan LiteLLM AI Servers for Critical Flaws Enabling RCE Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers are now scanning the internet for exposed LiteLLM servers. They want to chain two flaws that give them remote code execution (RCE) without a login.

The scans target a test endpoint in the LiteLLM AI gateway and abuse a weak spot in the Starlette web framework that it relies on.

LiteLLM sits between apps and AI model providers, so one compromised gateway can expose many secrets. Because it often holds provider API keys, a successful hit can give attackers a strong foothold in a company’s AI setup.

The two flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-42271 and CVE-2026-48710. Analysts at the Internet Storm Center (ISC) noted the scanning after their honeypots began receiving odd requests over a weekend.

Johannes Ullrich of SANS reported that the requests hit the /mcp-rest/test/tools/list path and appeared to target both CVEs. Horizon3.ai had earlier published a write-up showing how the two bugs work together.

Hackers Actively Scan LiteLLM AI Servers

The first flaw, CVE-2026-42271, sits in LiteLLM’s MCP test endpoints. In versions from 1.74.2 up to, but not including, 1.83.7, these endpoints accept a full server configuration.

That configuration includes the command, arguments and environment fields. The proxy then runs the supplied command on the host with its own privileges. On its own, the bug needs a valid proxy API key. Even a low-privilege internal-user key was enough.

The second flaw, CVE-2026-48710, removes that barrier. Starlette versions before 1.0.1 do not check the Host header. This weakness is known as “BadHost”.

Starlette builds a full URL from that unchecked value and uses it for access control decisions. A crafted header can confuse the logic and let a request slip past the login check.

The traffic seen by ISC shows the idea clearly. The request used a fake bearer token and a body that asked the server to run the id command through the stdio transport.

That command is a common way to test whether code runs. The attacker also tried strange Host values, such as localhost] and [localhost. These likely aim to slip past filters built around the public proof-of-concept.

The problem is not new. Ullrich noted that exploitation was reported back in July, and attackers keep tweaking old exploits to dodge filters and find new victims.

CISA also lists CVE-2026-42271 in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, where it was added on June 8, 2026. Teams that missed those early warnings may still be running exposed servers.

LiteLLM has been a repeat target this year. Earlier, attackers pushed a poisoned release through PyPI, as covered in this report on compromised LiteLLM packages from March. Another poisoned release followed in October.

Why Exposed AI Gateways Are Such a Rich Target

An AI gateway holds keys to many model providers, cloud accounts and internal tools. Wiz researchers scanned 3,074 internet-facing LiteLLM instances and found that 294, or 9.6%, accepted a default master key or had no authentication at all.

Our earlier look at LiteLLM flaws enabling root access explained how such a server can lead into a wider cloud environment. Attackers have also shown interest in the admin side.

Past activity included guesses at master keys such as sk-1234 and attempts to create new API keys and administrator accounts.

We covered this in more detail in a story on how hackers probed the LiteLLM admin API. A server that is open to the internet and unpatched gives such attackers an easy path.

The risk goes beyond one server. Once code runs on the proxy host, an attacker can read environment variables and stored provider keys.

They can then use those keys to run up costs or reach connected data. The October supply chain incident shows how far this can go, since one stolen key led to a poisoned release. The details are in our story on the compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 release.

The first step is patching. Upgrade LiteLLM to version 1.83.7 or later, and Starlette to version 1.0.1 or later. Both fixes are available. Teams should also pull LiteLLM admin and test endpoints off the public internet and place them behind a VPN or an authenticated reverse proxy.

ISC also offered advice for defenders who write filters. When building WAF rules, focus on the flaw instead of one exploit. Flag any character that should never appear in a hostname, or better, allow only known hostnames.

Developers should check a hostname before combining it into a URL. Ullrich also urged teams to reduce their attack surface, which he called the most important step after patching.

Finally, review web logs for requests to the test path and for the odd Host values below. If a vulnerable server was exposed, rotate the master key and every provider key it held.

articles.title: Hackers Use AI-Assisted PowerShell Toolkit With 41 Modules to Target African Stock Exchange
articles.description:
Hackers ran 41 PowerShell modules on a compromised server at a major African stock exchange in just three minutes and 12 seconds. The toolkit searched for passwords, cloud keys, and database credentials, then tested whether it could access the exchange’s investment application programming interface (API) and a securities depository gateway. The exchange was not named, […]

The post Hackers Use AI-Assisted PowerShell Toolkit With 41 Modules to Target African Stock Exchange appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers ran 41 PowerShell modules on a compromised server at a major African stock exchange in just three minutes and 12 seconds.

The toolkit searched for passwords, cloud keys, and database credentials, then tested whether it could access the exchange’s investment application programming interface (API) and a securities depository gateway.

The exchange was not named, and investigators could not determine whether any of the credentials worked. The activity took place on September 20, 2026.

A web shell, a script that lets someone issue commands on a compromised server, ran the modules through Microsoft Internet Information Services (IIS).

Earlier reporting on a suspected AI-written PowerShell backdoor documented a different use of AI-assisted scripting: maintaining remote access. At the exchange, the scripts focused on finding and testing credentials across several systems.

Researchers from Symantec identified the toolkit and detailed it in their November 19 report. They found repeated code patterns consistent with AI assistance but could not identify a model or prove how the scripts were written.

They also found six implants designed to maintain access on the same server, a separate finding that complicated efforts to establish who ran the toolkit.

Hackers Use AI-Assisted PowerShell Toolkit With 41 Modules

The modules searched shared policy folders and directories belonging to six business applications. They looked for Amazon Web Services (AWS) keys and database connection strings, which can contain the details an application needs to sign in to a database.

Other modules mapped SharePoint sites, software management servers, and source code infrastructure. A separate case involving AI-assisted Active Directory reconnaissance showed how a PowerShell script could map a Windows network.

Here, the toolkit also reached into cloud and financial systems. Four modules focused on financial interfaces. The operators tried a guessed password, reused a bearer token, and tested API keys against the securities depository gateway.

A bearer token can grant access to whoever presents it while it remains valid. The operators also checked a specific investor number.

Symantec said the choice of targets could point to financial motives, but the investor lookup and interest in internal information meant espionage could not be ruled out.

All 41 modules used the same basic script structure, error handling, and code for sending results through Domain Name System (DNS) queries.

That consistency was one reason researchers suspected AI assistance: a developer building a single toolkit might put the repeated code in a shared function instead.

Coverage of generative AI malware development puts the finding in context, but neither repeated code nor rapid execution proves a model wrote the scripts. The pace shows automation, not authorship.

The modules sent encoded output through DNS lookups to a public security testing service. Previous reporting on DNS malware delivery techniques examined a different use of the protocol: delivering malware rather than sending script output.

In the exchange case, Symantec could not see what the remote collector received. Researchers found no evidence of data theft or privilege escalation, but that visibility gap meant they could not determine whether the credential tests succeeded.

What the Witchetty Link Means for Defenders

Symantec attributed the six persistence implants to Witchetty, a China-linked espionage group, with high confidence. It did not attribute the PowerShell toolkit to the group.

The earliest evidence of malicious activity on the server dated to April 2026, though access may have begun earlier. Symantec had previously reported that Witchetty targeted the same exchange in 2022.

That history makes the overlap worth investigating, but it does not establish who ran the September scripts or how they gained access.

For security teams, the clearest signal is the combination of events: a web server worker process launching PowerShell, unusual DNS queries soon afterward, and attempts to access sensitive APIs.

Investigators can compare endpoint, DNS, and authentication logs to see whether those events occurred together and whether any tested credentials were accepted.

A matching file hash can help identify a known sample, but finding a Witchetty implant does not, on its own, connect that host to the 41-module toolkit.

articles.title: Wireshark 4.6.10 Released With Patch for 39 Security Vulnerabilities
articles.description:
Wireshark 4.6.10 has been released with fixes for 39 security vulnerabilities affecting protocol dissectors, capture file parsers, the dissection engine, and audio codecs. The update addresses crashes, processing loops, memory leaks, and a heap disclosure issue that could affect systems used for network troubleshooting and security analysis. The official release notes list security advisories wnpa-sec-2026-111 […]

The post Wireshark 4.6.10 Released With Patch for 39 Security Vulnerabilities appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Wireshark 4.6.10 has been released with fixes for 39 security vulnerabilities affecting protocol dissectors, capture file parsers, the dissection engine, and audio codecs.

The update addresses crashes, processing loops, memory leaks, and a heap disclosure issue that could affect systems used for network troubleshooting and security analysis.

The official release notes list security advisories wnpa-sec-2026-111 through wnpa-sec-2026-149. Developers said the large batch of fixes follows an internal review and a recent rise in AI-assisted vulnerability reports from outside researchers. That explains the volume of patches without suggesting that every issue has the same impact.

Many fixes target dissectors, the components that turn raw packet data into readable protocol fields. Affected protocols include RTSE, NBAP, IEEE 1609.2, IrDA, Matter, IEEE 1905, OpenWire, USB-PTP, ACN, PROFINET, and SDP. Several additional advisories group crashes across multiple dissectors, showing that the update reaches well beyond one protocol or network type.

Among the named flaws, CVE-2026-130455 fixes an infinite loop in the Kafka dissector. CVE-2026-130451 addresses infinite loops across multiple protocol dissectors.

While CVE-2026-130462 covers hangs in both dissectors and file parsers. These failures can leave analysis stuck rather than simply closing the application, making them important for teams that rely on timely packet review.

Wireshark 4.6.10 Released

Capture file handling also receives attention. Patches cover crashes in ERF, Android Logcat, and PEAK CAN TRC parsing, plus large loops in the Ascend and Tektronix K12xx readers.

The PEAK CAN TRC issue, tracked as CVE-2026-130467, specifically concerns builds using older GLib versions. This detail matters when assessing exposure across different operating system packages.

The release fixes a TLS dissector memory leak tracked as CVE-2026-130449 and further memory leaks across multiple dissectors under CVE-2026-130436.

Another grouped advisory, CVE-2026-130445, combines crashes, infinite loops, and memory leaks. Unlike an immediate crash, a leak can build resource pressure as processing continues.

An SCTP dissector heap disclosure is tracked as wnpa-sec-2026-147. The release notes also identify crash fixes for the iLBC and AMR audio codecs under wnpa-sec-2026-148 and wnpa-sec-2026-149. Those three entries do not display CVE identifiers in the notes, so the 39-advisory count should not be presented as 39 listed CVEs.

The update follows earlier security releases covered in Cybersecuritynews reports on Wireshark 4.6.9 and Wireshark 4.6.8. Those versions addressed 19 and 28 documented vulnerabilities, respectively, including flaws affecting packet decoding and capture file processing.

Windows and macOS installers now include Brotli 1.2.1, which fixes CVE-2026-111497. Windows packages also move from Npcap 1.88 to Npcap 1.89. These bundled component changes sit alongside the 39 Wireshark security advisories. Teams should include them when reviewing the update’s full scope.

Users can obtain installation packages and source code through the official Wireshark download page. Linux and Unix users can update through their platform’s package manager.

Security teams should prioritize updating analysis workstations and checking deployed package versions, particularly where staff handle outside capture files. The release adds no new protocols and focuses heavily on security and reliability fixes across existing analysis features.

articles.title: Hackers Leak Customer Data Linked to Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan After Third-Party Cyberattacks
articles.description:
Hackers published customer data linked to Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase on Thursday, November 19, after cyberattacks on third-party service providers. All three companies said their own networks were not breached. Visa said no card numbers were affected, Mastercard said the leak involved a limited group of cardholders in a benefits program, and JPMorgan said […]

The post Hackers Leak Customer Data Linked to Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan After Third-Party Cyberattacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers published customer data linked to Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase on Thursday, November 19, after cyberattacks on third-party service providers. All three companies said their own networks were not breached.

Visa said no card numbers were affected, Mastercard said the leak involved a limited group of cardholders in a benefits program, and JPMorgan said the attackers accessed marketing data.

The cyber extortion group n0n claimed responsibility and posted files it linked to the three companies. The disclosures point to vendor breaches rather than breaches at the financial companies themselves.

The companies have not publicly named the affected providers or said whether the incidents involved a shared vendor. They also have not disclosed how the attackers gained access.

As Cyber Security News reported in its initial coverage of the JPMorgan third-party data breach, the bank said the marketing records may include customer names and email addresses.

JPMorgan said it would contact affected customers where appropriate and offer support, including free credit monitoring. The bank said the incident was unrelated to a Chase outage earlier that week, which it traced to a software flaw.

Visa linked its exposure to a provider in the Asia-Pacific region. Mastercard said some email addresses were exposed, but its payment network and customers’ ability to use their cards were unaffected.

Mastercard said the exposure had been contained and it was working with the service provider to support affected cardholders. It did not disclose how many people were affected.

Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Data Leak

The Wall Street Journal reported that the published files contained data linked to thousands of customers. A Reuters review found more than 16,000 email addresses in files linked to JPMorgan, with phone numbers and postal codes in some entries.

American Banker reported that the records were tied to J.P. Morgan Reserve cardholders who received travel and concierge emails. The number of records is not a confirmed count of affected customers.

Reuters also found thousands of apparent customer email addresses in files linked to Visa, along with phone numbers and marketing campaign details from Asia-Pacific markets. Visa did not publish its own count.

The companies were investigating breaches at outside providers, not intrusions into their own networks. The public statements did not say whether the attackers encrypted any vendor systems.

Names, email addresses and details about card benefits can make a phishing message look legitimate. A fake email about a concierge service or a breach notice could direct a customer to a page that asks for a password or a one-time code.

Cyber Security News recently covered a separate campaign that stole U.S. bank logins, including Chase credentials. That campaign has not been linked to these vendor breaches.

Customers who receive an unexpected breach notice should verify it through their bank’s app or the number on the back of their card rather than clicking a link in the message. Chase says customers can forward suspicious emails to phishing@chase.com and should contact the bank promptly if they spot an unauthorized charge.

articles.title: Drupal Fixes Critical RCE Flaw That Could Let Unauthenticated Hackers Take Over Websites
articles.description:
Drupal released security updates on November 18 to fix a critical flaw that could let attackers take over vulnerable websites without logging in. The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-132165, affects the installer included with Drupal core. Under specific conditions, an attacker could use it to attempt to reinstall an existing site, leading to a takeover or […]

The post Drupal Fixes Critical RCE Flaw That Could Let Unauthenticated Hackers Take Over Websites appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Drupal released security updates on November 18 to fix a critical flaw that could let attackers take over vulnerable websites without logging in. The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-132165, affects the installer included with Drupal core.

Under specific conditions, an attacker could use it to attempt to reinstall an existing site, leading to a takeover or remote code execution (RCE). Drupal urges administrators to update immediately.

The installer is designed to set up new Drupal sites. The risk arises when it can be used against a site that is already running. Remote code execution means an attacker could run their own code on the server.

Drupal says successful exploitation could expose private data and allow attackers to change site information. The Drupal Security Team rated the flaw 18 out of 25 on its own risk scale. The advisory says no account is required, but exploitation is complex, and the affected setup is uncommon.

Drupal Fixes Critical RCE Flaw

Drupal credits Anthropic’s open-source software scanner with finding the bug. The official security advisory lists proof of exploitation but does not report attacks in the wild.

This is separate from the Drupal Field UI RCE flaw disclosed in October and the Drupal core SQL injection bug CISA flagged as exploited in May. That confirmed activity involved a different vulnerability and does not establish that attackers are using the installer flaw.

Sites on Drupal 11.3.x should move to 11.3.22, while those on 11.4.x should install 11.4.13. Sites on 10.6.x should update to 10.6.22.

Drupal 11.2.x and earlier 11.x branches, along with 10.5.x and earlier 10.x branches, no longer receive security fixes. Drupal 8 and 9 are also out of support. Administrators on those versions should move to a supported branch.

The updates also fix CVE-2026-132166, a separate issue Drupal rates as moderately critical. Known as a gadget chain, it involves existing code that could be misused to run attacker-controlled code.

Drupal says it cannot be exploited on its own. A site would need another flaw that allows the application to rebuild PHP data from untrusted input.

Administrators who cannot patch immediately should follow Drupal’s guidance for securing the installer. Preventing the web server from writing to or changing permissions on settings.php blocks some attack paths, but it does not replace the update.

Drupal Steward blocks known attack paths, though the security team still advises customers to upgrade in case others are found. The Drupal 11.3.22 release notes also flag a change for new installations.

If settings.php is not writable during setup, the installer now shows an error instead of trying to change the file’s permissions automatically. For existing sites, the priority is to apply the security update and verify the installed version in Drupal’s status report.

articles.title: KPMG Canada Confirms Cyberattack as Hackers Access Confidential Client Tax Documents
articles.description:
KPMG Canada confirmed on November 18 that an unauthorized third party accessed confidential tax documents belonging to some of its clients. The accounting and consulting firm said it acted immediately to contain the cybersecurity breach and secure its systems. It is contacting affected clients directly. KPMG did not disclose when the breach occurred, how many […]

The post KPMG Canada Confirms Cyberattack as Hackers Access Confidential Client Tax Documents appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
KPMG Canada confirmed on November 18 that an unauthorized third party accessed confidential tax documents belonging to some of its clients. The accounting and consulting firm said it acted immediately to contain the cybersecurity breach and secure its systems. It is contacting affected clients directly.

KPMG did not disclose when the breach occurred, how many clients were affected, or how many files were accessed. The firm also did not explain how the intruder gained access. Its public statement confirms that documents were accessed, but it does not establish whether the intruder copied them or what details the files contained.

KPMG spokesperson Sonja Cloutier-Bosworth told BNNBloomberg that the firm’s monitoring found no sign the affected information was available online or being misused. Technology analyst Carmi Levy cautioned that not finding the data online is not proof that it cannot be shared privately or used later.

Securing the affected systems stops further access through the same route if that route has been closed, but it cannot recover copies if any were taken.

For affected clients, the most useful detail is what was in their specific files. A document containing a Social Insurance Number or banking details calls for a different response than a file with no sensitive identifiers.

KPMG has not publicly confirmed that either type of information was exposed, so clients should ask the firm what its review found rather than assume every affected file carried the same risk.

Canada Warned of Fake Help Desk Calls

A separate October 28 alert from the Canadian Center for Cyber Security warned that callers were posing as internal IT staff at Canadian organizations, including legal and financial firms.

The campaign used phone and Microsoft Teams calls to direct employees to fake sign-in pages. KPMG has not linked its breach to that campaign or said that voice phishing was involved.

Cyber Security News has covered fake IT support calls on Microsoft Teams in separate incidents. The practical lesson for employees is to verify unexpected password or account reset requests through a known help desk number or service portal, not through contact details supplied by the caller.

The Credit Counseling Society recommends asking which information was exposed and considering a fraud alert on your credit file if sensitive details were involved.

It also advises monitoring bank and credit accounts for unfamiliar activity. If a breach notice arrives by email or text, verify it using a KPMG contact you already know before opening attachments or providing personal information.

Clients should also watch for messages that use tax details to make a request for payment or account access look genuine. Previous tax-season phishing campaigns in the United States show how scammers imitate tax agencies and preparation firms.

In Canada, anyone who spots unusual activity in their tax account should go directly to the Canada Revenue Agency’s fraud and identity theft guidance rather than follow a link in an unexpected message.
