articles.title: Hackers Deploy Overlord RAT That Survives Windows Resets and Crashes Systems When Terminated
articles.description:
A financially motivated hacking group is deploying Overlord RAT, a Windows remote access trojan that can return after a victim uses “Reset this PC.” The malware can also trigger a blue screen if a user or security tool forcibly ends its process. The two features turn familiar recovery steps into risks: killing the process can […]

The post Hackers Deploy Overlord RAT That Survives Windows Resets and Crashes Systems When Terminated appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A financially motivated hacking group is deploying Overlord RAT, a Windows remote access trojan that can return after a victim uses “Reset this PC.”

The malware can also trigger a blue screen if a user or security tool forcibly ends its process. The two features turn familiar recovery steps into risks: killing the process can immediately take the machine offline, while resetting Windows can give the malware another chance to run.

The campaign appears to target cryptocurrency holders, gaming account owners and users of internet calling software. File names and decoys included references to Viber, MicroSIP and a financial statement, suggesting that messaging users, call-center staff and finance teams could also be targets.

The evidence points to likely targets rather than confirmed victims, and the researchers did not observe how the initial files reached users.

Researchers at Cisco Talos identified the malware while examining an exposed staging server tied to a group they track as UAT-12643.

Their November 18 report assessed a possible North Korea link with low confidence, noting that other groups have used both Overlord and its blockchain-based server discovery technique.

Earlier coverage of the MALFEX npm malware campaign documented Overlord in a separate operation targeting Windows developers.

Hackers Deploy Overlord RAT

Overlord uses two forms of persistence, the term for how malware keeps a foothold after a restart or other interruption. Its first method adds a startup entry to the current user’s Windows registry so the malware can run again at sign-in.

Similar Windows RAT registry persistence has appeared in other campaigns, but what sets this Overlord variant apart is its ability to run during recovery, before the user signs in.

The second method tampers with the Windows Recovery Environment, or WinRE, which runs outside the normal Windows session.

Talos found that Overlord places a copy of itself in the recovery area and changes the reset configuration so Windows launches it during “Reset this PC.”

That is different from surviving a clean installation from trusted external media. The report describes abuse of the built-in recovery process, not a firmware infection.

The blue screen is a separate mechanism. If Overlord is already running with administrative privileges and successfully marks itself as critical, Windows treats its process like one the operating system cannot afford to lose.

Forcibly ending it can trigger the stop code CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED. A blue screen alone does not identify Overlord, but one that follows an attempt to stop a suspicious process gives responders a reason to preserve logs and investigate before trying again.

35 commands in the Go-based implant

Talos identified 35 commands in the Go-based implant, covering tasks such as recording keystrokes, capturing screens, accessing webcams and microphones, and transferring files.

Earlier reporting on live Overlord RAT activity showed how quickly that access can translate into data theft in a separate intrusion. In this campaign, Overlord retrieved encrypted server addresses from Solana transaction memos.

The blockchain stored the address, not the control server itself, allowing operators to change where infected machines connect without sending them a new copy of the malware.

The group’s other tools help explain the financial motive. The Good Game infostealer targeted browser credentials, account sessions, cryptocurrency wallet data and selected documents.

It uploaded archives to GoFile and sent download links through a Discord webhook. A separate clipboard hijacker replaced copied cryptocurrency addresses, potentially redirecting payments if victims pasted an address without checking it. Neither behavior should be confused with Overlord’s recovery mechanism.

articles.title: ruby2ßhell: Critical One-Byte Heap Overflow in Ruby Could Allow RCE Attacks
articles.description:
Ruby has patched a critical memory corruption flaw that can allow remote code execution (RCE) on vulnerable servers. Tracked as GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 and named ruby2ßhell by Veria Labs, the flaw affects Ruby’s string case conversion code. Researchers report that attackers can reach the vulnerable code over the network without logging in to applications running Ruby on […]

The post ruby2ßhell: Critical One-Byte Heap Overflow in Ruby Could Allow RCE Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Ruby has patched a critical memory corruption flaw that can allow remote code execution (RCE) on vulnerable servers. Tracked as GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 and named ruby2ßhell by Veria Labs, the flaw affects Ruby’s string case conversion code.

Researchers report that attackers can reach the vulnerable code over the network without logging in to applications running Ruby on Rails or classic-style Sinatra with default settings. A CVE identifier was still pending at disclosure.

The flaw occurs in case conversion routines for several legacy single-byte encodings, including some ISO-8859 and Windows-125x variants.

In those encodings, Ruby converts the German lowercase letter ß to SS when uppercasing it. That conversion produces two output bytes from one input byte, but the loop checks only whether the output buffer has room for one more byte. If the conversion needs two bytes and only one fits, the second write crosses the buffer boundary.

This is a heap buffer overflow because the output buffer sits in memory allocated at runtime. A subsequent copy of the converted string can also read one byte beyond the buffer.

The affected code dates back to Ruby 2.4.0 and can be reached through upcase, swapcase, downcase(: fold), and casecmp?. UTF-8 strings follow a separate code path and do not trigger this flaw.

ruby2ßhell – One-Byte Heap Overflow in Ruby

Ruby’s maintainers say proof-of-concept exploits have demonstrated code execution in some scenarios, not that every out-of-bounds write leads to RCE.

Affected releases include Ruby 3.3.0 through 3.3.13, 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, and 4.0.0 through 4.0.9. The flaw also affects older releases, including Ruby 2.4.0. Ruby 3.2 and earlier are end-of-life and have no fix for this issue.

Plain Rack is not exposed by default, according to Veria Labs. However, custom application code can still introduce exposure if it applies an affected case conversion to untrusted text in a legacy encoding.

Veria Labs identified affected Ruby runtimes bundled with GitLab 19.6.0, GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5, Mastodon 4.7.5, OpenProject 17.9.7, Discourse 2026.10.1, and Chatwoot 4.20.0.

Affected Ruby Web Frameworks

Affected Self-Hosted Software :

For administrators, the key detail is which Ruby runtime the application actually loads. Updating the host’s system Ruby does not replace a separate runtime shipped inside an application package, appliance, or container image.

The Ruby team released 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10 on November 18, 2026. The official Ruby security release addresses seven flaws across string case conversion and the regular expression engine.

These are separate from the earlier GitLab CI/CD regex vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-97229, which Cyber Security News also covered when CISA warned of active exploitation. That earlier exploitation does not establish that ruby2ßhell has been exploited in the wild.

Teams that manage their own Ruby runtime should upgrade to the fixed release for their branch or move to a supported branch if they run Ruby 3.2 or older.

Administrators of self-hosted products should install the vendor’s fixed build, then verify the Ruby version inside the running application environment. Prioritize internet-facing deployments where the vulnerable code is reachable without authentication.

The Veria Labs disclosure tracks affected products and vendor fixes. The researchers said they planned to publish a proof of concept about a week after disclosure.

articles.title: Splunk Patches Critical 9.9 RCE and Authentication Bypass Vulnerabilities in SOAR and Enterprise
articles.description:
Splunk has released security updates for Splunk SOAR and Splunk Enterprise to fix a critical remote code execution flaw and a separate authentication bypass. The SOAR flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-131253, scored 9.9 out of 10 and requires an account with specific permissions. The Enterprise flaw, CVE-2026-76535, lets someone who has not signed in run searches […]

The post Splunk Patches Critical 9.9 RCE and Authentication Bypass Vulnerabilities in SOAR and Enterprise appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Splunk has released security updates for Splunk SOAR and Splunk Enterprise to fix a critical remote code execution flaw and a separate authentication bypass. The SOAR flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-131253, scored 9.9 out of 10 and requires an account with specific permissions.

The Enterprise flaw, CVE-2026-76535, lets someone who has not signed in run searches under another user’s identity. The two bugs affect different products and require separate updates.

Splunk’s November 18 advisory says CVE-2026-131253 affects SOAR versions below 8.8.0. The flaw is in the App Wizard, which helps users build connectors between SOAR and other tools.

Splunk says a signed-in user who can edit apps and containers and run playbooks could execute code with the permissions of the account that runs SOAR. Playbooks are automated workflows that security teams use to investigate alerts and respond to incidents.

That level of access matters because code running under the SOAR service account could read or change data beyond what the user normally controls. The Splunk SOAR security advisory lists no workaround for the App Wizard flaw and recommends upgrading to 8.8.0 or later.

Splunk Patches Multiple Vulnerabilities

The same release fixes a separate 9.6-rated remote code execution flaw in the REST API, tracked as CVE-2026-131287, and a high-severity single sign-on bypass, tracked as CVE-2026-131297.

The update also addresses flaws that could expose data or let users make changes outside their assigned roles. One flaw could let a user change or delete integrations assigned to another tenant, a separate group within a shared deployment.

That matters for organizations that use one SOAR instance to serve multiple teams or customers. The November release follows Splunk’s October fixes for 24 Enterprise and SOAR vulnerabilities, which included four critical flaws.

The Splunk Enterprise security advisory identifies RapidDiag, a tool for collecting troubleshooting data, as the affected component. Improper username validation could let an unauthenticated user run Search Processing Language queries as a signed-in user.

Depending on that user’s permissions, the attacker could read or change data and settings. The reported impact is unauthorized searches, not the operating system code execution described in the SOAR advisory.

The RapidDiag bypass is separate from the Splunk Enterprise flaw CISA flagged as actively exploited in June. That earlier issue, CVE-2026-20253, involved a PostgreSQL component and had its own patches. Reports of attacks against the June flaw do not show attackers using the new RapidDiag bypass.

The fixed Splunk Enterprise versions for the RapidDiag flaw are 10.6.1, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17. Administrators should install the fix for their release branch or a later supported release.

Teams that run both products should track the upgrades separately. Patching Enterprise does not update SOAR, and the October SOAR 8.7.0 update does not include the November fixes.

After upgrading, verify the installed version on each affected instance and check that key searches, connectors, and response playbooks still work. If there are signs of earlier misuse, preserve logs and review unexpected searches, app changes, or playbook runs. The updates close the flaws, but they cannot tell you whether someone used them before the patches were installed.

articles.title: Ruby Patches 7 Security Vulnerabilities, Including Buffer Overflow and RCE Flaws
articles.description:
Ruby maintainers released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13, and 3.3.14 to fix seven security vulnerabilities in the language’s regular expression engine and string case-conversion code. Several flaws can allow remote code execution (RCE), which means an attacker could run code inside a vulnerable Ruby process. The maintainers said they know of proof-of-concept demonstrations that achieved code execution […]

The post Ruby Patches 7 Security Vulnerabilities, Including Buffer Overflow and RCE Flaws appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Ruby maintainers released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13, and 3.3.14 to fix seven security vulnerabilities in the language’s regular expression engine and string case-conversion code.

Several flaws can allow remote code execution (RCE), which means an attacker could run code inside a vulnerable Ruby process. The maintainers said they know of proof-of-concept demonstrations that achieved code execution in some scenarios and urged users to upgrade.

The advisory was published on November 19, 2026, at 00:00 UTC. At publication, the Ruby team had requested CVE numbers. However, none had been assigned, so the flaws are tracked by their GitHub Security Advisory IDs.

The advisory describes research demonstrations, not confirmed attacks against production systems. Two flaws affect the Ruby code used to change text case. The first flaw, GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5, lets Ruby write one byte beyond the memory reserved for its output in some text encodings.

The second, GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, starts with an integer overflow, where a calculation exceeds the range it can store. That error leads to a write outside the intended memory area. Ruby says both flaws can allow code execution in some scenarios.

Ruby Patches Security Vulnerabilities

Five flaws affect regular expressions, often called regexes, which applications use to search or validate text. The double-free flaw, GHSA-7x2q-68qv-6p8x, causes Ruby to release the same memory block twice while compiling a pattern.

A separate flaw, GHSA-3p8q-wmhx-vm2w, causes a buffer overflow during compilation. Ruby says both can lead to code execution when an application compiles patterns supplied by an attacker.

Another buffer overflow, GHSA-7whj-cfh7-xgm4, occurs when Regexp#to_s converts a regular expression to text. Ruby says the flaw can expose information or allow code execution.

GHSA-wpqw-5qxg-m68r involves a read beyond the intended memory area during case-insensitive matching. Ruby reports that a demonstration showed attacker-controlled memory corruption for this flaw, but does not say it demonstrated code execution.

The final flaw, GHSA-pvgc-g7gj-pv6h, can expose memory contents or crash the process during case-insensitive matching that reuses text captured earlier in the pattern.

The affected versions are Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, and 4.0.0 through 4.0.9. Upgrade to 3.3.14, 3.4.13, or 4.0.10, respectively, if you are on one of those maintained branches. Ruby 3.3 is in security maintenance.

Ruby 3.2 and older branches have reached end of life and will not receive these fixes, so teams still running them need to move to a supported branch.

These patches apply to the Ruby runtime itself, not to a Rails gem. That makes them different from the Rails Active Storage file-read flaw and the later Rails image-upload vulnerability previously covered by Cyber Security News. Updating Rails dependencies alone will not install a fixed Ruby runtime.

Start with internet-facing services that accept user-defined patterns or change the case of incoming text. Check the Ruby version in the environment where each app runs, not just on a developer’s laptop.

After upgrading, rebuild any container images that still bundle an older runtime, redeploy web services and background workers, and verify that the new instances are running a patched version.

Use the review to set patching priorities, not to delay updates elsewhere. The release fixes several distinct bugs, and an application does not need to use every affected feature to be exposed.

articles.title: Chinese Hackers Upgrade EggStreme Malware With Silent Backdoor to Evade Security Detection
articles.description:
A suspected Chinese cyberespionage group has rebuilt its EggStreme malware framework, adding a Windows backdoor that waits for an incoming connection instead of calling out to an attacker-controlled server. Bitdefender’s November 18, 2026, report tracks the changes as the group continues to target government organizations in the Philippines. Researchers also found signs of possible targeting […]

The post Chinese Hackers Upgrade EggStreme Malware With Silent Backdoor to Evade Security Detection appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A suspected Chinese cyberespionage group has rebuilt its EggStreme malware framework, adding a Windows backdoor that waits for an incoming connection instead of calling out to an attacker-controlled server.

Bitdefender’s November 18, 2026, report tracks the changes as the group continues to target government organizations in the Philippines. Researchers also found signs of possible targeting in Taiwan, but assessed that link with low to medium confidence.

Bitdefender first publicly documented EggStreme in September 2025 after investigating a compromise at a Philippine military company. The original EggStreme malware investigation described a modular toolkit that could run its main implant in memory and collect keystrokes.

The newer samples show that the operators can change how the backdoor communicates without abandoning the methods they use to run malware on compromised Windows systems.

ThreatCluster noted in its November 18 analysis that the overhaul went beyond changing servers or file hashes. It highlighted a new communications protocol, an expanded set of commands and a passive variant that does not send an outbound beacon.

The timing suggests public exposure may have prompted some of the changes, although Bitdefender found that some samples discovered after disclosure had been compiled earlier.

Chinese Hackers Upgrade EggStreme Malware

Bitdefender found two EggStremeAgent builds that operated in passive mode. A conventional backdoor often sends a beacon, or a recurring check-in, to tell its operators that a compromised machine is online.

These builds instead opened a listening port and waited for a connection. The distinction matters: a network rule that looks only for recurring outbound traffic may have nothing to flag.

A separate passive Windows backdoor called SLEEPWALKER illustrates the same monitoring gap, but it is not part of EggStreme.

The communications overhaul was not limited to passive mode. Newer EggStremeAgent builds dropped gRPC, a protocol for calling functions across a network, in favor of direct TCP connections while keeping mutual TLS.

That security mechanism requires both sides to present certificates. Bitdefender also found signs that the operators were moving away from one shared certificate authority toward campaign-specific ones.

If confirmed, that change would make it harder to link separate servers through a common certificate issuer. The newer agent builds analyzed by Bitdefender did not include the earlier keylogger, but they added ways to map Windows domains, query system information and run PowerShell in memory.

The missing keylogger does not mean the group has stopped collecting data, nor does it confirm that EggStremeWizard, a separate tool, has been retired.

Earlier coverage of Southeast Asian government espionage documented EggStreme components alongside other tools in a campaign where several activity clusters shared a victim network.

What Defenders Can Still Detect After the Rebuild

The malware still relies on DLL sideloading, in which a legitimate Windows program loads a malicious library. As other China-linked sideloading campaigns show, a trusted program name does not tell defenders whether every library it loads is safe.

For EggStreme, Bitdefender recommends checking whether system-named libraries load from unexpected folders and whether workstations begin listening on ports that do not match their usual roles.

Bitdefender also observed the operators using an unmanaged system reachable by workstations to stage malware. The researchers saw valid credentials and activity over Server Message Block (SMB), the Windows file-sharing protocol, but could not determine how the attackers first gained access.

That distinction matters in an investigation: a script launched from a file share can reveal how an intruder moved inside the network without identifying the original entry point.

Security teams should check which unmanaged devices can reach workstations and review internal file-share activity alongside endpoint alerts.

articles.title: AuditTeam Ransomware Gang Poses as Security Auditors and Use AV Drivers to Kill EDR Process
articles.description:
A ransomware group called AuditTeam is dressing up extortion as a paid security audit. Victims get a ransom note that reads like an audit log. It asks for an “Audit & Consulting fee” in return for a report on the holes the attackers used to get in. Before the note appears, the group has already […]

The post AuditTeam Ransomware Gang Poses as Security Auditors and Use AV Drivers to Kill EDR Process appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A ransomware group called AuditTeam is dressing up extortion as a paid security audit. Victims get a ransom note that reads like an audit log. It asks for an “Audit & Consulting fee” in return for a report on the holes the attackers used to get in.

Before the note appears, the group has already shut down security tools with a signed antivirus driver and encrypted the files.

The campaign ran from January 2026 through at least October 2026. It hit dozens of organizations, and a recent report on crews that disable EDR shows why this step matters so much to modern ransomware gangs.

Researchers at Securelist, the research arm of Kaspersky, identified the malware and named its framework OpsAgent. They first saw it on March 10, 2026, in an intrusion at a company in Hong Kong.

The tool looked like a normal penetration testing kit. Further digging showed the same tool in other countries.

The Securelist team says AuditTeam’s victims include organizations in Russia, Italy, the Philippines, Hong Kong, Senegal, Finland and China. The group’s leak site also lists victims in Turkey, Thailand, Ukraine, Argentina, South Korea, Japan and Spain.

AuditTeam Ransomware Gang Poses as Security Auditors

The EDR killer is an add-on module for OpsAgent. It installs a driver that poses as Beijing Jiangmin Antivirus, from the KV product series.

The driver carries a valid digital signature, which helps it load without raising alarms. This trick is called Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver, or BYOVD.

Attackers bring a trusted, signed driver onto a machine and misuse it to run code at the kernel level, where security tools have little power to fight back.

Once the driver is loaded, the malware talks to it through a filter port named \KvCorePortX0. When the driver gets the command 0x1D followed by a file name, it ends the matching process.

The kill list holds about 220 names. It covers Microsoft Defender (MsMpEng), ESET (ekrn) and Kaspersky (avp). It also covers monitoring tools such as Sysmon, splunkd and wazuh-agent.

Remote access tools like TeamViewer, backup services such as Veeam and Acronis, and database engines such as sqlservr, mysqld, mongod and redis-server are on it too.

Other gangs use the same idea. Earlier reporting on how GentleKiller abused vulnerable drivers showed one gang killing more than 400 security processes before it encrypted anything.

After the security tools go down, the cryptor module takes over. It encrypts files with AES-CBC or ChaCha20 and gives each file its own key.

It also uses X25519 key exchange, so victims cannot easily recover the keys. The module stops database and backup services, deletes shadow copies and empties the recycle bin.

When it deletes files, it overwrites them with random data first, which makes forensic recovery much harder. The same backup-wrecking habit appears in how DeadLock ransomware targets backups before locking files.

The ransom note says nothing about encryption. Because the cryptor module drops it, anyone who sees the note already has encrypted files.

OpsAgent Tooling, Infrastructure and Defense

OpsAgent does a lot. It manages files and processes, injects shellcode, steals tokens, logs keystrokes, takes screenshots and moves between machines.

Securelist says it rivals Cobalt Strike in features. Its loaders push code into msiexec.exe, and the newest Rust loader runs the payload inside its own process instead.

During the campaign, the authors rewrote the implant from C++ to Rust. Securelist also saw code patterns that suggest the authors used AI tools to help write it.

For command and control, the malware uses Amazon CloudFront subdomains. It finds them by reading a public GitHub repository.

Because CloudFront addresses are shared with legitimate traffic, blocking by IP address does not work well. The GitHub repository was removed in November 2026. The latest Rust samples have that feature switched off, so the campaign is probably still running.

Defenders should watch for new kernel driver installs, especially a file named kvcore.sys. They should alert on any security agent that stops reporting while its host stays online.

Turning on Microsoft’s vulnerable driver blocklist and limiting local admin rights also helps. Even trusted vendor tools can be turned against you, as research on how a Microsoft Defender driver abused can disable endpoint protection shows. Keep offline backups, because this gang destroys the online ones.

articles.title: Hackers Actively Exploit Critical Apache Roller RCE Flaw to Execute Code Without Authentication
articles.description:
Hackers are actively exploiting a critical vulnerability in Apache Roller that lets them run code on affected servers without signing in, the Apache Software Foundation warned on November 17. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-129448, affects versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 and carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8 out of 10. Apache says administrators should upgrade […]

The post Hackers Actively Exploit Critical Apache Roller RCE Flaw to Execute Code Without Authentication appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are actively exploiting a critical vulnerability in Apache Roller that lets them run code on affected servers without signing in, the Apache Software Foundation warned on November 17.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-129448, affects versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 and carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8 out of 10. Apache says administrators should upgrade to Roller 6.1.6 or later. Version 6.1.5 is also vulnerable, but Apache tracks it under a separate CVE.

Apache Roller is a Java-based blogging platform that can host multiple blogs and support teams of writers and editors. The vulnerability is in its XML-RPC endpoint, an interface that lets other software communicate with Roller.

The server accepts certain extended data types and rebuilds them into objects before checking whether the sender is allowed to use the service. That process, known as deserialization, is unsafe when the server reconstructs data supplied by an attacker.

The result is remote code execution, or RCE. An attacker who can reach the vulnerable service over the network can run code without a valid account or any action from a blog user.

Critical Apache Roller RCE Exploitation

Apache’s CVE record confirms active exploitation but does not identify the attackers, say how many systems have been targeted, or describe what attackers have done after gaining access.

The November disclosure expands the known affected range. Apache’s September advisory listed only version 6.1.5 under CVE-2026-82384.

The new record says the two CVEs describe the same underlying flaw across different releases. That matters for administrators who installed 6.1.5 to fix an earlier Apache Roller session vulnerability. That update fixed the session issue, not this code execution flaw.

Cyber Security News also covered active exploitation of a separate Apache Tomcat RCE flaw. The Roller issue is in the blogging application itself.

Apache Roller 6.1.6 turns off the affected extension types and rejects XML-RPC requests when the feature is turned off. On vulnerable releases, turning off XML-RPC in the administration interface is not enough.

Those versions can process incoming data before checking the setting, leaving the server exposed even when the dashboard shows the feature is disabled.

If an upgrade cannot happen immediately, Apache recommends setting enabledForExtensions to false in WEB-INF/web.xml or removing the /roller-services/xmlrpc servlet mapping. Both workarounds require a Roller restart.

Removing the mapping also takes the endpoint offline, so administrators should check whether any publishing tools depend on it before choosing that workaround. Neither option changes Apache’s recommendation to upgrade.

For teams managing several Roller deployments, first check the version running on each server rather than relying on the XML-RPC setting in the dashboard. Prioritize instances reachable from the internet, then verify that the fixed release is running after deployment.

Patching closes the flaw, but it doesn’t show whether a server was compromised before the update. Treat any suspected compromise as a separate investigation.

articles.description:

Symantec reported on November 18 that the attackers used a built-in scripting feature to copy the Active Directory database and launch malware that kept running after the collection activity. Researchers did not observe data leaving […]

The post Hackers Abuse CyberPower UPS Software to Execute SYSTEM Commands and Dump Active Directory Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Exploited CyberPower PowerPanel Business software for managing uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) to gain SYSTEM-level access to a Windows domain controller.

Symantec reported on November 18 that the attackers used a built-in scripting feature to copy the Active Directory database and launch malware that kept running after the collection activity. Researchers did not observe data leaving the network or see ransomware deployed.

PowerPanel Business helps businesses keep servers running during brief power interruptions and shut them down safely during longer outages. Its event settings let administrators run scripts when power drops or fails.

On Windows, the PowerPanel service, ppbed.exe, runs as SYSTEM, a built-in account with extensive local privileges. Scripts started by the service inherit those permissions. In the incident, Symantec traced unauthorized scripts to the PowerPanel web console on TCP port 3052.

The service launched Windows Command Prompt, and the resulting activity included downloading tools and running a PowerShell test that loaded a small .NET program into memory. The program only printed a greeting, but it showed that the attackers could run code in memory through a trusted service.

Symantec did not establish how the attackers first gained console access. Earlier advisories documented hard-coded credentials, a default administrator password and a file-upload flaw in PowerPanel Business.

Hackers Abuse CyberPower UPS Software

Stolen administrator credentials were another possibility. Cyber Security News previously covered security flaws in PowerPanel Enterprise, a separate CyberPower product. Those findings do not establish how this intrusion began.

The attackers repeatedly changed their collection scripts and checked the results before trying again. They eventually copied ntds. dit, the Active Directory database, and collected the SYSTEM registry hive.

As our earlier coverage of Active Directory database theft explains, access to both files can expose password hashes and other secrets used to authenticate domain accounts.

Symantec said the repeated adjustments suggested someone was operating the tools live. It did not name a threat group or determine the attacker’s motive.

The same PowerPanel process tree later led to upnpcont.exe, an executable named after a Microsoft component. It ran from an unusual location under the SYSTEM profile and loaded a malicious atl.dll.

The technique, known as DLL side-loading, uses a legitimate program to load a malicious code library. The link back to ppbed.exe gave defenders a way to connect the malware with the earlier activity.

Symantec recommends finding every PowerPanel Business installation and limiting access to TCP port 3052 to approved administrator workstations. Keep the console off the public internet and away from regular user networks.

Apply vendor updates, replace default passwords with unique credentials, and review the settings that link power events to scripts. Check the extcmd and temp\profile\extcmd folders for scripts that do not match a known configuration.

On domain controllers, review endpoint logs for unusual command shells, PowerShell activity, or database access linked to ppbed.exe. Use Symantec’s incident report to compare file names and hashes with evidence from affected hosts.

If the evidence shows that the directory database was copied, treat domain credentials as potentially exposed even without proof of an outbound transfer. Plan a coordinated reset of krbtgt, the account used to sign Kerberos authentication tickets, alongside wider credential rotation.

articles.title: Hackers Exploiting Java4Shell RCE Flaw Using ARTEX Disguise Themselves as Chrome
articles.description:
Cloudflare’s Cloudforce One reported a Java4Shell exploit attempt that looked like ordinary Google Chrome traffic in web logs. The team said a source IP first scanned a target using a User-Agent header that gave away the scanning tool. About 17 hours later, the same address sent an exploit attempt to the same target, this time […]

The post Hackers Exploiting Java4Shell RCE Flaw Using ARTEX Disguise Themselves as Chrome appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Cloudflare’s Cloudforce One reported a Java4Shell exploit attempt that looked like ordinary Google Chrome traffic in web logs. The team said a source IP first scanned a target using a User-Agent header that gave away the scanning tool. About 17 hours later, the same address sent an exploit attempt to the same target, this time claiming to be Chrome.

In a separate November 18 update, Cloudforce One said it had seen traffic linked to both ARTEX and Java4Shell from a single IP address for the first time.

The two updates do not establish that ARTEX sent the Chrome-disguised request or that either attempt led to a breach. The disguise was in the HTTP User-Agent header, which identifies the client making a web request, not in Chrome itself.

Java4Shell Puts Java Servers at Risk

Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, affects the Base64 decoder in OpenJDK’s HotSpot runtime. Base64 is a common way to represent binary data as text. On affected systems, the decoder can write outside its assigned memory when it processes invalid input. The flaw can crash a Java service, expose data held in memory, or allow remote code execution (RCE), meaning an attacker can run code on the target.

As Cyber Security News reported in its Java4Shell coverage, the flaw is in the Java runtime itself, not a library such as Log4j. It requires an unpatched Java build, an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support, and an application that passes attacker-controlled data to the affected decoder. ARM64 systems do not use that vulnerable code path.

Calif’s research demonstrated code execution without a login in default test setups of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, JFrog Artifactory, and PingFederate. Those tests show what is possible under the right conditions. They do not show that the target in Cloudforce One’s report was running any of those products or that the request succeeded.

The FBI’s November 13 advisory describes ARTEX as an AI-driven security testing framework that attackers have used to speed up intrusions. It cites separate campaigns involving South Korean financial institutions and ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers. Cyber Security News has also covered ARTEX consoles exposed to the internet. Neither report ties those earlier findings to the Java4Shell request that posed as Chrome.

Oracle and OpenJDK released fixes on November 17. Fixed OpenJDK builds include 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, and 27.0.1.1. Administrators should check their Java vendor’s advisory and prioritize internet-facing services. After restarting a service, verify the Java version it actually loads, not just the version returned by the host’s default Java command.

For incident review, compare web and application logs for repeat requests to the same service, then check host logs for unexpected Java crashes or unusual activity.

A Chrome label is not proof that a real browser sent the request, and a shared IP is not proof of a common operator. The FBI advises checking IP indicators against current network activity before using them to block traffic.

articles.title: WordPress 7.1.5 Patches 20 Security Issues, Including Potential RCE and SQL Injection Flaws
articles.description:
WordPress released version 7.1.5 on November 18, 2026, to address 20 security issues in WordPress Core. The update fixes a flaw that could allow someone without an account to run code on a vulnerable server, two SQL injection flaws, and a weakness that could let an administrator of one site take over a WordPress Multisite […]

The post WordPress 7.1.5 Patches 20 Security Issues, Including Potential RCE and SQL Injection Flaws appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
WordPress released version 7.1.5 on November 18, 2026, to address 20 security issues in WordPress Core. The update fixes a flaw that could allow someone without an account to run code on a vulnerable server, two SQL injection flaws, and a weakness that could let an administrator of one site take over a WordPress Multisite network. WordPress recommends updating immediately.

Security researcher Logan Homolka reported the flaw in the Template Part block, which WordPress uses for shared layout elements such as headers and footers.

The flaw lets an unauthenticated attacker gain permissions they should not have and could lead to remote code execution (RCE). The announcement does not report attacks exploiting it or identify which site configurations could allow code execution.

The Template Part flaw is separate from the update-process weakness covered in our WordPress 7.1.4 security release report. The new release also fixes a distinct Multisite issue, reported by Yuval Miller, that could let a site Administrator take over a Super Admin account. That distinction matters because a Super Admin can manage the entire network, not just one site.

SQL Injection, XSS, and Data Exposure

Christiaan Swiers reported SQL injection in WP_Meta_Query, which builds database queries based on metadata. WordPress security team member Rudy Faile reported the second flaw, which affects front-page previews in the Customizer. SQL injection can change how a database interprets a query. The two flaws are separate from the export-related issue fixed in WordPress 7.1.3.

Several fixes address cross-site scripting (XSS), which can let an attacker run a script in another user’s browser. One stored XSS flaw affects comments and does not require an account.

Other fixes cover the legacy media library, embeds, and the block editor. The update also closes a data leak that exposed private taxonomy terms, such as categories or tags, through REST API search without a login.

The official WordPress release announcement also lists a denial-of-service flaw involving XML-RPC pingbacks and a permissions bypass in comment editing. The 20 entries include two preventive changes: stricter checks for JSON content types and removal of an Imgur embed option whose provider was already gone.

How to Update WordPress

Open Dashboard → Updates → Update Now, then confirm the installed version. Sites with automatic background updates can receive the patch without manual action, but administrators should still verify that it installed.

For older deployments, the WordPress 7.1.5 documentation lists patched versions by branch, including 7.0.9, 6.9.12, and 4.7.40. WordPress 4.6 and earlier no longer receive security updates.

Patches for older branches give administrators a way to close these flaws if they cannot move to 7.1.5 right away, but WordPress says only the latest version is actively supported. WordPress 7.2 Release Candidate 2 also contains the applicable fixes.

The final 7.2 release is planned for December 8, but site owners should install the available security update now rather than wait.

articles.description:
The PHP security team plans to release security updates on Thursday, November 19, 2026, between 14:00 and 14:30 UTC. In its November 18 security notice, the team said the releases will address vulnerabilities across all supported PHP branches, with the highest severity rated critical. It urged users to prepare now and install the updates promptly […]

The post PHP Security Team Warns of Critical Vulnerabilities, Urges Users to Prepare for November 19 Updates appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The PHP security team plans to release security updates on Thursday, November 19, 2026, between 14:00 and 14:30 UTC. In its November 18 security notice, the team said the releases will address vulnerabilities across all supported PHP branches, with the highest severity rated critical. It urged users to prepare now and install the updates promptly once they are available.

The patches are part of PHP’s regular four-week release cycle. The team said the critical issues require non-default settings or uncommon setups.

An application might run a vulnerable PHP version without meeting the requirements for an attack. The team will release technical details and the corresponding fixed version numbers along with the updates.

PHP Session Upload Progress Flaw

One expected fix addresses CVE-2026-115560, a remote code execution flaw tied to PHP’s session upload progress feature. The feature lets an application track a file upload while it is still in progress.

Under certain conditions, the flaw could let an attacker run code on the server. PHP first flagged the issue on October 23, saying it requires an unusual combination of settings and application code.

For deployments covered by the advisory, PHP recommends disabling session upload progress as a temporary safeguard. Teams that have already turned it off should keep it disabled until they install the fix. PHP says applications that do not change how session data is stored while running can leave the feature enabled.

The patch window also falls on the planned launch date for PHP 8.6.0. Administrators do not need to move to the new feature release just to get the security fixes. The team plans to publish updates for existing supported branches.

October’s PHP2Shell Attacks

The November update follows October’s emergency PHP2Shell patches. That release fixed CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 in PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12. Both flaws scored 9.2 out of 10 and could let attackers run code on affected web servers without logging in.

As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of CISA’s PHP2Shell warning, the agency added both October flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after attacks were reported. That warning applies to the October flaws and does not establish that attackers are exploiting the issues covered by the November release.

Check which PHP versions actually serve web requests, including those bundled in containers or managed by hosting providers. Once the updates go live, consult the PHP 2026 release archive for the fixed version on your branch.

Install that build or your vendor’s patched package, restart the affected PHP workers, and verify that the web application is running the updated version. Checking only the command-line version may miss an older build still serving traffic.

articles.title: Fake FMCSA, DAT, and TIMOCOM Portals Attack US Logistics Firms
articles.description:
Attackers are impersonating carrier-verification, broker-onboarding, and load-board platforms to steal identities and fuel-card credentials, deploy backdoors, and take remote control of dispatch workstations. US trucking and logistics companies are being targeted by three separate cybercrime campaigns that disguise attacks as routine freight business, according to new research from ANY.RUN. The campaigns, tracked as HelloFriends, NodeRemote, […]

The post Fake FMCSA, DAT, and TIMOCOM Portals Attack US Logistics Firms appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers are impersonating carrier-verification, broker-onboarding, and load-board platforms to steal identities and fuel-card credentials, deploy backdoors, and take remote control of dispatch workstations.

US trucking and logistics companies are being targeted by three separate cybercrime campaigns that disguise attacks as routine freight business, according to new research from ANY.RUN.

The campaigns, tracked as HelloFriends, NodeRemote, and Fake Freight Portals, exploit the everyday steps carriers and brokers take on digital platforms: verifying a carrier, onboarding with a broker, reviewing paperwork, or booking a load.

Each one turns a normal business interaction into a way to steal data, plant malware, or gain hands-on access to company systems.

HelloFriends: Fake FMCSA Notices Harvest SSNs, Fuel-Card Logins, and OTPs

The largest operation by infrastructure, HelloFriends, impersonates the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA). ANY.RUN linked approximately 1,430 domains to the campaign in 2026.

The phishing emails are tailored to each target: they name the carrier and include its real USDOT number. Because the sending domains are controlled by the attackers, the emails pass SPF, DKIM, and DMARC checks.

Image: The lure names the carrier and its real USDOT number

Victims land on convincing clones of the SAFER and Motus portals, which display genuine carrier records alongside a “NOT AUTHORIZED” warning. From there, the scam escalates step by step:

  1. The victim is asked for an SSN, EIN, date of birth, and contact details, and is told about a $300 “administrative fee.”
  2. They are prompted to “connect” a fleet fuel provider: Relay, Comdata, WEX, EFS, or Fleet One.
  3. A fake provider login captures their credentials. In the observed Relay and Comdata flows, the first password is deliberately rejected so the victim enters a second one.
  4. Finally, the site requests an SMS or six-digit one-time code, which turns the stolen password into a usable account.

The stolen data is sent to Telegram through server functions hosted on Vercel. Researchers found message labels such as “FULL OBJECT” and “Hello Friends” marking each stage of the theft.

View the HelloFriends analysis in ANY.RUN’s sandbox

Identify up to 58% more threats with ANY.RUN. Gain broader visibility and strengthen your defenses with integrated analysis and intelligence from 16K+ orgs. Explore ANY.RUN Solutions

NodeRemote: Broker Paperwork That Installs a Self-Healing Backdoor

The second campaign, NodeRemote, targets dispatch teams and brokers with fake onboarding pages, bills of lading, insurance claims, and rate confirmations.

In one variant, a fake reCAPTCHA copies a PowerShell command to the clipboard and tells the victim to paste it into the Windows Run dialog, a ClickFix-style trick. Other variants deliver VBS scripts disguised as business documents.

In November 2026, an MSI installer pushed through a load-tracking lure was added.

Once it runs, the chain installs a Node.js runtime and an obfuscated main.js backdoor, which persists through scheduled tasks named NodeRemote{GUID}.

The backdoor stands out for how resilient its infrastructure is. It looks up its command-and-control relays from three independent sources:

  • a BNB Smart Chain contract
  • an encrypted DNS TXT record fetched over DNS-over-HTTPS
  • a GitHub gist

This lets operators swap servers without pushing new malware. Between October 25 and November 3, researchers watched six of twelve relay endpoints being replaced. An additional tool, higeleveltask_x64.exe, attempts a UAC bypass through fodhelper.exe and ComputerDefaults.exe.

A single compromised dispatch workstation, researchers warn, can expose broker portals, load boards, and email.

Fake Freight Portals: From “Terms and Conditions” to CastleRAT

The third campaign clones the TIMOCOM and DAT freight and load-board platforms. Visitors are asked to review “updated terms and conditions” or download booking documents.

Clicking “View PDF” opens a WebDAV share containing terms_and_conditions.pdf.lnk. The file is a Windows shortcut disguised as a PDF, and it launches an executable from the remote server.

That executable installs a MeshCentral agent, a legitimate remote administration tool. Through it, the operator took several hands-on steps:

  • Retrieved the BitLocker recovery password using manage-bde
  • Added Microsoft Defender exclusions for C:\Users and the payload
  • Deployed CastleRAT (also tracked as NightshadeC2) as C:\Users\SysmonDrivers.exe
  • Relaunched it with elevated privileges through a UAC bypass

CastleRAT uses a Steam Community profile as a dead-drop resolver to find its command server. Earlier waves of the campaign, seen in May 2026, used NetSupport Manager instead.

Researchers did not observe file encryption. However, they note that having BitLocker recovery keys, weakened defenses, and persistent remote control together creates serious risk for any organization.

Cut MTTR by 21 minutes per incident. Expand your SOC's capacity to respond faster, contain threats sooner, and reduce the impact of cyberattacks. Talk to ANY.RUN Experts

Indicators of Compromise (Selected)

How Logistics Security Teams Can Respond

Based on the research, defenders should prioritize the following:

  • Verify through official channels. Confirm FMCSA, broker, and load-board requests through known contacts, not links in emails.
  • Train dispatch and onboarding staff to recognize ClickFix-style prompts and “PDFs” that open Windows Explorer.
  • Hunt for WebDAV execution, such as rundll32.exe invoking davclnt.dll, followed by programs run from an external share.
  • Watch for unauthorized remote-management agents, especially when they appear alongside BitLocker queries or Defender configuration changes.
  • Monitor scheduled tasks for names like NodeRemote*, and outbound requests to /internal/clients/telemeter.
  • Detonate suspicious files and links in an Interactive Sandbox to see the full chain, from lure to payload to C2, before they reach production systems.

The Bigger Picture

All three campaigns succeed for the same reason: they look like routine freight work. As carriers, brokers, and shippers move more operations onto digital platforms, attackers are copying those platforms closely enough to slip past email filters and busy staff.

For logistics organizations, the researchers conclude, the defense lies in understanding these attack chains early, mapping the infrastructure behind them, and turning those findings into detections before a fake portal becomes a real breach.

articles.title: Hackers Use GhostMap eBPF Rootkit to Hide IronWorm Malware From Linux Security Tools
articles.description:
Hackers are using a Linux rootkit called GhostMap to hide IronWorm malware from tools administrators rely on to inspect running systems. The rootkit can make selected processes, files, and network sockets disappear from routine listings without removing them. In one test, a malware listener vanished from /proc/net/tcp but remained visible to ss, a Linux utility […]

The post Hackers Use GhostMap eBPF Rootkit to Hide IronWorm Malware From Linux Security Tools appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are using a Linux rootkit called GhostMap to hide IronWorm malware from tools administrators rely on to inspect running systems.

The rootkit can make selected processes, files, and network sockets disappear from routine listings without removing them.

In one test, a malware listener vanished from /proc/net/tcp but remained visible to ss, a Linux utility that reads socket information through a different interface.

GhostMap is the concealment component, not the entire implant. IronWorm is Rust-based malware delivered through compromised software packages.

Earlier reporting on the IronWorm supply chain attack documented its focus on developer secrets, including credentials and API keys.

The new research examined what happens after installation, when a Linux service starts the implant and the rootkit begins changing what local tools can see.

Researchers Dolev Mizrahi and Ivan Kosarev from Aqua Security (Aquasec) identified GhostMap in examined IronWorm and Atomic Arch payloads.

Their November 17 report found evidence that both payloads used the same rootkit implementation, but did not establish that the two campaigns had the same operator.

Hackers Use GhostMap eBPF Rootkit

Aqua examined the executable bundled with weavedb-sdk@0.45.3. When the researchers ran it with root privileges, it copied itself into /var/lib and created a persistent systemd service.

The process launched by that service loaded GhostMap. That distinction matters for investigators: following only the original installer’s child processes would have missed the process that loaded the rootkit. The test did not demonstrate privilege escalation or an unprivileged loading path.

GhostMap abuses eBPF, short for extended Berkeley Packet Filter, a Linux feature that lets small programs run at selected points in the kernel. Aqua counted 13 programs and 10 maps, which hold data the programs use.

As earlier coverage of LinkPro’s Linux rootkit activity shows, GhostMap is not the first malware to abuse eBPF for concealment. Aqua’s contribution was to measure exactly what disappeared and what remained observable.

In six altered directory listings, Aqua found that changing one byte was enough to make the reader skip selected records. The entries were still in memory, and the amount of data returned did not change.

Test processes dropped out of ps output but remained accessible through their known /proc/PID paths. When the rootkit stopped, the processes appeared in the listings again.

The socket tests exposed another limit. IronWorm’s local collector disappeared from /proc/net/tcp in all three checks, but the tested build of ss still showed the listener each time, without identifying its owning process.

The collector stored test records in an extended file attribute called user.d. Aqua verified local storage but did not observe successful external delivery or authenticated remote command execution.

Detecting GhostMap and Investigating Exposed Linux Hosts

Aqua also found matching eBPF program and map names in the Atomic Arch sample. Earlier coverage of the Atomic Arch supply chain traced that campaign to compromised Arch User Repository build scripts.

The overlap gives defenders a reason to look beyond npm package names, but Aqua’s detailed concealment and detection tests apply to the examined IronWorm specimen.

Tracee, Aqua’s open-source runtime security tool, flagged three eBPF programs with application-memory write capabilities when they attached. It also retained all 48 directory-reader calls in the test.

This demonstrated detection, not prevention. Reporting on SANSAR Linux mining malware illustrates a similar lesson: a normal-looking system reading does not mean the activity behind it has stopped.

On potentially exposed hosts, investigators should compare process listings with retained execution records and known /proc/PID paths.

They should also review unexpected systemd services and eBPF attachments, then preserve executable metadata, including extended attributes, before removing suspect components. A matching hash identifies a specific artifact; a path or attribute name alone does not confirm infection.

articles.title: Hackers Use Hidden Cron Jobs to Reinstall Malware on Firewalls and Routers Every 5 Minutes
articles.description:
A Linux botnet is hiding in a place most network teams never look: the scheduled jobs on their firewalls, routers and switches. If a responder kills the malware and deletes the file, a hidden cron job downloads it again within five minutes. The botnet is called Evooo1Bot. FortiGuard Labs first described it on August 13, […]

The post Hackers Use Hidden Cron Jobs to Reinstall Malware on Firewalls and Routers Every 5 Minutes appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A Linux botnet is hiding in a place most network teams never look: the scheduled jobs on their firewalls, routers and switches.

If a responder kills the malware and deletes the file, a hidden cron job downloads it again within five minutes. The botnet is called Evooo1Bot. FortiGuard Labs first described it on August 13, 2026.

It goes after internet-facing devices such as routers, firewalls, IP cameras, phone systems and storage boxes.

The malware reuses the attack engine from the leaked Mirai source code, and its authors have added encrypted control traffic, a password-guessing scanner and a proxy feature.

Analysts at Eclypsium noted this weakness in a November 17 report. They warned that killing the process does not clean a compromised device when a scheduled job quietly puts the malware back. Many teams treat that step as the end of cleanup, and that is where this botnet wins.

Hackers Use Hidden Cron Jobs

Cron is the standard Linux job scheduler. It runs tasks at set times, and many network operating systems are built on Linux, so they include it. The legitimate jobs on a firewall are usually small. They rotate logs, clean up files and run health checks.

Evooo1Bot abuses this. One bot command, !persist, installs several ways to stay on the device at once. The cron entry runs every five minutes.

It uses wget or curl to download a script and pipes it straight into a shell. If the bot process is killed and the binary is deleted, the next five-minute mark pulls everything back.

The cron job is only one layer. The same command also creates a systemd service with the harmless-sounding name “Apache HTTPD Cache Manager,” an init script, an /etc/rc.local entry and a login script under /etc/profile.d/.

Removing the cron line alone leaves those in place. The malware also lowers its priority for the system’s out-of-memory killer and keeps the watchdog file open, so a hardware reboot is less likely to interrupt it.

Cron is not how the botnet gets in. According to FortiGuard, it spreads by exploiting known flaws in devices from D-Link, Tenda, NETGEAR, Telesquare and others, and by guessing SSH passwords.

All the exploit callbacks pointed to one loader address. Once inside, the bot can turn a device into a SOCKS proxy. FortiGuard called that the most important feature, because the attacker can hide behind your device and move deeper into your network.

This is not a one-off trick. Flare researchers described the SSHStalker botnet in February 2026. It uses a cron job that runs every minute and restarts the malware if it disappears.

Our earlier report on a legacy IRC botnet campaign showed how that one-minute watchdog brings bots back in about 60 seconds.

How Defenders Can Find and Remove Hidden Jobs

Appliances are easy to miss. Admins work in the vendor’s command line, and configuration tools track the vendor settings, not the Linux crontab underneath.

Endpoint agents usually do not run on these devices. As we have seen when hackers target edge devices, that blind spot is exactly why attackers like them.

Eclypsium advises starting in the device’s Linux shell. On Arista EOS, the bash command opens one. On Cisco NX-OS, the bash shell must be enabled first, and many deployments leave it off. If you cannot enable it, record that cron was not inspected. Do not record the device as clean.

Read the scheduler files directly. Check /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d/, the hourly, daily, weekly and monthly folders, and the spool files under /var/spool/cron/.

Do not rely on crontab -l alone. An attacker with root can write straight into the spool folder without ever running that command. The spool path also differs by Linux family, so check both /var/spool/cron/crontabs/ and /var/spool/cron/.

Then search for risky patterns. A curl or wget command piped into sh or bash points to Evooo1Bot. References to /dev/tcp, nc or ncat suggest a reverse shell, and a long base64 string suggests a hidden command.

Jobs that run every minute or at boot deserve a closer look, but some vendors run their own frequent jobs, so treat those as suspicious and not proof. Any job that downloads and runs code should go to incident response.

Order matters during cleanup. Save a copy of the cron file and its timestamps, remove the cron entry first, and only then kill the process. Doing it the other way gives the scheduler another chance to run.

After that, check the other startup spots, and look at vendor schedulers such as NX-OS EEM applets or Arista event handlers, which are not cron. Eclypsium also warned that it has not tested whether a cron entry survives a reboot or upgrade on every platform.

Patching helps stop the first break-in, but it will not remove a job that is already there. In the stealthy PEERSTITCH malware implant case, attackers also relied on weak visibility inside firewalls.

articles.title: AI Hacking Framework CyberStrikeAI Runs 221 Tool Executions Without Human Approval
articles.description:
An exposed CyberStrikeAI workspace recorded 221 tool executions in a single session on November 16, 2026. The logs show no human decision at the framework’s tool approval gate, and the saved configuration later showed that the gate had been switched off. A person still directed the AI agent through chat. The difference matters: telling an […]

The post AI Hacking Framework CyberStrikeAI Runs 221 Tool Executions Without Human Approval appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
An exposed CyberStrikeAI workspace recorded 221 tool executions in a single session on November 16, 2026. The logs show no human decision at the framework’s tool approval gate, and the saved configuration later showed that the gate had been switched off.

A person still directed the AI agent through chat. The difference matters: telling an agent what to do is not the same as approving each action before it runs.

CyberStrikeAI is an open-source penetration testing framework, not a newly discovered malware family. It connects a language model to security tools and stores their results.

Earlier reporting on CyberStrikeAI multi-agent activity described a separate case involving 44 agents. In the November 16 session, every recorded tool call came from one main agent, even though the workspace was configured in supervisor mode.

Researchers from huntback identified the exposed workspace and examined its conversation database, diagnostic log and application source.

Their CyberStrikeAI workspace investigation did not establish who operated the framework or whether the testing was authorized. The researchers reviewed the artifacts without running recovered programs, replaying requests or contacting the services under test.

AI Hacking Framework CyberStrikeAI

The runtime logged 240 tool calls, but only 221 had execution IDs that matched entries in the database’s execution table.

The other 19 were local actions, such as updating plans and reading files, that did not receive those IDs. Of the stored executions, 209 were marked completed and 12 failed.

A completed status meant the tool finished running, not that the action it attempted succeeded. Some completed runs returned authentication or application errors.

The database recorded four approval rejections, all issued by an automated reviewer after it failed to get a response from its model. None was a human decision.

At 09:48:15 UTC, the saved configuration showed approval enforcement was off. Huntback could not determine who changed the setting and found no evidence that the AI agent bypassed the control on its own.

The operator later asked the agent to list potentially harmful write and delete actions for review, then approved the proposed items in chat.

That approval did not restore the software control that could stop a tool call before execution. The repeated instructions also distinguish this session from cases covered in the FBI’s ARTEX security warning, where some intrusions reached privileged access in under three hours.

What the CyberStrikeAI Session Actually Proved

The strongest evidence was that a compute service returned node and job data. The retained outputs did not establish that the agent gained a shell, reached an internal network, breached a data lake or made a destructive database change.

A search result showing at least 10,000 matches did not establish that 10,000 records were downloaded. Likewise, a script reported collecting 260 node entries, but it did not check for duplicates, and researchers did not recover the full list.

The agent entered nine findings in the database, but those were not nine independently verified vulnerabilities. A newly generated wallet did not prove that someone else’s credentials were stolen, and a catalogue of available tools did not establish permission to run them.

As coverage of AI attack automation trends shows, agents can drive real tool activity. Investigators still need returned data and system logs to verify what that activity achieved.

For security teams running AI agents, the clearest detection opportunity is the sequence: reviewer errors, a change to approval settings and renewed tool activity.

Huntback also recommends checking whether file servers or backup routes expose conversation databases, uploaded documents or runtime logs, even when the main application requires authentication.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
New York City, United States, November 18th, 2026, CyberNewswire

OffSec built 14 labs on real CVEs in two weeks. Its Level 20 offer takes $550 off Learn One for learners ready to train against threats like these.

OffSec, the world’s leading provider of hands-on cybersecurity training and certifications, released more than 80 hands-on labs in the last two weeks of October as Black October crippled government and university websites across Europe.

The labs give security teams a safe place to attack and defend the same kinds of flaws making headlines. Fourteen are built on real CVEs disclosed this year. They include a free lab on PHP2Shell, the PHP flaw at the center of the month’s disclosure wave.

Black October is the name the security community gave to a cluster of critical disclosures in late October. At its center was PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619).

The flaws let attackers run code on web servers without logging in. Researchers at Calif and Wiz found the flaws with help from AI models. Amazon spotted an exploitation attempt on Oct. 17, four days before public disclosure.

CERT-EU told organizations that could not patch right away to isolate internet-facing apps from public networks. CISA urged immediate patching. The same day GitLab patched a maximum-severity flaw that let unauthenticated users run code on its servers.

CrowdStrike reported four threat actors running campaigns in which AI agents make decisions and execute commands.

The pace reflects a larger shift. AI now helps find flaws and turn them into working exploits. An AI agent can compare a vulnerable release against its patched version and see exactly what changed. That shrinks the window defenders have to understand a flaw and act on it.

“AI has lowered the skill ceiling for attackers,” said Alex “Sickness” Uifalvi, Security Researcher and architect at OffSec. “Going from a patch to a working exploit used to take a skilled team up to a week.

An agent can cut that by a big chunk. Defenders need to get their hands on these flaws while they are still in the news. That is why our team builds labs on real CVEs as fast as we can. You learn what an attack looks like by running it and stopping it yourself.”

OffSec’s new labs, listed in its Oct. 19–25 and Oct. 26–Nov. 2 weekly updates, cover both sides of an incident, and include:

  • Offensive Labs built on recent CVEs in Kestra, Hermes WebUI, WordPress 7.0.2, the Algernon web server and a chained Vite and Uptime Kuma exposure.
  • Defensive Labs where learners secure vulnerable versions of Spring, Kestra and Next.js.
  • Incident Investigations modeled on real attack types. These include ransomware that began with a help desk call, an email compromise that rerouted a client payment, a breached SSL VPN appliance and an intrusion at a hydroelectric plant.
  • AI Targets such as an AI-driven tool marketplace with an automated reviewer and agent.

OffSec CEO Ning Wang said fast-moving flaws like PHP2Shell are now the norm.

“These vulnerabilities are being found by AI agents and that will happen more and more,” said CEO Wang. “You need to very quickly understand how a flaw works and how to defend against it.

When PHP2Shell hit, we acted instantly to develop a new lab and a blog to begin teaching people how the attack works and how to stop it. Every organization that cares about its business risk needs to be on top of these things. Your red team and your blue team both need to know how to use AI to do their jobs. It’s no longer a nice-to-do. It’s a must-do.”

Level 20: Same Game, New Level

OffSec is marking 20 years of hands-on training with Level 20, a year-end offer for individual learners. Learn One is $550 off through Jan. 4, 2027.

Security professionals who want to learn AI red teaming can now train for OSAI (OffSec AI Red Teamer) through Learn One. This is the first time OSAI is part of a Learn One offer.

Its AI-300 course covers attacks on AI models, large language models and autonomous agents.

A Learn One Subscription Includes:

  • One 200- or 300-level OffSec course such as PEN-200 for the OSCP penetration testing certification or AI-300 for OSAI
  • 365 days of course and lab access
  • Two attempts at the certification exam
  • More than 200 Proving Grounds Practice labs
  • Bonus KLCP and OSWP courses and exams

The PHP2Shell lab is free to use on Proving Grounds Play. Claim the Level 20 offer at learn.offsec.com/level-20-promo.

Built on a foundation of excellence, integrity, and the relentless “Try Harder” ethos, OffSec empowers individuals and organizations to outsmart evolving cyber threats through rigorous, hands-on learning.

From its beginnings to today, OffSec has set the elite standard for cybersecurity proficiency, earning global recognition and the implicit trust of the world’s most elite security teams.

articles.title: NGINX HTTP/2 Flaws Could Allow Memory Corruption and Remote Code Execution on Web Servers
articles.description:
Two critical vulnerabilities in NGINX could let remote attackers run code on vulnerable web servers without logging in. The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, were disclosed on November 18, 2026. Both require NGINX to accept HTTP/2 connections from clients, but the conditions differ. One affects certain reverse proxy setups, while the other can affect […]

The post NGINX HTTP/2 Flaws Could Allow Memory Corruption and Remote Code Execution on Web Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Two critical vulnerabilities in NGINX could let remote attackers run code on vulnerable web servers without logging in. The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, were disclosed on November 18, 2026.

Both require NGINX to accept HTTP/2 connections from clients, but the conditions differ. One affects certain reverse proxy setups, while the other can affect a server that does nothing more than serve static files.

The flaws are in NGINX itself, not the websites or APIs behind it. NGINX often handles HTTPS and routes incoming requests to several applications. That means a single vulnerable proxy can put multiple services at risk even when their application code is secure. Depending on what the NGINX process can access, a successful attack could expose sensitive data, alter website content, or interrupt service.

Wiz Research named Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint as independent finders across the two disclosures. Both flaws carry a critical score of 9.2 under the CVSS 4.0 severity scale. The findings show that remote code execution is possible under the reported conditions. They do not, on their own, establish that attackers have used either flaw against production systems.

Netcraft counted more than 225 million sites using NGINX in its September 2026 web server survey. That figure shows how widely the software is used, not how many sites are vulnerable. Exposure depends on the installed version and how the server handles HTTP/2. Multiple sites can also share the same NGINX deployment, so a site count is not a count of affected servers.

These are separate from the NGINX flaws F5 disclosed in October. An organization that applied those fixes may still need another update. F5 lists NGINX Open Source 1.31.8 as affected by CVE-2026-123633, so running a build newer than October’s security release does not mean it contains the November fixes.

NGINX HTTP/2 Vulnerabilities

In its advisory for CVE-2026-123633, F5 describes a use-after-free bug, which means a worker process can reuse memory after it has been released. The issue affects setups where NGINX accepts HTTP/2 client connections and forwards requests to a backend. F5 says the worker must also be running low on available connections. The flaw can crash the worker or, under certain conditions, let an attacker run code.

CVE-2026-123007 has a wider reach. It affects NGINX Open Source releases dating back to 1.9.5, which shipped in 2015. In its disclosure report, Wiz said it demonstrated code execution on an NGINX server serving ordinary static files, with no backend application or third-party modules. A basic site should therefore be part of the patch review, not just API gateways and reverse proxies.

The two November flaws are also distinct from the NGINX HTTP/2 proxy and gRPC vulnerability patched in June, which depended on a different set of configuration options. For this update, administrators should check whether NGINX accepts HTTP/2 from clients. Checking only the protocol NGINX uses to reach a backend can miss the client-facing exposure.

Fixed NGINX versions

The fixes for both flaws are listed for NGINX Open Source 1.31.9 on the mainline branch and 1.30.7 on the stable branch. For NGINX Plus, the minimum fixed builds differ by CVE.

Administrators should check F5’s CVE-2026-123007 advisory alongside the CVE-2026-123633 advisory and choose a build that covers both. If the current branch has no fix listed, F5 recommends moving to one that does.

Start with internet-facing servers, then check internal proxies and static sites. For NGINX installed through a Linux distribution or bundled with another product, check the supplier’s security notice for the package or image that contains both fixes.

After updating, verify the version actually running on every instance. A configuration reload alone does not replace the running NGINX binary, so restart the service or roll out replacement containers as appropriate.

If a fixed build is not yet available through your update channel, temporarily turn off client-facing HTTP/2 on affected listeners where the service can tolerate the change.

Afterward, test from the client side to confirm the endpoint no longer accepts HTTP/2, and check that websites and APIs still work. Disabling HTTP/2 reduces exposure to these two flaws, but it does not fix the underlying flaws. Install the security update before turning the protocol back on.

Every approved nomination also enters Community Choice, a separate public vote that does not influence jury results. Outstanding Gold winners may be considered for Best in Class distinctions throughout the year, without requiring another nomination.
