The post SpyCloud’s 2027 Forecast: Attackers Will Exploit Trusted Access, From Hijacked Sessions to AI Agents appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Austin, TX, USA, November 17th, 2026, CyberNewswire

New predictions drawn from SpyCloud’s research teams and a survey of security professionals show why stolen sessions, API keys, and vendor connections will drive the most damaging attacks in 2027.

SpyCloud, the leader in identity threat protection, today released its SpyCloud 2026 Forecast Report, outlining several predictions for 2027 drawn from the company’s experts across security research, product, investigations, and data science, plus a survey of 50 security professionals at large enterprises.

The predictions are ordered by expert confidence, with the most certain listed first. 

AI is speeding up attackers and defenders alike, but organizations are adopting it faster than they can govern it. Attackers are using that gap to automate phishing and evolve malware, shortening their path to the access they want.

“The clearest pattern heading into 2027 is that attackers are gaining access through vectors that organizations already trust: active employee sessions, vendor connections, and even insider threats,” said Aurora Johnson, Director, Threat Research & Intelligence at SpyCloud.

“Security measures like multifactor authentication are good, but defenders need to be mindful that they’re not enough these days. Criminals have developed new tactics to effectively bypass these protections.”

Cybersecurity Threats SpyCloud Anticipates in 2027

  1. Attackers will keep slipping past MFA by taking over the session or the device it trusts. SpyCloud experts expect phishing kits to keep moving to methods MFA does not stop, including device code phishing and relay attacks, also known as adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attacks.Some attackers will skip the kit altogether and work inside the victim’s own browser through browser-in-the-middle (BitM) attacks, and the kits that remain will keep adapting.
  2. The API keys and tokens behind AI tools and agents will become attackers’ next favorite target. WardenStealer and Aoki, two commodity infostealers, already collect the tokens, keys, and session cookies that AI coding tools store on developer machines, and SpyCloud has recaptured more than 127,000 WardenStealer infections since August. Stolen AI access retains much of its reach after a password reset, and criminals already sell it well below list price. These non-human identity (NHI) credentials will only grow more valuable as AI tools and agents reach more enterprise systems.
  3. The most damaging compromises will come through access the organization already trusts, from a vendor integration to an employee insider threat. Attackers keep reaching big targets through connections granted long ago. SpyCloud experts expect the next wave to include both negligent and potentially malicious insiders, and integrations that still hold admin scope years after someone approved them. In the survey, 68% of security professionals reported being affected by a breach at a vendor, contractor, or SaaS provider.
  4. Fraudsters will stitch together convincing identities from real stolen data and AI-generated faces, voices and documents. Stolen personal data is plentiful, and AI makes it cheaper to turn into a believable face, voice, or document. Experts expect fraud cases to become harder to identify and crack as these identities improve and AI agents open accounts at volume.
  5. Only 6% of survey respondents have seen this activity, so this call runs ahead of what most teams see today.
  6. Attackers will start phishing AI agents the same way they have always phished people. AI agents now hold as many tokens, keys, and sessions as the people they work beside, and they read tickets, logs, and résumés all day without anyone checking each one. Early signs include malicious skills on an AI agent marketplace that tell agents to download infostealer malware. In SpyCloud’s 2026 Identity Threat Report, 91% of security leaders said their organizations used AI tools or agents with access to internal systems.
  7. Threat actor groups will keep changing names and members, and their conversations will keep hopping between chat apps. As forums are taken down, only to resurface under new names, more cybercriminal activity is moving to chat apps that are free, feature-rich, and easy to join. SpyCloud experts agree the conversation will stay on chat apps but are split on where. Some expect Telegram to hold, while others expect a move to invite-only platforms such as Session, SimpleX and Matrix, which is why SpyCloud rates this call medium-confidence.
  8. Fully autonomous attacks will grab the headlines in 2027, but ordinary attacks running faster will do most of the damage. Familiar attacks built on stolen sessions, tokens, and vendor connections will keep doing the most damage, with AI making them cheaper and quicker to run, even if autonomous attacks take the spotlight. Autonomous attacks have not yet shown up in SpyCloud’s recaptured data, so SpyCloud rates that half of the call low-confidence. Of the security professionals surveyed, 46% expect attackers to gain ground in the first half of 2027.

Several of these predictions point to the same shift in what attackers want: not just employee passwords, but the tokens, keys, and service accounts that connect SaaS platforms, vendors, and AI tools.

“With the proliferation of more SaaS and less on-prem services, NHIs have become as valuable if not more valuable than everyday traditional username/email password pairs,” said Joe Roosen, Senior Director, Security Research at SpyCloud.

“Because of this, commodity infostealers will pivot to seeking out NHIs as a preference.”

Security Implications of AI Driven Threats

Drawing on more than one trillion recaptured identity assets, SpyCloud helps organizations identify compromised identities and automate remediation before stolen access can enable session hijacking, account takeover, ransomware, fraud, and other cyberattacks.

“AI is making familiar attacks faster and easier to scale,” said Jason Lancaster, Chief Investigations Officer at SpyCloud. “Stolen sessions, API keys, and tokens already give criminals access to business systems, and as AI tools and agents hold more of those credentials, organizations need greater visibility into what has been exposed and the ability to remediate compromised access before attackers can exploit it.”

To read the full insights and report users can visit spycloud.com. 

About SpyCloud

SpyCloud transforms recaptured darknet data to disrupt cybercrime. Its automated identity threat protection solutions use advanced analytics and AI to accelerate investigations and protect workforce, consumer, and supplier identities from the threats that matter most: authentication bypass, session hijacking, malicious insiders, account takeover, ransomware, and fraud.

Its data from malware-infected devices, successful phishes, combolists, and third-party breaches also powers many popular dark web monitoring and identity theft protection offerings.

Customers include 7 of the Fortune 10, along with hundreds of global enterprises, mid-sized companies, and government agencies worldwide.

Headquartered in Austin, TX, SpyCloud is home to more than 250 cybersecurity experts whose mission is to protect businesses and consumers from the stolen identity data criminals are using to target them now.

To learn more and see insights on your company’s exposed data, users can visit spycloud.com.

Armornet, an AI cybersecurity company, is accepting teams into the private alpha of its platform, which gives an automatically discovered, continuous view of the vendors a company’s teams relies on.

Procurement and risk review each vendor at signing. First- and third-party engineering teams ship thousands of lines of code a day. As that code changes, so does how teams use each vendor and where that vendor stands on breaches, exploits and patching. The review done at signing captures none of it.

After teams connect their version control, compliance and workspace tools, Armornet lists the vendors and packages they rely on and how they use them.

Armornet’s Agent Mesh monitors everything from package installs to the breach notifications, counting each block and response against the vendor’s risk score. 

Open-source malware grew 75% in 2025, according to Sonatype’s 2026 State of the Software Supply Chain report. In May, GitHub said a hacking group took about 3,800 of its internal repositories through a poisoned code-editor extension on an employee’s device.

“A vendor review is a snapshot, but vendor risk changes every day. Breaches, exploits and patches keep coming, and the teams relying on that vendor are typically the last to find out,” said Tony Ramos, founder and CEO of Armornet.

“Armornet gives procurement, security and engineering teams one shared, continuously monitored record of each vendor they rely on, so everyone works from the same picture.”

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
New York, United States, November 18th, 2026, CyberNewswire

New technology monitors critical vulnerabilities and supply chain threats, automatically assessing customer exposure and guiding remediation

OX Security, a leader in AI-native application protection, today announced the launch of OX Radar and Response Center, giving security teams one place to track high-priority cyber threats, determine whether their organizations are affected, and manage remediation.

OX Radar continuously monitors emerging vulnerabilities, compromised software dependencies, and actively exploited threats.

Integrated with OX Security’s application security platform, the Response Center automatically checks supported threats against customer environments, identifying affected assets and providing the context and guidance needed to respond.

Separately, a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed provides broader security research and findings across the software and AI supply chain.

When a major vulnerability or supply chain attack emerges, security teams often spend hours searching advisories, checking inventories, and correlating findings across tools to answer the question that matters most: Are we affected? As new software and AI components proliferate, investigating every potential threat manually is becoming increasingly impractical.

“The question isn’t just whether a new threat is dangerous. It’s whether it’s dangerous to you,” said Neatsun Ziv, CEO and co-founder of OX Security. “AI is accelerating software development, expanding the supply chain, and generating more security alerts than teams can realistically investigate.

Security teams need to know immediately which threats affect their organization, which don’t, and what action is required.”

From Breaking Threats to Customer Action

To help security teams stay ahead of threats requiring urgent attention, OX Radar scans CVE databases, known-exploited vulnerability catalogs, security advisories, and vendor research approximately every 10 minutes.

The customer-facing capabilities focus on high-priority threats, including compromised or malicious dependencies, exploited vulnerabilities, and critical-severity CVEs.

The Response Center connects supported OX Radar threats to each customer’s environment, checking whether vulnerable components are present and assessing their exploitability.

It combines intelligence from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogs, EPSS exploit predictions, and VEX exploitability status with OX Security’s AI-generated exploit checks and runtime visibility to determine whether vulnerable libraries are affected.

Through the Response Center, security teams can:

  • Track threats: Follow high-priority incidents as new intelligence and findings emerge.
  • Assess exposure: Identify affected assets and examine supporting evidence.
  • Prioritize risk: Evaluate severity, exploitation, code usage, and reachability.
  • Manage remediation: Access safe versions and guidance, and create or track tickets and fix pull requests.
  • Document response: Maintain records of findings and remediation activity.

For each supported incident, the Response Center indicates whether a vulnerability has been detected in the customer’s environment, provides evidence of its potential exploitability, and incorporates available VEX information to help teams determine whether action is required.

Teams can also initiate investigations using a CVE identifier, GitHub Security Advisory identifier, or advisory URL.

Expanding Threat Visibility Through Public Research

Alongside the customer-facing capabilities, OX Security is introducing a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed with a broader catalog of security findings.

Powered by OX Security’s independent research and scanning, the feed analyzes newly published npm and PyPI packages, AI skills, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.

OX Security will continue expanding the range of threats assessed against customer environments, bringing more findings from its public research into the Response Center over time.

Availability

OX Radar and Response Center are available to OX Security customers as part of OX Security’s AI-Native Application Protection Platform (AINAPP). The broader OX Radar research feed is publicly accessible through the OX Security website.

About OX Security

OX Security is the first AI-Native Application Protection Platform built to secure software from prompt to production runtime.

Its platform includes VibeSec, OX Code, OX Cloud, and OX Agentic Pentester, giving security teams a unified system for securing AI-driven development, applications, and cloud environments.

articles.title: Microsoft Unveils Windows Server 2028 With Hundreds of Security Protections Enabled by Default
articles.description:
Microsoft has released Windows Server 2028 in public preview. The biggest change is that a new server now starts in a locked-down state rather than an open one. Hundreds of security settings are on from the first boot, so admins no longer need to harden the system by hand after setup. Microsoft announced the release on November […]

The post Microsoft Unveils Windows Server 2028 With Hundreds of Security Protections Enabled by Default appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has released Windows Server 2028 in public preview. The biggest change is that a new server now starts in a locked-down state rather than an open one.

Hundreds of security settings are on from the first boot, so admins no longer need to harden the system by hand after setup. Microsoft announced the release on November 17, 2026.

For years, Windows Server shipped in a “compatible by default” form. Admins had to apply the Security Baseline or their own scripts to secure it. Until that work was done, every new server ran in a weaker state, and the gap was easy to miss.

In its Hardened Server Core announcement, Microsoft says this approach is changing. Admins now start from a hardened setup and relax only what a workload needs.

Hardened Settings in Windows Server 2028

The change starts with Windows Server Insider Preview build 29706, where Server Core installs hardened. The settings line up with industry benchmarks such as CIS and DISA STIG.

This closes the window in which a freshly deployed server sits exposed while it waits to be hardened. Microsoft grouped the settings by layer, and it says they were validated together so they work as a set. On identity, Kerberos is preferred over NTLM, LSASS is protected, and strong passwords and account lockout are on. Consumer accounts are not allowed.

On the network side, the server talks only over signed, encrypted, and authenticated channels. SMB signing and encryption are on, and the firewall runs in every profile. Legacy name resolution and unauthenticated RPC are off.

Cryptography also gets stronger. TLS is limited to modern cipher suites, and key exchange uses hybrid post-quantum protection with ML-KEM. Admins must approve privilege elevation, and Guests cannot sign in. The sign-in process runs only Microsoft-signed code, and the paging file is encrypted.

For remote access, RDP needs NLA and TLS. WinRM blocks Basic and Digest logins and unencrypted traffic. Audit logs now record command lines, PowerShell script block logging is on, and event logs are larger.

These choices target problems that defenders have seen for years. Cyber Security News has covered how Windows SMB client flaws let intruders take over Active Directory when relay protections are weak. Many of those cases worked because SMB signing was optional on most servers.

A proof-of-concept for CVE-2026-24294 showed the same pattern. It gave SYSTEM-level access on a default Windows Server 2025 install where signing was not enforced. Microsoft fixed that path in March 2026.

The research still warned that as long as NTLM stays common and signing stays optional, new tricks will keep appearing. Turning on signing, encryption, and Kerberos preference at install time removes much of that room. It also matches the advice researchers keep repeating.

Cymulate noted that turning off NTLM alone is not enough and that anti-relay protections must be enforced on every service. Microsoft delivers the hardened values as policy in the HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies hive wherever a component supports it. Policy wins over local settings, so a script or installer cannot quietly weaken a default.

In Microsoft’s test, trying to turn on WinRM Basic authentication was refused because policy controls it.Admins keep control. OSConfig, Group Policy or another management tool can manage the settings, and whichever tool sets a value owns it. One surprise is that gpresult and RSOP report these settings as Not Configured.

The defaults are built into the image, so there is no policy file for those tools to read. A new PowerShell module called MSHardenedPolicyEval ships in the box. The Get-MSHardenedPolicyScore cmdlet scores the server by category. In Microsoft’s example output, the server passed 191 of 237 checks, an overall score of 80.59 percent.

Restore-MSHardenedPolicy removes hardened values for one category or the whole server. Set-MSHardenedPolicy applies them again. Both support -WhatIf, so admins can preview a change before making it.

Microsoft warns that names may change in later previews, and that scores below 100 percent are expected on this build. Microsoft says some things that worked on Windows Server 2025 may break. Older protocols, legacy authentication, and some management tools and scripts are the likely trouble spots.

Teams should test apps and admin tooling against the hardened setup first. They should relax only the specific setting a workload needs.

Some protections are also still missing from this preview. These include NTLM blocking, Secure Boot and DMA protection requirements, kernel shadow stacks, and Windows Protected Print. Print and RPC hardening is also on the list, along with extra settings such as the logon banner.

The wider release adds more protection. Trusted Launch helps guarantee boot integrity across virtual machine fleets. Confidential VM support begins a path toward integrity-protected runtimes on supported hardware.

Microsoft is also working on automatic certificate management and post-quantum cryptography. Windows Server 2028 also adds native NVMe storage by default, along with NVMe over TCP and RDMA. Intune management for Windows Server is in preview, and Windows Admin Center Virtualization Mode is now generally available.

Microsoft further plans AI inference on local servers, with AMD Instinct MI350P cards in preview from the first half of 2027. The preview is open through the Windows Server Insider Program. Teams that want early access and direct contact with engineers can apply to the Windows Server Technology Adoption Program at aka.ms/WSTAP.

Admins should try the build in a lab, score it, and report any workload that breaks. Microsoft says this feedback will shape the defaults before general availability.

For now, keep patching current servers and enforce SMB signing and Kerberos where possible. Doing so will make a move to Windows Server 2028 much smoother when it arrives.

The post Microsoft Unveils Windows Server 2028 With Hundreds of Security Protections Enabled by Default appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: New Hello Again Attack Bypasses Windows Hello and BitLocker PIN Lockout Protection
articles.description:
Researchers have shown that someone with a laptop and a few cheap parts can guess a Windows Hello PIN in about 40 hours. With the lockout working as designed, the same job would take 69 days. The same trick also cuts the worst-case time to crack a default 6-digit BitLocker startup PIN from 19 years […]

The post New Hello Again Attack Bypasses Windows Hello and BitLocker PIN Lockout Protection appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Researchers have shown that someone with a laptop and a few cheap parts can guess a Windows Hello PIN in about 40 hours. With the lockout working as designed, the same job would take 69 days.

The same trick also cuts the worst-case time to crack a default 6-digit BitLocker startup PIN from 19 years to 20 days. The work is called “Hello Again” and comes from a paper on arXiv that is also tied to ACM CCS ’26.

Windows Hello is the main sign-in method on more than one billion Windows 11 devices, and it allows PINs as short as four digits. A short PIN is only safe because the TPM, the security chip that guards keys, locks down after too many wrong guesses. Microsoft explains that the TPM protects against PIN brute-force attempts on lost or stolen devices, and the device locks after too many bad tries.

BitLocker works the same way. Microsoft’s BitLocker countermeasures page says TPM anti-hammering is built to stop people from guessing a startup PIN. The whole design depends on the chip keeping an honest count of failed guesses.

Hello Attack Bypasses Windows Hello and BitLocker

Most modern x86 PCs use a firmware TPM, or fTPM, which runs inside the processor and has no private storage of its own. It saves its state, including the failed-guess count, on the SPI flash chip on the motherboard. If someone copies that saved state and writes it back later, the count goes back too. To stop this, newer boards use Replay Protected Monotonic Counters, or RPMC.

These are counters inside the flash chip that can only move up. The researchers did the first practical security study of RPMC in real x86 PCs and found several weak spots.

The first flaw is in Winbond flash chips. Winbond is the top NOR flash maker, with more than 25 percent of the market. The team found that a short voltage glitch makes the chip leak its HMAC key, the secret used to sign counter values. With that key in hand, they could forge any counter value they wanted.

The second flaw is in AMD’s non-volatile controller. It never checks that a counter actually went up. A small board sitting between the processor and the flash chip can block the increase, say it worked, and the PC accepts the old state without noticing.

AMD PCs without RPMC flash looked even weaker. On two AMD desktops, writing an old flash image back reset the fTPM’s lockout counters, and no special board was needed. The paper says these rollbacks work on AMD, Intel, and Pluton fTPM state.

The researchers tested the idea on locked and encrypted hardware from start to finish. Each time the TPM locked them out, they rolled back the saved state and kept guessing. This brought a 4-digit Hello PIN down to 40 hours, and the BitLocker TPM+PIN protector fell the same way.

A stolen Hello PIN also opens device-bound keys and Hello-based single sign-on at work, so the damage can reach company accounts and not only the laptop.

AMD has published bulletin AMD-SN-7079 for the flaw. It tracks the issue as CVE-2026-43613 and gives it a CVSS score of 5.1. AMD says the Secure Processor firmware does not properly confirm that an RPMC increase finished, allowing someone with physical access to suppress counter updates.

AMD notes that physical attacks sit outside its normal threat model. It adds that RPMC exists to stop exactly this kind of interposer trick, so it plans firmware fixes. Some target dates for affected Ryzen, EPYC, and Athlon lines are in November 2026.

Until the fixes arrive, AMD tells users to keep systems under physical control and watch for signs of tampering. The Winbond key leak is a chip design problem, and the paper’s findings suggest that only new flash designs can close it.

Other BitLocker Bypasses

This is not the first time BitLocker’s physical protections have been tested this year. Cyber Security News covered the YellowKey BitLocker zero-day, which let someone with physical access skip BitLocker through the Windows Recovery Environment. We also reported on Microsoft’s YellowKey mitigation, tracked as CVE-2026-45585.

Microsoft’s advice after YellowKey was to move from TPM-only mode to TPM+PIN. Hello Again shows why that advice needs a second step. A short PIN is only as strong as the lockout behind it. The GreatXML bug, which we covered in our GreatXML report, points to the same pattern of physical-access bypasses.

The risk is real but narrow. It requires physical access, special tools, and time, so it mainly worries owners of lost or stolen laptops that carry valuable data. Longer PINs are the easiest fix, because each added digit multiplies the number of guesses needed.

Microsoft’s guidance also suggests using a longer, enhanced alphanumeric PIN with BitLocker when strong protection is needed. Admins can raise the minimum PIN length in Group Policy, turn on enhanced startup PINs, and install AMD firmware updates once vendors release them. Companies that store sensitive data should also treat a stolen laptop as a possible data exposure, even when the drive was encrypted.

articles.title: Microsoft’s AI Uncovers 99 Security Issues in Express, ImageMagick and Other Open-Source Projects
articles.description:
Microsoft and GitHub sent 99 verified security reports to six open-source projects, including Express and ImageMagick, after an AI pilot identified thousands of potential vulnerabilities. In its Nov. 17 announcement, GitHub said maintainers had fixed 55 issues as of Nov. 15. However, only 14 of those fixes had made it into software releases. The other […]

The post Microsoft’s AI Uncovers 99 Security Issues in Express, ImageMagick and Other Open-Source Projects appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft and GitHub sent 99 verified security reports to six open-source projects, including Express and ImageMagick, after an AI pilot identified thousands of potential vulnerabilities.

In its Nov. 17 announcement, GitHub said maintainers had fixed 55 issues as of Nov. 15. However, only 14 of those fixes had made it into software releases.

The other four projects, Caddy, AutoGPT, FastMCP, and Netty, also participated in the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund, with maintainers approving the scans before the pilot began.

Microsoft’s Codename MDASH scanned the projects with an earlier version of the MAI Cyber model and suggested code fixes. A GitHub Security Lab AI tool removed duplicates, filtered out reports that didn’t hold up, and prioritized higher-impact issues.

Seven Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers then manually reviewed the remaining findings. Microsoft had previously used MDASH to find Windows vulnerabilities.

Microsofts AI Uncovers 99 Security Issues

GitHub sent the verified reports through its private vulnerability reporting system. Each report included evidence of the issue and a proposed patch.

According to GitHub, maintainers could accept, modify, or replace suggested patches and decide when to release fixes without receiving raw scan results. Caddy fixed all 22 reported issues within a week, while ImageMagick’s two-person team also received 22 reports.

One looked like a problem the team had seen before, but the report explained what was different and pointed to the relevant code. The team pushed a fix in 15 minutes. Those findings are separate from previously reported ImageMagick memory corruption flaws.

AutoGPT’s team received a report about a newly added security check three days after it shipped. The maintainers went beyond the suggested patch, wrote their own fix within a day, and put it into production in less than a week. Express maintainers said the reports helped them cut through the noise from other vulnerability submissions.

The pilot covered only six projects, and the human review took about two days per project. That makes the results an early test of how AI can help small teams, not proof that the approach can work at the same pace across thousands of repositories.

The work also does not end when a maintainer writes a patch. Users need a release that contains the fix, and they still need to install it.

GitHub plans to offer reviewed AI scans to all alums of its Secure Open Source Fund and deliver findings privately. For developers who rely on open-source packages, GitHub recommends enabling Dependabot alerts to catch known vulnerabilities in their dependencies.

Once a public advisory is reviewed for the GitHub Advisory Database, Dependabot can notify repositories that use the affected package. Teams can then check the advisory against the version they actually run and confirm that their next update includes the fix.

articles.title: Hackers Steal Exposed AWS Credentials From Docker Hub Images in Just 8 Seconds
articles.description:
Automated bots used a decoy Amazon Web Services (AWS) access key just 7.86 seconds after researchers published the Docker Hub image containing it. That was the fastest case in a controlled Stony Brook University study, not the average. Still, the median time to the first AWS request was just 51.19 seconds, and all 100 keys […]

The post Hackers Steal Exposed AWS Credentials From Docker Hub Images in Just 8 Seconds appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Automated bots used a decoy Amazon Web Services (AWS) access key just 7.86 seconds after researchers published the Docker Hub image containing it. That was the fastest case in a controlled Stony Brook University study, not the average.

Still, the median time to the first AWS request was just 51.19 seconds, and all 100 keys in the first round were used within 15 minutes. The study did not report a break-in at Docker Hub. It showed how quickly a secret left inside a public image can be found and used.

Researchers Billy Tsouvalas and Nick Nikiforakis published 300 test images across eight public container registries over four months. They planted AWS, OpenAI, and Anthropic API keys, along with decoy SSH and database credentials.

In the first round alone, 100 unadvertised Docker Hub images were downloaded 58,819 times. The AWS keys inside them drew 66,321 requests from 3,842 distinct IP addresses. Those addresses indicate where requests came from, not how many attackers were involved.

A container image packages an application and its files in layers. The researchers saw no signs that anyone ran the images in the first round, despite heavy use of the planted keys.

That points to bots reading the image layers directly. It also explains why watching running containers would miss this kind of leak. A file removed in a later build step can still be present in an earlier layer.

Exposed AWS Credentials From Docker Hub Images

AWS logs showed that some requests checked whether a key worked, while others tried to list cloud resources or use paid services. The study’s first-round restrictions blocked attempts to consume AWS resources.

However, requests made with planted OpenAI and Anthropic keys drained the researchers’ test balances. The difference illustrates why permissions matter. A separate investigation covered by Cyber Security News found 768 exposed corporate AWS credentials with full admin access.

Scan the built image before uploading it, not just the source code. The scan should cover image layers and metadata because a clean project folder does not guarantee a clean image.

If a build needs a password or token, use Docker BuildKit secret mounts to make it available only during the build step that needs it. Avoid putting secrets in Dockerfile ARG or ENV instructions. For applications running on AWS, prefer roles that issue temporary credentials with only the permissions the application needs.

If an AWS key has already shipped in a public image, deactivate it immediately and replace it if the application still needs one. Removing the image does not invalidate a copied key.

Review AWS CloudTrail logs from the time of publication for unfamiliar requests, permission changes, and unexpected resource creation. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of AWS key quarantine, automatic restrictions can block some actions without revoking the key.

The researchers shared their findings with Docker, whose security team acknowledged the report. They proposed checking images for secrets before publication and limiting access to the public feed of new and updated images. For developers, the most useful change is one they can make now. Put the secret check before the upload, when a failed scan can still stop a leak.

articles.title: The Gentlemen Ransomware Gang Allegedly Claims to Have Breached NVIDIA
articles.description:
The Gentlemen ransomware gang listed NVIDIA on its dark web leak site on November 18, 2026, but the post does not prove that the group broke into the chipmaker’s systems. The listing shows a countdown and references ransom talks, but includes no sample files. NVIDIA has not publicly confirmed a breach, and there is no […]

The post The Gentlemen Ransomware Gang Allegedly Claims to Have Breached NVIDIA appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The Gentlemen ransomware gang listed NVIDIA on its dark web leak site on November 18, 2026, but the post does not prove that the group broke into the chipmaker’s systems.

The listing shows a countdown and references ransom talks, but includes no sample files. NVIDIA has not publicly confirmed a breach, and there is no verified evidence that the group stole data or encrypted company systems.

The screenshot shows NVIDIA’s logo, its NVDA stock ticker, and a revenue figure of $303 billion with no reporting period. It also shows the words “DATA INFO – SOON” and a reference to Tox, a messaging service.

The countdown reads 237 hours, 50 minutes and 39 seconds, or just under 10 days. It does not say what will happen when the timer reaches zero.

NVIDIA Ransomware Listing

The company details in the post are not evidence of access to an internal network. The image does not show which systems the gang claims to have reached, what files it claims to hold, or when any intrusion may have occurred. Without that evidence, it is not clear whether the claim concerns NVIDIA’s own systems, a third party, or neither.

The Gentlemen emerged in 2025 and operates as a ransomware-as-a-service group, meaning affiliates use the group’s tools to carry out attacks. As Cyber Security News previously reported in its profile of The Gentlemen, the group uses double extortion: stealing data and threatening to publish it while also locking files. That history does not establish that either happened at NVIDIA.

Previous Cyber Security News coverage of the gang’s attacks cited a Sophos review of 15 incidents. In some cases, attackers disabled endpoint security tools and backup services before encrypting systems less than 24 hours after gaining access. Those findings describe past attacks, not the NVIDIA claim. The leak post offers no technical evidence that the same methods were used here.

Ransomware tracker Breach House indexed the NVIDIA listing on November 18 and marked its leak status as pending. Its record documents when the claim appeared, not whether the gang accessed NVIDIA’s systems.

The listing also follows NVIDIA’s November 12 announcement that Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO after co-founder Jensen Huang resigned. No evidence links that leadership change to the ransomware claim.

A company disclosure or independently verified files could help establish whether data was taken and where it came from. Even a genuine sample would not, on its own, show how the data was obtained or whether ransomware ran on company systems. Until such evidence emerges, the countdown marks a deadline set by the gang, not proof of a breach.

articles.title: Chinese APT Hackers Target Global Banks to Steal Financial Intelligence and Spy on Microsoft 365 Accounts
articles.description:
Chinese state-linked hacking groups are going after banks around the world, and their goal is intelligence rather than cash. Several of these groups are also reading email in Microsoft 365 accounts, according to new infrastructure research. The shift matters because nation-state hackers have usually hit banks to steal money. In 2020, CISA described North Korea’s […]

The post Chinese APT Hackers Target Global Banks to Steal Financial Intelligence and Spy on Microsoft 365 Accounts appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Chinese state-linked hacking groups are going after banks around the world, and their goal is intelligence rather than cash.

Several of these groups are also reading email in Microsoft 365 accounts, according to new infrastructure research. The shift matters because nation-state hackers have usually hit banks to steal money.

In 2020, CISA described North Korea’s BeagleBoyz bank robbery scheme, which targeted ATMs and SWIFT terminals to fund the regime.

The Chinese groups now in focus want to watch the economy, not drain accounts. Analysts at Team Cymru identified and tracked the malware servers behind these operations.

Their report, published on November 17, 2026, builds on CrowdStrike’s 2026 Financial Services Threat Landscape report. Between January 1 and June 1, 2026, Team Cymru counted 64 ShadowPad command-and-control (C2) servers and 115 Vshell servers.

Chinese APT Hackers Target Global Banks

CrowdStrike names the Chinese groups with a “Panda” label. The report lists HOLLOW PANDA, VAULT PANDA, GENESIS PANDA, MURKY PANDA and VERTIGO PANDA. They focus mostly on the Americas, the Middle East and Southeast Asia.

HOLLOW PANDA was seen going after Check Point VPNs at financial firms in South America and Southeast Asia. It then installed ShadowPad, a modular backdoor shared among many China-linked actors.

Older reports show how this path works, including a Check Point VPN zero-day that was used to drop ShadowPad on victim networks.

GENESIS PANDA hit a financial institution in Southeast Asia and a fintech company in North America. It used Vshell, a remote access tool, and Fscan, a network scanner.

Team Cymru found one Vshell-tagged IP address with an open directory. Two files in it, named “fscan” and “vs”, turned out to be Fscan and Vshell programs.

MURKY PANDA takes a different route. CrowdStrike says it runs an Operational Relay Box (ORB) network to reach Microsoft 365 email accounts worldwide.

An ORB is a set of hacked devices that hides where the attacker’s traffic really comes from. Banks were among the sectors this group hit most often. Our earlier coverage of MURKY PANDA espionage activity shows it also targets government, legal and technology firms.

Microsoft 365 is a common goal for China-linked actors. Another recent report covers how China-linked hackers use ARTEX to try stolen credentials against more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants.

The research gives four reasons banks are valuable to spies:-

  • Central and commercial banks reveal trade volumes, currency moves and foreign investment, which helps in trade talks and economic planning.
  • Bank databases hold passport numbers, addresses, job history and debt details. These can be used to profile politicians, military leaders and dissidents.
  • A large regional bank can give a view into government networks, clearinghouses and multinational firms.
  • The focus on South and Southeast Asia fits China’s Belt and Road Initiative. Knowing a country’s debts and finances gives China leverage in deals.

Shared Tools Make Attribution Hard

Team Cymru did not link any of the servers it tracks to a specific Panda group. ShadowPad, Vshell and ORB networks are shared by many China-nexus actors, so the same infrastructure can serve several teams at once.

The servers match known ShadowPad and Vshell patterns, but a pattern match does not prove who runs them. This is why defenders should look at infrastructure as well as malware. Team Cymru uses NetFlow data, which records which systems talk to each other.

That data can show scanning and probing of a bank’s perimeter before a break-in happens. Teams can also watch for ShadowPad IIS listener module activity, which turns hacked servers into relay points.

Banks should patch VPN and edge devices quickly, turn on strong multifactor authentication for Microsoft 365, and review sign-in logs for logins from odd locations.

They should also block traffic to known C2 servers and check for open directories or scanning tools on their own systems. In July 2026, a project called ORBITAL was released to track and help disrupt ORB networks used by China-nexus groups.

articles.title: Hackers Impersonate Microsoft Exchange Online Alerts to Trick Users During Microsoft 365 Outage
articles.description:
Hackers used a real Microsoft 365 outage to send fake Exchange Online alerts claiming that four emails were being held and would be deleted unless recipients restored them. The messages borrowed a genuine Microsoft incident number and sent users through several redirects to a page that looked like Microsoft’s sign-in screen. The outage was real; […]

The post Hackers Impersonate Microsoft Exchange Online Alerts to Trick Users During Microsoft 365 Outage appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers used a real Microsoft 365 outage to send fake Exchange Online alerts claiming that four emails were being held and would be deleted unless recipients restored them.

The messages borrowed a genuine Microsoft incident number and sent users through several redirects to a page that looked like Microsoft’s sign-in screen. The outage was real; the request to recover mail was not.

The phishing emails began arriving on November 13, 2026, a day after Exchange Online users started having trouble accessing their mailboxes.

The disruption also affected Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and other cloud services. Microsoft’s preliminary outage incident report traced the disruption to an infrastructure failure.

The phishing operators took advantage of the confusion, but there is no evidence they caused the outage. Researchers Ernesto Fernández Provecho and Duy-Phuc Pham from Trellix identified the credential-phishing activity through the company’s SecondSight threat hunting service.

They counted 252 emails sent to more than 30 organizations across the United States, Europe, the Middle East and Asia-Pacific in about three and a half hours. Their report describes a web-based phishing campaign, not a confirmed malware infection.

Hackers Impersonate Microsoft Exchange Online Alerts

The emails copied the look of Microsoft service notices, using its logo, sender display names such as “Service Health,” and the real Exchange Online incident number, EX1550543.

As noted in Microsoft’s credential phishing warning, some messages told users they had 24 hours to recover their mail. That deadline gave employees who were already expecting delayed messages a reason to click before checking with IT.

Trellix tracked four waves between 17:04 and 20:38 UTC. The largest delivered 124 emails in 33 minutes. Most subjects paired “Outage” with a short code, while smaller waves used “Restore — 4 messages” or switched to a security checkup.

The messages came from three domains through SendGrid, a legitimate email delivery service. Some also carried an invisible image that let the sender track when recipients opened the email.

The recovery button led first to a tracking link unique to each recipient. From there, visitors passed through pages designed to show automated scanners harmless content while sending people onward.

A later page passed along the recipient’s email address so the final sign-in form arrived prefilled. That made the prompt look routine, even though the address bar showed a domain unrelated to Microsoft.

The final page used AiTM phishing, short for adversary-in-the-middle phishing. Instead of simply copying Microsoft’s login screen, the site relayed the live sign-in process.

This setup could capture both the password and the session issued after a user completed multifactor authentication, or MFA.

Earlier reporting on Microsoft 365 account hijacking shows why that session matters: someone who steals it may be able to reuse an already authenticated login. The reports do not establish that anyone’s account was taken over in this outage campaign.

Employees who receive an outage alert should verify it through their help desk or an administrator rather than use the email’s recovery button.

Security teams can look for “Outage” subjects alongside phrases such as “messages held after the outage” and check mail and click logs for affected users.

A click alone does not prove compromise. If a user entered credentials, responders should reset the password, revoke active sessions and review sign-in activity.

articles.description:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has warned that attackers are exploiting a critical vulnerability in Perforce Puppet Enterprise. The agency added CVE-2026-115731 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 17, 2026, citing evidence of active exploitation. The flaw lets an attacker run code on a vulnerable Puppet Server with the […]

The post CISA Warns of Puppet Enterprise Vulnerability Actively Exploited in Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has warned that attackers are exploiting a critical vulnerability in Perforce Puppet Enterprise.

The agency added CVE-2026-115731 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 17, 2026, citing evidence of active exploitation. The flaw lets an attacker run code on a vulnerable Puppet Server with the permissions of the Puppet service account.

Perforce disclosed the flaw on November 3 and assigned it a critical CVSS 4.0 score of 9.4. U.S. federal civilian agencies have until December 1 to address the vulnerability.

CISA’s alert does not name the attackers or say how many organizations were affected. For other organizations, confirmed exploitation is a reason to move Puppet Server updates ahead of routine maintenance.

Puppet Enterprise Flaw Actively Exploited

Puppet helps administrators keep software and system settings consistent across many machines. That makes the central server a sensitive point in the network: a change made there can reach managed systems during their regular Puppet runs. Cyber Security News’ coverage of system administration tools explains Puppet’s role in managing infrastructure through code.

The flaw is in the way Puppet Server reads reports sent by its agents. It involves unsafe deserialization, which happens when software rebuilds structured data from a report without safely checking what it contains.

In this case, a client with a certificate signed by the Puppet certificate authority can cause the server to run code. The code runs as the Puppet service user, not necessarily as root.

The certificate requirement offers less protection when Puppet automatically signs requests without strong checks. In that setup, an attacker who starts without credentials could obtain a trusted certificate.

If the server is compromised, its certificate-signing key and the settings it sends to managed systems could be at risk. That wider exposure is also why flaws in central management tools such as N-able N-central deserve fast attention.

The advisory lists three affected Puppet Enterprise branches. The 2023.8 branch is affected from 2023.8.0 up to, but not including, 2023.8.13. The 2025 branch is affected from 2025.0.0 up to, but not including, 2025.12.1. Version 2026.0.0 is also affected. The first fixed release in that branch is 2026.0.1. Administrators should check the installed version on each Puppet Server and upgrade to a fixed release.

If an update cannot be applied immediately, Red Hat recommends restricting network access to Puppet’s report service and avoiding automatic certificate signing unless requests are strongly verified. These steps reduce exposure but do not fix the flaw.

Security teams should also review certificate issuance records for unexpected enrollments and check host logs for unusual processes started by Puppet Server.

If those checks suggest a breach, investigate whether the signing key was accessed or managed configurations were changed. Installing the patch closes the flaw, but it does not undo changes an attacker may already have made.

The post CISA Warns of Puppet Enterprise Vulnerability Actively Exploited in Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.description:
Google began rolling out Chrome 158 to Windows, macOS, and Linux on November 17, 2026, with 204 security fixes. The desktop release notes list six critical memory bugs that could lead to code execution. However, Google did not spell out the impact of each flaw. The patched builds are 158.0.8127.36 for Linux and 158.0.8127.36 or […]

The post Chrome 158 Fixes 204 Vulnerabilities, Including Critical Code Execution Flaws appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Google began rolling out Chrome 158 to Windows, macOS, and Linux on November 17, 2026, with 204 security fixes. The desktop release notes list six critical memory bugs that could lead to code execution.

However, Google did not spell out the impact of each flaw. The patched builds are 158.0.8127.36 for Linux and 158.0.8127.36 or 158.0.8127.37 for Windows and macOS. Google said the update would reach users over the coming days and weeks.

Three critical flaws are use-after-free bugs. They affect WebView (CVE-2026-130963), garbage collection (CVE-2026-131008), and WebAudio (CVE-2026-130975).

A use-after-free happens when software keeps using memory after releasing it. That can crash a browser process or corrupt data. In some cases, this kind of memory error can let an attacker run code inside the affected process. That is not the same as gaining control of the entire device.

The other three critical flaws affect graphics and media processing. CVE-2026-131031 is an out-of-bounds write in the GPU component, while CVE-2026-131054 is the same type of bug in ANGLE, a graphics layer Chrome uses.

CVE-2026-131060 is a buffer overflow in Media. Both error types can cause Chrome to write beyond the memory set aside for data, potentially overwriting nearby information.

Google reported the WebView and ANGLE flaws. Xinyang Ge reported the other four critical issues, and Google credited Anthropic’s Claude with assisting on the GPU and Media reports.

Chrome 158 Fixes 204 Vulnerabilities

The release notes do not say whether any of the six were used in attacks or whether any could break out of Chrome’s sandbox, which limits what browser processes can access.

Critical Flaws :

The update fixes high-severity bugs in V8, Chrome’s JavaScript engine, as well as in Autofill, extensions, and downloads. Not all of the fixes address memory errors. Some correct permission checks were missing or applied incorrectly.

Google listed a $4,000 reward for Arni Hardarson of Neonix Security for reporting CVE-2026-130910, a high-severity failure in an ANGLE protection mechanism.

The release follows Chrome 157’s launch, which included 213 security fixes, and a separate November patch for a Chrome zero-day already used in attacks. Unlike that zero-day notice, Google’s Chrome 158 announcement does not flag active exploitation.

The company says it may restrict access to bug reports until most users have installed the fix, or keep reports closed longer if other projects still use an affected third-party library.

On Windows or macOS, open Chrome’s three-dot menu and go to Help, then About Google Chrome. The page checks for updates. When the download finishes, select Relaunch.

Linux users who installed Chrome through their distribution’s package manager should check for the update there, then restart the browser. After restarting, return to About Google Chrome and confirm that it shows the patched build for your platform or a newer version.

For IT teams, the rollout announcement is not proof that every managed device has installed the update. Check which Chrome version is running across the fleet, and follow up on devices that downloaded the patch but are still waiting for a browser restart.

Users who do not see Chrome 158 yet should check again as the rollout reaches their devices. The restart is what puts the new version into use.

articles.title: Hackers Hijack Old Bitly Links in Burger King, McDonald’s and Trump Posts to Redirect Users
articles.description:
Old Bitly links shared by Burger King, McDonald’s, and other prominent X accounts now redirect users to unrelated websites, videos, and offensive content, exposing long-standing social media posts to link hijacking. According to CNN’s reporting, affected posts dated from 2009 to 2014. At least a dozen Trump posts contained links that led somewhere other than […]

The post Hackers Hijack Old Bitly Links in Burger King, McDonald’s and Trump Posts to Redirect Users appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Old Bitly links shared by Burger King, McDonald’s, and other prominent X accounts now redirect users to unrelated websites, videos, and offensive content, exposing long-standing social media posts to link hijacking.

According to CNN’s reporting, affected posts dated from 2009 to 2014. At least a dozen Trump posts contained links that led somewhere other than their intended destination. Other affected accounts included Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the Department of Defense.

In a statement posted Sunday, Bitly said it had identified an issue that allowed bad actors to repurpose certain old, inactive links. The company said it suspended the accounts involved and was disabling affected URLs. At the same time, its Trust and Safety team worked to strengthen protections.

The available information does not establish that attackers accessed the affected X accounts. Instead, the reported changes involved where their shortened links sent visitors. This allowed old posts to carry unexpected content while still appearing under the names of public figures, companies and government agencies.

Hackers Hijack Old Bitly Links

Burger King told CNN it had no involvement in the redirects and was working to correct or delete affected posts. One restaurant location post from 2011 reportedly redirected to a Wikipedia list of Nazi concentration camps. Another was linked to a page about Adolf Hitler.

A McDonald’s post from 2011 redirected to information about the September 11 attacks. Trump’s affected links pointed to Geometry Dash, a baby image, and a Wikipedia page on the Epstein files. An FBI post about infected computers instead opened a seal image.

A shortened URL acts as an intermediate address, forwarding visitors to another webpage. That extra step means the address visible in an old post can remain unchanged even when its destination changes.

However, normal link expiry should not be treated as the confirmed cause. Bitly’s documentation says its links never expire. Deleted links should return a 404 error, while links hidden inside an account continue working. Bitly has not publicly explained the precise failure behind this incident.

The broader risk resembles earlier X advertising redirect abuse, where attackers changed shortened link destinations after advertisements displayed a trusted website name. That case involved a different method, but also exploited the gap between what users expected and where they landed.

Cyber Security News has also covered URL shorteners used in phishing campaigns, showing how redirect services can hide routes to credential theft and malware. Those outcomes have not been established in this incident.

Carnegie Mellon professor Ari Lightman warned that neglected social media posts create opportunities for misuse. He also raised concerns that AI could help attackers find old links at scale. The supplied reporting does not confirm that AI was used here.

For account owners, the practical lesson is to review links in older posts, not just secure current logins. Security teams should track final destinations and remove unsafe references.

Readers should check the destination before entering passwords, downloading files, or sharing payment details, even when a link appears in an authentic post from a familiar brand or public official.

articles.title: Anthropic Reduces Vulnerability Disclosure Deadline from 90 to 30 Days as AI Quickly Identifies Flaws
articles.description:
Anthropic is shrinking the time it gives software makers to fix serious security flaws before the details go public. The company says AI is now finding bugs so fast that the old 90-day window no longer makes sense. In an update to its coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) policy, Anthropic cut the deadline for high- and […]

The post Anthropic Reduces Vulnerability Disclosure Deadline from 90 to 30 Days as AI Quickly Identifies Flaws appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Anthropic is shrinking the time it gives software makers to fix serious security flaws before the details go public. The company says AI is now finding bugs so fast that the old 90-day window no longer makes sense.

In an update to its coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) policy, Anthropic cut the deadline for high- and critical-severity issues from 90 days to 30 days. All other issues now get 45 days.

The new timelines apply to reports sent to vendors and maintainers on or after January 1, 2027. Reports already in progress on that date keep their current deadlines.

Anthropic will shorten vulnerability coordination from 30 to 15 days and publish full technical details 30 days after patches, down from 45, while keeping the rest of its policy unchanged.

Some older reports are affected too. Anthropic says several high and critical findings reported more than 90 days ago have passed the current deadline and are still private.

Maintainers of those projects have 30 more days. After that, Anthropic will publish the reports on its dashboard, in line with the new policy starting January 1, 2027.

Anthropic Cuts Critical Vulnerability Disclosure Deadline

Anthropic says existing vulnerability disclosure rules are outdated because they predate AI-driven bug discovery and assume human-speed fixes and fewer duplicate findings.

The company says neither idea holds up today. Models can now help write fixes, and a bug one model finds is more likely to be found by another.

Anthropic says it is already seeing more cases of the same flaw being found twice. That raises the risk that a bug kept private for three months is already known to someone else.

The scale backs this up. The dashboard shows 5,087 vulnerabilities disclosed across 680 open-source projects as of November 2, 2026. Only 629 of them are known to be patched.

Anthropic also notes that human review is the slowest step. Its models found more than 29,000 candidate flaws, but only about 6,000 have been manually reviewed.

Security teams have seen this pace before. Cyber Security News reported that Claude Mythos Preview found 271 zero-day flaws in Firefox, all fixed in a single release. Mozilla later said it patched 423 Firefox security bugs in April 2026 alone.

Anthropic admits some bugs cannot be fixed in 30 or 45 days. Software that is hard to deploy, such as systems used in critical infrastructure, is one example.

Flaws that need a change to a specification or RFC are another. In those cases, Anthropic says it will agree on a fix timeline with the vendor. The seven-day window for bugs under active attack stays the same.

The update also does not cover AI findings without human review. That includes results from OSS Scanner, the free opt-in service Cyber Security News covered in its report on the new Anthropic OSS Scanner tool.

Anthropic knows the shorter clock adds pressure on small teams. It says each report will include clear steps, plus a patch or workaround when possible. It will also agree on a steady pace with maintainers before sending a large batch to one project.

Support programs are available as well. Critical open-source projects can apply to OSS Scanner at no cost. Eligible maintainers can get six months of Claude Ultra through the Claude for Open Source Program. Security professionals can join the Cyber Verification Program, which adjusts Claude’s safeguards for defensive work.

Teams that depend on open-source software should plan for faster public details and shorter patch windows. Track the dashboard, keep an up-to-date list of the components you use, and be ready to apply fixes within weeks, not months.

articles.title: Tails Released Emergency Tor Browser Update to fix uBlock Origin Flaw
articles.description:
The Tor Project released Tails 7.17.1 on November 17, 2026, to fix a critical security flaw in uBlock Origin, the ad blocker bundled with Tor Browser in Tails. The emergency update temporarily removes the extension. A malicious website could trick a visitor into clicking once and then run its own code on another site the […]

The post Tails Released Emergency Tor Browser Update to fix uBlock Origin Flaw appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The Tor Project released Tails 7.17.1 on November 17, 2026, to fix a critical security flaw in uBlock Origin, the ad blocker bundled with Tor Browser in Tails.

The emergency update temporarily removes the extension. A malicious website could trick a visitor into clicking once and then run its own code on another site the visitor opens. The Tails team said it was not aware of any attacks using the flaw when it announced the update.

The official release notes say the flaw affects the Standard and Safer security levels in Tor Browser. The Safest level is not affected. Tails plans to restore uBlock Origin as soon as possible but did not give a date. Users do not need to wait for the extension to return before upgrading.

The bug is a one-click universal cross-site scripting flaw, often shortened to universal XSS. In a typical cross-site scripting attack, unsafe code runs on a site with its own flaw. Here, the weak point was the browser extension. That meant the targeted site did not need its own cross-site scripting bug.

Tails Fixes uBlock Origin Flaw

The issue involved uBlock Origin’s element picker, a feature that lets people choose parts of a page to hide. The flaw let a malicious site make the extension save a rule it shouldn’t have accepted.

That rule could then make the browser run JavaScript, the code that controls many parts of a web page, on another site. For example, a person could click on a malicious page and later open webmail. Code running in the webmail page could read information visible there or change what the person sees.

The flaw differs from the website-level problems covered in our reporting on Firefox’s built-in XSS protection. In this case, the extension crossed the boundary that normally keeps one website’s code away from another.

Restarting Tails clears any malicious uBlock Origin settings left by the attack. However, it cannot undo data theft that may already have happened. A restart is not a substitute for the update.

Users running Tails 7.0 or later can upgrade automatically to 7.17.1. Start Tails from your existing USB stick, connect to Tor, and follow the upgrade prompt. If the automatic upgrade fails or the USB stick no longer starts afterward, use the official manual upgrade guide.

Both upgrade methods preserve Persistent Storage, the space on the USB stick where Tails keeps files and settings you choose to save between sessions.

For a new USB stick, follow the Tails installation guide. Do not choose a fresh install on an existing Tails USB stick if you want to keep its saved data. Installing instead of upgrading erases Persistent Storage on that stick. Tails also offers a USB image for flash drives and an ISO image for DVDs and virtual machines.

The update also moves the Linux kernel to version 6.12.117. It refreshes firmware for newer hardware, including graphics cards and Wi-Fi adapters. That follows earlier work on wireless hardware support covered in our Tails 6.13 release report. The immediate reason to upgrade, however, is to remove the vulnerable extension from Tor Browser.

articles.title: Atlassian Patches 318 Security Vulnerabilities Across Jira, Confluence, Bitbucket and Other Products
articles.description:
Atlassian’s November 2026 security bulletin lists fixes for 318 vulnerability entries across Jira Software, Jira Service Management, Confluence, Bitbucket, Bamboo, Crowd, Fisheye and Crucible. Published on November 17, the bulletin covers fixes shipped in product releases over the previous month. Atlassian counted 266 high-severity entries and 52 critical entries involving third-party components. Some CVE identifiers […]

The post Atlassian Patches 318 Security Vulnerabilities Across Jira, Confluence, Bitbucket and Other Products appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Atlassian’s November 2026 security bulletin lists fixes for 318 vulnerability entries across Jira Software, Jira Service Management, Confluence, Bitbucket, Bamboo, Crowd, Fisheye and Crucible.

Published on November 17, the bulletin covers fixes shipped in product releases over the previous month. Atlassian counted 266 high-severity entries and 52 critical entries involving third-party components.

Some CVE identifiers appear under more than one product, so the total does not represent 318 distinct flaws or mean every installation is affected by all of them.

The November total rose from 176 entries in October’s Atlassian security update, which listed 162 high-severity entries and 14 critical third-party entries. Atlassian says the critical scores describe flaws in components made by other developers.

The company assessed the risk as lower and non-critical based on how its own products use those components. It publishes separate advisories when a flaw poses an immediate critical risk to customers.

The Confluence Data Center fixes include CVE-2026-4800, a remote code execution flaw in the Lodash JavaScript library with a severity score of 9.8 out of 10.

Atlassian Patches 318 Security Vulnerabilities

Remote code execution means an attacker could run code on a vulnerable system under the flaw’s conditions. Atlassian also addressed CVE-2026-21605, an 8.7-rated path traversal flaw in Confluence that can allow access to files outside their intended location.

The Jira Software Data Center fixes include three path traversal flaws rated 8.7 and two stored cross-site scripting flaws. Stored cross-site scripting can cause a browser to run malicious code when a user views affected content.

The Bitbucket bulletin also lists denial-of-service flaws in Netty and Bouncy Castle that can disrupt service, along with a certificate issue affecting Docker images that appears under several Atlassian products.

For Jira Software Data Center, Atlassian recommends 11.3.13 or 10.3.27, both long-term support (LTS) releases. Jira Service Management Data Center also lists both builds, with 11.3.13 recommended.

The company recommends Confluence Data Center 10.2.20 LTS, Bitbucket Data Center 10.2.9 LTS, Bamboo Data Center 12.1.13 LTS, Crowd Data Center 7.2.6, and Fisheye or Crucible 4.9.16.

Administrators should check the November security bulletin and current release notes before choosing a build, especially if they run an older branch or a Server edition.

Confluence teams on the 9.2 LTS branch should pay particular attention to the version number. The monthly bulletin lists both 9.2.27 and 9.2.28, but Atlassian’s separate critical advisory identifies 9.2.28 as the fix for CVE-2026-90436.

That flaw affects older Confluence Data Center installations with the legacy Remote API enabled. Confluence 10.x and later and Atlassian Cloud are not affected by that separate issue. Cyber Security News previously reported on active exploitation of the Confluence flaw.

For teams managing several Atlassian products, the first step is to record each installation’s edition and version. Match each one against the bulletin and check the separate advisories before scheduling upgrades. If a release branch has no listed fix, Atlassian recommends moving to a current supported release rather than assuming the installed version is safe.

articles.title: Researchers Break AMD SEV-SNP Security to Read Encrypted Virtual Machine Memory Using a GPU
articles.description:
An attack called Mior uses a graphics card to bypass AMD SEV-SNP, allowing access to confidential virtual machine memory, modification of guest memory, and making altered VMs appear to run trusted software. Tracked as CVE-2026-0462, the flaw carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 5.9. AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization with Secure Nested Paging, or SEV-SNP, is […]

The post Researchers Break AMD SEV-SNP Security to Read Encrypted Virtual Machine Memory Using a GPU appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
An attack called Mior uses a graphics card to bypass AMD SEV-SNP, allowing access to confidential virtual machine memory, modification of guest memory, and making altered VMs appear to run trusted software. Tracked as CVE-2026-0462, the flaw carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 5.9.

AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization with Secure Nested Paging, or SEV-SNP, is designed to protect data while a virtual machine is running. It encrypts each guest’s memory and uses hardware checks to prevent the hypervisor from accessing it.

This software runs virtual machines and prevents the hypervisor from reading or changing protected pages. That separation matters in the cloud because the provider controls the host, while the customer may be processing data the provider should never see.

The GPU did not crack the encryption or recover the key. Instead, the researchers showed that a malicious host could interfere with setting up the Reverse Map Table, which records who owns each memory page and who can access it.

In the lab, some of the AMD Platform Security Processor’s setup writes reached graphics card memory instead of system memory. That left holes in the table’s protection, undermining the checks that keep the host away from guest data.

AMD SEV-SNP GPU Attack

The ACM research paper shows that the Mior attack gained read and write access to a production-style guest VM with debugging disabled.

The attack also allowed a modified VM to spoof a legitimate guest’s launch measurement, potentially undermining attestation checks used to verify VM trustworthiness before handling sensitive data.

The team demonstrated Mior on a Zen 5 AMD EPYC 9135 server. The setup required control of the hypervisor and system firmware, along with access to a PCIe device such as a graphics card.

This was not a remote break-in by an ordinary cloud customer. It tested what a highly privileged host could do to a guest that SEV-SNP was built to protect.

Mior follows earlier findings covered by Cyber Security News. RMPocalypse also exposed a weakness in how the Reverse Map Table is set up.

At the same time, BadRAM exploited how AMD systems interpreted information from memory modules. Mior shows that the route a security processor’s writes take can matter just as much as the checks it performs.

In its November 10 security bulletin, AMD lists SEV-SNP as affected, but not the older SEV or SEV-ES modes. It lists SEV firmware fixes dated August 12, 2026, for EPYC 7003, 8004, 8005, 9004 and 9005 server processors.

AMD targets December 2026 for the related platform firmware releases to server makers. Several embedded EPYC models have separate target dates in 2027.

Server operators should check with their hardware vendor for the BIOS update that matches their model. Cloud customers should ask whether the fix is active on the hosts that run their workloads and check attestation reports against the values AMD lists for the updated firmware.

A guest operating system update alone cannot address a flaw in host firmware. The key question is not whether a patch exists, but whether the host running the workload has received it.

articles.title: 4-Year-Old NVIDIA Linux GPU Flaw Lets Users Hijack Entire Shared Servers
articles.description:
A four-year-old NVIDIA Linux GPU driver flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-47501 and dubbed ForgePtr, could let users with access to a vulnerable GPU take control of the entire server. The flaw allowed Stealthium researchers to gain root, the highest level of access on Linux, from inside an unprivileged container. The finding puts shared GPU servers used […]

The post 4-Year-Old NVIDIA Linux GPU Flaw Lets Users Hijack Entire Shared Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A four-year-old NVIDIA Linux GPU driver flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-47501 and dubbed ForgePtr, could let users with access to a vulnerable GPU take control of the entire server.

The flaw allowed Stealthium researchers to gain root, the highest level of access on Linux, from inside an unprivileged container. The finding puts shared GPU servers used for AI training and inference at particular risk.

Stealthium senior security researcher Branislav Brzak traced ForgePtr to version 515.43.04, the first public release of NVIDIA’s open GPU kernel modules in May 2022. The team found the flaw in source through version 610.57.04 and confirmed root access in tests on that release and 610.43.02.

NVIDIA shipped the fix in 615.71.09 on September 9, 2026, and disclosed the flaw on September 30. Stealthium published its findings on November 12 without releasing proof-of-concept code.

The flaw starts with a missing error check when the driver sets up an event buffer. If the driver fails to turn a supplied reference into a valid memory address, it does not stop. The result is an out-of-bounds write, meaning the driver can change kernel memory outside the area it should use.

The researchers’ full demonstration also relied on a separate leak to locate live kernel addresses. The attack requires local access to the affected driver. However, the team did not need an administrator account or a privileged container.

That local access is what makes ForgePtr dangerous for GPU rental providers. A tenant may be allowed to run code inside a container and use the GPU without being trusted to manage the server.

4-Year-Old NVIDIA Linux GPU Vulnerability

Stealthium showed that ForgePtr could turn that limited access into root on the host. A compromised host could expose other tenants’ model weights, job data, and credentials. NVIDIA rated the flaw 7.8 out of 10, but Stealthium recommends treating it as critical on shared GPU nodes.

In testing, researchers also loaded an unsigned kernel module on a machine running Secure Boot. They did not break the signed boot chain.

Instead, they changed the running kernel’s security state, weakening the checks that normally block unsigned modules. Hardware controls that limit where the GPU can access memory did not stop the attack because the kernel itself performed the write.

For the Linux display driver, administrators should move to 615.71.09 or a later release that includes the fix. Operators using NVIDIA vGPU should check the advisory for their specific product and branch rather than assume the display driver version applies.

Until affected hosts are patched, Stealthium recommends withholding GPU device access from untrusted tenants and containers. Tightening container settings does not repair the driver.

Security teams should investigate unexpected changes to host-wide crash handling, kernel lockdown, or module-signature enforcement, especially when they can tie the changes to a container workload.

A process crash alone is not evidence of exploitation. Stealthium says its demonstration used ordinary-looking driver activity, so the surrounding host events matter more than the crash itself.

Unlike the earlier NVIDIAScape container escape and CVE-2025-23359, ForgePtr is a driver flaw, not a Container Toolkit flaw. Updating the toolkit alone leaves the vulnerable host driver in place.
