articles.title: Hackers Target US Trucking Companies With Fake Freight Portals to Steal Credentials and Deploy Malware
articles.description:
Hackers are targeting US trucking companies with fake freight portals, bogus carrier verification notices, and phony broker paperwork. Some sites collect fleet fuel card passwords and one-time codes. Others disguise malware as routine downloads, turning what appears to be a load confirmation or a terms update into a way to gain remote access to a […]

The post Hackers Target US Trucking Companies With Fake Freight Portals to Steal Credentials and Deploy Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are targeting US trucking companies with fake freight portals, bogus carrier verification notices, and phony broker paperwork. Some sites collect fleet fuel card passwords and one-time codes.

Others disguise malware as routine downloads, turning what appears to be a load confirmation or a terms update into a way to gain remote access to a Windows workstation.

The campaigns target different people in the same business. A carrier owner might receive a warning that their operating status needs attention, while a dispatcher might be asked to review an insurance claim.

Someone booking a load could land on a site that looks like DAT or TIMOCOM. Earlier reporting on the Diesel Vortex campaign showed how freight and fuel payment accounts had already become valuable targets for credential thieves.

Researchers at ANY.RUN identified malware and credential theft across three distinct campaigns in a November 17, 2026, report. HelloFriends focused on stealing personal information and fuel account credentials.

NodeRemote used broker paperwork to deliver a persistent backdoor. The campaign called Fake Freight Portals used lookalike load boards to install remote administration software and, in one observed case, deploy CastleRAT.

Hackers Target US Trucking Companies With Fake Freight Portals

Fake Freight Portals, observed since December 2025, targeted workers who book and confirm loads. In May 2026, freight-themed downloads installed the legitimate NetSupport Manager client.

By October, researchers had seen a fake terms update lead to a remote WebDAV share, which lets Windows access files hosted on a server. The supposed PDF was a Windows shortcut that launched an executable and installed MeshCentral, another legitimate remote administration tool.

The operator used that connection to retrieve a BitLocker recovery password, add Microsoft Defender exclusions, and deploy CastleRAT, a remote access Trojan also known as NightshadeC2.

Researchers did not observe encryption. Earlier reporting on remote access tool abuse documented how similar software gave criminals access to freight operations in a separate investigation.

The presence of MeshCentral alone does not establish a compromise; where it came from and what happened after installation matter more.

HelloFriends took a different route. A fake Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration email used the recipient’s real USDOT number, and cloned SAFER or Motus portals made carrier verification appear urgent.

The sites requested Social Security numbers, business tax IDs, and a supposed $300 administrative fee. Fake fuel provider pages then asked for passwords and one-time codes.

C2 Infrastructure and Privilege Escalation

ANY.RUN associated about 1,430 domains with HelloFriends in 2026, a count of infrastructure rather than confirmed victims. NodeRemote went after dispatch personnel with fake onboarding pages, bills of lading, and insurance claims.

One page used fake CAPTCHA verification prompts to trick workers into running a Windows command. Other variants used script files or a Windows installer.

Once installed, the Node.js backdoor used scheduled tasks to maintain access, potentially exposing broker portals, load boards, and email sessions already open on a dispatch computer.

For trucking companies, the clearest rule is to open carrier and freight portals from saved bookmarks rather than from links in unexpected messages. Verify changed terms or paperwork with the broker using a number already on file.

Security teams should investigate unfamiliar remote access agents alongside Defender changes, BitLocker recovery activity, or new scheduled tasks. Proofpoint’s separate cargo theft research also recommends restricting remote management software to tools approved by IT.

Indicators of compromise (IoCs):-

Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.]) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM.

articles.title: Hackers Impersonate Major Defense Companies to Spread GravityRAT Spyware and Steal Sensitive Data
articles.description:
Hackers are using the logos of major defense and aerospace companies on a fake recruitment website to spread GravityRAT spyware. The site promises connections to overseas employers and offers an Android résumé builder that can steal text messages, location data, and files. Lockheed Martin, Airbus, and BAE Systems are among the brands displayed as supposed […]

The post Hackers Impersonate Major Defense Companies to Spread GravityRAT Spyware and Steal Sensitive Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are using the logos of major defense and aerospace companies on a fake recruitment website to spread GravityRAT spyware.

The site promises connections to overseas employers and offers an Android résumé builder that can steal text messages, location data, and files.

Lockheed Martin, Airbus, and BAE Systems are among the brands displayed as supposed clients. Their logos are part of the lure, not evidence that the companies were breached or involved.

The campaign appears to focus on people in India seeking jobs with foreign defense contractors. Mobile security data showed GravityRAT detections on 14 devices in India over a 12-month period.

That figure reflects what researchers could see, not the total number of infections. Defense and military personnel in other countries may also be targets, but the public report did not confirm infections outside India.

Researchers from Lookout identified the active campaign and detailed their findings in a November 12 threat report. They traced GravityRAT back to at least 2015 and linked it to Pakistan-aligned threat actors tracked as SpaceCobra and Cosmic Leopard.

The spyware began as a Windows tool before expanding to Android and macOS, an evolution covered in our earlier reporting on GravityRAT’s cross-platform expansion as researchers uncovered versions targeting more devices.

Hackers Impersonate Major Defense Companies to Spread GravityRAT Spyware

The site calls itself “Global Recruiter” and offers automated résumé tools alongside promises of job connections. Its “Our Clients” section displays nine company logos, including those of Thales, Rheinmetall, Northrop Grumman, Saab, Rolls-Royce, and Safran.

The use of a fake defense recruitment portal echoes a separate Nimbus Manticore campaign that targeted aerospace and defense professionals. Here, the download is GlobalRecruiters.apk, an Android app with the package name com.resumee.resumebuilder.

The Google Play button does not open the official store. Instead, a pop-up claims the app is under review and asks visitors to download the Android package directly.

The message makes sideloading, or installing an app outside the store, sound like a temporary workaround. Researchers found no evidence that the apps they analyzed were distributed through Google Play.

Similar fake Play Store prompts have been used in other Android spyware campaigns, though GravityRAT’s operators framed the download as part of a job search rather than a software update.

The researchers also found a related Windows lure called DropDeckX by examining domains that shared registration dates and name servers with the mobile campaign.

DropDeckX was advertised as a cloud storage utility, but the analyzed sample could collect credentials and system information, stay on the device through Windows Task Scheduler, and download additional malware.

Lookout said similar variants have been tracked as HeavyLift. The finding shows the operation was not limited to Android downloads.

What GravityRAT Steals and How to Spot It

GravityRAT can upload collected data to servers controlled by its operators at intervals ranging from one to 30 minutes. It can collect contacts, incoming and outgoing call logs, missed calls, past and current SMS messages, and GPS coordinates.

It can also take documents, photos, audio files, Wi-Fi network details, device account information, and the phone’s IMEI, a hardware identifier. That combination can reveal who a target communicates with, where they go, and what they keep on their phone.

Earlier reporting on GravityRAT’s WhatsApp backup theft documented a capability that persists in this campaign. Lookout found that the spyware targets encrypted backup files with extensions including .crypt12, .crypt13, .crypt14, .crypt18, and .crypt32.

Copying an encrypted backup is not the same as decrypting it. The public report identifies the files GravityRAT can collect, but does not establish that the operators could read the contents of stolen backups.

Job seekers should verify vacancies through the employer’s official careers page and treat requests to install a résumé or interview app outside an official store as a warning sign. Defense organizations can use the indicators below to check app inventories, endpoint records, and network logs.

An installed package or a matching file hash is a stronger lead than a DNS lookup alone, which does not show that someone installed the app. Anyone who installed the fake recruiter app on a device used for work should report it promptly to their security team.

articles.title: Japan Shuts Down Fugaku Supercomputer After Hackers Breach Internal Servers
articles.description:
Japan’s RIKEN research institute suspended operations of its Fugaku supercomputer on November 14, 2026, after an intruder breached the system’s internal operations network and installed malicious software on some servers. The breach may have exposed account information for up to 4,597 users across Fugaku and RIKYU. RIKEN also confirmed that the intruder used some stolen […]

The post Japan Shuts Down Fugaku Supercomputer After Hackers Breach Internal Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Japan’s RIKEN research institute suspended operations of its Fugaku supercomputer on November 14, 2026, after an intruder breached the system’s internal operations network and installed malicious software on some servers.

The breach may have exposed account information for up to 4,597 users across Fugaku and RIKYU. RIKEN also confirmed that the intruder used some stolen credentials to try to connect to other systems. Investigators have not determined whether those attempts caused further damage.

RIKEN traced the intrusion to a public dashboard that showed Fugaku’s operating status. The intruder used the page as a starting point to reach the internal network between November 10 and 13.

RIKEN confirmed that multiple internal servers were tampered with, but it has not disclosed exactly how the intruder got in. Suspicious network traffic on November 12 prompted RIKEN to investigate with the contractor that maintains the affected system.

Investigators confirmed the breach at 4:33 p.m. on November 13 and isolated the system used in the intrusion at 10:07 p.m. that night. RIKEN suspended Fugaku operations and blocked external access at 4:30 a.m. the next morning, then replaced its administrative keys that evening.

Japan Shuts Down Fugaku Supercomputer

According to RIKEN’s original Japanese notice, the account records at risk included names, email addresses and user IDs for up to 4,222 Fugaku users, plus names and email addresses for up to 375 RIKYU users.

The total is an upper limit, not a confirmed count of people whose data was taken. RIKEN described the intrusion as a breach of Fugaku’s operations network, not a separate break-in at RIKYU.

The inquiry also covers files in users’ home directories, including SSH private keys and other access keys used to connect to supercomputers and services outside RIKEN.

The institute said it had no concrete evidence that research data was taken. It is still checking whether the files under review contain personal information about other people.

The risk does not end when Fugaku goes offline. A stolen SSH private key can remain useful wherever the matching public key is still trusted.

Cyber Security News covered a similar risk in separate reports on the Barracuda cloud account breach and the Cursor data breach, where exposed credentials gave attackers access beyond the original point of compromise.

RIKEN stopped all running and queued computing jobs when it emailed users at 4:18 p.m. on November 15. It also turned off all users’ public login keys for Fugaku.

In its English notice, the institute asked anyone who stored an SSH private key on Fugaku to remove the matching public key from every external service that accepts it and generate a new key pair. Users should also revoke and replace other credentials stored on Fugaku through the services that issued them.

RIKEN warned users to watch for phishing emails that pretend to come from Fugaku or the institute. It said it would never ask for passwords or other personal information by email.

RIKEN notified Japan’s education and science ministry and its personal information regulator. The institute did not give a restart date in its notice. It said Fugaku would resume operations after it fixes software weaknesses, rebuilds compromised servers, reviews the network setup, and adds security measures that use AI.

articles.title: Hackers Use Stolen FortiGate VPN Credentials to Access Corporate Networks and Deploy Custom Malware
articles.description:
A threat actor known as “tcherber” is selling and using stolen FortiGate VPN logins to get into company networks. The same person also builds custom malware, including a stealer, a remote desktop tool, and ransomware. The campaign shows how one weak VPN password can open the way to data theft and file encryption. The actor […]

The post Hackers Use Stolen FortiGate VPN Credentials to Access Corporate Networks and Deploy Custom Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A threat actor known as “tcherber” is selling and using stolen FortiGate VPN logins to get into company networks. The same person also builds custom malware, including a stealer, a remote desktop tool, and ransomware.

The campaign shows how one weak VPN password can open the way to data theft and file encryption. The actor does not need a new Fortinet bug. Many of the logins come from guessing weak passwords, using default ones such as guest/guest and admin/admin, or reusing leaked ones.

This is the same pattern seen in the FortiBleed credential campaign that hit Fortinet devices worldwide earlier this year.

Researchers at Cyderes studied the operation and traced it back to one build path in the malware. Analysts at the firm’s Howler Cell team noted that a Rust binary leaked the folder name “/home/tcherber”.

That clue linked the malware to a Go-based VPN toolkit, a ransomware strain, and a live control panel. Their full technical report covers the findings in detail.

Hackers Use Stolen FortiGate VPN Credentials

Cyderes found a database holding more than 500 FortiGate VPN credentials from many countries. Logs showed the actor connecting with full root-level tunnels into several victim networks during May and June 2026. Some sessions lasted for hours.

The toolkit is written in Go and works mostly on its own. It connects to the VPN, waits about 20 seconds for the tunnel to settle, and then maps the internal routes.

Next it queries Active Directory over LDAP and writes the results into report files. Other modules scan ports, list SMB shares, and test which logins work on Windows machines. The toolkit also has a SonicWall module. Its comments and messages are in Russian.

The actor also advertises on a forum called rehubcom.pro. The posts offer access to FortiGate and other appliances, plus custom loader builds.

The seller skips targets in CIS countries and sorts victims by company revenue. This points to a business that sells access to other criminals. It is similar to the access-broker behavior seen in FortiGate attacks on edge devices, where stolen logins were sold and reused.

Once inside, the actor can use the VPN to reach the internal network like a normal employee. Stolen passwords are hard to spot in logs because the logins look valid. That is why a leaked VPN password can be worse than an unpatched bug.

Custom Malware: Fake Windows Update, Rust Loader, and Enigma Ransomware

The malware chain starts with a file named setup.exe that pretends to be a Windows Update installer. It shows a short “Installing… Please wait” window while it quietly drops a PowerShell script.

The script adds the C: drive to the Defender exclusion list. It then downloads a file called loader.cer and decodes it with certutil. A similar certutil trick appeared in a BlankGrabber stealer chain earlier this year.

The decoded file is a Rust loader. It checks for sandboxes by looking at memory size, disk size, usernames, and tools such as Wireshark and x64dbg.

If the checks pass, it downloads two more payloads. The first is a stealer that takes browser passwords, cookies, wallets, FTP and email data, and files from the Desktop and Documents folders. It sends a ZIP file to the attacker over HTTP and through a Telegram bot.

The second payload is an HVNC implant. HVNC opens a hidden desktop, so the attacker can use the victim’s logged-in browser without the user seeing anything.

The implant uses AES-256-GCM encryption for its traffic. It also patches AMSI and ETW, which weakens Windows scanning and logging. It can bypass UAC and set up persistence.

The same developer built Enigma ransomware. It deletes shadow copies and turns off recovery. It also clears event logs, stops Hyper-V machines, and kills 125 processes, including database and backup software.

Files are encrypted with ChaCha12 and get the .ENIGMA extension. Ransom notes are named README_ENIGMA.txt and list the contact Enigma1@aol.com. Cyderes found no data upload feature in the ransomware.

Cyderes also found an open control panel at 158.94.209.138 with 178 active bots. It showed builds dated September 2026, so the infrastructure was still active. Groups such as The Gentlemen ransomware crew also use Fortinet VPNs as their main way in.

Reset all FortiGate and SonicWall VPN passwords. Turn on multi-factor authentication for every remote user. Remove default accounts and review VPN logs for long or odd sessions. Block the IPs below and hunt for the file names and registry values listed in the report.

Look for a Run key named “SecurityHealth” and scheduled tasks named “S0”, “MU”, “Upd”, and “WindowsUpdate”.

articles.title: Hackers Hijack AI Coding Agents Through Malicious GitHub Repositories to Steal Developer Credentials
articles.description:
Hackers are planting poisoned files in GitHub repositories to make AI coding assistants run hidden malware. The malware steals developer credentials, and it also uses them to spread to other projects. The campaign targets tools such as Claude Code and Cursor, and 22 malicious GitHub links have been found so far. The trick is simple. […]

The post Hackers Hijack AI Coding Agents Through Malicious GitHub Repositories to Steal Developer Credentials appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are planting poisoned files in GitHub repositories to make AI coding assistants run hidden malware. The malware steals developer credentials, and it also uses them to spread to other projects.

The campaign targets tools such as Claude Code and Cursor, and 22 malicious GitHub links have been found so far. The trick is simple. Files that AI tools read to understand a project now carry secret orders.

Once a developer opens the repository, the assistant may run a script without any warning. That script runs with the developer’s own access and permissions.

Analysts at Bitdefender Labs identified the malware, and thge researcher Andrei Anton-Aanei found the 22 malicious links and mapped how they work. The team says the campaign abuses the files, rules, hooks and settings that AI coding tools use to automate work.

Hackers Hijack AI Coding Agents Through Malicious GitHub Repositories

Many projects include files such as AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md. These notes tell an AI assistant how to run tests or follow coding rules. In this campaign, the same files carry a different message. They tell the assistant to run a file named setup.js.

The text is written to sound official. It calls the script a “sealed binary artifact” that has been cryptographically signed. It tells the assistant not to read or show the contents, to run it at session start, and to hide the output.

If a user asks for help before setup has run, the assistant is told to run node scripts/setup.js without asking. This language is meant to make a risky step feel routine.

This is a form of indirect prompt injection attack, where harmful instructions sit in content the AI reads instead of in what the user types. Researchers have already shown that a clean-looking repository can push an agent into opening a reverse shell.

There is also a second path that needs no AI prompt at all. Bitdefender found settings files, such as .claude/settings.json, that use session-start hooks.

Once a developer trusts the repository, the hook can run a command in the user’s shell. The configuration file does the work, and the AI never has to follow an instruction.

The setup.js file is a multi-stage loader built to hide its purpose. The outer file is a 3.75 MB single-line script. It decodes a large hex value, applies ROT13 and runs the result.

That reveals a Node.js stager with two AES-128-GCM encrypted blobs. One blob unpacks into a 4.67 MB bundle. The stager then downloads or finds the Bun runtime and passes the bundle to it.

The final payload goes after credentials. It targets CI/CD systems and GitHub Actions, cloud platforms, package registries, browser-stored logins and password managers.

It also takes Windows Credential Manager data, SSH keys, .env files, API keys and source-control tokens. It can check whether stolen tokens still work, then encrypt and batch the data. Extra modules sit in a compressed _bz field in package.json.

Self-Spreading Through Stolen Tokens and Agent Settings

This is more than a password stealer, because it is built to spread. After it runs, it searches the victim’s home folder for AI agent settings, such as mcp.json, .cursorrules, .windsurfrules and .github/copilot-instructions.md.

It keeps results that match 14 agent names: Claude, Codex, Gemini, Copilot, Kiro, OpenCode, Cline, Aider, Tabby, Amazon Q, Cody, Bolt, Continue and Cursor. It then adds its own instructions, hooks or MCP server settings to those files.

The spread also reaches other repositories. The malware checks stolen GitHub and GitLab tokens for account details, repositories, scopes and push rights.

For GitHub it looks for the repo, public_repo and workflow scopes. By default it is capped at 25 target repositories through a MAX_TARGET_REPOS setting. For each target it can inspect up to 50 branches and skip automated ones, such as dependabot/ and copilot/.

If the account has enough rights, it commits files that trigger AI tools, including AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .mcp.json and .vscode/tasks.json.

It can also edit package data and workflows. It may try to republish infected packages through npm, PyPI, RubyGems and JFrog. The pattern echoes the Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm, which also searched for Claude Code settings and VS Code task files.

A recent case of 4,837 hijacked GitHub accounts shows how fast stolen tokens can reach tens of thousands of repositories.

Developers should review unfamiliar repositories before opening them in an AI-enabled editor. Check AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and the .claude/, .cursor/ and .gemini/ folders.

Look at MCP server definitions, session-start hooks, VS Code tasks and unknown setup scripts. Treat any text that says not to inspect a file, hides output or skips confirmation as a warning sign. Earlier research on a Claude Code deny-rule bypass showed that a CLAUDE.md file alone can be enough to cause harm.

Bitdefender says its AI Guardian tool inspects instruction files such as CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md before the agent acts. In internal tests on November 10, it detected all 22 samples.

The company notes that new variants may give different results. If a system ran any of these files, rotate every token, key and cloud secret that the machine could reach.

articles.title: Google Reveals How Russian Hackers Used One Cloud Breach to Compromise Another US Organization
articles.description:
Russian state-sponsored hackers broke into a U.S. organization’s Google Workspace environment in late 2025, stole its staff directory and cloud files, and used information from the breach to target a second U.S. organization in 2026. Google and Mandiant said the hackers posed as an employee of the first victim, turning a familiar professional identity into […]

The post Google Reveals How Russian Hackers Used One Cloud Breach to Compromise Another US Organization appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Russian state-sponsored hackers broke into a U.S. organization’s Google Workspace environment in late 2025, stole its staff directory and cloud files, and used information from the breach to target a second U.S. organization in 2026.

Google and Mandiant said the hackers posed as an employee of the first victim, turning a familiar professional identity into a way to steal cloud credentials from the second. Neither organization was named.

In its November 17 case study, Google identified the group as COLD RELIC, previously tracked as COLDRIVER and also known as Star Blizzard or Callisto.

The U.S. Justice Department has tied Callisto to Russia’s Federal Security Service, or FSB. Google’s researchers said they saw evidence of fresh phishing activity as recently as November 2026.

Google Cloud researchers previously identified the group’s LOSTKEYS document theft malware in a separate 2025 campaign. The new report does not identify a malware payload in either U.S. breach.

Instead, it shows how stolen credentials, unauthorized authentication methods, and convincing impersonation were enough to steal cloud files and reach another organization.

Google Reveals How Russian Hackers Used One Cloud Breach

The first intrusion began with stolen credentials for a Google Workspace Super Admin account. The attackers sent repeated multi-factor authentication (MFA) prompts until the user approved one, a tactic known as MFA fatigue.

They signed in through a residential proxy near the victim, making the connection look geographically routine. Once inside, they registered a device model the organization had not seen before.

With administrator access, the group downloaded the organization’s entire cloud drive, both by retrieving files directly and by sharing them with an attacker-controlled email account.

The hackers also exported the staff directory, started a tenant-wide Google Workspace Customer Takeout export, and deleted security alerts.

Some attacker-enrolled passkeys remained usable after password and session resets because responders had not revoked the passkeys themselves.

Once removed from the first organization’s systems, the hackers used accounts impersonating its employees to approach staff and professional contacts.

Social engineering conversation (Source – Google Cloud)

That tactic fits a pattern seen in earlier Star Blizzard campaigns, where the group opened with what looked like ordinary professional correspondence. In the second U.S. breach, the conversation began on an encrypted messaging app, not in the victim’s work inbox.

Previously targeted WhatsApp

The group had previously targeted WhatsApp with malicious QR codes, but Google did not name the messaging app in this case.

Investigators found a stronger link between the two breaches: a phishing redirect submitted to VirusTotal in June 2026 contained a reference to the first organization, matching the identity the hackers used in the chat.

The phishing links targeted Microsoft Entra ID, which the second organization used for single sign-on to Google Workspace. That setup lets staff use their Microsoft identity to access Google services.

After stealing login information, the hackers added an MFA device and downloaded files available to the compromised user. Unlike the first breach, Google did not report an organization-wide drive theft in the second.

Singapore’s CSA warned of active exploitation on November 17, […]

The post Critical Apache HTTP Server RCE Vulnerability Actively Exploited in Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Apache’s HTTP/2 module, mod_http2, has a critical flaw tracked as CVE-2026-119618 that reportedly allows unauthenticated remote code execution.

Apache released version 2.4.71 on November 11 to fix the flaw, which it rates as critical, while Singapore’s CSA assigns it a high-severity CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1/10.

Singapore’s CSA warned of active exploitation on November 17, 2026, urging administrators to patch immediately. It also noted that a public PoC was available but provided no details about victims or attack scale.

Wiz Research had reported no known exploitation when it published its analysis on November 11. The later alert changes the urgency for administrators who have not yet applied the update.

The bug sits in assign_headers(), a function in the module that handles HTTP/2 traffic. Apache says the function does not properly control how multiple threads access a shared resource.

This creates a race condition, meaning the result depends on which task gets to the resource first. The bug can corrupt the heap, an area of memory the server uses while it runs.

Apache HTTP Server RCE Exploitation

A successful attack can turn that memory corruption into remote code execution (RCE), allowing an attacker to run commands with the web server process’s permissions.

Apache credited Anthropic’s OSS Scanner, which reported the issue on October 26, and Google Cloud researchers Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell, who reported it independently on November 3.

Cybersecurity News previously covered the Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 patch and a separate Apache HTTP/2 code execution flaw fixed in May. The earlier fix does not protect servers from this vulnerability.

The Apache security advisory lists versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 as affected when mod_http2 is enabled. It also lists standalone mod_h2 releases 2.0.8 through 2.0.42 as affected, including 2.0.42 itself.

Servers configured to serve only HTTP/1.1 are not exposed to this flaw. Administrators should check the server’s active protocol settings rather than relying on the version number alone.

Wiz found that 64% of the cloud environments it examined had resources running affected versions, while 51% had publicly exposed instances.

Those figures do not account for whether HTTP/2 was enabled. They show where teams should check first, not how many environments could be exploited or how many were breached.

Administrators should install Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 or later, or apply a package their operating system vendor confirms contains the fix.

If an update must wait, temporarily disable HTTP/2 by setting Protocols http/1.1 and checking that individual virtual hosts do not still allow h2 or h2c. After reloading the service, verify that the affected Apache listeners no longer accept HTTP/2.

Start with internet-facing servers, but include internal deployments in the patch plan. For systems that were exposed before the update, keep relevant logs and review them for signs of compromise. Installing the fix closes the vulnerability, but it cannot tell you whether someone exploited it before the upgrade.

Backing starts at $399, with shipping estimated for July 2027. The campaign runs from November 17 through December 17, 2026, making this a crowdfunding launch rather than immediate retail availability. The device […]

The post Flipper Devices Launches Flipper One Linux-based Multi-tool With Advanced Network Security Tools appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Flipper Devices has launched a Kickstarter campaign for Flipper One, a portable Linux computer built for network testing, hardware projects, and security research. Backing starts at $399, with shipping estimated for July 2027.

The campaign runs from November 17 through December 17, 2026, making this a crowdfunding launch rather than immediate retail availability.

The device combines Wi-Fi 6E, two Gigabit Ethernet ports, and an expansion system for cellular modems, software-defined radios, and storage. Its main appeal is bringing several network tools into one standalone unit, giving researchers a portable platform for checking networks and building custom testing setups.

Flipper One Linux Multi-tool

Flipper One is not a replacement for Flipper Zero. Zero focuses on NFC, RFID, infrared, sub-GHz radio, and other direct hardware links. One targets IP networks and Linux applications.

As covered in our earlier Flipper One report, the two products serve different tasks rather than forming a simple upgrade path.

Flipper One supports up to five network uplinks, with options for routing, failover, load balancing, firewall rules, and VPN tunnels. It can act as both a Wi-Fi client and hotspot. Two independent 1 Gbps Ethernet ports also let users place it between wired devices as a transparent bridge or traffic sensor.

Its network scanner is designed to discover active hosts, identify open ports and services, and map network layouts. Flipper also describes passive monitoring that can detect network attacks and report unusual activity.

These functions could help administrators find exposed services and investigate traffic, although their real value will depend on software quality and testing.

According to the official product page, its MediaTek wireless hardware supports Wi-Fi 6E across the 2.4, 5, and 6 GHz bands, with monitor mode support. Flipper is still testing advanced wireless features.

Packet injection appears among its development goals, so buyers should not treat every planned Wi-Fi testing function as finished.

An eight-core Rockchip RK3576 processor runs Linux, user applications, and high-speed interfaces. A separate Raspberry Pi RP2350 microcontroller handles the screen, buttons, battery, power states, and boot control.

The firmware documentation explains this split, which keeps core device controls separate from the Linux system.

That separation matters when a custom Linux build fails or the main processor is switched off. Users retain access to the built-in interface instead of depending entirely on a working operating system.

Flipper also supports charging and SSH access through one USB-C cable, while desktop mode combines display output, power, and USB peripherals through a compatible connection.

Flipper is working with Collabora to bring the RK3576 platform into mainline Linux. This approach aims to reduce reliance on vendor-specific board support packages that can become difficult to maintain.

For researchers, upstream support offers a clearer path to kernel updates, code review, and custom builds without maintaining large private patches.

However, the open-source claims need context. In its May development update, Collabora said a proprietary DDR training component remained in the boot chain.

Hardware video decoding and the AI accelerator were also unfinished. Those findings describe development status at that time, not proof that every limitation remains today.

The internal M.2 slot supports PCIe, USB, and SATA connections for compatible modems, radios, and SSDs. A 5G modem is required to use the built-in eSIM for cellular data.

GPIO accessories offer another route for custom hardware. This extends the community-driven approach seen in Flipper Zero firmware development, but on a different computing platform.

For security teams, Flipper One promises a compact network lab rather than an automatic hacking device. Buyers should separate announced features from tested performance and treat the delivery date as an estimate.

Its strongest potential lies in combining open Linux software, wired traffic analysis, wireless monitoring, and expandable hardware in one field-ready design.

articles.description:
Hackers published two malicious versions of Microsoft’s agent-framework package on the Python Package Index (PyPI) on November 17, 2026. Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 contained a credential stealer that could run during normal Python startup, even if an application never imported Agent Framework. The malware targeted Azure identities, GitHub credentials, and secrets used in automated builds. […]

The post Microsoft’s Agent Framework PyPI Package Hacked to Steal Azure and GitHub Credentials appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers published two malicious versions of Microsoft’s agent-framework package on the Python Package Index (PyPI) on November 17, 2026.

Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 contained a credential stealer that could run during normal Python startup, even if an application never imported Agent Framework. The malware targeted Azure identities, GitHub credentials, and secrets used in automated builds.

Wiz traced the first upload to 20:35 UTC and the second to about 21:08 UTC. Both versions were no longer available on PyPI by 21:30 UTC. Wiz identified 1.26.0 as the latest known clean release and put normal package traffic at about 41,000 downloads per week. It indicates the package’s overall use, not downloads of the malicious versions or the number of victims.

Microsoft’s Agent Framework PyPI Compromised

Both releases placed a .pth file in site-packages, the directory where Python stores installed libraries. Python processes these files during normal startup and can run executable lines in them.

That meant an unrelated Python script could trigger the stealer simply by running in the affected environment. Cyber Security News documented a similar startup mechanism in its coverage of the elementary-data PyPI compromise.

The two versions left different files behind. Version 1.26.1 used agent_framework_meta.pth and a collector named _telemetry.py. Version 1.26.2 restored the package’s original initializer and moved the malicious code into af_runtime_diag.py, triggered by af_runtime_diag.pth.

A check limited to the first release’s files could therefore miss the second, even though both ran in the background and sent data to the same destination.

Researchers found the malicious releases under the legitimate Microsoft-associated PyPI publisher, not under a lookalike name. Wiz found no matching python-1.26.1 tag or release in Microsoft’s GitHub repository and no malicious code on its main branch.

The first malicious release also appeared only as a wheel, a ready-to-install Python package, rather than alongside a source archive and a matching agent-framework-core release. Those differences suggest it may have bypassed the usual build process, but the entry point remains unconfirmed

Azure and GitHub Actions Credentials

Socket’s analysis found that both versions searched environment variables, readable process data and local files for secrets. Targets included Azure CLI data, Azure DevOps agent credentials, Git credential stores, Docker and npm configuration, and application .env files. The stealer also tried to obtain fresh Azure managed identity and Azure DevOps tokens instead of relying only on credentials already stored on the system.

Version 1.26.2 added requests for GitHub Actions OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens in workflows that could issue them. OIDC lets a build job prove its identity without storing a cloud password.

If Microsoft Entra ID trusts that workflow, a stolen token could be exchanged for Azure access within the permissions granted to that identity. An earlier Microsoft durabletask supply chain incident also targeted build and cloud credentials, but Wiz has not linked the two attacks.

Both versions sent compressed, encoded data to a specific webhook[.]site address. Wiz said the destination used the service’s free tier and that no more than 50 requests were captured. That is not a count of affected systems or exposed credentials. A single accepted request could contain several working secrets, including cloud tokens and package registry credentials.

Search dependency lockfiles, build logs, Python environments, container images, and package caches for either version. If you find one, isolate the affected host or runner and avoid starting Python in that environment to inspect it.

Check proxy logs for the specific webhook path listed in Socket’s indicators. Then rebuild from a known-good image or dependency set and pin agent-framework to 1.26.0. Removal from PyPI does not remove copies already installed or cached.

From a clean system, revoke or rotate credentials that were available to the affected environment. Review Azure sign-in and activity logs for unexpected use of managed identities and service connections.

For GitHub Actions jobs that installed 1.26.2 with id-token: write, check the Entra ID trust settings and sign-ins for the linked application.

articles.title: Critical Java4Shell Flaw Lets Hackers Execute Code Without Authentication on OpenJDK Servers
articles.description:
A critical flaw in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder can let a remote attacker run code on an affected server without signing in. The vulnerability, dubbed Java4Shell and tracked as CVE-2026-114938, can also crash the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) or expose sensitive data held in its memory. Oracle released security updates on November 17, 2026, and the […]

The post Critical Java4Shell Flaw Lets Hackers Execute Code Without Authentication on OpenJDK Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A critical flaw in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder can let a remote attacker run code on an affected server without signing in. The vulnerability, dubbed Java4Shell and tracked as CVE-2026-114938, can also crash the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) or expose sensitive data held in its memory.

Oracle released security updates on November 17, 2026, and the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) urged organizations to patch immediately.

The flaw sits in HotSpot, the JVM that runs Java applications in many OpenJDK distributions. That differs from Log4Shell, which affected the Log4j logging library. Updating an application’s Java libraries will not replace a vulnerable runtime. Administrators need to identify the Java build each service actually runs, including any copy shipped by the application vendor.

Security firm Calif rated Java4Shell 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, which puts it in the critical range. OpenJDK’s advisory lists a score of 8.1 under CVSS 3.1. The scores use different versions of the severity standard. Both describe a serious flaw, but neither means every Java server can be exploited. Exposure depends on the runtime, the processor, and how the application handles outside data.

Calif researcher, Quang Luong, found the flaw while examining OpenJDK HotSpot with help from an AI coding tool. The disclosure follows Calif’s work on PHP2Shell and the emergency PHP patches. Both investigations found memory flaws in shared runtimes, but the PHP flaws and Java4Shell have different causes and require separate fixes.

Base64 represents binary data as text so applications can pass it through systems that expect text. It is common in sign-in flows, file uploads, and network messages.

On supported processors, HotSpot uses a faster decoder that handles several bytes at once. A mistake in that code can make the decoder write past the end of its allocated buffer before Java rejects the bad input. Rejecting it does not undo the memory damage.

Java4Shell Exposes Java Applications

Calif reported remote code execution without a login in default test setups of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira and Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate. Its tests against Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker required authentication. The researchers also demonstrated code execution in sample applications built with Apache Struts and Spring Boot. These results describe the setups Calif tested, not every installation of those products.

The risk is not limited to servers that accept incoming requests. Calif also reported a client-side demonstration in which a Java program could be compromised after opening an encrypted TLS connection to a malicious server.

The researchers compared the memory exposure to Heartbleed because a successful attack could reveal data already held by the process, such as session tokens or private keys. The two flaws do not share the same cause.

The vulnerable decoder requires an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support, a feature available on some Intel Xeon and newer AMD processors. ARM64 systems are not affected by this code path. The earlier Cybersecurity News report on the Java 17 flaw focused on that release line. The OpenJDK advisory now identifies fixes for Java 17, 21, 25 and 27. Oracle also lists a specific Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack build and certain GraalVM builds as affected.

There is no single exploit that works across all Java applications, according to Calif. WatchTowr also expects attacks to be tailored to individual products because the CPU, JDK, and the way the application uses Base64 all matter. The research demonstrations establish that code execution is possible, but they are not evidence of attacks against production systems.

How to patch Java4Shell and Fix Versions

Oracle’s fixed Java SE releases include 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1. Organizations using Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Azul Zulu, or another distribution should check their vendor’s advisory for the build that fixes this CVE.

CISA recommends patching internet-facing systems first and checking for runtimes bundled with third-party software, container images, and appliances. Those copies may not appear as separate entries in a software inventory.

Where patching must wait, Calif recommends starting affected JVMs with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to turn off the optimized Base64 routines. Another option on x86-64 is -XX:UseAVX=2, which disables AVX-512. Do not add the second flag to ARM startup settings because it can prevent Java from starting.

CISA also recommends restricting unauthenticated access, validating Base64 input before it reaches the decoder, and enforcing input-size limits while teams prepare updates. These are temporary controls, not replacements for a patched runtime.

After updating, restart each affected service or redeploy it with a rebuilt container image. Verify the version used by the running process rather than checking only the host’s default Java installation.

CISA also recommends watching for unexpected JVM crashes, unapproved runtimes, and suspicious Java processes. A crash alone does not prove exploitation, but an unexplained crash on an exposed, unpatched system deserves investigation.

articles.title: Malicious iOS Scripts Now Behind 1 in 5 Advertiser Suspensions as Coruna Exploit Kit Hides Inside Ad Landing Pages
articles.description:
Malicious iOS scripts accounted for roughly 20% of advertiser account suspensions in 2026 across advertising platforms protected by ADEX, according to the company’s newly released State of Ad Fraud 2026: ADEX Trust & Safety Report. It is the first year the anti-fraud platform has tracked device-targeted attacks as a standalone category, and the figure places […]

The post Malicious iOS Scripts Now Behind 1 in 5 Advertiser Suspensions as Coruna Exploit Kit Hides Inside Ad Landing Pages appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Malicious iOS scripts accounted for roughly 20% of advertiser account suspensions in 2026 across advertising platforms protected by ADEX, according to the company’s newly released State of Ad Fraud 2026: ADEX Trust & Safety Report.

It is the first year the anti-fraud platform has tracked device-targeted attacks as a standalone category, and the figure places iPhone-specific exploitation alongside cloaking as one of the leading reasons advertisers are removed from ad networks.

The finding reflects a shift in how malware reaches mobile users. Rather than relying on malicious apps, operators are buying legitimate ad inventory and pointing it at landing pages that quietly fingerprint each visitor’s device before deciding what to serve.

One URL, two very different pages

At the center of the report is an investigation into approximately 50 advertiser accounts that ran campaigns with sharply different creatives and landing-page designs but near-identical delivery mechanics underneath.

ADEX found hidden iframes checking visitors’ iOS versions and filtering scripts designed to screen out bots, crawlers, and manual reviewers. A platform moderator loading the page would see an ordinary offer; a user on a vulnerable iPhone would receive an exploit chain.

That chain was assembled by the Coruna exploit kit, which selected payloads matched to the device’s iOS version and chipset. The kit has been documented in previous campaigns leveraging 23 exploits to compromise thousands of iPhones, and Apple has already shipped emergency updates for older devices specifically to blunt Coruna attacks. The documented chains in ADEX’s investigation covered iOS 13.0 through 17.2.1, meaning fully patched devices were not affected but any phone running outdated firmware remained exposed.

The payload was delivered under a filename ending in .min.js, blending into the minified JavaScript libraries found on virtually every commercial website. The final implant targeted digital wallets and financial applications and scanned the device for cryptocurrency recovery seed phrases, a technique consistent with DarkSword and Coruna operations previously observed stealing wallet recovery phrases.

Why the accounts were only visible together

ADEX noted that reviewing each landing page in isolation would likely have missed the operation entirely. The connection between the 50 accounts emerged only from shared infrastructure: the same device-check logic, the same script patterns, and the same redirect behavior repeated behind constantly rotating designs and offers. The company passed its findings to affected clients for review and enforcement, and said the investigation has since allowed its moderation systems to recognize the same attack pattern even when it appears behind a brand-new landing page.

The approach mirrors a broader trend in which attackers abuse legitimate ad platforms as a distribution layer, as seen when malicious Instagram ads were used to infect iPhones with spyware without any user interaction. In both cases, the ad network’s trust and reach become the delivery mechanism.

Cloaking declines as a share, new categories emerge

The report also shows the enforcement mix changing. Cloaking accounted for about 45% of advertiser suspensions in Q3 2026, down from roughly 75% across 2025. Messenger-based phishing, observed on services including WhatsApp and Telegram through third-party abuse, was broken out as its own category during the year.

ADEX cautioned that platforms log a single primary reason for each suspension even when several techniques appear together. An iOS-targeted campaign typically also uses cloaking to hide its payload from reviewers, so the 20% figure for malicious iOS scripts likely understates how often device-targeting appears in practice.

For traffic-quality teams, the report’s practical takeaway is to follow the delivery infrastructure rather than the creative. Shared scripts, servers, device checks, and redirect chains are harder to rotate than page designs, and they expose coordinated operations that individual account reviews cannot.

The full State of Ad Fraud 2026: ADEX Trust & Safety Report is available from ADEX, a global anti-fraud and traffic-quality platform within AdTech Holding that analyzes billions of impressions, clicks, and conversions to protect AdTech products and partners from malware-driven and invalid traffic.

The post Malicious iOS Scripts Now Behind 1 in 5 Advertiser Suspensions as Coruna Exploit Kit Hides Inside Ad Landing Pages appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: How a Five-Analyst MSSP Increased SOC Capacity by 25% with Threat Intelligence
articles.description:
Every managed security service provider eventually hits the same wall. New clients bring more endpoints, more log sources and more alerts, while SLAs get tighter and qualified analysts stay expensive and hard to hire. The obvious fix is headcount.  A US-based MSSP with one SOC manager and five analysts chose a different route: it changed […]

The post How a Five-Analyst MSSP Increased SOC Capacity by 25% with Threat Intelligence appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Every managed security service provider eventually hits the same wall. New clients bring more endpoints, more log sources and more alerts, while SLAs get tighter and qualified analysts stay expensive and hard to hire. The obvious fix is headcount. 

A US-based MSSP with one SOC manager and five analysts chose a different route: it changed how its team gets threat context, and ended up handling about 30% more alerts with the same people.

This article walks through what that MSSP changed, why MSSP threat intelligence matters more for providers than for single-company SOCs, and what other service providers can take from the approach.

The problem: growth that outpaces the team

The provider, which asked to remain anonymous, serves a growing list of customers, including enterprises with thousands of endpoints.

As the client base expanded, three pressures arrived together: rising alert volume, stricter SLA commitments and pressure on staffing costs.

Its investigation workflow was typical of many mid-sized MSSPs. Alerts were enriched inside the SIEM, and analysts then checked suspicious indicators against open-source IOC sources by hand.

That works at low volume. At higher volume, every unfamiliar domain, hash or IP address turns into a small research task, and those tasks pile up across clients.

The team considered hiring. As the company’s Head of SOC put it, “Hiring more analysts was one option, but we also wanted to improve the way we worked.”

The real question was whether some of the threats the analysts were researching could have been recognized earlier, before anyone spent time on them.

Why MSSPs feel the context gap harder

An in-house SOC defends one environment and learns its normal behavior over time. An MSSP defends many environments at once, each with different software, users and risk.

The same suspicious file might appear at three clients in a week, and without shared, current intelligence, three analysts may each investigate it from scratch.

This is where threat intelligence earns its cost for a provider. Fresh, verified indicators let the SOC recognize known-bad activity on arrival.

Rich context (which malware family, which campaign, which infrastructure) lets analysts decide quickly whether an alert matters. Both reduce the number of alerts that need full manual research, which is the most expensive work a SOC does.

Give your MSSP earlier visibility into up to 30% of unique malicious IOCs and strengthen detection without adding manual research.Protect More Clients with Less Work

Step 1: sandbox analysis built into the SOC workflow

The MSSP’s adoption happened in stages, which is part of why it worked. Analysts first used the ANY.RUN Interactive Sandbox individually to detonate suspicious files and URLs and watch their behavior.

After several months, the company moved to an enterprise plan and connected the sandbox to its SIEM through the API, so analysis became part of the standard investigation path rather than an ad hoc tool.

Behavioral analysis answers the question static indicators cannot: what does this sample actually do? For a provider, getting that answer in minutes instead of hours across many clients is a direct gain in capacity.

Step 2: threat intelligence feeds that catch threats on arrival

About six months after the sandbox rollout, the MSSP added ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence Feeds and connected them to the SIEM through an out-of-the-box integration. Indicators that matched the feed were tagged as malicious automatically.

That change moved part of the work from investigation to detection. Instead of an analyst opening an alert, pulling an IOC and researching it, a known-malicious indicator arrived already labeled. 

According to ANY.RUN’s own analysis of sandbox sessions, around 30% of unique malicious IOCs were already present in its feeds before they were investigated, which shows how much research time early visibility can remove.

The feeds draw on sandbox activity from what the company says are more than 16,000 SOCs and 700,000 security professionals.

Step 3: lookup for the alerts that still need a human

Feeds cover what is already known. For everything else, the team added Threat Intelligence Lookup, which analysts use manually to research indicators, connected infrastructure and related activity across industries. 

When an alert does not match a feed, the analyst can quickly see whether a domain or hash has appeared in other attacks, which malware it relates to and what else belongs to the same campaign.

This gave the SOC a consistent research method across all customer environments, rather than leaving each analyst to assemble context from scattered open sources.

The results: more alerts, same team

Once all three pieces were in place, the provider reported:

  • About 30% more alerts handled with the same five analysts. “We were handling around 30% more alerts with the same team,” the Head of SOC said.
  • 25% greater SOC capacity, which the company could use to take on more clients without immediately adding staff.
  • Easier SLA compliance, because fewer alerts stalled waiting for manual research.
  • Less time per alert and fewer manual checks, as feed matches and sandbox verdicts replaced repetitive lookups.

The business effect matters as much as the operational one. For an MSSP, capacity is revenue. Freeing a quarter of the team’s capacity is roughly the output of an extra analyst, gained without the cost and ramp-up time of a new hire.

Cut response time by up to 21 minutes with context-rich threat intelligence while keeping your MSSP’s investigation costs under control.Boost Your MSSP’s Efficiency

Lessons for other MSSPs

  1. Measure where analyst time goes. Track how many alerts need manual IOC research and how long that takes. That number shows how much a feed or lookup service could save.
  2. Integrate, do not just subscribe. Intelligence that lives in a separate portal still costs analyst time. Push feeds into the SIEM or SOAR so matches are tagged automatically.
  3. Roll out in stages. This MSSP proved value with the sandbox first, then added feeds, then lookup. Each step was easier to justify with results from the previous one.
  4. Standardize research across clients. A shared lookup method gives every customer the same triage quality, regardless of which analyst is on shift.
  5. Tie the metrics to the business. Report capacity and SLA results in terms leadership understands: clients served per analyst and cost per investigation.

How ANY.RUN helps MSSPs scale

The approach in this story is built on three ANY.RUN products that work together. The Interactive Sandbox shows how a file or URL behaves in a live environment, so analysts reach a verdict quickly.

Threat Intelligence Feeds deliver fresh, verified IOCs from real sandbox analysis straight into the SIEM, catching known threats before an analyst touches them.

Threat Intelligence Lookup provides deep context for the indicators that still need investigation.

ANY.RUN says more than 2,170 MSSPs already use its services. For a provider facing the same squeeze between growth and headcount, the practical starting point is to connect the feeds to the existing stack and measure how many alerts arrive already resolved.

Integrate TI Feeds into your existing security stack to close detection gaps and protect more clients.Expand Detection Coverage

articles.title: TheMailer – Self-hosted Phishing Platform that Runs on Claude and ChatGPT
articles.description:
TheMailer, a self-hosted phishing platform identified by Varonis Threat Labs, brings commercial AI models into almost every stage of an email attack. Rather than only fixing grammar or writing convincing messages, it uses AI to build lures, change templates, test delivery, and manage replies. Operators supply their own API keys to connect services including Claude, […]

The post TheMailer – Self-hosted Phishing Platform that Runs on Claude and ChatGPT appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
TheMailer, a self-hosted phishing platform identified by Varonis Threat Labs, brings commercial AI models into almost every stage of an email attack.

Rather than only fixing grammar or writing convincing messages, it uses AI to build lures, change templates, test delivery, and manage replies. Operators supply their own API keys to connect services including Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, Mistral, and DeepSeek.

According to the research, TheMailer has been advertised on a cybercrime network since March 2026. Its sales thread has attracted more than 24,000 views, although that figure does not confirm customer numbers or successful attacks. Advertised lifetime licenses range from $3,000 to $6,000, depending on the package and whether it includes AI modules.

Buyers receive installation help and support, while supplying their own mail servers, proxies, and target lists. A Telegram sales channel and automated cryptocurrency payment bot help handle purchases.

The setup reduces the technical work needed to start a campaign by packaging email delivery and AI tools in an interface that resembles ordinary marketing software.

The approach builds on tools such as SpamGPT, an AI-powered phishing platform, which combines message generation, mail account management, delivery testing, and campaign tracking.

TheMailer takes that model further by linking AI rewriting directly to feedback about where test messages land. That connection turns content creation into an ongoing process rather than a single preparation step.

Its most notable feature, Inbox Loop, sends a test email and checks a connected mailbox through IMAP to determine whether the message reached the inbox or spam folder.

When a test lands in spam, the platform asks AI to rewrite the template and tries again. This tests delivery conditions, but does not guarantee access to every recipient’s inbox.

The Varonis Threat Labs report describes an AI Letter Builder that creates HTML email from short prompts. It can also import genuine messages from a connected mailbox and use them as templates.

This gives attackers an easy starting point for copying familiar brand layouts and language without designing each lure themselves.

Templates and subject lines can be rewritten for individual recipients. One example uses a Robinhood account warning with a changing reference number. Other presets turn messages into security alerts or routine transaction notices.

Options advertised as removing “AI patterns” aim to make the wording seem human, but the report does not establish that these options reliably defeat detection.

An AI Autopilot module groups recipients by mailbox provider and applies provider-specific sending limits and content guidance. Supported groups include Gmail, Microsoft, GMX, Yandex, and French providers.

A screenshot shows a list containing 145,133 entries, largely Japanese business and university domains. That is evidence of a displayed target list, not proof that those organizations were compromised.

The platform also advertises account warm-up, delivery testing, and reply management. AI WarmUP appears designed to exchange messages between sending accounts so they look established.

Inbox Finder tests delivery settings against a seed mailbox. A separate reply manager gathers responses and offers AI sorting and answering, extending automation beyond the initial message.

TheMailer’s attachment tools convert HTML templates into personalized PDFs, including filenames based on recipient names. Embedded links and changing metadata produce files with different hashes, making simple file blocklists less useful.

Other features create SVG redirects and calendar invitations. Branding shown in sample lures includes Robinhood and IONOS, alongside financial alerts and hotel booking callback themes.

The delivery features include randomized headers, sender profiles, and redirects that place trusted Google domains ahead of another destination.

These features can complicate review, but a familiar opening domain does not make the final page safe. Likewise, changing a message or file hash does not remove the phishing request or stop deeper analysis of its links and behavior.

The main defensive lesson is to assess intent, identity, and behavior rather than writing style alone. As explained in Cybersecurity News’ coverage of AI-written phishing detection, identifying machine-written text is different from identifying a malicious request.

Teams should check sender history, authentication results, reply-address mismatches, redirect chains, and attachment behavior.

Unexpected requests for passwords, payments, or verification codes deserve review even when every sentence looks natural. Staff should verify sensitive requests through a known contact channel rather than details supplied in the message.

articles.title: Critical Java 17 RCE Vulnerability Puts Servers at Risk as Oracle Releases 11 Security Fixes
articles.description:
A remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Java 17 has prompted warnings for server admins, especially as Oracle released 11 new Java SE security updates on the same day. The bug is tracked as CVE-2026-114938. Public reports say it needs no login and affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later. The details are still unconfirmed. Security firm […]

The post Critical Java 17 RCE Vulnerability Puts Servers at Risk as Oracle Releases 11 Security Fixes appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Java 17 has prompted warnings for server admins, especially as Oracle released 11 new Java SE security updates on the same day. The bug is tracked as CVE-2026-114938. Public reports say it needs no login and affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later. The details are still unconfirmed.

Security firm watchTowr said on X that it is aware of public reports of an unauthenticated RCE in Java. It told teams to review their Java environments and watch for vendor news. Reports rate the flaw 9.2 out of 10 under CVSS 4.0, which is Critical.

South Korea’s National Intelligence Service sent a warning to public bodies about a Java flaw that could allow remote code execution without authentication.

Open questions remain. The CVE record is still reserved with no public description. Early reports point to memory corruption. No fixed build, proof-of-concept code or sign of real-world exploitation has been published.

The reports also don’t name the weak component or say whether a special setup is needed. Running Java 17 does not prove you are exposed. Risk depends on whether outside data can reach the weak code.

Update: Researchers now call the flaw behind CVE-2026-114938 “Java4Shell.” It is a memory bug in the Base64 decoder of OpenJDK’s HotSpot runtime, and it can allow code execution without a login. It can also crash the JVM or leak data held in memory. Oracle released its fixes on November 17, and CISA urged organizations to patch right away. Our full Java4Shell report has the details.

What Oracle Fixed in November

Oracle’s November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update covers 652 new patches across its products. Java SE gets 11 of them, and all can be used over a network without credentials. The highest CVSS 3.1 score among them is 8.1. Fixes also cover GraalVM and JavaFX.

Oracle lists these builds as affected: Java SE 8u511, 11.0.33, 17.0.21, 21.0.13, 25.0.5 and 27.0.1. It has not tied any of the 11 fixes to CVE-2026-114938. Oracle’s JDK release notes are the place to find the replacement builds. Astra also notes that a secondary report lists 17.0.21.1 and 21.0.13.1 as scheduled releases.

Java 17 is a long-term support release, so many banks, cloud services and back-end systems still run it. Version 17.0.6 shipped in January 2023, so the reported range covers almost four years of builds. Because OpenJDK is sold in many vendor builds, the fix may arrive on different dates under different version names. South Korean officials told teams to check the exact JVM, vendor, and build in use, including Java inside containers and apps.

This is not the first Java scare this season. Oracle already issued an emergency Java update in October for CVE-2026-91403, a certificate trust bug rated 9.1. Our earlier report on Oracle’s 943-patch August update showed how fast these bundles are growing. Java apps are also under pressure elsewhere. Rapid7 reported exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 in Apache Axis, which affects Confluence Data Center.

Start with a full list of Java runtimes, including those inside containers. Close any internet access that the business does not need. Test the November update in a staging system, then roll it out quickly. Keep backups ready in case an update fails. Oracle’s only advice so far is to apply the update as soon as possible, and no workaround exists for this CVE.

Watch Oracle’s advisory, your OpenJDK vendor, and the CVE record for updates. Until a fix is confirmed for your build, treat every exposed Java 17 server as a priority.

articles.title: Hackers Abuse Microsoft SharePoint and GitHub to Hide GraphDoor Backdoor Attacks on Government Networks
articles.description:
Hackers are hiding a backdoor named GraphDoor inside normal Microsoft and Ably traffic. The goal is to spy on government networks in Asia and Africa. Kaspersky’s GReAT team detailed the findings on November 17, 2026, in the second part of its Operation ShadowCloud research. The report also lists the plug-ins GraphDoor loads and points to […]

The post Hackers Abuse Microsoft SharePoint and GitHub to Hide GraphDoor Backdoor Attacks on Government Networks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are hiding a backdoor named GraphDoor inside normal Microsoft and Ably traffic. The goal is to spy on government networks in Asia and Africa.

Kaspersky’s GReAT team detailed the findings on November 17, 2026, in the second part of its Operation ShadowCloud research. The report also lists the plug-ins GraphDoor loads and points to Chinese-speaking threat groups as possible owners of the tools.

GraphDoor first opens a named pipe built from its own process ID, in the form \\.\pipe\p%lu. Later plug-ins write their results to this pipe. The malware then creates an Intel_Log folder inside ProgramData, with a random GUID folder inside it.

Next, it collects system details. These include the network adapter, Windows version, public and private IP addresses, user name, host name, and a list of running processes. To hide its Windows API calls, it hashes function names with the DJB2 method.

It also uses a vectored exception handler, which forces an error on purpose so that a small routine runs the target call. The data is then encrypted with AES, Base64 encoded, and sent out.

GraphDoor SharePoint Backdoor

GraphDoor does not use a normal command server. It connects to login.microsoftonline.com and signs in as a malicious app, not as a person, using a client ID and secret stored inside the malware. That sign-in returns a token for the Microsoft Graph API.

With that token, the malware uploads the stolen host data to a SharePoint document library. The file is named main.<victim code>.js.map, which makes it look like a harmless JavaScript source map.

The victim code is a random eight-character string. Researchers saw the SharePoint site buildersemp.sharepoint[.]com used for this. A second site, cskautogo[.]sharepoint[.]com, is also listed in the report.

The malware then asks SharePoint lists for three plug-ins. They are scr.ts for screenshots, pr.ts for process lists, and kl.ts for key logging. It only fetches the keylogger if a file named log.lock already exists on the machine.

After that, it checks the same lists for command files that start with its own victim code and end in .js, .swp, .tmp, .kmap, .pmap, or .apmap.

This design is not new. Cisco Talos found a similar Rust backdoor named Antino, which uses Outlook and OneDrive for control, as Cyber Security News reported. In both cases, defenders see only calls to a trusted Microsoft service.

GraphDoor supports the same commands as its sibling, GitDoor, and adds two more. The shell command runs text through cmd.exe /C.

The adsmload command hides payloads as fake MAC addresses inside Base64 text, then turns them back into bytes with the Windows call RtlEthernetStringToAddressA.

Each plug-in is a small loader followed by a COFF object, with an entry point named go. The keylogger saves keystrokes and mouse clicks to %APPDATA%\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\Cache\logs.dat, locked with a random XOR key.

The screenshot plug-in sends JPEG images through the pipe. The process plug-in turns on the SeDebugPrivilege right before it lists running programs. A moveDir.ts plug-in copies the backdoor files to a new folder and can delete the old copies.

Three proxy plug-ins give the actors a path into the network. One is a patched copy of the open-source reverse proxy Erfrp, and it reads its settings from shared memory instead of a file.

Another uses the Ably real-time messaging service through its official Go SDK. The third is a SOCKS5 proxy that moves TCP traffic over Ably’s Pusher-compatible WebSocket endpoint.

Because the C2 host name comes through these proxy plug-ins or through an Ably channel, the backdoor holds no fixed C2 domain. Defenders cannot simply pull a domain out of the sample and block it.

Sophos also saw ably[.]net and ably[.]io in a separate China-linked case, which Cyber Security News covered here. Kaspersky says it cannot yet name one group. Still, GitDoor files appeared in the same folders as tools from FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle, within one day of each other.

In one case, a renamed Avast file called excint.exe loaded a bad wtsapi32.dll on March 6, 2026, and GitDoor files landed in the same folder on March 5. The DLL used the RC4 key iotrh^%4CFGTj, which ESET has tied to FamousSparrow.

In the CopperTurtle case, pdfset.exe in the PDF24 folder loaded the PLEAD RAT on May 3, 2026, and GitDoor followed on May 4. Kaspersky says this does not prove a direct link. Cyber Security News also covered FamousSparrow’s newer Exchange intrusions, which show how active that group still is.

Two IP addresses, 103[.]106[.]230[.]33 and 123[.]58[.]205[.]105, resolve to ms[.]twnic[.]top and ekmt[.]tw. Both domains also served as Cobalt Strike beacon servers on machines infected with GraphDoor. The report lists many more proxy server IPs for defenders to check.

Kaspersky notes that calls to Microsoft Graph, GitHub, and Ably look like normal business traffic, so network tools often miss them. Teams should watch for odd app sign-ins in Entra ID, unknown SharePoint sites, and files with names like .js.map in document libraries.

They should also treat any new remote tool, such as MeshCentral Agent, as suspicious. Defenders should also hunt for sideloaded DLLs in folders such as PDF24 and ProgramData\excint. The report’s hashes, domains, and IPs can be added to blocklists.
