articles.description:
Hackers used a cloud access key exposed through an unnamed AI vendor to enter Barracuda’s cloud environment and reach about 10 accounts in roughly 44 hours. The November 1–2 intrusion crossed cloud services, data analytics, source code, and Kubernetes systems as the attacker collected credentials to keep moving. Barracuda said the key remained active after […]

The post Hackers Exploit Exposed AI Vendor Key to Breach 10 Barracuda Cloud Accounts in 44 Hours appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers used a cloud access key exposed through an unnamed AI vendor to enter Barracuda’s cloud environment and reach about 10 accounts in roughly 44 hours. The November 1–2 intrusion crossed cloud services, data analytics, source code, and Kubernetes systems as the attacker collected credentials to keep moving.

Barracuda said the key remained active after the vendor finished its project. Its security advisory, updated November 13, confirmed that the credential was stored in a configuration file inside the vendor’s GitHub repository.

Attackers obtained it after compromising the vendor’s development environment in October. Other Barracuda credentials in that file had expired or were later revoked.

According to Barracuda’s account, the first recorded request arrived at 04:33 UTC on November 1. Within minutes, the attacker checked what the key could access and read stored secrets, including AWS access keys and Azure service principal secrets.

Over the next day, those credentials gave the attacker access to a data analytics system, then a source code token, and finally Kubernetes clusters. Each newly found secret became another route into the environment.

Early on November 2, the attacker pushed temporary branches to several repositories to trigger build workflows. These workflows printed build secrets into job logs.

Encoding the values helped bypass controls designed to hide secrets in those logs. The technique echoes credential theft through malicious GitHub Actions workflows, where trusted build systems become tools for stealing cloud and AI keys.

Barracuda Cloud Account Breach

Barracuda linked the activity to ARTEX, an open-source AI-driven penetration testing framework, based on matching resource names, workflow patterns, and automated credential searches, though this does not identify the attacker.

The attacker searched infrastructure state files, server metadata services, and Kubernetes service accounts for credentials. Commands also searched for WALLET, MNEMONIC, SEED, and PRIV environment variables, Ethereum keystores, private keys, and wallet-related Kubernetes secrets. Barracuda said no wallet material existed on those systems.

A container deployed inside one Kubernetes cluster mounted the underlying server’s file system. Although access was read-only, it allowed credential harvesting. An attempt to create a new administrative cloud identity was blocked.

Barracuda traced the unusual account activity reported on November 4, removed the affected container that evening, and rotated credentials across affected systems.

One reached system stored integration credentials for Barracuda XDR. Investigators found no direct evidence that these credentials were accessed, but incomplete logging prevented them from ruling it out.

Notified customers must recreate integration credentials and review connected systems’ activity from November 1. Customers not notified need no action under the advisory.

The incident follows the Railway AI credential breach, where stolen keys generated about $740,000 in unauthorized charges. Railway’s report describes attackers targeting AI provider credentials for possible resale.

Barracuda has not confirmed that same goal, though AI service credentials were within reach. Barracuda is removing long-lived keys, improving audit logs, and tightening Kubernetes controls to limit future credential theft and reduce cross-system access.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit macOS ß vs ss Filename Trick to Bypass Developer Tool Security Checks
articles.description:
A Unicode normalization flaw allows attackers to bypass macOS file exclusion checks, affecting Deno, libarchive, HashiCorp go-slug, and Python setuptools across four CVEs. The flaw comes from two parts of the system disagreeing about what a file name is. Apple File System (APFS) resolves paths in a way that treats different Unicode spellings of one […]

The post Hackers Exploit macOS ß vs ss Filename Trick to Bypass Developer Tool Security Checks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A Unicode normalization flaw allows attackers to bypass macOS file exclusion checks, affecting Deno, libarchive, HashiCorp go-slug, and Python setuptools across four CVEs.

The flaw comes from two parts of the system disagreeing about what a file name is. Apple File System (APFS) resolves paths in a way that treats different Unicode spellings of one name as the same file.

The affected tools compare paths as raw bytes. A byte comparison sees “ß” and “ss” as different strings, while the file system sends both to the same file on disk.

An attacker uses this gap. They give a tool a path spelled in a form that misses its exclusion rule or deny list. The tool allows the path. APFS then resolves it to the protected file.

CERT/CC says a local attacker can overwrite files anywhere the process has write access. That can lead to data corruption, configuration hijacking, or code execution.

Hackers Exploit ß vs ss macOS Flaw

CVE-2026-45110 affects libarchive. It has a file-overwrite bypass and a directory-exclusion bypass. An attacker can place a look-alike name, such as a variant of “password,” in an archive. APFS treats the entry as /etc/passwd, and the extraction silently overwrites it.

CVE-2026-49401 affects Deno. Its permission system checks a requested path against values passed to –deny-read, –deny-write, –deny-run, and –deny-ffi on macOS, and that check used raw-byte matching. A different Unicode spelling of a denied path could pass the check, even though APFS treats it as the same file.

CVE-2026-14978 affects HashiCorp go-slug. Path matching handled Unicode normalization badly, so an attacker with local filesystem access could bypass .terraformignore rules. Sensitive files could then end up in Terraform slug uploads.

CVE-2026-59890 affects setuptools. Before version 83.0.0, FileList applied MANIFEST.in directives such as exclude, global-exclude, recursive-exclude and prune by matching glob patterns against on-disk names without normalization.

On APFS or HFS+, a file name in NFD form could slip past an exclusion rule written in NFC form. The file would then be packed into a source distribution. Version 83.0.0 fixes it.

CERT/CC also opened a general tracker, VU#604762.8, for a related problem. On case-insensitive or normalization-insensitive file systems, some libraries fail to lock colliding paths like ß and ss. Both paths can then be processed in parallel during archive extraction. That creates a race, and a protected file can be overwritten.

The risk is highest in automated workflows. CERT/CC says backup tools, forensic workflows, and CI/CD pipelines are exposed to unwanted file changes. A poisoned archive or package could corrupt build steps. A weak exclusion rule could also push secrets into a published artifact.

This is not the first time Unicode handling has caused trouble. We covered a DNN Unicode normalization bypass earlier this year. We have also reported on a macOS Gatekeeper bypass that shows how Apple’s security layers can be sidestepped when software trusts a path too much.

CERT/CC advises updating affected software to the latest version. Apple is listed as “Not Affected.” Many other vendors, including Docker, Helm, IBM, and Node.js, show an “Unknown” status for now.

Developers should stop comparing paths as raw bytes. Security filters should normalize paths and fold case the way the operating system does, before they compare anything.

Security teams should check which archive and packaging tools run on macOS build hosts and update them. They should also watch for unexpected file writes during extraction. The attack needs local access, and CERT/CC reports no exploitation in the wild.

A software bug at JPMorgan Chase disrupted banking services on November 16, 2026, leaving thousands of customers reporting trouble with account access and payments. Complaints also appeared for Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Zelle, though reports did not establish separate outages at each bank. Chase linked the disruption to a temporary software […]

The post Chase Software Bug Disrupts Banking Services as Customers Report Outages at Major US Banks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A software bug at JPMorgan Chase disrupted banking services on November 16, 2026, leaving thousands of customers reporting trouble with account access and payments. Complaints also appeared for Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Zelle, though reports did not establish separate outages at each bank.

Chase linked the disruption to a temporary software issue in its “on-premise hardware systems,” meaning equipment within its own computing setup. The bank said there was no evidence of a cyberattack and described the problem as isolated rather than a failure across the wider banking system.

Customers reported problems checking balances, viewing transactions and completing transfers. Some Chase users also faced trouble withdrawing money, while delays affected both online services and branch transactions. Chase said customers retained access to their accounts and funds, although some requests were taking longer than usual to complete.

Chase Outage Affected Other Banks

The wider impact came from transactions involving Chase, not confirmed failures inside every bank named in customer complaints. Chase said other institutions could experience slower processing when it was involved in a payment. Bank of America and Citigroup were not experiencing failures in their own banking services.

U.S. Bank made a similar distinction, saying its systems were not directly affected. Customers sending or receiving Zelle payments involving another financial institution could still face delays. This explains why reports across several banking brands did not mean every institution had suffered its own technical failure.

Zelle said its network was “operating as it should.” Its operator, Early Warning Services, linked delayed payments to problems at financial institutions. As the Associated Press explained, customers using other banks could encounter delays when sending money to, or receiving money from, a Chase customer.

The available evidence points to a service availability problem, not a confirmed data breach. CNN reported that an update to Chase’s physical computer systems caused the issue, citing a person familiar with the matter. Chase’s public explanation identified a software bug without naming the affected component or releasing a detailed technical report.

That distinction matters when assessing banking disruptions. Cyber Security News previously covered DDoS attacks causing financial-sector outages, but Chase reported no evidence of such activity here. The incident also followed the separate Microsoft 365 service outage, with no established connection between the two events.

Chase Reports Recovery

By Monday evening, Chase said transactions were posting normally, according to NBC News. The recovery update marked an improvement after hours of customer complaints. It did not provide a full breakdown of the software fault, leaving the exact failure mechanism and steps to prevent a repeat unclear.

articles.description:
On 16 November 2026, attackers planted malicious JavaScript inside the Optimizely Web experimentation platform. The code reached visitors of 178 organizations. The list includes some of the busiest sites on the internet, such as Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock. Researcher Scott Helme of Report URI found the […]

The post Hackers Infect 178 Major Websites via Optimizely to Steal Credit Cards and Target iPhones appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
On 16 November 2026, attackers planted malicious JavaScript inside the Optimizely Web experimentation platform. The code reached visitors of 178 organizations.

The list includes some of the busiest sites on the internet, such as Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock. Researcher Scott Helme of Report URI found the campaign. He confirmed that crypto has already been stolen and traced the transactions to wallets controlled by the attackers.

This was not a simple skimmer. The malware worked as a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses, stole payment card details, grabbed cookies and screenshots, and pushed the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits to iPhone and iPad users.

What makes the case worrying is that none of the affected websites had to be hacked directly. The bad code came through a trusted third-party script that each site loaded on every page.

Optimizely Snippet Was Abused

Optimizely Web works by having each customer load a JavaScript “snippet” from cdn.optimizely.com. The file holds Optimizely’s code, the customer’s experiments, and an optional field called Project JavaScript. Optimizely’s documentation says Project JavaScript is the first code to run in the snippet and can affect every experiment in a project.

The attacker wrote a small loader into this field and left the rest of the snippet untouched. The file was still served from Optimizely’s domain with Optimizely’s certificate, so browsers and security tools treated it as normal. In Zoom’s snippet, the added code quietly created a new script tag that pulled a file called track.js from the domain 1688360.cc.

Report URI found three versions of the loader. Most snippets used a plain script tag. Others hid the same URL in base64 with atob(), so a simple search for “1688360.cc” would miss it.

A third version carried a full inline copy of the payload and ran it through eval if the attacker’s domain was blocked. Smartsheet cleaned the snippet at one point, then re-infected it with the base64 version, showing the attacker still had access. Sites that serve the snippet from their own domain, such as Scheels and Vodafone Australia, were also affected because the content came from the same Optimizely project.

What the Malware Stole

The crypto clipper scanned each page for wallet addresses on Bitcoin, Ethereum, TRON, Solana, TON, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash and Dogecoin. It swapped them for attacker addresses in page text, in the clipboard, and in outgoing web requests. By 19:25 UTC, the attacker’s wallets had received about $7,040. Stolen funds were moved to exchanges at around 13:03 UTC.

The attacker added a card skimmer at 13:43 UTC. It watched form submissions for a card number, expiry date and CVV, then sent the details to 1688360.cc/card.php. Cards typed into hosted payment frames such as Stripe or Adyen were out of its reach.

Cards entered into a site’s own form fields were not. The script also sent page URLs, readable cookies and html2canvas screenshots to 1688360.cc/hit.php.

iPhones Targeted With Coruna and DarkSword

On Apple mobile devices, the script loaded a router file from .icu domains and chose an exploit chain based on the iOS version. Devices on iOS 13 to 17 received Coruna. Devices on iOS 18 received DarkSword. A separate chain for iOS 26 only fingerprinted the device.

Google’s Threat Intelligence Group says Coruna contains 23 exploits across five full chains. DarkSword links six vulnerabilities against iOS 18.4 to 18.7. Readers can find more background in our earlier reports on the Coruna exploit kit and the DarkSword iOS exploit chain.

Indicators of Compromise

Report URI says it does not know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects. The researchers ruled out CDN cache poisoning. The snippets for Optimizely’s own sites, including login.optimizely.com, also carried the malicious code.

Report URI said it had not heard back from Optimizely when it published its findings. Most of the code was gone by 21:52 UTC, when only TalkTalk’s snippet was still infected, down from 169 at 20:56 UTC.

Optimizely Web customers should open every Project JavaScript field and every experiment’s custom code. They should look for 1688360.cc, atob( and any script they did not write.

Optimizely’s change history logs all Project JavaScript changes. It also shows whether each change came through the REST API or the web interface. Teams should review users, API tokens and integrations, then rotate their credentials. Cards entered on 16 November, and any secrets stored in non-HttpOnly cookies, should be treated as exposed.

Content Security Policy made a clear difference. Of the affected organizations whose own websites Report URI checked, 68 had no CSP at all, and only 24 blocked the payload completely. Allowing ‘unsafe-eval’ or ‘strict-dynamic’ let the code through. Users should update to iOS 18.7.3 or later, or iOS 26.3 or later. They should also double-check any crypto transfers and card statements from that day.

Update: Optimizely said it contained the Web Experimentation incident, blocked the vulnerable path, removed injected code, and contacted affected customers directly. Further updates are available on its status page.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Patch management tools remain critical for IT security and operational efficiency in 2026, automating the discovery, testing, and deployment of software updates across diverse endpoints.

Leading solutions NinjaOne, Automox, Kaseya VSA, ManageEngine Patch Manager Plus, SolarWinds Patch Manager, and Ivanti Patch Management deliver automated patching for Windows, macOS, Linux, and third-party applications.

Key capabilities include customizable deployment policies, multi-OS support, detailed compliance reporting, and real-time monitoring.

Cloud-native platforms eliminate on-premises infrastructure needs while enabling remote endpoint management.

Standouts like NinjaOne extend beyond patching with remote remediation, asset management, and intuitive dashboards for streamlined security operations.

Here Are Our Picks For The Best Patch Management Tools in 2026

  • SolarWinds: Robust patch management with automated discovery and deployment capabilities.
  • Kaseya VSA: Integrated patch management and IT automation for streamlined updates.
  • Saner CVEM (SecPod): Continuous vulnerability and exposure management platform with automated vulnerability assessment, risk-based prioritization, patch management, endpoint remediation, and compliance monitoring.
  • Endpoint Central: Unified endpoint management with extensive patching features for multiple platforms.
  • Salt: Scalable configuration management and patching with SaltStack automation.
  • Pulseway: Mobile-first patch management solution for remote IT monitoring and management.
  • ConnectWise: Integrated patch management with IT automation for comprehensive system updates.
  • Acronis: Cyber protection platform with integrated patch management and backup.
  • Datto, Inc.: Comprehensive patch management with backup and disaster recovery integration.
  • Ivanti (formerly Landesk): Advanced patch management with real-time endpoint vulnerability assessment.
  • Jamf: Specialized patch management for Apple devices, ensuring timely updates.
  • VMware: Centralized patch management for virtualized environments and VMware products.
  • GFI LanGuard: Network security scanner with comprehensive patch management.
  • BigFix: Real-time visibility and control over patch deployment across diverse environments.
  • SysAid: Integrated ITSM with automated patch management for improved security.

Features Of Best Patch Management Software

1. SolarWinds

SolarWinds Patch Manager simplifies patch implementation in extensive networks and virtual environments with its versatile and scalable automatic patch management software that interfaces with third-party apps.

Patch Manager uses Microsoft WSUS and pre-built and pre-tested packages to distribute patches reliably. It also offers configurable alarms and scheduled patch reports.

Wake on LAN improves software scan security by reactivating sleeping devices and turning them off afterward. It monitors and manages third-party software, virtual machines, and Adobe and Java fixes, surpassing WSUS and SCCM.

Companies can eliminate software vulnerabilities and manage security with real-time security monitoring and thorough compliance reporting. IT managers must keep up with software patches to keep networks secure and efficient. SolarWinds Patch Management helps.

2. Kaseya VSA

Kaseya VSA automates and streamlines device and operating system software and security patch deployment.

The software automatically discovers and applies missing updates on target devices, supporting many software applications, operating systems (Windows, macOS, Linux), and third-party apps.

Patch scanning and inventory detects all patches, checks endpoints for missing updates, and keeps a complete inventory of installed software and patch levels to monitor all managed devices.

Kaseya VSA administrators manage patches. They authorize patches before distribution, create patching procedures, and schedule company and customer-specific installs.

Prioritizing critical updates for immediate deployment resolves security issues and provides flexible patch deployment options for various scenarios. The program permits automated, manual, and patch deployments during non-business hours to minimize disruption.

3. Saner CVEM


Product overview 

SecPod ‘s Saner Patch Management is an automated patch management solution that helps organizations identify missing patches, prioritize vulnerabilities, and deploy security updates across their IT environments.

It supports Windows, Linux, macOS, and more than 550 third-party applications, allowing IT and security teams to manage patching activities from a centralized platform. 

Unlike traditional patching tools that primarily focus on deploying software updates, Saner connects patch management with vulnerability intelligence, risk-based prioritization, and remediation.

This helps organizations address critical security gaps, maintain patch compliance, and reduce the time spent on manual patching activities. 

With automated patch deployment, flexible scheduling, continuous scanning, and centralized reporting, Saner simplifies patch operations across on-premises, remote, and hybrid environments. 

Key features 

  • Patch rollback: Restore a previous stable state when a deployed patch causes operational issues. 
  • Firmware and configuration remediation: Address firmware vulnerabilities and security configuration gaps alongside software patches. 
  • Patch compliance reporting: Monitor patch status, identify noncompliant endpoints, and track remediation progress. 
  • Continuous patch assessment: Run real-time, scheduled, continuous, or on-demand scans to identify missing updates. 
  • Third-party application patching: Manage security updates for more than 550 third-party applications. 
  • Risk-based prioritization: Prioritize patches using CVSS, EPSS, CISA KEV, and SSVC-aligned risk context. 
  • Automated patch management: Identify missing patches and automate deployment across operating systems and third-party applications. 

Key differentiators 

Saner combines vulnerability assessment, patch prioritization, and remediation within a unified workflow.

Its integrated vulnerability intelligence helps teams understand which missing patches present the greatest security risk rather than relying solely on patch availability or severity.

The solution also supports patch management for remote and distributed endpoints through a lightweight agent and centralized cloud-native management console. 

Relevant use cases 

  • Addressing firmware and configuration-related security risks. 
  • Managing patches for remote employees and hybrid IT environments. 
  • Prioritizing actively exploited and business-critical vulnerabilities. 
  • Maintaining patch compliance across distributed endpoints. 
  • Reducing vulnerability remediation backlogs. 
  • Automating operating system and third-party application patching. 

Current pricing  

Pricing given on demo and trial request. 

4. Endpoint Central

Endpoint Central is an automated tool for patch management that supports Windows, Mac, Linux, and third-party applications.

Critical features of Endpoint Central include a user-friendly dashboard, an updated vulnerability database, periodic patch scanning, system health policies, automated antivirus updates, the ability to decline patches for specific applications, and the option to disable automatic updates.

Endpoint Central uses a central patch repository maintained by Zoho Corp, which is regularly synchronized with the client’s server. Scanning for missing patches is done automatically, and system health can be classified based on patch status.

The tool simplifies antivirus updates and allows administrators to schedule them to reduce bandwidth consumption. It also enables patch testing and automated approval with configurable installation options.

articles.title: Researchers Reveal How Claude Code VS Code Extension Can Access Files Outside Trusted Workspaces
articles.description:
Security researchers have found that the Claude Code extension for Visual Studio Code can show a permission prompt that hides where a file really sits. A user may approve access to a path that looks safe, while the file lives outside the trusted workspace. Anthropic reviewed the report and does not treat it as a […]

The post Researchers Reveal How Claude Code VS Code Extension Can Access Files Outside Trusted Workspaces appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Security researchers have found that the Claude Code extension for Visual Studio Code can show a permission prompt that hides where a file really sits.

A user may approve access to a path that looks safe, while the file lives outside the trusted workspace. Anthropic reviewed the report and does not treat it as a security issue.

The extension has more than 29 million installs, so the problem could reach a very large number of developers. The extension is Anthropic’s official add-on that lets developers use Claude Code inside the VS Code editor. It asks for approval before the AI agent reads or writes files, and that prompt is meant to protect the user.

The same type of weakness was seen before in the command-line version of the tool. A Claude Code symlink import issue reported earlier also showed how a link inside a project can quietly point to files outside it.

The new finding shows the editor extension still has a similar gap. Researchers at Ultrastrike identified and described the issue in a blog post published on November 11, 2026. Carl Pearson wrote the report. He found it while reviewing several VS Code plugins for flaws.

Claude Code VS Code Extension Can Access Files

The problem centers on symlinks, which are shortcuts that point to another file or folder. In the test, a folder named ./helpdocs inside the workspace was a symlink to a location outside it.

When the agent asked to write a file called test.txt, the prompt showed only the workspace path. It gave no sign that the file would land elsewhere.

The roots of this go back to May 2026. Adversa AI published research showing that the Claude Code command-line tool had the same display flaw.

A link at ./link that pointed to /etc/ would show as ./link/passwd in the prompt, not the real /etc/passwd. Anthropic reportedly called that report not a security issue, but Adversa says the company fixed it quietly a few weeks later.

The command-line tool now shows the real file location. It also warns the user when a symlink leads outside a trusted folder. The VS Code extension never got the same change. Pearson says it still fails to show the link target in version 2.1.322, the latest at the time of writing.

The risk grows when an agent is tricked. A rogue agent, or one fooled by a malicious instruction, could get a user to approve access that seems harmless.

Attackers already target tools like this, as seen in how attackers can hijack AI coding agents with planted text. The real impact depends on which symlinks exist. A link to the home folder, for example, could expose SSH keys stored in ~/.ssh/.

Anthropic’s Trusted Workspace Argument

Pearson reported the issue to Anthropic through its HackerOne program. Anthropic closed the report as informative. It said the prompt alone is enough and that the text shown in it is not part of the security control.

It also said symlinks fall outside the permission threat model, although Ultrastrike says the public program guide does not list that exclusion.

Anthropic’s view rests on a trust model. Once a user opens a workspace, the tool trusts everything in it, including symlinks. Pearson questions this logic.

If the workspace is fully trusted, he asks, why does the tool ask for permission at all? A prompt suggests a security boundary, and that boundary only works if the user sees accurate details.

He also points to two cases where the trust model can fail. First, a developer’s account in the same company may be compromised. The attacker can push a bad commit with a symlink, and it lands in every teammate’s workspace on the next sync, because Git supports symlinks.

Second, depending on the permission mode, the extension can rename files without asking. A known link could be renamed, and the user would no longer spot it in the prompt.

These risks matter more as teams lean on AI tools. Other recent research on AI coding agent flaws shows that weak guardrails around permissions are a repeated pattern, not a one-off bug.

No patch exists yet, so Ultrastrike suggests a manual check. Before approving a request, copy the path from the prompt and run realpath <path displayed in permission dialog> in a terminal.

The command prints the true location on disk. If that location is outside the workspace, the agent’s request may involve a symlink and should be denied.

Developers should also review repositories for unexpected symlinks after each sync. Teams should be careful with extensions too, since a malicious Claude Code extension recently appeared in extension marketplaces and showed how much trust these tools carry.

articles.title: Hackers Use AI-Powered Marketplace to Find Infected Computers With Corporate VPN and Cloud Access
articles.description:
A new underground marketplace is making stolen computer data much easier to search. It adds a short written profile to each infected computer, so buyers can look for the exact kind of victim they want. They no longer have to dig through raw files. The service was advertised on a cybercrime forum on November 14, […]

The post Hackers Use AI-Powered Marketplace to Find Infected Computers With Corporate VPN and Cloud Access appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new underground marketplace is making stolen computer data much easier to search. It adds a short written profile to each infected computer, so buyers can look for the exact kind of victim they want. They no longer have to dig through raw files.

The service was advertised on a cybercrime forum on November 14, 2026. Buyers can type plain-language searches and narrow the results by country, operating system, and price.

One example search read “citrix access to healthcare provider,” which shows how quickly a criminal could hunt for corporate VPN and cloud access.

Analysts at Infostealers, the research hub run by Hudson Rock, identified several logs sold on the marketplace. They matched those logs to infection records already in their own database.

The operator claims tens of millions of logs, more than one billion parsed accounts, and AI analysis of every log, with prices from $0.25. The researchers stress that these are the seller’s claims and have not been independently confirmed.

Hackers Use AI-Powered Marketplace

Infostealers are malware that quietly copy saved passwords, browser cookies, and other files from a computer. Criminals then sell this stolen data in bundles called logs.

As we covered in how infostealer logs fuel cloud breaches, these logs are often the first step into company networks, VPN gateways, and cloud services.

This marketplace adds a description to every log. A stolen machine may be shown as a clinic’s front desk, a defense contractor’s home computer, or a government worker’s family PC.

Buyers can also search by domain, email, cookies, and files. The listings carry tags and scores, but the screenshots do not explain how those scores are worked out.

The clearest example was a $10 listing called “The Ophthalmology Clinic Front Desk Dump.” It describes a Canadian clinic computer with medical software, billing activity, and Citrix VPN credentials. The seller shows 11 password entries and 574 cookies.

Those are inventory counts, not proof of working logins. Hudson Rock matched this listing to its own data using a Firefox profile name visible in the file preview.

Its records showed the computer was labeled “Reception” and held saved Citrix-related login links and billing usernames. Hudson Rock’s AI agent, Enki, also judged the machine to be a front-desk workstation.

Other listings followed the same pattern. A $9 listing described a defense-industry contractor’s home computer with a 100/100 score. Another $10 listing claimed a Washington, D.C. government employee’s family PC.

A third claimed an AI researcher’s machine in New Delhi with “valid Anthropic Claude API session tokens.” These are the seller’s words, and the researchers could not confirm them.

Why Searchable Victim Profiles Raise the Risk for Companies

Descriptions save criminals time. Buyers once had to read through large logs to work out who owned a computer and what it could reach. Now a short summary does that work.

Hudson Rock believes this could cut the manual effort, though the screenshots do not measure how well the system works. The idea is not entirely new. The U.S. Department of Justice said in 2023 that Genesis Market let buyers search by location and account type.

Cisco Talos also described how VOLTA malware uses AI to rate what stolen data is worth. Hudson Rock found no link between VOLTA and this marketplace.

Stolen cookies matter as much as passwords. A valid session cookie can let someone back into an account without a new MFA prompt, as explained in how session cookie theft leads to SaaS account takeovers.

Criminals can also pay little for bulk data and more for targeted access, a trend covered when stolen credentials flood criminal markets at record levels.

Readers should avoid overstating the findings. The account search returned rows for uber.com and fbi.gov, but that does not show either organization was breached.

A listing shows an asking price, not a completed sale. Saved passwords also do not prove a working login, and the “Saved” dates in password files are not infection dates.

Hudson Rock suggests defenders follow three steps. First, map the stolen items to the affected accounts and the job the computer did.

Second, clean the infected computer, reset passwords from a trusted device, and revoke active sessions and tokens. Third, review sign-in and audit logs for unfamiliar sessions or account changes.

articles.title: Retadup USB Worm Returns After 7 Years, Spreading CoffeeLoader Malware to Windows Systems
articles.description:
The Retadup USB worm is again being used to deliver malware to Windows systems, seven years after French authorities dismantled its botnet. The latest findings connect the worm to CoffeeLoader, a malware loader that uses graphics hardware during decryption and can download and run additional payloads on infected computers. The timeline needs an important distinction: […]

The post Retadup USB Worm Returns After 7 Years, Spreading CoffeeLoader Malware to Windows Systems appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The Retadup USB worm is again being used to deliver malware to Windows systems, seven years after French authorities dismantled its botnet.

The latest findings connect the worm to CoffeeLoader, a malware loader that uses graphics hardware during decryption and can download and run additional payloads on infected computers.

The timeline needs an important distinction: Retadup’s infrastructure began returning in 2024, rather than suddenly reappearing in 2026.

Previously used command-and-control domains were registered again and used to deliver SmokeLoader before switching to CoffeeLoader in early 2025. The identity of whoever revived those servers remains unknown.

Researchers from Securelist identified a new CoffeeLoader variant in August 2026 and described its connection to Retadup in a technical report published November 16.

Their findings show how old USB infections can become useful delivery channels when attackers regain control of the domains those infections still contact.

Retadup USB Worm Returns After 7 Years

First discovered in 2017, Retadup was written using AutoIt and AutoHotkey. It copies itself onto connected USB flash drives and external drives, using hidden files and Windows shortcuts.

When someone moves an infected drive to another computer and opens the malicious shortcut, the worm spreads to that system. The technique relies on user interaction, not simply inserting a drive.

Similar deception appears in weaponized Windows shortcut attacks that hide genuine files and present misleading replacements, showing why familiar document names do not prove that removable storage is safe.

In July 2019, French law enforcement took control of Retadup’s command servers. Infected computers received instructions to remove the worm when they checked in, leading to more than 850,000 systems being disinfected within weeks.

However, Securelist documented a 2017 variant still communicating successfully with revived infrastructure in 2026. Retadup’s command protocol is relatively simple: plaintext instructions are encoded with Base64 and then converted to hexadecimal.

That simplicity leaves researchers unable to determine whether the original developer or another party restarted operations. The revived servers initially distributed SmokeLoader packed with a 32-bit Armoury version.

Kaspersky blocked Retadup infection attempts on around 15,000 systems during the first three quarters of 2026, mainly in Peru, Angola, Russia, and Bolivia.

These are blocked attempts, not confirmed CoffeeLoader infections. Separately, reporting on PlugX USB worm activity illustrates the continued use of removable drives for malware distribution, without establishing any connection between the campaigns.

CoffeeLoader Adds GPU Decryption and a New Download Stage

The observed CoffeeLoader installer drops a modified library belonging to the popular 7-Zip archiver and executes it through a legitimate Windows utility.

Attackers replaced part of the library’s code with self-decrypting shellcode belonging to an updated Armoury packer. This is a maliciously altered file, not evidence of a vulnerability in 7-Zip.

Armoury previously used OpenCL to decrypt its payload through the GPU. The new version switches to OpenGL, a graphics interface commonly associated with rendering applications.

It also introduces an intermediate downloader that combines installation, persistence, process injection, and retrieval of CoffeeLoader’s main body.

For persistence, the downloader copies its library into application-data folders and creates a registry startup entry. Folder names, library names, and registry values use eight hexadecimal characters derived from system volume information.

It also changes startup-approval settings to prevent users from disabling its autorun entry through Task Manager. The downloader then injects itself into one of several Windows processes and retrieves encrypted shellcode over HTTPS.

It verifies a digital signature and the decrypted payload’s checksum before executing the downloaded code in memory. CoffeeLoader retains three execution options: process injection, launching an executable, or running a downloaded DLL.

The findings support checking removable drives alongside endpoint and network telemetry. Earlier coverage of CMoon worm propagation methods describes another malware family using USB shortcuts, reinforcing the value of investigating suspicious replacements rather than trusting displayed file names.

articles.title: Apple Reveals How Secure Exclaves Prevent Hidden Camera and Microphone Access on iPhones
articles.description:
Apple has detailed how Secure Exclaves protect camera and microphone data, aiming to stop attackers from secretly collecting sensitive recordings even if they compromise the main operating system. The architecture combines hardware isolation, strict data-sharing rules, and protected privacy indicators to separate background sensing from active recording. According to the supplied technical description, Apple uses […]

The post Apple Reveals How Secure Exclaves Prevent Hidden Camera and Microphone Access on iPhones appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Apple has detailed how Secure Exclaves protect camera and microphone data, aiming to stop attackers from secretly collecting sensitive recordings even if they compromise the main operating system.

The architecture combines hardware isolation, strict data-sharing rules, and protected privacy indicators to separate background sensing from active recording.

According to the supplied technical description, Apple uses these protections for sensor indicators on iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo. The design also supports background recognition features, where devices must detect faces or wake words without exposing raw audio or video to apps.

Secure Exclaves divide sensor use into ambient and active modes. In ambient mode, protected software processes camera frames or microphone input and shares only limited results, such as whether it recognized a familiar voice. Raw sensor data stays inside the protected environment and is discarded after processing.

Active mode allows full sensor data to reach the operating system for tasks such as FaceTime or a Siri request. Before that transfer begins, a secure controller must confirm that the relevant privacy indicator is visible.

Apple Reveals Secure Exclaves

This addresses a practical problem with background sensing. A light that glowed whenever wake-word detection ran would stay on constantly, making it harder to distinguish passive processing from actual recording.

The foundation is a small operating system built around an Apple microkernel. Components receive explicit permissions for memory and communication rather than broad access by default.

Memory protection relies on the Secure Page Table Monitor. Apple’s platform documentation confirms that this component operates above the kernel and protects memory mappings even when attackers gain kernel write capabilities. Secure Exclaves extend that separation to keep their private memory outside the main system’s reach.

Protected Neural Engine queues support demanding recognition models while keeping their workloads separate. Local storage is cleared when switching from isolated to standard queues to reduce data leakage.

Secure IPC, written in Swift, restricts communication to approved interfaces. Only narrowly defined results should cross the boundary, not unrestricted audio buffers or camera frames.

The Exclave Indicator Controller acts as the gatekeeper. It releases full sensor data only after confirming the indicator has appeared for long enough.

On iPhones, a separate display exclave checks the indicator’s actual pixels, including its shape, color, brightness, and visibility. This means drawing a dot is not enough if another screen element hides it.

During “Hey Siri” detection, the Always-On Processor first checks for possible wake words. Protected exclaves then clean and verify the audio. The main operating system initially receives only a wake signal. Audio is released after the indicator check, and the indicator remains visible for at least three seconds.

The approach complements Apple’s Memory Integrity Enforcement, which targets memory corruption used in advanced attacks. It also adds context to ongoing warnings about mercenary spyware affecting selected iPhone users.

Apple says mathematical verification has helped uncover deep microkernel bugs, but coverage remains incomplete. Its broader formal verification work likewise stresses that proofs depend on defined assumptions. Secure Exclaves therefore raise the barrier to hidden sensor access rather than establish that an entire device cannot be compromised.

articles.description:
AI-powered penetration testing tools are helping hackers automate reconnaissance, vulnerability testing, and follow-on attacks with less hands-on work. Cisco Talos warns that these platforms can connect familiar security utilities with AI agents, allowing operators to pursue targets faster and run several tasks at once. The danger comes from how legitimate testing capabilities are being used […]

The post Cisco Talos Reveals How Hackers Use ARTEX, PentAGI, and HexStrike AI to Automate Cyberattacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
AI-powered penetration testing tools are helping hackers automate reconnaissance, vulnerability testing, and follow-on attacks with less hands-on work.

Cisco Talos warns that these platforms can connect familiar security utilities with AI agents, allowing operators to pursue targets faster and run several tasks at once.

The danger comes from how legitimate testing capabilities are being used against organizations without permission. ARTEX, PentAGI, and HexStrike AI illustrate different approaches to this automation.

Instead of simply suggesting commands, these frameworks connect AI models with tools that perform security tasks. Their growing availability lowers technical barriers for attackers, while giving experienced operators ways to scale operations and shorten the time defenders have to respond.

Cisco Talos researchers identified growing malicious use of these frameworks in a November 13 report, including ARTEX activity associated with credential theft and malware deployment.

The distinction matters: these platforms are dual-use security tools, not malware families themselves. Earlier reporting on ARTEX AI attack automation explains how agents turn operator goals into connected technical actions.

Hackers Use ARTEX, PentAGI, and HexStrike AI

ARTEX appeared on GitHub in July 2026 under the developer name Autumn-27. An operator supplies a target and objective, and a planner agent divides the work into tasks.

Worker agents execute those tasks using security tools, while a shared graph records discovered assets, findings, and progress. This structure lets subsequent actions build on earlier results with relatively little operator input.

PentAGI provides a self-hosted, multi-agent testing environment with a web interface for monitoring activity and viewing attack-chain graphs. Talos found more than 700 reachable PentAGI instances online.

HexStrike AI connects with Claude Code, VS Code, and other clients supporting Model Context Protocol, or MCP. These differences concern how operators connect, manage, and observe automated workflows, rather than proving equivalent malicious activity across all three platforms.

ARTEX has the clearest campaign evidence in the report. Talos cites Microsoft findings that Storm-0940 used compromised ConnectWise application credentials to accelerate sign-in attempts against more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 tenants.

The previously documented Microsoft 365 tenant attacks show how trusted application access can extend a compromise into connected customer environments.

Other reported activity involved password spraying, weak administrative credentials, missing API authentication, command injection, and authorization flaws.

Agents also searched public repositories for exposed secrets. In one Microsoft-observed case, the transition from GitHub searches to Azure Key Vault data theft took five minutes. Reporting on GitHub secrets theft automation details how leaked credentials became a bridge into cloud resources.

Detection and Containment Must Match Automated Attack Speeds

Talos identified more than 2,500 ARTEX-associated infrastructure IP addresses and examined tools present during overlapping periods. These included PentAGI, VShell, AdaptixC2, Mimikatz, Cobalt Strike, and several scanners.

However, shared infrastructure does not prove that ARTEX launched every tool or that one operator controlled everything. ARTEX also does not ship with a traditional command-and-control framework, although MCP allows operators to add compatible servers.

That distinction matters when assessing alerts. A recognizable tool or user agent can provide an investigative lead, but defenders need supporting evidence.

Talos recommends correlating authentication, endpoint, and cloud API logs for rapid requests, unfamiliar applications, unusual token use, and privilege changes. Its findings reinforce the concerns described in the FBI ARTEX security warning about attackers compressing intrusion timelines.

Organizations should patch exposed systems, remove default passwords, enforce multifactor authentication, and apply rate limits against credential attacks.

Public repositories need secret scanning, while exposed credentials require immediate revocation and rotation. Least-privilege application permissions can reduce downstream access.

Talos also advises endpoint tamper protection and tested procedures for disabling suspicious applications, revoking tokens, and isolating affected systems quickly.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are no longer just asking AI chatbots for help. They now run AI agents that can scan, break in, and move through networks with very little human input.

In its latest AI Threat Tracker, published on November 16, 2026, the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant said AI misuse has reached a “critical inflection point” across cybercrime, spying, and influence campaigns.

The findings come from Mandiant incident response cases, global tracking of threat groups, and Google’s own platform defenses. Google says attackers are using AI to shorten attack timelines, grow their operations, and run multi-stage intrusions at machine speed.

Google AI Agent Cyberattacks

Google says threat actors are actively using open-source, multi-agent hacking frameworks such as ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI. GTIG saw CAIRN and PentAGI used in the wild and spotted testing of CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike AI.

CAIRN was used in intrusions against US aerospace targets. A custom platform built on PentAGI scanned many organizations in Asia between late August and early October 2026.

ARTEX remains the best-known example. Cyber Security News earlier reported how hackers use ARTEX AI agents to automate Active Directory attacks, with single bursts of activity lasting just 2 to 25 seconds.

Wiz researchers also tracked an ARTEX-using actor, overlapping with Microsoft’s Storm-0940, that went after Okta, Entra, and Cognito identity systems at IT and software vendors.

There is a weak spot. Google says these tools trade stealth for speed, leaving noisy traffic, known names, and clear code traces behind. Even so, they still reach their goals, and Google expects less human involvement and better stealth over time.

For the first time, GTIG found attackers using AI to find and exploit flaws with no human in the loop. An exposed staging server hosted a framework called “exploit_agent” that compares web software code before and after patches, finds bugs, writes exploits, and runs them on its own.

Russian comments in its setup files pointed to a pilot project. The operator focused on French media, entertainment, and education websites.

Real cases back this up. After two PaperCut flaws (CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078) were exploited as zero-days in August 2026, GreyNoise reported an AI-assisted campaign that hit hundreds of organizations and reached domain admin within minutes.

Zero-day exploits climbed from 8 per month in 2025 to 11 per month in 2026, then jumped to 22 in August.

Money-driven groups keep stealing AI keys and cloud access, then reselling it through “LLM Mixers.” Google’s LLMJacking research found fake charges topping $100,000 in a single day, with some victims reaching $1 million. Our earlier report on LLM Hijacking attacks and million-dollar cloud bills explains how attackers test stolen keys with tiny requests to avoid alerts.

A suspected North Korean cluster, MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE, used fake recruiter profiles with AI-made images and ClickFix lures to break into crypto firms. It then changed .claude/settings.json files so Claude Code would download the SOMBERMEME backdoor at startup. It also hid its tracks with GitHub tokens named after Microsoft Copilot.

Influence groups now use AI as part of their normal work. One contractor used the Gemini API while building a platform designed to run over 100,000 social media accounts with cloud phone farms. Fake accounts were “aged” by AI that copied normal scrolling and viewing habits before posting political messages.

Google SecOps has released behavior-based rules to detect ARTEX. Mandiant’s five-layer defense guide advises teams to lock down admin systems, use short-lived credentials, limit access, split networks, and watch for sudden spikes in API and identity activity.

For AI services, teams should set budget alerts, scan code for leaked keys, and treat any unexpected AI service activation as a serious warning.

As Google notes, the methods have not changed. AI simply lets attackers chain them together much faster, so defenders have less time to respond.

articles.title: Mustang Panda-Linked Hackers Deploy LOTUSLITE V2 Through Malicious Zoho WorkDrive Downloads
articles.description:
Hackers linked to Mustang Panda are distributing LOTUSLITE V2 through public Zoho WorkDrive downloads, using an Indo-Pacific assessment lure to draw victims into running malware. The campaign, focused on Thailand, combines a trusted PDFgear executable, malicious DLL loading, registry persistence, and encrypted command-and-control communications to establish access to Windows systems. The operation shows how attackers […]

The post Mustang Panda-Linked Hackers Deploy LOTUSLITE V2 Through Malicious Zoho WorkDrive Downloads appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers linked to Mustang Panda are distributing LOTUSLITE V2 through public Zoho WorkDrive downloads, using an Indo-Pacific assessment lure to draw victims into running malware.

The campaign, focused on Thailand, combines a trusted PDFgear executable, malicious DLL loading, registry persistence, and encrypted command-and-control communications to establish access to Windows systems.

The operation shows how attackers can reuse familiar delivery methods while changing the backdoor underneath. Earlier reporting on LOTUSLITE espionage targeting India documented a Microsoft-signed launcher, whereas this campaign uses PDFgear software as its execution cover.

Both approaches place malicious code beside a legitimate application so that running the trusted program also activates the attacker’s payload.

Researchers from Antares Research identified the malware as a modernized .NET successor to LOTUSLITE in their November 15 technical analysis.

Authors Kyaw Pyiyt Htet and PHYO PAING HTUN assessed the lineage with high confidence, citing shared protocol design, execution methods, persistence techniques, and regional targeting.

That assessment links the activity to Mustang Panda, also known as Earth Preta, rather than establishing attribution through geography alone.

Mustang Panda-Linked Hackers Deploy LOTUSLITE V2

The infection chain starts with a public WorkDrive link that immediately downloads an assessment-themed ZIP archive when clicked.

Inside are an executable named to resemble the promised assessment and a companion malicious library. Downloading the archive is the delivery step; execution follows when the victim runs its executable. The report does not establish how the link initially reached each target.

The use of a business file-sharing platform gives the download a familiar setting. Separate reporting on Zoho WorkDrive malware delivery described unrelated PureRAT distribution through shared folders, showing why a legitimate hosting service cannot establish a file’s safety.

Here, the evidence describes abuse of a public download link, not exploitation of a Zoho vulnerability. After launch, the assessment-themed executable stages two components in a Microsoft-themed directory beneath ProgramData.

A trusted PDFgear executable then loads the malicious library from that location through DLL sideloading. The signed application provides the execution path, but its signature does not make the adjacent library trustworthy. This distinction matters when investigators review apparently legitimate software activity.

The malware establishes persistence through conditional registry changes. When running as SYSTEM, it writes a system-wide Run entry; otherwise, it uses the current user’s Windows Load value.

It also changes PDFgear’s file-opening association to point to an attacker-controlled launcher, forwarding the selected document path. These changes provide multiple routes for restarting execution during normal Windows use.

Encrypted Communications and Detection Priorities

LOTUSLITE V2 moves from the family’s earlier native C++ implementation to managed C#. Previous Mustang Panda cloud abuse involved WorkDrive-based command exchange and data theft, but the roles differ here: WorkDrive delivers the archive, while this implant contains two hardcoded command-server addresses. Keeping those functions separate helps defenders avoid treating all cloud-related activity as the same technique.

The configuration stores those addresses in byte arrays decoded at runtime with a single-byte XOR key. Antares describes UDP communication and secure WebSocket options across several ports, alongside progressively longer connection retries.

Its network evidence includes process-attributed outbound traffic, giving investigators a way to connect suspicious communications with the staged executable rather than relying on destination addresses alone.

The backdoor also introduces a versioned protocol marker and application-layer AES-256-GCM encryption. Unlike encryption supplied only by a transport connection, this additional layer protects the payload itself.

The implementation calls Windows cryptographic functions directly through a compatibility wrapper, which researchers say supports older Windows endpoints without relying on .NET’s higher-level encryption wrapper.

Defenders should correlate unexpected PDFgear execution, registry changes, unusual library loading, and outbound connections. Earlier Mustang Panda sideloading techniques show why execution behavior remains useful even when filenames change.

Antares also warns that signatures matching older LOTUSLITE protocol markers will miss the updated identifier. Its conclusions remain subject to revision as further evidence emerges.

Indicators of compromise (IoCs):-

Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.]) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM.

articles.description:
New York, USA, November 16th, 2026, CyberNewswire AI attribution has linked more than 3,913 high-impact leaks to 1,532 companies since spring; security experts handle critical disclosures to enterprise security teams. GitGuardian, the secrets security platform, today announced the Enterprise Good Samaritan Program, an expansion of its longstanding responsible disclosure efforts aimed at strengthening security across […]

The post Leaked Credentials Are an Enterprise Problem: GitGuardian Extends Its Good Samaritan Program to Security Teams appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
New York, USA, November 16th, 2026, CyberNewswire

AI attribution has linked more than 3,913 high-impact leaks to 1,532 companies since spring; security experts handle critical disclosures to enterprise security teams.

GitGuardian, the secrets security platform, today announced the Enterprise Good Samaritan Program, an expansion of its longstanding responsible disclosure efforts aimed at strengthening security across the broader digital ecosystem.

Combining AI-powered attribution with expert security analysis, the program identifies high-impact credential leaks that could give attackers a path into an organization’s systems or data.

It traces these exposures to affected companies and delivers actionable disclosures to their security teams, showing how an attacker could exploit the credentials and what they could gain access to.

For the first time, GitGuardian can extend these warnings to any company in the world, regardless of its size or whether it’s a GitGuardian customer.

Since 2018, GitGuardian’s original Good Samaritan Program has detected more than 83 million exposed secrets on public GitHub, sending 11.9 million alerts to 5.9 million developers.

But notifying a developer doesn’t necessarily lead to revocation. Approximately 90% of valid secrets remain unrevoked a week after the developer responsible for the leak has been alerted.

To date, the Enterprise Good Samaritan Program has linked more than 3,913 high-impact leaks to 1,532 companies. GitGuardian followed up with them, typically reaching at least five people at each organization. 

The scale of the problem is growing. GitGuardian’s 2026 State of Secrets Sprawl report found that 28.65 million new secrets were exposed on public GitHub in 2025, a 34% year-over-year increase.

The Enterprise Good Samaritan Program gets exposed credentials to the security teams that can revoke them.

“For years, we’ve warned developers, but they’re not always the ones who can revoke it. Our expertise combined with AI now helps us identify at scale the organizations behind serious exposures at scale, and our researchers work to reach the people who can respond. Attackers now have the ability, with AI offensive harnesses like ARTEX, to use these credentials to target companies at scale. Those companies deserve to know, whether they’re our customers or not. And if a company has no clear way to receive a warning, the warning doesn’t help. Every company needs a door for these reports, and someone behind it.” — Eric Fourrier, CEO at GitGuardian

Extending Responsible Disclosure To The Enterprise

The Enterprise Good Samaritan Program combines continuous public monitoring, AI-assisted analysis, and human-led disclosure to identify serious credential exposures and help organizations respond.

GitGuardian monitors public sources, including GitHub and Docker Hub, for exposed credentials. Its AI agents now screen more than 1 million public incidents each month and investigate over 100,000 in depth, helping identify the affected organizations and assess the potential impact of exposure, including credential validity, permissions, and the systems or data at risk.

Human experts review high-impact findings before disclosure, providing the affected organization with the context needed to investigate and remediate the exposure.

Rather than relying exclusively on notifications to individual developers, GitGuardian contacts multiple people within affected organizations, works to reach the relevant security teams, and escalates manually when automated outreach goes unanswered.

The value of this escalation was demonstrated in May 2026, when GitGuardian researchers identified a public GitHub repository containing sensitive CISA-related data and valid cloud credentials.

Nine automated alerts had failed to resolve the exposure. After GitGuardian researchers escalated through CERT/CC and established contacts, the repository was taken offline within 26 hours of human escalation.

The need for timely disclosure is becoming more urgent as attackers automate credential discovery and exploitation. In November 2026, Microsoft documented attackers using agentic AI to search public GitHub repositories for exposed credentials.

In one observed case, an AI agent went from searching for a leaked secret to extracting data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

The speed of these attacks makes unresolved credential exposures especially dangerous, and reinforces the need for organizations to have a reliable way to receive and act on external security disclosures.

Making Organizations Easier To Warn

With only 35% of contacted organizations responding to the program’s outreach, GitGuardian is calling on companies to establish clear, monitored channels for receiving security disclosures from external researchers, such as a security.txt file and a staffed security inbox.

The Enterprise Good Samaritan Program operates under GitGuardian’s published disclosure principles, which emphasize timely notification, non-destructive verification, transparency, traceable research activity, and persistent follow-up.

Organizations receive the full details of their exposures without needing to sign up or become customers.

To learn more about the Enterprise Good Samaritan Program and GitGuardian’s responsible disclosure principles, visit GitGuardian’s Enterprise Good Samaritan Program Page.

Organizations can also assess their exposure on public GitHub using GitGuardian’s GitHub Security Audit.

About GitGuardian

GitGuardian is the secrets security platform built to protect the credentials that let code, machines, and AI agents access critical systems.

The platform helps organizations detect exposed credentials across code, endpoints, and public sources; remediate incidents at scale with identity context, risk prioritization, and guided workflows; and prevent new leaks with security controls embedded in developer and AI coding workflows.

More than 600,000 developers worldwide trust GitGuardian. Enterprise customers include DigitalOcean, ING, BASF, Datadog, Euronext, and Bouygues Telecom.

For more information, visit the GitGuardian website. 

Contact

Holly Hagerman

hollyh@connectmarketing.com

The post Leaked Credentials Are an Enterprise Problem: GitGuardian Extends Its Good Samaritan Program to Security Teams appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: Microsoft Releases Out-of-band Update to Address Windows Licensing and Activation Errors
articles.description:
Microsoft released an out-of-band Windows update on November 13, 2026, to fix licensing and activation errors affecting a limited number of enterprise devices. The issue appeared after the November 2026 Windows security update and mainly affects organizations that use scripts or automated tools to manage Windows licenses. Affected operations may fail with error 0x80041008, shown […]

The post Microsoft Releases Out-of-band Update to Address Windows Licensing and Activation Errors appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft released an out-of-band Windows update on November 13, 2026, to fix licensing and activation errors affecting a limited number of enterprise devices.

The issue appeared after the November 2026 Windows security update and mainly affects organizations that use scripts or automated tools to manage Windows licenses.

Affected operations may fail with error 0x80041008, shown as “Invalid parameter,” when using the Software Licensing Management Tool, commonly called SLMGR.

Microsoft says devices that were already activated remain activated. Existing Key Management Service configurations are also unaffected when no additional slmgr.vbs commands are required.

The problem affects certain licensing tasks carried out through slmgr.vbs, including configuring Key Management Service activation, installing product keys, and managing Windows licensing. Microsoft’s release notes identify the affected operations but do not explain the underlying code fault.

Microsoft Windows Licensing Error

Microsoft’s SLMGR documentation describes the tool as a built-in Visual Basic script for managing activation from the command line. Administrators can use /ipk to install a product key, /ato to request activation, and /dlv to display detailed license information. These functions explain why the bug matters to teams using automated licensing workflows.

KMS lets organizations activate Windows devices through a host on their local network. The reported fault concerns licensing management operations rather than a general loss of activation across previously activated systems. This limits the immediate impact, although affected scripts may still interrupt routine administration.

Microsoft has issued separate packages for the affected Windows releases. Windows Server 2025 receives KB5136489, while Windows Server 2022 receives KB5136487. Windows Server 2019 and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2019 receive KB5136490.

Windows 11 version 23H2 receives KB5136483. Windows 10 version 22H2 devices covered by Extended Security Updates, along with Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021, receive KB5136493.

These optional, non-security updates are cumulative and include improvements from the November security release. Microsoft’s out-of-band update guidance explains that such releases address problems that cannot wait for the next scheduled update. The release timing alone does not mean a new security threat exists.

Microsoft has previously used this approach for Windows reset and recovery failures and Remote Desktop credential prompt failures. Those cases involved different faults but show how targeted fixes can restore functions disrupted by earlier updates.

For the listed Windows Server and Windows 10 releases, the packages are available only through the Microsoft Update Catalog. Windows 11 version 23H2 users can also open Settings > Windows Update > Advanced options > Optional updates.

Before deployment, administrators should match the package to the affected Windows version, check prerequisites and restart requirements, and test it on representative devices. Microsoft advises installing optional non-security OOB updates on systems experiencing the issue. Unaffected organizations can generally wait for a later cumulative update that includes the fix.

articles.title: New OWASP Top 10 Exposes Hidden Security Weaknesses in Neocloud and AI Infrastructure
articles.description:
A new OWASP Incubator Project highlights an overlooked AI security gap: the servers, networks, and data centers supporting AI systems receive far less attention than models, apps, and agents. The OWASP Top 10 Neocloud and AI Data Center Security Risks tries to fix that. It gives neocloud providers, their customers, and AI data center operators […]

The post New OWASP Top 10 Exposes Hidden Security Weaknesses in Neocloud and AI Infrastructure appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new OWASP Incubator Project highlights an overlooked AI security gap: the servers, networks, and data centers supporting AI systems receive far less attention than models, apps, and agents.

The OWASP Top 10 Neocloud and AI Data Center Security Risks tries to fix that. It gives neocloud providers, their customers, and AI data center operators one shared list of the biggest infrastructure risks.

AI data centers pack thousands of GPUs, fast network fabrics, remote management controllers, shared storage, and complex scheduling tools into one place.

Much of this gear came from high-performance computing, where users were trusted. Today, the same parts run commercial GPU clouds, where unrelated companies share the same hardware. A flaw once considered minor can now put many customers at risk.

Many security tools also cannot see this layer. They watch operating systems, apps, and normal networks. They often miss firmware, management ports, and the special links that join GPU nodes. If the base is compromised, nothing running on top can be trusted.

Michael Katchinskiy and Yakir Kadkoda of the security firm Lava lead the project. The team selected risks from security research, incident reports, published CVEs, vendor documents, and practitioner talks.

Each candidate was scored on likelihood, impact, and detectability. Reviewers came from companies and schools such as Dell, Nebius, Google, IBM, and the University of Basel.

OWASP Top 10 Exposes Neocloud AI Risks

The project does not cover prompt injection or model abuse. Other frameworks, including the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and MITRE ATLAS, handle those.

OWASP ranks the risks from most to least severe. The first five are rated critical. These are hardware and firmware tampering, weak networks between GPUs, poor separation between tenants, unsafe out-of-band management, and supply chain compromise.

Lower on the list are weak facility systems, careless handling of data and model files, gaps in certifications and provider honesty, unsafe operations tools, and slow patching.

Firmware and management controllers deserve a close look. A baseboard management controller, or BMC, lets admins control a server even when its operating system is off. If a hacker takes it over, the access can survive a reinstall and follow the server to the next customer.

OWASP Top 10 Risks:

This is not just theory. Researchers recently found 36,872 internet-exposed IPMI interfaces, and about 67 percent leaked password-based authentication data before login.

Some belonged to GPU and bare-metal cloud providers. Earlier, a flaw in AMI MegaRAC software (CVE-2024-54085) let attackers skip login on affected servers.

Our own BMC firmware vulnerabilities report showed how weak Supermicro patches left the door open. Tenant isolation is another weak spot.

The NVIDIAScape container escape flaw, CVE-2025-23266, let a malicious container gain root access on a GPU host. It hit toolkit versions up to 1.17.7. That is the exact kind of problem the OWASP list warns about.

The framework notes that attackers have begun targeting AI infrastructure. It cites a TIME report about a US tech firm whose AI data center lost intellectual property.

It also cites a conviction for stealing AI data center designs and claims of a 10-petabyte theft from China’s Tianjin supercomputing center. The authors also warn that GPU shortages mean customers often pick whatever provider has capacity, not the most secure one.

Providers can use the list to review their setups and show maturity. Customers can use it when buying, writing contracts, and comparing vendors. Ask a provider whether its audit covers the GPU hardware, and whether it resells capacity from someone else.

Security teams should keep BMCs off the public internet, patch firmware, and put management traffic on its own network. Our AI data center security checklist offers a 60-day plan to do that.

The post Australia’s Supermarket Chain Coles Investigates Cyber Security Incident appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Australian supermarket chain Coles is investigating a cybersecurity incident, with outside experts helping secure its systems. The retailer disclosed the incident on November 16, 2026, and said stores and online shopping remain open. Investigators have found no evidence that customer, employee or supplier data has been compromised or removed.

Coles is working with the Australian Cyber Security Center and global cyber security experts to contain the incident and protect its IT environment. The company said it would continue engaging with relevant agencies and regulators as its investigation develops, while closely monitoring systems for signs of further security problems.

The current finding is not a final guarantee that no data was affected. Coles qualified its statement as being based on its investigation so far. Its public update does not identify an attacker, explain how the incident began, name affected systems, or confirm whether ransomware was involved. Those details remain unknown.

Customers can continue using the Coles app and website normally. Flybuys accounts show no indication of impact, while Coles Plus, Coles Plus Delivery and QuiteLike subscriptions remain available. Gift cards also continue working. These updates distinguish the confirmed incident from claims of widespread service failure or account compromise.

Coles Investigates Cyber Security Incident

However, Coles acknowledged that a small number of customers were experiencing problems with Liquorland click-and-collect orders. The retailer is investigating those issues but has not publicly explained their cause or confirmed a connection to the security incident. It currently says customers do not need to take any incident-specific action.

The official Coles incident update remains the main source for confirmed findings. Other retail incidents provide context, not evidence about this case. Cyber Security News previously covered retail chains facing cyberattacks, including Marks & Spencer, Harrods and Co-op. Their experiences should not be treated as proof of the methods used against Coles.

Separate reporting on the Harrods customer data breach shows why retailers must distinguish attacks on their own systems from incidents involving suppliers. Coles has not named a third-party provider as the source of this incident. No public technical findings currently support attributing it to a particular group, tool or entry method.

Coles warns customers to watch for unexpected emails, texts, calls and requests for personal details. It says unsolicited emails or SMS messages will never request passwords or sensitive account information. Customers should avoid suspicious links, use unique passwords, and verify doubtful messages.
