articles.title: Claude Gets VirusTotal Threat Intelligence Capabilities for AI-Assisted Malware and URL Analysis
articles.description:
Claude users can connect VirusTotal threat intelligence to their investigations, bringing file, URL, domain, and IP reports into an AI workflow. The connection lets analysts review detection findings, analysis dates, coverage, and source links without treating an AI answer as a security verdict. The integration uses Model Context Protocol, or MCP, to connect Claude with […]

The post Claude Gets VirusTotal Threat Intelligence Capabilities for AI-Assisted Malware and URL Analysis appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Claude users can connect VirusTotal threat intelligence to their investigations, bringing file, URL, domain, and IP reports into an AI workflow. The connection lets analysts review detection findings, analysis dates, coverage, and source links without treating an AI answer as a security verdict.

The integration uses Model Context Protocol, or MCP, to connect Claude with VirusTotal AI, known as VTAI. Users authenticate through browser OAuth without providing a personal VirusTotal API key. Organization rules may require an owner to approve the connector before employees can use it.

For security teams, the main benefit is evidence review. An analyst can provide a file hash or suspicious address and ask Claude to explain the report. This brings the checks described in Cyber Security News’ VirusTotal research guide into a conversation, while keeping the underlying findings available for review.

Report lookups remain separate from submissions. Only an explicit user request authorizes file uploads, URL submissions or domain and IP reanalysis. Before uploading a file, the service checks its verified hash. Original bytes are uploaded only after confirmed absence, not after a permission error or failed lookup.

The approach extends a workflow covered in the VirusTotal ChatGPT integration. However, missing reports and zero detections do not establish safety. Analysts still need to consider report age and coverage rather than reading an empty result as approval to open a file or link.

Local File Analysis and Privacy Limits

According to VirusTotal’s Claude Code documentation, an optional plugin adds a threat intelligence skill and local file hook. The hook checks permitted paths, original bytes, size, and SHA-256 before transfer. It blocks common credential filenames for human review. Claude chat does not run this local hook, and the remote connector cannot read local paths.

When explicitly requested, submit_attachment can retrieve original file bytes from a public HTTPS download link. This does not establish native Claude attachment support. VirusTotal documents authenticated testing in Claude Code, while noting that hosted Claude chat report workflows, renewal, and writes remain unverified.

The official connection guide lists free access at 60 queries per minute and 1,000 per UTC day, shared across account connections. Repeated reports and explicit analysis reads count each time. New file contributions and owned receipt recovery use no query quota, but separate contribution limits apply.

Standard submissions are shared with VirusTotal’s community and security partners, so private documents, internal code, credentials and personal data require permission before disclosure. URL queries expose the complete address, including parameters and fragments.

Users can revoke access through Your connections, but removing the plugin does not erase prior submissions or receipts already held by the service.

articles.title: Nine Underground Listings Reveal How Hackers Sell Access to Enterprise VPNs, Cloud, and CI/CD Systems
articles.description:
Nine underground advertisements show how hackers package alleged access to enterprise VPNs, cloud accounts, software delivery systems, and business applications for sale. The offers range from individual remote-access accounts to bundles of cloud keys, database credentials, and authenticated sessions that could expose connected systems if genuine. The listings illustrate a market where permissions and business […]

The post Nine Underground Listings Reveal How Hackers Sell Access to Enterprise VPNs, Cloud, and CI/CD Systems appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Nine underground advertisements show how hackers package alleged access to enterprise VPNs, cloud accounts, software delivery systems, and business applications for sale.

The offers range from individual remote-access accounts to bundles of cloud keys, database credentials, and authenticated sessions that could expose connected systems if genuine.

The listings illustrate a market where permissions and business reach matter more than password counts. As reporting on initial access broker operations explains, sellers can supply entry points that other criminals use for ransomware, theft, or fraud.

However, these advertisements do not independently prove any breach. ThreatMon researchers identified the nine listings across DarkForums, Exploitin, and PwnForums between November 2 and November 9, 2026.

Their November 11 research report documents access-sale claims rather than a newly identified malware family. Several sellers had little forum history, and advertised privileges, prices, and sale status remained unverified.

Nine Underground Listings

One detailed November 5 listing concerned a Nordic warehouse-automation group. Seller marlowfinch42 claimed a TeamCity account with SYSTEM_ADMIN rights, Windows SYSTEM access on a domain-joined build host, and SQL Server 2017 sysadmin privileges.

The deployment environment allegedly included 28 databases and 1,133 targets across 130 customer environments.

That combination could expose software delivery workflows and deployment secrets. Crucially, the seller denied possessing Domain Admin credentials and described TeamCity access through an existing user record, not an exploit.

Patching alone would therefore not necessarily invalidate the claimed account. Neither the permissions nor customer exposure was independently confirmed.

Remote-access offers carried clearer prices. BigTuna advertised Pulse Secure VPN access to a Turkish manufacturer for $980, claiming “Enterprise Admin” privileges and more than 10,000 hosts.

Separately, SCP-2013 requested $4,000 for alleged FortiGate, SSH, and FortiSSLVPN access to a US manufacturer, referencing 81 hosts without establishing their reachability.

A broader ERP SaaS offer bundled 180 Aliyun key pairs, allegedly including 114 active pairs, with 525 ECS instances, 237,498 plaintext MySQL credentials, and 44,807 API tokens.

Coverage of infostealer logs fueling breaches provides wider context for credential resale, although ThreatMon did not establish how this seller obtained the advertised material.

Another seller offered a mobile game publisher’s repositories, deployment server, and cloud keys, initially referencing more than 1,000 EC2 instances.

A Mexican-Canadian VPS provider listing instead promoted hosting infrastructure for ransomware and botnet operations, but supplied little technical evidence about the systems or permissions available.

The remaining offers covered French RDP access, a US industrial distributor’s connected services, and an insurance agency’s PandaDoc session.

The distributor package named AWS S3, FTP, Slack, Twilio, and BrowserStack. The $250 PandaDoc offer allegedly exposed more than 8,000 documents, including insurance records and personal information. Both claims remained unconfirmed.

Why Access Sales Require More Than Password Resets

The French RDP seller marked the offer sold and claimed on November 7 that the access had been used. A reference to SGS was not evidence of a breach.

Across the sample, “sold” labels and seller reputation provided context, not proof of working access or subsequent attacks.

The PandaDoc advertisement highlights why defenders must examine sessions alongside passwords. Reporting on stolen browser session cookies explains how authenticated sessions can remain useful without another login.

Depending on platform controls, changing a password may not terminate every active session or invalidate every refresh token. ThreatMon recommends reviewing remote-access accounts, enforcing multifactor authentication, and removing unused identities.

Build platforms need checks covering administrators, service accounts, deployment secrets, and build agents. Cloud teams should inventory keys and tokens, restrict permissions, and rotate exposed credentials; SaaS investigations should include session revocation and connected-application reviews.

Security teams should preserve authentication and endpoint evidence when a credible listing matches their environment. Unusual database queries, new service accounts, unexpected administrative access, and deployment changes warrant investigation.

These nine posts are a limited snapshot, not a market-wide measurement, but they show why exposure monitoring must extend beyond VPN gateways.

articles.description:
Hackers are using ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration-testing framework, to automate intrusions and shorten the time needed to gain powerful access. In multiple attacks linked to Storm-0940, Microsoft observed attackers moving from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours, according to research published by ExtraHop on November 15, 2026. Originally built for authorized […]

The post Hackers Use ARTEX AI Agents to Automate Network Intrusions and Gain Privileged Access in Under 3 Hour appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are using ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration-testing framework, to automate intrusions and shorten the time needed to gain powerful access.

In multiple attacks linked to Storm-0940, Microsoft observed attackers moving from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours, according to research published by ExtraHop on November 15, 2026.

Originally built for authorized security testing, ARTEX connects large language models with agents that run commands, review results, and choose their next steps.

Its developer removed the original GitHub repository on October 8 following criminal adoption, but copies and forks remain available. The FBI warning on ARTEX describes how attackers use this automation across several intrusion stages.

Researchers from ExtraHop’s Reveal Labs identified network behaviors associated with ARTEX while testing ScopeWeaver, an English-language fork, in a controlled environment.

Their technical analysis of ARTEX concerns a dual-use attack framework, not a newly discovered malware family, and separates laboratory findings from reported real-world compromises.

Hackers Use ARTEX AI Agents

ARTEX reduces manual work by dividing an operator’s objective into smaller tasks. A planner assigns those tasks to worker agents, which can run simultaneously using existing security tools.

Workers store findings in PostgreSQL, allowing the framework to adjust its approach as new information arrives or commands fail. Operators can configure local models or cloud-based services.

That workflow has supported attacks against cloud environments. ExtraHop’s report summarizes Microsoft’s findings that Storm-0940 used compromised ConnectWise Cloud Backup application credentials to attempt authentication against more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants.

The ARTEX Microsoft 365 campaign exploited existing application trust; the targeting count does not mean every tenant was breached. In some environments, attackers used Microsoft Graph to discover resources, modify application credentials, and establish persistence.

These actions show why privileged application access matters: attackers can operate through permissions already granted to trusted software.

The under-three-hour finding describes observed attacks, not a guaranteed capability or a result reproduced by ExtraHop’s laboratory tests.

During those tests, researchers supplied valid and invalid credentials and asked ScopeWeaver to access a Windows host and obtain a domain-controller shell.

Initial SSH and RDP attempts failed. The framework then scanned with Nmap, found Windows Remote Management services, and tried alternative remote-access tools rather than stopping after its first unsuccessful attempts.

The experiment also exposed a reliability problem. ScopeWeaver confirmed WinRM connectivity but failed to establish a remote shell, yet reported success.

In a separate simulation, it successfully used Impacket’s PsExec to change a Windows lock-screen setting. That change demonstrated remote configuration control, but researchers explicitly noted that it did not establish persistence.

Detecting ARTEX Activity Before Attackers Gain Control

ARTEX’s speed does not make its activity invisible. ExtraHop detected scanning, repeated authentication attempts, remote-service activity, PowerShell remoting, and plaintext credential transmission during testing.

Its findings complement reporting on ARTEX enterprise attack automation, showing that familiar intrusion techniques remain useful detection targets even when agents select and execute them.

Visibility depends on where the framework runs. Internal worker messages and model requests may be observable when ARTEX operates inside a monitored network.

When attackers run it externally, those communications may never enter the victim’s environment. Inspecting supported encrypted model traffic also requires appropriate session keys; network monitoring alone does not automatically expose request contents.

Defenders should correlate bursts of failed logins, scanning, changing access methods, and remote execution involving the same systems. ExtraHop recommends investigating related events within short windows instead of relying only on infrastructure lists.

Its research into publicly exposed ARTEX consoles also highlights an important distinction: an exposed framework does not, by itself, prove criminal activity.

articles.title: Hackers Use Falcon C2 to Hijack Government Browsers and Steal Passwords, Emails, and Session Cookies
articles.description:
Hackers have compromised government webmail portals and internal applications using Falcon C2, a browser-based command-and-control framework that steals passwords, emails, session cookies, and private communications. By planting malicious JavaScript inside trusted websites, the attackers turned routine browsing into an entry point for surveillance and account compromise. The activity affected government entities in one Middle Eastern […]

The post Hackers Use Falcon C2 to Hijack Government Browsers and Steal Passwords, Emails, and Session Cookies appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers have compromised government webmail portals and internal applications using Falcon C2, a browser-based command-and-control framework that steals passwords, emails, session cookies, and private communications.

By planting malicious JavaScript inside trusted websites, the attackers turned routine browsing into an entry point for surveillance and account compromise.

The activity affected government entities in one Middle Eastern country and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026. Targets included foreign affairs, defense, and interior ministries, alongside law enforcement agencies.

The selection points toward intelligence collection rather than widespread financial theft, although the affected countries remain unnamed.

Researchers from Unit42 identified Falcon, also called XG or Xiàng Gē, and documented its browser implants, malicious extensions, and delivery of the Antino backdoor.

Their technical analysis of Falcon shows how attackers combined website compromise with persistent browser access to monitor sensitive government work.

Hackers Use Falcon C2

Falcon begins when someone opens an infected website. An injected script requests a JavaScript implant from the attacker’s server, which generates a differently obfuscated version for each browser session.

The script uses numeric encoding and a decoder to hide its contents before execution. The implant establishes a persistent WebSocket connection protected by TLS.

It can additionally encrypt messages using AES-256-CBC after exchanging key material through RSA. Operators can then execute JavaScript, collect information, and label sessions to distinguish victims. The initial page implant remains limited to its browser context.

Researchers found strong technical similarities with PeckBirdy, including matching delivery patterns and tracking conventions. Earlier reporting on PeckBirdy command and control provides context for these overlaps.

Unit42 assessed with high confidence that Falcon and PeckBirdy are variants of the same underlying framework, rather than unrelated tools sharing isolated features.

Browser extensions expand Falcon’s reach. Available for Chrome and Firefox, they disguise themselves as a PDF viewer.

The analyzed Chrome extension requests 40 permissions and access across visited websites, allowing collection of credentials, cookies, browsing history, downloads, clipboard activity, and network traffic.

The extension can also turn a victim’s browser into a proxy. Requests use the victim’s existing credentials and cookies, letting operators access resources under that person’s identity.

Custom commands can retrieve Gmail messages and attachments, while separate functions collect Discord data, Zalo communications, and visible X direct messages.

Falcon’s management interface hides its login until an operator presses F9 three times. Victim-facing servers displayed Tetris or Snake games.

These disguises echo the broader practice of hiding espionage infrastructure online behind ordinary-looking content, although the specific infrastructure and campaigns should not be treated as identical.

Targeted Webmail Intrusions and Antino Delivery

In April 2026, investigators found Falcon injected into a Middle Eastern foreign ministry’s Roundcube portal. They identified 39 affected Roundcube instances within that country.

The malicious script could intercept login credentials and operate inside authenticated webmail sessions, exposing inbox contents and account settings.

At a Southeast Asian police entity, attackers first harvested usernames from an internal application. They then showed selected users a fake Adobe Flash Player update prompt designed to deliver Antino.

This selection reduced unnecessary exposure by restricting the lure to accounts already marked as valuable. Antino is a separate Rust-based Windows implant, not merely another browser module.

The sample analyzed by Unit42 uses Microsoft OneDrive for commands, status updates, and file transfers. Previous coverage of Antino cloud control channels describes related Microsoft 365 abuse, but implementation details differ between reported versions.

Another intrusion involved a malicious extension sideloaded in Chrome’s developer mode at a justice-related entity. It communicated for more than three weeks, stole plaintext credentials, and supported a screenshot of an internal document.

Researchers also recorded more than 20 additional document-routing page views during the monitoring period. The extension installation method remains uncertain. Researchers saw references to silent installation utilities but did not recover them.

Defenders should investigate unauthorized developer-mode extensions, unexpected external scripts in internal portals, unusual browser WebSocket connections, and OneDrive activity involving outside tenants. Blocking unapproved extensions and reviewing portal integrity directly address the observed entry points.

articles.title: BlackNevas Ransomware Wipes VMware ESXi Infrastructure and Backups Without Exploiting Any Flaws
articles.description:
A ransomware attack linked to BlackNevas destroyed an organization’s VMware environment during a 10-day intrusion, targeting four ESXi hosts, every hosted virtual machine, two vCenter Server Appliances, and connected backup infrastructure. The attackers used legitimate management interfaces rather than exploiting virtualization vulnerabilities, showing how stolen administrative access can undermine hypervisor security. The distinction matters: investigators […]

The post BlackNevas Ransomware Wipes VMware ESXi Infrastructure and Backups Without Exploiting Any Flaws appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A ransomware attack linked to BlackNevas destroyed an organization’s VMware environment during a 10-day intrusion, targeting four ESXi hosts, every hosted virtual machine, two vCenter Server Appliances, and connected backup infrastructure.

The attackers used legitimate management interfaces rather than exploiting virtualization vulnerabilities, showing how stolen administrative access can undermine hypervisor security.

The distinction matters: investigators found no guest-to-host escape or hypervisor memory corruption. Credentials stolen from systems outside the virtualization environment opened access to vCenter.

Earlier reporting on BlackNevas ransomware encryption tactics documented the group’s operations, but this investigation shows how management access enabled broader destruction.

Researchers Elsayed Elrefaei and Mohamed Ghobashy, writing for Securelist’s ESXi ransomware investigation, identified BlackNevas in the ransom notes.

Their November 13 report explains that the ESXi payload was unavailable for analysis, limiting binary-level attribution and verification of some command-line options.

BlackNevas Ransomware Wipes VMware ESXi Infrastructure and Backups

The attackers extracted stored credentials after gaining administrative execution on backup infrastructure. Those systems became a bridge into other infrastructure, illustrating why backup servers require protection beyond their role as recovery tools.

Valid-account access also made malicious activity harder to distinguish from normal administration. On the disaster-recovery vCenter appliance, the intruders authenticated as root through SSH and deployed MeshAgent just 43 seconds later.

The initial session lasted two minutes and 26 seconds. Roughly four hours afterward, they returned through MeshAgent and installed a persistent Ligolo-ng reverse tunnel using a VMware-looking systemd service.

Next, the attackers abused vCenter Host Profiles, a legitimate feature for enforcing host configurations. They changed the TSM-SSH service state to enable direct SSH access on ESXi hosts.

From the first configuration read to SSH becoming available, the sequence took approximately eleven minutes. Subsequent connections originated from vCenter itself, a normally trusted management source.

This exposed a major monitoring gap. Security agents inside virtual machines cannot directly observe the hypervisor process modifying their virtual disks.

Separate research into GhostFrame ESXi credential theft highlights the same visibility problem, although investigators did not connect that toolkit to this incident.

The payload arrived through SFTP, and authentication logs recorded a FlowSsh client identifier. A self-test ran for approximately 16 seconds around three hours before destructive execution, creating a potential detection window.

On the disaster-recovery host, all virtual machines stopped within 23 seconds; investigators could not establish the exact shutdown technique.

The final execution targeted VMFS storage with wiping and directory-traversal options. Artifacts indicated that roughly the first 2 KB of virtual-disk files had been overwritten.

That damage can prevent booting, but it does not prove every disk is unrecoverable: surviving backup partition metadata and the extent of other damage determine recovery prospects.

Backup Destruction, Detection, and Recovery Lessons

The attackers weakened recovery before disrupting production. Antivirus protection in the backup environment was disabled days earlier.

They later stopped backup services, encrypted recovery infrastructure, and disrupted administrative access before triggering the ESXi payload. This sequence left defenders without their expected restoration path when virtual machines failed.

Previous cases involving ransomware targeting Veeam backups demonstrate the wider interest in recovery systems. However, those incidents involved vulnerability exploitation; Securelist did not observe the Veeam flaws discussed in its report being exploited here.

Shared credentials and connected management systems were central concerns in this case. Defenders should correlate unexpected Host Profile changes with SSH enablement, new connections from vCenter, executable staging, and mass VM shutdowns.

Authentication, shell, host-management, and vCenter task logs provide essential evidence. Forwarding those logs outside the affected environment reduces the chance that attackers or a reboot erase the investigation trail.

Securelist recommends separate administrative identities for production, virtualization, and backups, alongside restricted management access and tested recovery procedures.

Immutable storage alone is insufficient when attackers can compromise the accounts, servers, or network paths needed to restore it.

articles.title: Apple Fixes iOS Flaw That Let Sandboxed Apps Secretly Record Microphone Audio Without Permission
articles.description:
Apple has patched a privacy bug in iOS, iPadOS, and macOS that let an app record microphone audio after the user said no. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-65339. On an earlier iOS 27 beta build, the orange microphone dot stayed off, and the system logs did not name the app. Apple’s own note was […]

The post Apple Fixes iOS Flaw That Let Sandboxed Apps Secretly Record Microphone Audio Without Permission appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Apple has patched a privacy bug in iOS, iPadOS, and macOS that let an app record microphone audio after the user said no. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-65339.

On an earlier iOS 27 beta build, the orange microphone dot stayed off, and the system logs did not name the app. Apple’s own note was short. It said only that “an app may be able to leak sensitive user information” and that “a logic issue was addressed with improved checks”. That wording hides how serious the bug was.

Apps do not decide for themselves whether they can use the microphone. The request goes through Apple’s Transparency, Consent, and Control system, known as TCC, and the decision depends on who is asking. The weak point was audiomxd, Apple’s audio media daemon. A daemon is a background system service.

The researchers who wrote up the bug say audiomxd trusted an audit token supplied by the app. An audit token is a 32-byte value that identifies a process.

The app could forge this token and pass it off as the daemon itself. The daemon has a shortcut for audio it hosts internally. Suppose the client looks like the daemon recording is allowed with no TCC check. The forged token triggered that shortcut.

Apple Fixes iOS Vulnerability

The recording was then credited to the daemon, not the app. That is why the logs showed nothing, and the orange dot stayed dark. The microphone prompt still appeared on the first launch.

But declining it didn’t stop the recording, and the prompt never returned on later launches. The bypass covered microphone capture only through this audio path. It did not give the app general TCC permissions.

A sandboxed app could not simply look up the daemon’s process ID. The researchers found another route. The app sent a malformed request to the audio service and read the kernel-attached trailer on the error reply.

That trailer exposed the daemon’s real process ID and process version. The app then wrote a forged token through the public AudioUnitSetProperty call, using property 2009. Guessing the version number also worked and took about 70 seconds in testing.

Similar mistakes have happened before. In 2014, Ian Beer of Google Project Zero found a related identity bug in OS X networkd, fixed as CVE-2014-4492. Developers are usually told to take identity from the connection’s kernel-supplied token, never from the message body.

In the patched build, the property handler now checks the real caller’s token. It requires a private entitlement called com.apple.private.audio.client-audit-token-override before it accepts a replacement identity. An app cannot grant itself that entitlement.

Apple fixed the bug in iOS 27.0 beta 5 on 10 August 2026. It shipped to the public on 17 August 2026 in iOS 26.6.1, iPadOS 26.6.1 and macOS Tahoe 26.6.2. Fixes reached macOS Sequoia 15.8, tvOS 27, watchOS 27 and visionOS 27 on 14 September, and iOS 18.7.11 followed on 26 October.

Mustafa Calap and Meta Red Team X’s Nik Tsytsarkin reported the vulnerability to Apple on July 7, 2026; it was not remotely exploitable.

A user had to install a malicious app first. Still, a hidden recorder in a normal-looking app is a real risk. Keep your devices updated, and install apps only from sources you trust. Remember that the orange indicator was the safety net here, and on the vulnerable build, it failed.

This is not the first Apple privacy bypass of its kind. Cyber Security News covered a macOS TCC bypass tracked as CVE-2025-43530 that let attackers reach the microphone without consent.

It also reported on the August 2026 Apple update that fixed 28 flaws, which included this audio bug. For references, see Apple’s security notes for iOS 26.6.1 and macOS Tahoe 26.6.2, and the Project Zero report on networkd.

A criminal complaint accuses Zyaire Dontaevious Zamarion Wilkins of helping fund and promote the operation, which ran from at least May 2024 through February […]

The post FBI Reveals How Hackers Hid Malware in Video Games to Steal $220,000 From Cryptocurrency Wallets appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The FBI has detailed an alleged cryptocurrency theft scheme in which hackers hid malware inside video games, infected about 8,000 users’ devices, and stole at least $220,000 from roughly 80 wallets.

A criminal complaint accuses Zyaire Dontaevious Zamarion Wilkins of helping fund and promote the operation, which ran from at least May 2024 through February 2026.

The July complaint charged Wilkins with conspiracy to obtain computer information for private financial gain. Prosecutors filed a further computer access charge on November 9, according to KING 5. The claims remain allegations, not findings of guilt.

According to the criminal complaint, an unnamed developer created accounts using stolen identities and released eight games containing malware. The filing does not name the game store. However, the FBI’s separate victim notice identifies Steam and lists several matching titles.

The complaint names DASHVERSE, Lunara, PirateFi, BlockBlasters, and Lampy. Investigators allege that Lampy received a malicious update in January 2026, showing that the threat could arrive after a game was already available.

FBI Cryptocurrency Theft Warning

The group allegedly promoted downloads through Discord, Telegram, X, and LinkedIn. Bots helped identify people with large cryptocurrency holdings and send targeted messages. This approach combined broad game distribution with direct contact aimed at users whose wallets could offer larger payouts.

Once installed, the malware allegedly collected account credentials, browser cookies, user tokens, and autofill data. The group searched that stolen information for details that could unlock cryptocurrency accounts, then used those details to take funds.

Earlier BlockBlasters malware reporting described a staged infection involving batch files, hidden scripts, a backdoor, and the StealC information stealer. That analysis provides technical context for one named game. However, the complaint does not establish that every title used the same payload.

Cyber Security News has also explained how gaming account theft through infostealers can expose saved passwords and session tokens. These stolen browser records give attackers another route into accounts beyond simply guessing a password.

Signal messages recovered during the investigation allegedly linked Wilkins to the name “Sibel.eth.” In one exchange, that user discussed spending $10,000 on a remote access Trojan and adding stealers.

Other messages discussed wallet draining, including tricking victims into approving transfers or entering wallet recovery phrases on phishing sites. The suspects discussed these methods, but that does not prove every victim lost funds the same way.

Investigators followed Bitcoin payments to Bitrefill, where an account purchased more than 150 gift cards. Uber records then connected food delivery purchases to a phone number and addresses linked to Wilkins. Google account records and other provider data added further links, according to the complaint.

Agents later seized devices and wallet recovery phrases. One Monero wallet showed about $382,000 in transfers, but that activity is separate from the alleged $220,000 minimum stolen from victims.

The FBI’s victim reporting page asks affected players to provide information. Its notice identifies eight games, including Chemia, Tokenova, and Beyond the Dark, as well as titles named in the complaint. Reports could help investigators assess the campaign’s broader impact and identify additional affected users and losses.

articles.title: Meta Hit With €805 Million Fine Over Facebook’s Unauthorized Access to Android Photo Galleries
articles.description:
Italy’s Data Protection Authority has fined Meta Platforms Ireland Limited €805 million after finding that Facebook accessed Android users’ photos, videos, and related metadata without specific consent. Announced on November 14, 2026, the decision affects around 20 million Android users in Italy. It requires Meta to change how its gallery suggestion feature works. The Italian […]

The post Meta Hit With €805 Million Fine Over Facebook’s Unauthorized Access to Android Photo Galleries appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Italy’s Data Protection Authority has fined Meta Platforms Ireland Limited €805 million after finding that Facebook accessed Android users’ photos, videos, and related metadata without specific consent.

Announced on November 14, 2026, the decision affects around 20 million Android users in Italy. It requires Meta to change how its gallery suggestion feature works.

The Italian regulator’s announcement concerns a Facebook feature available since 2023 that suggests pictures and videos from a phone’s gallery while users browse their feed. The investigation began in July 2025 following a complaint from the Bolzano Consumer Protection Center and included technical checks by the authority.

Investigators found that Facebook used one app permission to support several functions with different needs. Before requesting access, the app displayed a generic message about enabling other features. According to the regulator, this wording did not clearly explain that users were also allowing Facebook to suggest content from their galleries.

The gallery suggestion feature was also switched on by default. When users granted full access, the permission allowed Facebook to read the phone’s entire photo archive on an ongoing basis. The authority said neither users nor investigators could verify exactly which information the feature used.

Meta Hit With €805 Million Fine

The case centers on consent rather than an Android security flaw. In the regulator’s findings, granting an app technical access to stored media did not provide valid consent for every feature using that access. Facebook needed to explain the gallery suggestion function and obtain a separate, informed choice.

Cyber Security News previously covered a separate Meta Android tracking technique that linked browser activity to Facebook and Instagram apps through local connections. That research concerned web tracking, not gallery access, but also raised questions about how clearly users understood background data collection.

The authority based its decision on Article 122 of Italy’s Privacy Code, which implements the European ePrivacy Directive. It said information stored on smartphones falls within a person’s private sphere and requires free, informed consent for access, regardless of whether data leaves the device or proven harm occurs.

Meta argued that the Irish authority had jurisdiction. Italy rejected that objection because the ePrivacy rules do not include the “one-stop-shop” system. Separately, Cyber Security News reported on Meta’s €91 million plaintext password fine, issued by Ireland’s Data Protection Commission under GDPR in 2024.

Within 60 days, Meta must introduce a separate consent request, explain gallery access and disabling options, and keep suggestions off by default, including for previously authorized users. Without valid consent, the feature cannot be activated after the deadline. Progress reports are due within 30 and 90 days.

The fine reflects the number of affected users, the violation’s duration, a previous 2019 decision, and limited cooperation. Changes made after the complaint reduced the penalty but were considered late. The investigation did not determine whether gallery content trained AI, which Meta denies. A newer cloud processing feature may face separate checks.

articles.description:
Japan recorded 233 publicly disclosed cybersecurity incidents in October 2026, roughly 2.4 times its previous monthly record, according to Trend Micro data reported by TV Asahi. The surge has affected businesses, service providers, and public institutions, raising concerns about how quickly attackers are finding weaknesses in systems holding customer information. An analysis by MM Research […]

The post Japan Reports Record 233 Cyber Incidents as 185 Million Personal Records Are Put at Risk appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Japan recorded 233 publicly disclosed cybersecurity incidents in October 2026, roughly 2.4 times its previous monthly record, according to Trend Micro data reported by TV Asahi.

The surge has affected businesses, service providers, and public institutions, raising concerns about how quickly attackers are finding weaknesses in systems holding customer information.

An analysis by MM Research Institute estimated that approximately 185 million personal information records were exposed or potentially exposed in incidents disclosed during October.

That is nearly four times the total reported throughout 2025. Thirty incidents involved at least one million records each. These figures measure records at risk, not necessarily separate individuals or confirmed data theft in every case.

Researchers at Socket.dev noted the attacks in a November 12 analysis, highlighting evidence of AI-assisted exploitation and suspicious files consistent with AI-generated code.

However, the report did not identify a single malware family behind Japan’s broader surge, and researchers have not established how much AI contributed to the overall increase.

Japan Reports Record 233 Cyber Incidents

The October figures followed an already difficult year. TrendAI counted 607 publicly disclosed incidents between January and September 2026, exceeding the 594 recorded throughout 2025.

Unauthorized access accounted for 331 incidents, while another 62 involved information exposed through compromised service providers. Ransomware disclosures increased only slightly, from 79 to 82 across the same nine-month comparison period.

Email distribution provider Arara illustrates how one intrusion can affect hundreds of organizations. Its November 6 update confirmed the theft of approximately 81.3 million email addresses, with up to 380 corporate customers potentially affected.

Depending on the customer, additional exposed information could include names, birth dates, telephone numbers, addresses, and membership details.

The consequences reached major brands. The SEGA newsletter data breach exposed 2,196,044 email addresses through Arara, although SEGA said its separate account platform was unaffected.

Across Arara’s wider incident, attackers also abused the email service to distribute up to 7.13 million fraudulent messages impersonating credit card companies between October 28 and October 30.

Another provider, Ymir Link, confirmed that attackers extracted approximately 47.9 million email distribution records from 49 Cuenote FC systems. Investigators found software exploitation, stolen session information, and misuse of legitimate CSV export functions.

That combination shows how attackers can turn ordinary business features into tools for large-scale data theft after gaining access.

Macnica separately identified 288 web-system intrusion incidents involving possible data theft through October, compared with 84 throughout 2025.

October alone accounted for 168 disclosures. Its dataset excluded ransomware, credential stuffing, and duplicate customer disclosures arising from a shared provider breach, so those numbers should not be treated as interchangeable with the broader national totals.

AI-Assisted Exploitation Increases Pressure to Patch

JPCERT/CC’s October 21 investigation found attackers using AI to scan known vulnerabilities and conduct attacks through application programming interfaces.

Investigators also discovered efforts to analyze Android applications for backend endpoints and test weaknesses such as server-side request forgery, which can make a server send requests on an attacker’s behalf.

The findings fit a wider pattern of automation. Separate reporting on CyberStrikeAI automated attack workflows described 44 coordinated agents checking weaknesses at 19 organizations, including 16 in Japan.

However, testing a target did not establish a successful breach, and the platform itself is a legitimate penetration-testing tool rather than a newly discovered malware family.

Investigators also found Blutter and jadx on attack infrastructure. These reverse-engineering tools can reveal application endpoints and authentication mechanisms.

Macnica observed attackers exploiting application-specific authentication and access-control weaknesses, while TrendAI found suspicious code artifacts and attempts that adapted after failures.

Those observations support AI-assisted activity, but not attribution of every incident to one campaign. Japan’s response also reflects the urgency of software exposure.

Coverage of public PHP2Shell exploit code shows how quickly working exploits can threaten unpatched websites. On November 5, Japan’s National Cybersecurity Office urged organizations to address unsupported software, known vulnerabilities, API weaknesses, and contractor-operated systems.

The following day, the government announced a 10 billion yen emergency cybersecurity package covering intelligence gathering, AI-assisted vulnerability detection, and incident-response support.

The post Microsoft Reveals How a Hidden Windows Bug Took Down Microsoft 365 Services Worldwide appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has traced the worldwide Microsoft 365 outage on November 12–13, 2026, to a hidden Windows bug that overwhelmed servers handling cloud connections.

Its preliminary incident report, dated November 15, describes how a software change shifted traffic and reduced server capacity, which combined to cause widespread failures. Exchange Online suffered the greatest impact.

The disruption lasted from 4:20 PM UTC on November 12 until 4:10 PM UTC on November 13. Most users could not reach Exchange Online mailboxes through Outlook or other clients, while many faced delayed emails

As covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s initial Microsoft 365 outage report, the incident also affected other Microsoft cloud services.

Hidden Windows Bug Triggered Failures

The defect came from a fix prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. Deployment began in July, and the change ran globally for more than three months without visible problems. Microsoft says neither the defect nor that fix applies to general Windows deployments, separating this incident from a Windows desktop issue.

Inside an internal Windows process, competing tasks were waiting for access to shared resources, a problem called lock contention. Under certain traffic conditions, this exhausted processor and memory capacity.

Connection requests piled up until servers stopped responding. Microsoft’s tests missed the issue because they focused on weaker machines, while the fault became worse on newer hardware with more cores.

Two conditions exposed the bug. Around fifteen hours before the outage, Teams traffic moved from an alternative gateway to the primary gateway shared with Exchange Online.

Meanwhile, nearly 14% of gateway server capacity was unavailable because of an unrelated issue. Microsoft says the remaining capacity was sufficient on its own, but the combined conditions triggered the defect.

Automatic Recovery Made Things Worse

When servers failed, automated systems moved connections to healthy endpoints. That extra work triggered the same fault elsewhere, spreading failures across regions in less than two hours. More than 80% of servers became unresponsive at the worst point. Microsoft-hosted incident discussions also recorded unavailable servers placing extra load on remaining infrastructure.

A separate failure in the boundaries designed to contain faults allowed the outage to spread globally. Restarted servers quickly failed again when waiting traffic returned, matching Cybersecuritynews.com’s coverage of unsuccessful recovery efforts. Teams, SharePoint, and OneDrive could move eligible traffic away, but Exchange Online could not fully switch paths at its operating scale.

Engineers developed an update that returned Windows connection handling to its earlier working state. They removed large server groups from service, applied the change, restarted them, and restored traffic gradually. Microsoft also added capacity and extended the email delivery window so queued messages would not be returned as undeliverable.

The report remains preliminary, with repair details due November 20. For administrators, incidents EX1550543 and MO1550821 identify the disruption in service health records. Microsoft’s published guidance said tenant or device configuration changes were unnecessary. The failure was within Microsoft’s cloud infrastructure, not customer Windows systems.

Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
CAASM exists because every security tool keeps its own asset list and they all disagree: the same laptop under three names, the server EDR sees but the scanner doesn’t, the cloud workload nobody’s CMDB ever met.

These platforms aggregate asset truth from the tools you already run, merge the duplicates, and let you query the gaps unencrypted devices touching production, internet-exposed hosts missing EDR. Axonius takes 1; JupiterOne and runZero complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Axonius the connector-breadth and merge-accuracy benchmark.

• Podium: Axonius, JupiterOne (graph-query depth), runZero (discovery-native truth for what connectors miss).

• Model split: connector-aggregators (Axonius, JupiterOne, Sevco) versus discovery-native engines (runZero, Lansweeper, Armis) what your tools know versus what’s actually on the wire.

• 2026 theme: the gap queries CAASM’s value is the questions it answers in seconds that used to take three weeks of spreadsheet reconciliation.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: connector breadth and quality, merge/correlation accuracy, query ergonomics, discovery-native capability, coverage-gap workflow (findings to owners), and pricing clarity.

Weights: merge accuracy 25%, connector breadth 20%, query ergonomics 20%, discovery capability 20%, gap workflow 15%.

The 2026 CAASM Power Rankings

Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Axonius — Best Connector-Aggregation Benchmark

Snapshot: Per-asset tiers | Largest connector catalog claim | Query + enforcement actions

Why it earns 1: Axonius defined the category and still sets its benchmark: hundreds of connectors pulling asset truth from EDR, MDM, cloud, identity, and scanners; correlation that merges the three-named laptop into one record; queries that answer gap questions in seconds; and enforcement actions that open tickets or trigger fixes when answers demand them.

Pros: Connector breadth; merge accuracy reputation; query-to-action workflow.

Cons: Leader pricing; value tracks connector-match to your stack.

Bottom line: The aggregation benchmark the category measures against.

2. JupiterOne — Best Graph-Query Asset Model

Snapshot: Asset/tier pricing| Graph model of assets and relationships | J1QL query language

Why it ranks here: JupiterOne models the estate as a graph assets, identities, policies, and their relationships so queries traverse connections: which internet-facing hosts can reach the crown-jewel database, owned by whom, protected by what.

The relationship lens cloud-native estates think in.

Pros: Graph-relationship depth; query expressiveness; cloud-native fit.

Cons: Graph thinking is a learning curve worth budgeting.

Bottom line: The estate as a queryable graph.

3. runZero — Best Discovery-Native Truth

Snapshot: Asset-based tiers; free tier | Active+passive discovery engine | Finds what connectors can’t

Why it ranks here: runZero (HD Moore’s lineage) answers the question aggregators can’t: what’s on the network that no tool knows about? Research-grade active and passive discovery fingerprints the unagented, unmanaged, and forgotten the OT device, the shadow server, the switch nobody inventoried feeding ground truth into whatever aggregates above.

Pros: Discovery-engine pedigree; unmanaged-asset truth; accessible entry.

Cons: Connector-aggregation breadth pairs with the leaders.

Bottom line: The ground truth under everyone’s inventories.

4. Armis — Best Unmanaged/IoT-OT Asset Lens

Snapshot: Per-asset tiers | Agentless device intelligence | IoT/OT/medical depth

Why it ranks here: Armis sees the estate agents never will: passive device intelligence across IoT, OT, and medical fleets, behavioral profiling of what each device should do, and asset context at hospital-and-factory scale.

Where unmanaged devices dominate the risk, the lens is the platform.

Pros: Unmanaged-device depth; behavioral profiling; OT/medical fluency.

Cons: IT-connector aggregation breadth versus the benchmark.

Bottom line: The census of everything that can’t run an agent.

5. Sevco Security — Best Correlation-Transparency Challenger

Snapshot: Per-asset tiers | Source-attributed correlation | Real-time inventory telemetry

Why it ranks here: Sevco security shows its correlation work: every merged asset record carries source attribution which tool said what, when so coverage-gap findings (in EDR, missing from MDM) arrive with evidence attached.

The transparency-first challenger for teams burned by black-box merges.

Pros: Source-attributed merging; gap evidence; telemetry freshness.

Cons: Ecosystem breadth versus incumbents.

Bottom line: Correlation you can audit.

6. Qualys (CSAM) — Best Platform-Native Asset Estate

Snapshot: Platform module | CyberSecurity Asset Management on the Qualys agent/scan estate | EASM pairing

Why it ranks here: Qualys CSAM builds the inventory where its sensors already live: agent and scan telemetry unified with business context, unmanaged-asset flagging, and external-surface pairing asset truth as a module of the platform consolidators already run.

Pros: Platform-native truth; sensor leverage; consolidation economics.

Cons: Third-party-tool aggregation breadth versus pure CAASM.

Bottom line: The asset estate inside the Qualys stack.

7. Lansweeper — Best IT-Discovery Value Lane

Snapshot: Per-asset value tiers | Deep IT discovery lineage | OT expansion

Why it ranks here: Lansweeper brings two decades of IT-discovery craft at value economics: agentless scanning that fingerprints hardware and software across Windows-heavy estates, OT modules expanding the reach, and pricing mid-market budgets clear.

The inventory workhorse below the enterprise platforms.

Pros: Discovery depth; value pricing; mid-market fit.

Cons: Security-correlation workflow versus the CAASM purists.

Bottom line: The value-lane inventory engine.

8. Panaseer — Best Controls-Assurance Metrics Lane

Snapshot: Enterprise platform | Continuous controls monitoring | Coverage-metrics focus

Why it ranks here — scoped honestly: Panaseer uses asset aggregation for a specific mission: continuous controls monitoring measuring, with evidence, what percentage of the estate each control actually covers, trended for boards and regulators.

CAASM machinery pointed at assurance metrics rather than operational queries.

Pros: Controls-coverage metrics; board/regulator outputs; evidence discipline.

Cons: Operational-query lane sits with the generalists.

Bottom line: The controls-coverage scoreboard.

9. Noetic Cyber — Best Graph-Automation Challenger

Snapshot: Platform tiers | Graph model + automation workflows | Rapid7-family adjacency

Why it ranks here: Noetic cyber pairs a graph-based asset model with automation: continuous correlation feeding workflows that fix gaps automatically untagged asset tagged, uncovered host ticketed.

A challenger with automation instincts, now in the Rapid7 family orbit; confirm packaging.

Pros: Graph+automation pairing; gap-fix workflows.

Cons: Family-era packaging confirmation; ecosystem scale.

Bottom line: The graph that files its own tickets.

10. Balbix — Best Risk-Quantified Asset Lens

Snapshot: Platform subscriptio | Asset inventory + breach-likelihood math | Dollar-ranked exposure

Why it ranks here — scoped honestly: Balbix enters CAASM from the risk side: continuous inventory joined to per-asset breach likelihood and business-criticality weighting, exposure expressed in currency.

Less the operational query engine, more the quantified lens atop asset truth ranked as what it is.

Pros: Risk quantification; criticality weighting; ROI ranking.

Cons: Operational CAASM queries pair from the generalists.

Bottom line: Asset truth, priced in currency.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Audit the Merge, Define the Queries, Mind the Connector Calendar

CAASM pilots live or die on merge accuracy with your data: feed finalists the same week of your real tool exports and measure duplicate-collapse quality the three-named laptop merged correctly, and nothing merged that shouldn’t be (Sevco security-class source attribution makes that auditable).

Define the justifying queries up front unencrypted devices touching production, internet-exposed hosts missing EDR, stale admin accounts on live assets and run them live in evaluation, because those answers are the product.

Respect the connector calendar: approvals for read credentials across EDR, MDM, cloud, and identity are the real deployment timeline, so sequence by evidence value.

Pair models honestly aggregators tell you what your tools know; discovery-native engines (runZero/Armis/Lansweeper-class) find what nothing knows and most estates need one of each.

Settle the CMDB question early (corrected from CAASM findings, or quietly replaced), route gap findings as owned tickets with SLAs, and track the metric that justifies renewal: coverage-gap count per control, trending down quarter over quarter.

FAQs

What are the best CAASM tools in 2026?

Axonius as the aggregation benchmark, JupiterOne for graph queries, runZero for discovery-native truth, Armis for unmanaged estates, with Sevco, Qualys CSAM, Lansweeper, Panaseer, Noetic, and Balbix by model and mission.

CAASM versus ASM/EASM?

CAASM aggregates internal asset truth from your own tools; EASM maps the external attacker-reachable estate complementary maps, and mature programs run both.

Aggregator or discovery-native?

Both: aggregators unify what your tools already know; discovery engines find what nothing knows the unagented, unmanaged, and forgotten.

Does CAASM replace the CMDB?

It corrects or quietly supersedes it: decide explicitly whether CAASM findings flow back or become the operational source ambiguity breeds parallel inventories.

What proves CAASM value?

Gap queries answered in seconds (uncovered hosts, missing controls) and coverage-gap counts trending down reconciliation weeks collapsed into live answers.

Verdict

Ten tools, two models, one merge test that decides: your data, duplicates collapsed, nothing over-merged.

Axonius benchmarks the aggregation, JupiterOne graphs the relationships, runZero and Armis and Lansweeper find what nothing else sees, Sevco shows the work, Qualys rides its sensors, Panaseer scores the controls, Noetic files the tickets, Balbix prices the estate audit the merge, define the queries, sequence the connectors, and let the shrinking gap count renew the contract.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
External attack surface management answers the question attackers answer daily and most defenders never have: what of yours is actually reachable from the internet right now? • Roster notes: IBM’s Randori lineage carries portfolio-era packaging questions; Detectify enters from the payload-testing side both scoped honestly.

• 2026 theme: freshness velocity the new cloud bucket appearing in your map in hours versus weeks is the operational difference between EASM and archaeology.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: discovery depth and attribution accuracy, refresh velocity, exploitability validation, ownership-routing workflow, supply-chain/subsidiary reach, and pricing clarity.

Weights: attribution accuracy 25%, discovery depth 20%, freshness 20%, validation 20%, workflow 15%.

The 2026 ASM Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Palo Alto ( Xpanse) — Best Internet-Scale Attribution

Snapshot: Cortex module structure | Continuous internet-wide discovery | Ownership attribution depth

Why it earns 1: Xpanse scans the way adversaries do the whole internet, continuously and attributes what it finds with the depth that makes findings actionable: this forgotten subdomain, that acquisition’s server, your cloud bucket spun up Tuesday.

Inside Cortex, discoveries route toward automation; standalone, the attribution engine is the draw.

Pros: Internet-scale discovery; attribution depth; freshness velocity; Cortex routing.

Cons: Platform economics; validation stage pairs elsewhere.

Bottom line: The attacker’s reconnaissance, running for you.

2. Microsoft (Defender EASM) — Best Estate-Bundled Surface Mapping

Why it ranks here: Defender EASM maps the external estate and joins it to the internal one Microsoft already watches: discoveries linked to Defender device and identity context, findings flowing into Security Exposure Management’s attack paths.

For Microsoft estates, outside-in truth arrives pre-integrated.

Pros: Estate fusion; bundled-adjacent economics; exposure-path integration.

Cons: Internet-scan authority depth versus the dedicated engines.

Discovery plus proof in one pass.

Pros: Subsidiary-graph discovery; active testing; risk-ranked output.

The unification argument for Falcon shops.

Pros: Console unity; adversary-informed ranking; internal-external join.

Cons: Dedicated-engine discovery depth race.

For Tenable programs, the surface is one more input to the one queue.

The noise-economy pick fewer findings, more of them true.

Cons: Ecosystem gravity versus the anchors.

The recon-to-attack pipeline stays differentiated; portfolio-era packaging and roadmap deserve written confirmation.

Cons: Portfolio packaging clarity.

The pilot is an attribution audit: seed each candidate with known assets (including two subsidiaries and one acquisition) and count both misses and false attributions over-attribution floods teams with other companies’ infrastructure, and it’s the complaint that kills programs.

Time freshness empirically (spin up a cloud asset, measure hours-to-map), weigh validation philosophy (CyCognito/IONIX-class active testing versus discovery-pure engines fewer, truer findings versus maximal coverage), and pre-agree the ownership-resolution process before the first run, because unattributed discoveries age indefinitely and week one will produce orphans.

Price by seed-domain and subsidiary counts honestly (they drive cost more than asset totals), demand API access so discoveries flow into existing queues rather than another portal, and route the whole feed into your CTEM prioritization the surface map is scope-and-discover fuel, not a destination dashboard.

Portfolio-era packaging (Randori) and jurisdiction posture (Group-IB) get confirmed in writing where shortlisted.

FAQs

Cortex Xpanse for internet-scale attribution, Defender EASM for estate fusion, CyCognito for attacker-logic discovery with testing, Censys for scan-data authority, with Falcon Surface, Tenable, IONIX, IBM (Randori), Group-IB, and Detectify by lens.

How fast should discoveries appear? Hours-class for new cloud assets at the leaders time it empirically in the pilot, because freshness is the operational difference between EASM and archaeology.

Should ASM findings be actively tested? Validation-inclusive engines (CyCognito, IONIX, Randori-lineage) cut noise dramatically; discovery-pure engines maximize coverage choose by whether your bottleneck is finding or believing.

Verdict

Ten tools, one audit that decides: seed the assets, count the false claims. Xpanse runs the adversary’s recon at scale, Microsoft and CrowdStrike and Tenable wire the outside map to the inside one, CyCognito and IONIX prove what they find, Censys holds the scan record, Randori ranks by temptation behind a packaging check, Group-IB watches the fraud routes, Detectify fires the crowd’s payloads audit the attribution, time the freshness, resolve the orphans, and feed it all into the exposure cycle where maps become fixes.

CTEM fails as a SKU and succeeds as a calendar: name owners for all five stages (several hats on one head is fine; unnamed stages are not), then compose honestly a discovery-and-prioritization anchor (Tenable/Microsoft/CrowdStrike-class by estate gravity) plus a validation spine (XM Cyber’s paths, Cymulate/Picus’s control tests), with external truth (Xpanse/IONIX-class) if your internet estate sprawls.

Refuse to skip validation: unvalidated exposure lists are vulnerability management rebranded, and the proof is one quarter’s choke-point fixes severing measured paths.

Start scoped one crown-jewel business service end-to-end publish the first exposure-reduction number inside ninety days, and let breadth follow credibility.

Inventory connectors against your real stack before any contract (CTEM consumes scanners, cloud posture, identity, and ticketing on both ends), run the Skybox status check before evaluation hours, and hold the program to its two numbers: validated paths severed per quarter, and median days from prioritized finding to mobilized fix.

XM Cyber for path validation, Cymulate for validation-to-exposure convergence, Tenable for discovery breadth, with Xpanse, Microsoft, CrowdStrike, Picus security, Rapid7, IONIX, and Skybox (status-gated) mapped by stage.

A program a five-stage operating rhythm most estates run on two composed platforms plus owned process; no single SKU covers the cycle honestly.

Validation and mobilization: exposures proven exploitable along real paths, and fixes routed as owned work without those stages, it’s VM with new branding.

Validation budget for safe exploit simulation or path confirmation, because unvalidated lists regress to scanner output.

Validated attack paths severed per quarter, and days from prioritized finding to mobilized fix exposure reduction you can prove, not counts.

Ten platforms, five stages, one rule: compose, don’t believe the single-SKU story.

articles.title: NoisyTCP: 11-Year-Old Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Crash Servers Remotely
articles.description:
NoisyTCP is an 11-year-old Linux kernel bug. It lets a remote attacker crash a server without logging in. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-99288. Hyunwoo Kim (@v4bel) reported and patched it, and he released the NoisyTCP advisory on GitHub after the Linux distribution embargo ended. The flaw sits in the kernel’s TCP code, which handles […]

The post NoisyTCP: 11-Year-Old Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Crash Servers Remotely appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
NoisyTCP is an 11-year-old Linux kernel bug. It lets a remote attacker crash a server without logging in. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-99288. Hyunwoo Kim (@v4bel) reported and patched it, and he released the NoisyTCP advisory on GitHub after the Linux distribution embargo ended.

The flaw sits in the kernel’s TCP code, which handles almost all network traffic on Linux. Kim says it can be triggered against plain TCP listeners.

A server doesn’t need unusual settings, firewall rules, or special sockets. It only has to call listen() and receive packets from the attacker. That puts Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers in their default setups at risk, as well as proxies.

The attacker needs a server with two or more receive queues, or one with Receive Packet Steering (RPS) turned on. Both are common on modern hardware.

The attacker sends IPv4 fragments and normal TCP packets that land on different CPUs. This creates a race condition, where two parts of the kernel touch the same memory at the same moment.

NoisyTCP Linux Kernel Flaw

In the first trigger path, one CPU finds an existing half-open connection record. Another CPU frees that record and quickly reuses the same memory for a new SYN cookie request with the same connection details.

The first CPU grabs the new object and passes its checks. But the new object has no listener attached. The kernel then reads a NULL listener and panics.

The result is a remote denial of service. Kim warns that a crash from a containerized web server takes down the whole host, not only the app. A second path could cause a remote use-after-free, but it needs several races to succeed in a row and is much harder to pull off.

Timing matters here. On virtual machines such as QEMU/KVM, the tests took about 5 seconds to 2 minutes. On a quiet bare-metal server with 8 receive queues, the tuned proof-of-concept needed about 14 hours. Cloud and virtualized servers are therefore the most exposed.

This is not a remote code execution bug, at least for now. Kim says he has only built a limited, lab-specific exploit for VM servers and is still researching a general one. A reliable crash is still serious for any internet-facing service.

The bug was introduced in commit 079096f103fa on October 3, 2015. The fix, commit 4e2b3ef19e0e, landed on November 3, 2026. That means nearly every Linux distribution has carried the flaw for about 11 years. Administrators should install updated kernels from their vendors as soon as they are available and reboot.

If patching must wait, Kim suggests two stopgaps. The first is to turn off SYN cookies with sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=0. This setting applies per network namespace, so each container with its own namespace needs it too.

It also weakens protection against SYN floods, a common way to knock servers offline. The second is to cut the network interface down to one receive queue and disable RPS and RFS, which stops the race.

Linux networking code has had a rough few weeks. Cyber Security News recently covered attackers scanning for the Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-98432, a critical TCP/IPv4 bug with a 9.8 score.

It also reported on a Linux kernel TCP flaw that sat hidden for seven years. Race conditions like these are hard to spot in code review, and they often stay hidden for years.

Teams that run public Linux servers should check kernel versions now, test vendor patches, and watch for unexplained reboots. For background on the SYN cookie feature involved, see this LWN.net explainer.

The post AWS Restores Services in US-EAST-1 After Hours-Long Outage Disrupts Cloud Operations appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Amazon Web Services restored operations in its US-EAST-1 region on November 15 after an outage disrupted account signups, authentication, and network connections. Problems began at 3:05 a.m. PST, and the last network issue was resolved at 6:21 a.m. PST, leaving some customers affected for more than three hours.

The disruption affected customers using IAM Identity Center to access the AWS Console and services including Kiro and Amazon Connect. AWS also reported failed sign-up requests. Its initial service notice confirmed that engineers were investigating connectivity issues alongside problems with account access and new registrations.

Authentication Restored Before Network Recovery

AWS engineers were automatically engaged at 3:10 a.m. PST, five minutes after the incident began. Teams investigated the cause while working to restore service. Authentication issues were fully resolved by 5:20 a.m. PST, when most affected AWS services also returned to normal operation, according to the company’s update.

However, network recovery took longer for a subset of customers using Network Load Balancers, or NLBs, within a single cell. Those customers continued to experience connectivity problems until 6:21 a.m. PST. The separate recovery times show why successful authentication alone did not mean every affected service connection had recovered.

In its final recovery statement, AWS listed the main disruption window as 3:05 a.m. to 6:10 a.m. PST while separately confirming the final NLB fix at 6:21 a.m. PST. The company advised customers to retry failed requests and said all AWS services were operating normally.

Previous Cloud Outages

The incident follows earlier problems in the same region. Cyber Security News previously covered AWS US-EAST-1 delays affecting EC2 deployments, which also disrupted related container services in October 2025. That event provides historical context, but available evidence does not establish a shared cause with the latest outage.

The disruption also came after a major Microsoft 365 outage affected Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, and Defender XDR. Microsoft reported unavailable servers, failed health checks, and capacity problems during recovery. The separate incidents highlight how failures in shared cloud systems can interrupt access to several business and security services at once.

AWS’s recovery statement did not disclose a detailed root cause or identify a cyberattack. Its findings described authentication and connectivity failures. Until further technical details emerge, the incident should be treated as a service availability event rather than evidence of malicious activity or a confirmed security breach.

articles.description:
The Tor Project has released Tor 0.4.9.17 in an urgent response to an ongoing distributed denial-of-service attack that is overwhelming network relays. Announced on November 13, 2026, the stable release includes several security fixes, including one that addresses IPv6 handling in relay denial-of-service defenses. Tor says the attack has affected most relay operators and urges […]

The post Tor Releases Emergency Security Update as Ongoing DDoS Attack Overwhelms Network Relays appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The Tor Project has released Tor 0.4.9.17 in an urgent response to an ongoing distributed denial-of-service attack that is overwhelming network relays.

Announced on November 13, 2026, the stable release includes several security fixes, including one that addresses IPv6 handling in relay denial-of-service defenses. Tor says the attack has affected most relay operators and urges them to upgrade immediately.

The attack involves a massive flood of client circuits, according to a release announcement from Tor Network Team developer David Goulet. These circuits are the connections handled across Tor’s relay network.

By flooding relays with circuit activity, the attackers are placing heavy demand on the systems that carry user traffic. Tor has not published traffic volumes or identified those responsible in the announcement.

IPv6 Fix Strengthens Relay Defenses

The most important disclosed change concerns how relay DoS defenses handle IPv6. However, Tor’s public announcement does not explain the underlying code error, provide a CVE number, or describe the exact conditions needed to trigger it. The confirmed finding is narrower: the developers consider this fix especially important to relay protection during the current attack.

That distinction matters because a security update does not automatically mean the wider attack has ended. Tor says its developers are still testing additional defenses and expect more releases soon. Version 0.4.9.17 should therefore be understood as an immediate response to an active problem, rather than a confirmed end to the disruption across the network.

Tor has previously added other defenses against denial-of-service activity. Cyber Security News covered its proof-of-work protection for onion services, which makes clients complete a small computing task before their requests receive service. That earlier feature addresses onion-service access and should not be confused with the IPv6-related relay fix announced in this release.

Relay Operators Urged to Update

In the official security announcement, Goulet gave operators a direct instruction: “If you run a relay, please upgrade as soon as possible.” The project states that no further action is required after upgrading. It does not ask operators to apply extra configuration changes or manually adjust IPv6 settings as part of this release.

The urgency reflects Tor’s reliance on volunteer-run infrastructure. Its relay operations guidance explains that volunteers provide the bandwidth supporting bridges, guards, middle relays, and exit relays. When many operators face the same circuit flood, the problem reaches beyond one server and becomes a shared network availability issue.

This release targets Tor’s core relay software, not a newly announced Tor Browser build. Readers should distinguish it from browser updates, such as the previously reported Tor Browser security releases, which also address Firefox-based browser components. The immediate upgrade instruction in this announcement is specifically directed at relay operators.

Tor also thanked operators sharing information through the tor-relays mailing list. Their continued reports are helping developers respond while the attack remains active. For now, the confirmed response is to install 0.4.9.17 promptly and follow further official release announcements as additional defenses become available.

articles.description:
A car owner says an AI coding agent helped him read, copy, and then run code inside the engine computer of a 1994 Jeep Cherokee. The work took about a week. He used a $3 Arduino Nano, and the Jeep passed California’s smog test at the end. Muhammad Zulali shared the full story in a […]

The post Claude Cracks 32-Year-Old Jeep ECU Using a $3 Arduino and Reverse Engineers Its Engine Computer appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A car owner says an AI coding agent helped him read, copy, and then run code inside the engine computer of a 1994 Jeep Cherokee. The work took about a week. He used a $3 Arduino Nano, and the Jeep passed California’s smog test at the end. Muhammad Zulali shared the full story in a YouTube video on November 10, 2026.

The Jeep had no modern OBD2 port, so common scan tools could not talk to it. It failed the smog test at 25 mph because of high NOx, a gas that rises when an engine runs lean. Zulali first swapped the oxygen sensor, but the result got worse at 15 mph. Each test cost about $100, so he asked Claude Code to find a better way.

Claude found that the engine computer speaks an old, slow Chrysler protocol called SCI. The signal wire is flipped compared with a normal serial port, so a small translator was needed. A $3 Arduino Nano on a breadboard did the job, and the full parts list came to about $15.

Claude Cracks 32-Year-Old Jeep ECU

Tom’s Hardware reported that the link ran at about 7,800 baud. Only three wires from the six-hole diagnostic plug were used. One hole carries 12 volts with the key on, and touching it can fry the board.

The first reading came at 1:30 a.m. and showed only coolant temperature and battery voltage. Later data looked odd, with a fuel trim that seemed to add 22 percent extra fuel. Zulali tested fuel pressure and found a very low 10 PSI.

Claude then switched the fuel pump on by itself for about 10 seconds. He called this the moment the tool went from read-only to controlling the car.

The AI also made a mistake, and the cause was a public tool. Claude later found that the ChryslerScanner parameter table was wrong for his Jeep. The computer was removing fuel, not adding it. The scanner’s author, László Dániel, is credited in the project for the parameter tables.

Next, Claude copied the engine computer’s whole program to a laptop. The code showed a California-only fuel table that cuts fuel at the same load used in the smog test. This likely explained the high NOx. Reflashing the chip was the obvious fix, but the computer was built in December 1993, about four months too early to be reflashable.

That is where OpenAI’s Codex stepped in. It found a way to send a tiny program over the same three wires and have the computer run it. The first version was wiped out within seconds, so Codex moved the code into EEPROM, a memory that survives a dead battery. Zulali said Claude did most of the diagnosis and Codex did the memory work, while he handled wiring and driving.

The project is open source under the GPLv3 license. The xj-scanner repository on GitHub had 252 stars and 30 forks at the time of writing. It was tested on one car, a 1994 Cherokee XJ with a 4.0L engine, and the author warns that use is at your own risk.

For security readers, the lesson is about how fast AI agents can learn forgotten systems. Researchers once showed that car computers could be pushed to turn off brakes through physical access. Agents now cut the skill and time needed for that kind of work.

Our earlier report on Claude Code finding a hidden model backdoor shows the same pattern. Agents also carry their own risk, as seen when hackers hijacked Codex and Claude Code with files in Downloads. Anthropic’s Claude Code security guide advises users to review commands before approval.

Zulali admits he is not a mechanic and that some of his engine claims may be wrong. The owner reported the result himself, so it has not been independently tested.
