articles.title: Researchers Find Six 0-Days Allowing Unauthorized Takeover of Supermarket Refrigeration Systems
articles.description:
Six pre-authentication remote code execution flaws were found in the Danfoss AK-SM800A supermarket fridge controller, allowing remote takeover in about an hour, according to Midnight Blue researcher Carlo Meijer. The flaws are stack-based buffer overflows. They affect every firmware version up to and including 5.3.2, and no CVE numbers have been assigned yet. Since October […]

The post Researchers Find Six 0-Days Allowing Unauthorized Takeover of Supermarket Refrigeration Systems appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Six pre-authentication remote code execution flaws were found in the Danfoss AK-SM800A supermarket fridge controller, allowing remote takeover in about an hour, according to Midnight Blue researcher Carlo Meijer.

The flaws are stack-based buffer overflows. They affect every firmware version up to and including 5.3.2, and no CVE numbers have been assigned yet.

Since October 11, waves of cyber attacks have hit internet-exposed Danfoss and Copeland fridge controllers across Europe. Attackers started defrost cycles, and the losses reached tens of millions of euros.

Some stores even had fires, according to Wikipedia’s incident summary. Cyber Security News has followed the story from the start, including its report on the 4,980 exposed Danfoss hosts.

Who is behind the incidents is still debated. France has blamed Iran’s Shahid Kaveh unit, but SentinelOne says attribution remains open and the incidents may not share one operator. The French agency ANSSI also said its early findings pointed to exposed admin pages and weak passwords, not the older published bugs.

Meijer did not use fuzzing or AI. He downloaded the public firmware, ran the main program in an emulator, and looked for places where the code calls strcpy.

This old C function copies data without checking its size, so a long input can overflow memory. One unauthenticated web handler crashed after he sent a long string of “A” characters. He found at least five bugs of this kind in a small part of the code.

The binary also lacked stack canaries and PIE, two basic protections that make such bugs harder to use. The program runs as root, so a successful exploit gives full control.

Supermarket Fridge Controller Takeover

Midnight Blue showed a working root exploit on an older firmware version. The team is withholding technical details while it works with Danfoss on coordinated disclosure.

Danfoss added session control in later firmware, and “strict” became the default from version 4.0. This setting blocks most of the web attack surface for unauthenticated users, and CERT-FR lists it among its official mitigations.

Even so, the researchers found another overflow in sm_fcgi_app, the component that checks logins, and it still works on the latest firmware with strict mode on.

The team also warns about what comes after a break-in. The controller does not use the i.MX6 chip’s secure boot features. An attacker with root access could therefore plant an implant that survives a factory reset.

They could also wipe the flash memory or push bad firmware to brick the device. That would force stores to replace hardware, and freezers could sit idle for days. Midnight Blue compares this to the wiper-style tactics seen in the December 2025 attack on the Polish electric grid.

The researchers say patching one bug at a time is a poor use of limited staff time. Owners should find every exposed controller, including those behind integrators’ 4G modems. They should then move remote access behind a VPN, a private APN, or a strict IP allow list. CERT-FR warns that allow lists are only a short-term fix.

Exposure is still high. Censys sees hundreds of Danfoss devices online, plus over 1,000 Copeland and Dixell units. Earlier Cyber Security News coverage of Copeland XWEB Pro flaws showed the same pattern. Until these controllers leave the open internet, new bugs will keep putting food and medicine at risk.

articles.title: FBI Reveals How Hackers Use ARTEX AI Agents to Gain Privileged Access in Under Three Hours
articles.description:
The FBI has warned that hackers are using ARTEX AI agents to automate network attacks, with some intrusions reaching privileged access in under three hours. Its November 13, 2026, FLASH alert describes how attackers combine stolen credentials, exposed applications, and cloud permissions to shorten the gap between discovery and compromise. ARTEX is an open-source security […]

The post FBI Reveals How Hackers Use ARTEX AI Agents to Gain Privileged Access in Under Three Hours appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The FBI has warned that hackers are using ARTEX AI agents to automate network attacks, with some intrusions reaching privileged access in under three hours.

Its November 13, 2026, FLASH alert describes how attackers combine stolen credentials, exposed applications, and cloud permissions to shorten the gap between discovery and compromise.

ARTEX is an open-source security testing framework, not a malware family. Written in Go, it connects external large language models to agents that turn instructions into commands.

Operators set objectives while agents scan targets, run tools, review results, and adjust failed steps with limited human input throughout an attack campaign.

ARTEX Accelerates Enterprise Attacks

As covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s ARTEX enterprise attack analysis, the framework links familiar weaknesses rather than relying on a single new exploit. Agents can investigate cloud permissions, map Active Directory, and test access paths. Google observed individual automated bursts lasting two to 25 seconds, leaving defenders little time to assess connected events.

The FBI lists attacks involving SQL injection, missing API authentication, exposed passwords, and abuse of trusted cloud connections. After entry, agents have added credentials to existing applications, deployed web shells, and attempted credential theft. Other activity included searching for Windows systems without endpoint protection and mapping over 110,000 directory objects.

Microsoft previously linked ARTEX to Storm-0940, a China-state-aligned group targeting Microsoft 365 environments through compromised ConnectWise application credentials.

Attackers attempted access to more than 2,250 tenants using permissions customers had already approved. That number measures targeting, not confirmed breaches, and successful sign-ins alone do not establish customer data theft.

The FBI advisory brings these findings together, warning that ARTEX also targets overlooked supplier portals, sales tools, and mobile backends. Its under-three-hour figure describes some observed intrusions, not a fixed capability. Publicly exposed consoles exceeded 1,600 by early November, although exposed installations do not automatically prove malicious use by their operators.

A separate WorkOS breach report shows the risk to internal business applications. WorkOS detected unauthorized access to a sales application containing customer contact details and conversation records, including Slack excerpts. Its CEO identified ARTEX involvement, while the company reported no evidence that production services or WorkOS application data were affected.

Another Microsoft investigation documented ARTEX agents searching GitHub for exposed secrets. In one case, an agent progressed from repository searches to stealing Azure Key Vault data within five minutes. The activity illustrates how leaked application credentials can become cloud access, particularly when those identities hold broad permissions across connected services.

Researchers also examined servers exposed by an operator linked to South Korean financial attacks. The files revealed AI routing tools, reusable instructions, proxy services, and stored credentials. Those attacks affected roughly 67,000 people. However, shared ARTEX use does not establish that this operator, Storm-0940, and the WorkOS attacker were connected.

What Security Teams Should Monitor

The FBI recommends restricting exposed administration tools, reducing application permissions, and scanning repositories for secrets. Defenders should connect unusual application sign-ins with credential additions, role changes, and rapid API activity.

Preserve evidence during containment, investigate secondary access paths, and validate historical indicators against current logs before blocking shared cloud infrastructure.

The messages copy Microsoft service health notices and cite the real Exchange Online incident EX1550543, making the requests appear linked to an ongoing business problem. Microsoft Threat Intelligence detected emails […]

The post Microsoft Warns of Active Password Stealing Attack Exploiting the Microsoft 365 Service Disruption appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has warned of an active phishing campaign using the November 12 Microsoft 365 service disruption to lure users into opening fake email recovery links.

The messages copy Microsoft service health notices and cite the real Exchange Online incident EX1550543, making the requests appear linked to an ongoing business problem.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence detected emails on November 13 claiming that messages held during the outage would be deleted within 24 hours unless recipients clicked to restore them.

That deadline creates pressure to act quickly, particularly for employees already worried about missing customer messages, delayed payments, or other urgent business communications.

The warning follows the Microsoft 365 outage that affected Exchange Online and other cloud services. The phishing campaign takes advantage of that disruption, but it should not be confused with its cause. Microsoft’s outage updates said there was no indication that malicious activity had caused the underlying service failure.

Active Password Stealing Attack

The phishing emails use subject lines following the pattern “Outage – [six-character code].” Sender display names include organization-specific prefixes followed by “Outage Notification” or “Service Health.”

These details make the messages look like workplace notices, while the genuine incident number gives recipients another reason to believe the request is valid.

Microsoft identified three sender domains: moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com, and newbooker[.]com. Embedded links use recipient-specific SendGrid click tracking before redirecting to reallifeaccounting[.]com, including the path /themelist0.html. Similar messages reached organizations across multiple US sectors, showing that the activity was not limited to one company.

In its public threat intelligence warning, Microsoft described the activity as consistent with credential phishing. However, it has not confirmed credential collection or malware delivery.

The distinction matters. The observed emails and redirects support a phishing assessment, but they do not establish that passwords were successfully stolen or that devices were infected.

SendGrid links also appeared in a separate credential phishing campaign previously covered by Cybersecuritynews.com. That earlier reporting provides context for how attackers misuse trusted email services. It does not establish a connection between the campaigns, and Microsoft’s current warning does not identify the operator behind these outage-themed messages.

Microsoft recommends using Defender for Office 365 Threat Explorer and Defender XDR advanced hunting to investigate suspicious messages. The EmailEvents, EmailUrlInfo, and UrlClickEvents tables help teams examine email activity, embedded links, and user clicks. Investigators can use the reported sender domains, subject pattern, and redirect destination to guide their searches.

Organizations should also verify their Defender for Office 365 Safe Links policies. When properly configured, Safe Links provides time-of-click protection against malicious URLs.

Microsoft advises security teams to investigate potential user interactions rather than relying only on whether a suspicious message was delivered, because a recorded click needs further review.

For users, the key check is straightforward: confirm service disruptions directly through the Microsoft 365 admin center. An email citing a genuine outage number is not proof that its recovery link is safe.

articles.description:
Cursor has traced its October security breach to an access key exposed by Fireworks AI. The attacker used that key to steal historical coding agent records, find more credentials, and eventually place backdoored Claude Code extensions in Cursor’s marketplace cache. Its November 13 update connects the vendor exposure to the malicious packages discovered on October […]

The post Cursor Reveals How a Leaked Fireworks AI Key Led to a Backdoored Claude Code Extension appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Cursor has traced its October security breach to an access key exposed by Fireworks AI. The attacker used that key to steal historical coding agent records, find more credentials, and eventually place backdoored Claude Code extensions in Cursor’s marketplace cache. Its November 13 update connects the vendor exposure to the malicious packages discovered on October 29.

The stolen key, which Cursor had issued to Fireworks, provided read-only access to a shared storage bucket. It held limited coding agent traces, mostly from 2025, from sessions outside Privacy Mode that Cursor was permitted to use for model training. Some records contained credentials that had not been removed.

Cursor said fewer than 0.05% of users had coding agent traces exposed, while less than 0.01% of customers had API credentials exposed. These figures describe different parts of the incident and should not be treated as the number of users who installed malware.

Using credentials found in those records, the attacker reached selected software services used by Cursor. The exposed information included archived, non-production source repositories, limited support records and emails, usage metrics, contact details, conversation summaries, and some credentials customers had sent to support.

On October 29, a credential stolen from exposed internal data allowed the attacker to place modified Claude Code packages directly into the cache serving Cursor’s VS Code extension marketplace. Cursor said Anthropic did not publish the packages, its product was not vulnerable, and Open VSX never hosted the malware. This corrects earlier reporting that placed the package on Open VSX.

Claude Code Backdoor Worked

According to Cursor’s incident update, at most 5,000 users requesting specific cached versions potentially received malicious builds during roughly 11 hours. The affected packages were Anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for Windows and macOS. That is a potential distribution count, not confirmation of 5,000 successful backdoor connections.

Cyber Security News’ initial technical analysis described injected JavaScript that ran when the extension loaded, without requiring a Claude conversation. It collected host details, added an SSH key labeled svc-telemetry, and attempted a reverse SSH tunnel to 134[.]209[.]82[.]225. The initial data upload included environment variable names, not their values.

Its follow-up on Cursor’s confirmation detailed macOS LaunchAgent persistence and a Windows scheduled task with a Startup-folder fallback. Scripts retried connections about every 60 seconds. Cursor said coding errors and missing administrator rights blocked remote login on most hosts, but did not prevent other malicious changes or host data collection.

Wider Fireworks AI Breach Impact

The Fireworks AI breach report covered broader exposure involving account and billing records, selected datasets, and incomplete model weights. Fireworks’ November security update also described access through a cloud provider hosting development machines. Those broader findings do not establish that every customer lost the same data.

Other customers reported separate impacts. Notion’s disclosure involved AI chat transcripts used by Insights across fewer than 1% of workspaces, without a breach of Notion’s systems. Uber’s disclosure concerned personal information, including driver’s license details, belonging to thousands of U.S. drivers. Neither disclosure establishes involvement in Cursor’s extension attack.

Cursor moved inference traffic away from Fireworks, revoked vendor access, rotated internal credentials, rebuilt the extension marketplace, and expanded secret scanning and network restrictions. It also redeployed production infrastructure as a precaution. The company believes the incident is contained and said the last observed attacker activity, on November 1, was blocked. Privacy Mode prompts, customer code repositories, and official Cursor updates were unaffected.

Affected developers should follow Cursor’s cleanup notice. Removing the extension alone may leave SSH keys and startup scripts behind. Cursor advises checking endpoint evidence, isolating affected machines, removing persistence, rotating accessible credentials from a trusted system, and assessing whether rebuilding is needed.

articles.description:
CISA has warned that attackers are exploiting a Check Point security flaw that lets a local user gain root access on affected appliances. The agency added CVE-2026-123039 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 13, 2026, confirming that the vulnerability is being used in real attacks. Check Point said it observed exploitation against “a […]

The post CISA Warns of Check Point 0-Day Vulnerability Exploited to Gain Root Access appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
CISA has warned that attackers are exploiting a Check Point security flaw that lets a local user gain root access on affected appliances. The agency added CVE-2026-123039 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 13, 2026, confirming that the vulnerability is being used in real attacks.

Check Point said it observed exploitation against “a couple of dozen customers.” The flaw carries a CVSS score of 7.8 and affects the DynamicCLI service in Gaia OS. Successful exploitation allows commands to run with the highest operating system rights, putting affected firewalls and management systems at risk.

Check Point Root Access Vulnerability

The weakness sits in dynamic_server, a process that runs as root and handles extended command-line functions. It receives requests through /tmp/dynamic_socket, a local communication socket. On vulnerable systems, this socket has permissions set to 0777, allowing any local user to write to it without proper access restrictions.

The service also fails to authenticate the process sending a request. It executes the received command as root, turning limited local access into full system control. However, this is not a standalone remote code execution flaw. An attacker must already have local code execution on the appliance before exploiting it.

Cybersecurity News previously covered Check Point firewall attacks involving PHP2Shell, where attackers used this privilege escalation flaw after gaining initial access. That distinction matters because fixing an entry point alone does not remove every weakness attackers could use after reaching a device or gaining a service account.

Affected Products and Available Fixes

According to Check Point’s security advisory, affected products include Force Firewalls, Management and Log Servers, Multi-Domain management and logging systems, and Maestro Orchestrator. Vulnerable releases span R81, R81.10, R81.20, R82, R82.10, and R82.20. Check Point Spark Firewalls and Smart-1 Cloud are not affected by this flaw.

Check Point has released fixes in Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator updates. Protected releases start at R82.20 Take 14, R82.10 Take 52, R82 Take 132, and R81.20 Take 174. The correction blocks and logs unauthorized DynamicCLI requests. R81 and R81.10 are listed as end-of-support versions in the advisory.

For temporary mitigation, administrators can stop the service and prevent its restart by running dbset process:dynamic_server, followed by dbset :save. Check Point warns that this disables the Dynamic CLI commands described in its documentation. Administrators should account for that operational impact rather than treating the workaround as a permanent replacement for patching.

The daemon records received commands in /var/log/dynamicCli.log. Requests that lack the expected Clish wrapper need investigation. Check Point also recommends checking for unusual commands involving account creation, SSH keys, downloads, or sensitive files. After patching, /tmp/dynamic_socket should show permissions of 0660, owned by root and the config group, rather than 0777.

Earlier Check Point VPN zero-day coverage showed how gateway flaws can expose sensitive information. This case requires local access, but confirmed exploitation makes patching and compromise checks urgent. CISA’s alert urges organizations to prioritize known exploited vulnerabilities.

The exposed information includes driver’s license details. Uber is notifying affected people, but it has not disclosed the total number impacted nationwide. The incident became known to Uber […]

The post Uber Confirms Data Breach – Hackers Stole Users’ Personal Information appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Uber has confirmed a data breach involving the personal information of thousands of U.S. drivers after hackers accessed records held by Fireworks AI, a third-party technology provider.

The exposed information includes driver’s license details. Uber is notifying affected people, but it has not disclosed the total number impacted nationwide.

The incident became known to Uber on October 9, 2026, when its service provider reported that an unauthorized party had compromised internal login credentials. Those credentials allowed the attacker to access Uber’s account with the provider, creating a path to personal records stored outside Uber’s own systems.

Uber said it immediately cut its data connections with the provider and opened an investigation. On October 13, investigators confirmed that the attacker had accessed Uber data, including personal information belonging to people now receiving breach notices. The notification letter is dated November 10, 2026.

Stolen Credentials Exposed Driver Records

State notices show that the breach affected 2,567 people in Massachusetts, 3,430 in South Carolina, and approximately 1,873 in Rhode Island. Together, those figures cover 7,870 people across three states. Additional notifications involve other states, meaning this count does not represent the full scale of the breach.

The public California notice leaves the exposed data fields blank rather than listing specific information. However, state filings reviewed by TechCrunch identified driver’s license information among the stolen records. The available evidence concerns drivers and should not be read as confirmation that all Uber riders or accounts were affected.

An Uber spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch that Fireworks AI was the vendor involved. Cyber Security News previously covered the wider Fireworks AI data breach, which exposed customer records and some datasets. However, those broader findings do not establish which additional data, if any, belonged to Uber.

The same provider also handled data involved in the Notion AI chat transcript breach. Notion said fewer than 1% of customer workspaces were affected and that its own systems were not breached. These separate disclosures show how one provider’s security incident can expose information belonging to several customers.

Protection for Affected Drivers

Uber’s official breach notice says it had not identified misuse of the affected information when the letter was issued. The company is offering free credit monitoring and fraud assistance through Cyberscout, a TransUnion company. Recipients must enroll within 90 days of the letter’s date using their activation code.

Affected drivers should review their individual letters, check account statements, and report suspicious activity. Uber also recommends considering fraud alerts or credit freezes. The Federal Trade Commission explains that a credit freeze limits access to credit reports, making fraudulent new accounts harder to open.

Researchers have found that mistyped addresses of popular AI tools lead to fake verification pages, hidden commands and malware installers. The technique is called TypoPrompting. The research traced 186 lookalike domains across 27 AI brands, including Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Perplexity, Midjourney, […]

The post New TypoPrompting Attacks Turn Mistyped AI Website Addresses Into Malware Installation Traps appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A simple typing mistake can now cost you more than a failed page load. Researchers have found that mistyped addresses of popular AI tools lead to fake verification pages, hidden commands and malware installers. The technique is called TypoPrompting.

The research traced 186 lookalike domains across 27 AI brands, including Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Perplexity, Midjourney, ElevenLabs and Cursor.

A small slip, such as “cloude.ai” for Claude, can send a visitor down a chain of redirects that ends in a ClickFix lure, a Microsoft Store-signed hijacker or a search-changing browser extension. This follows other reports of fake AI brand lures used to push harmful files and commands.

Analysts at Island identified the campaign and named the pattern TypoPrompting. They describe it as AI-app lookalikes that turn an attempt to reach a familiar tool into a prompt to verify, install or run something else. The research was published on November 12, 2026, by lead security researcher Oleg Zaytsev.

New TypoPrompting Attacks Turn Mistyped AI Website Addresses

The typos are ordinary. In “clsude.ai” the finger hits S instead of A. In “cluade.ai” two letters swap places. In “caude.ai” a letter goes missing. ChatGPT has the most lookalikes at 25, followed by Claude with 18 and DeepSeek with 16.

What happens next depends on the visitor. A parked page hands the browser to a traffic distribution system. That system picks a destination based on the visitor’s location, operating system and browser.

One person sees a harmless parked page, while another gets a malicious lure. Some of these names are years old. Several were registered in July 2023 and later joined a monetized portfolio of 81 domains tied to the redirector a11[.]click.

The Claude typo “cloude.ai” shows the full chain. A Windows visitor is sent through several redirect hops to a gate that fingerprints the browser and solves a small proof-of-work challenge. Only selected visits get an answer.

That answer is a fake human check, and fake Cloudflare verification pages have been seen in other ClickFix campaigns too. The page tells the user to open the Windows Run box, paste a command and press Enter.

The pasted command uses curl to save a script named W901.ps1 in the temporary folder. It then runs the script in a hidden PowerShell window with the execution policy bypassed.

The download address is written as the single number 3112851459. This is the IP address 185.138.88[.]3 in decimal form, so a filter looking for dotted IP addresses would miss it.

The gate behind this chain is much larger than one typo. Researchers found 550 matching scan records across 211 entry domains.

These include lookalikes of Scotiabank, Charles Schwab, Verizon and Microsoft Azure. Mac users get a fake Terminal prompt instead, and others are offered an archive to unpack and run.

Store-Signed Malware and Search Hijacking

A second route ends somewhere that looks far safer. Eight typos of Claude, DeepSeek, Copilot, ElevenLabs and Voice AI led through deezyj[.]com to fake “Security Check” pages.

These pages delivered Net Guard, an app sold as a Wi-Fi and DNS scanner. The installer matches the real Microsoft Store listing and carries Microsoft’s signature, so victims get a genuine Store package with a browser-control engine inside.

Net Guard is built on a module called buntai-sdk and takes its orders from remote configuration. It can change the default search engine while the user is idle.

It can also run remote JavaScript through browser DevTools and edit browser profiles to install extensions. In the code the researchers analyzed, all of these features are on by default.

The app also checks for a debugger and for enterprise browser management. Privacy Keeper and MyFlixly Browser share the same code and were also classed as malicious browser hijackers.

The third route starts at “preplexity.ai”, a Perplexity typo. It leads to an installation page for a Chrome extension that needs no permissions.

Its listing promises Bing search, but its manifest quietly sends every address-bar search through find.flashysearches[.]com. It is one of 30 extensions built from one kit.

Thirteen have been removed, and the 17 still listed showed 972,000 users on November 3. This matches the pattern in a recent report on Chrome extensions hijacking searches at a much larger scale.

Island advises organizations to give staff direct links to approved AI services and to watch for lookalikes of those tools.

It also suggests linking browsing activity to Run-dialog or Terminal use, checking the publisher and hash of MSIX installers, and setting a fixed search provider.

Security teams should hunt across the whole route, from entry domain to endpoint change. The same human-error risk appears when slopsquatting targets AI coding agents, where a wrong name leads to malware. Users can lower the risk by bookmarking the AI tools they use. A real verification page never asks you to paste a command.

articles.title: Hackers Use SANSAR Linux Malware to Hide Crypto Mining by Faking 0% GPU Usage
articles.description:
Hackers are hiding cryptocurrency mining on Linux GPU servers by changing the readings administrators use to spot heavy workloads. The toolkit combines a Rust-based controller called SANSAR, a kernel rootkit, and a modified NVIDIA monitoring library that reports 0% GPU utilization while mining continues in the background. The intrusion reached three Linux GPU hosts through […]

The post Hackers Use SANSAR Linux Malware to Hide Crypto Mining by Faking 0% GPU Usage appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are hiding cryptocurrency mining on Linux GPU servers by changing the readings administrators use to spot heavy workloads.

The toolkit combines a Rust-based controller called SANSAR, a kernel rootkit, and a modified NVIDIA monitoring library that reports 0% GPU utilization while mining continues in the background.

The intrusion reached three Linux GPU hosts through an exposed Ray job agent. Ray supports distributed computing, including AI training and inference, making these systems valuable targets.

Unlike campaigns involving fake utility download traps, this attack entered through infrastructure that accepted remote computing jobs without authentication.

Researchers from Elastic Security Labs identified the activity as REF3364 in a November 12, 2026, technical analysis of SANSAR.

Their findings describe coordinated tools for mining, hiding processes, maintaining access, and opening remote shells—not simply a miner running unnoticed.

Hackers Use SANSAR Linux Malware

The deception targets NVIDIA Management Library, or NVML, the interface used by monitoring tools such as nvidia-smi. The attacker’s wrapper forwards requests to the genuine NVIDIA library, then changes selected results before returning them.

GPU utilization becomes zero, while temperature and power readings are replaced with random values between 36–46 degrees Celsius and 100–200 watts.

This makes apparently normal monitoring output unreliable. The GPU is not necessarily idle; the software reporting its activity has been altered.

SANSAR can also rebuild and reinstall the wrapper from recovered source files, giving the operator a way to maintain the modified monitoring layer.

A separate kernel rootkit hides selected processes, files, and socket entries. It intercepts directory listings and other system operations, removing matching records or returning errors when tools inspect hidden processes.

Similar Linux rootkit mining attacks have used kernel-level concealment, but this toolkit adds falsified GPU measurements to obscure resource use.

SANSAR itself supervises publicly available mining software rather than performing every mining task internally. Its CPU branch uses XMRig, while its GPU branch launches SRBMiner-MULTI.

The controller supplies pool addresses, wallet or login details, algorithms, and other settings. Elastic found no hardcoded fallback pool or wallet in those launch paths.

Exposed Ray Jobs Enable Persistent Remote Access

Recorded activity began with external probes on October 22, followed by a GPU inventory query on October 24. On October 25, the attacker submitted a Python reverse-shell job.

Although the Ray head-node dashboard listened only on localhost, the job agent remained internet-accessible and accepted unauthenticated submissions. The initial shell ran under the account owning the Ray session. The attacker then added an SSH key for continued access.

After obtaining root, the operator installed the toolkit, built its kernel module through Dynamic Kernel Module Support, and added an early-boot loader. Elastic’s account does not explain the precise method used to obtain root.

Control extends beyond mining. SANSAR communicates over Tor and supports interactive Bash shells, miner configuration changes, output forwarding, and TCP SYN traffic generation.

Its shell setup suppresses saved command history. These capabilities make the compromise broader than stolen computing capacity alone.

A separate backdoor retrieves its controller address from an Ethereum smart contract, then connects directly over TCP. This creates another route for shell access.

Earlier Discord controlled mining campaigns also combined mining with remote control, although their communication methods differed from this intrusion.

For defenders, Elastic highlights two priorities: check who can submit Ray jobs and verify whether GPU monitoring libraries have changed.

A zero reading from an altered library cannot establish that a server is clean. Investigations should also account for persistent access and kernel-level hiding rather than treating the visible miner as the entire infection.

articles.title: Hackers Use 2,700 Passwords to Break Into Microsoft SQL Servers and Deploy Remote Access Malware
articles.description:
A new campaign is guessing its way into internet-facing Microsoft SQL Server systems. The attackers use a list of more than 2,700 passwords and then install a cryptocurrency miner and a remote access trojan (RAT) on the hacked machines. The campaign has been running since at least early October 2026. Database servers hold valuable data, […]

The post Hackers Use 2,700 Passwords to Break Into Microsoft SQL Servers and Deploy Remote Access Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new campaign is guessing its way into internet-facing Microsoft SQL Server systems. The attackers use a list of more than 2,700 passwords and then install a cryptocurrency miner and a remote access trojan (RAT) on the hacked machines.

The campaign has been running since at least early October 2026. Database servers hold valuable data, so they are a favorite target. This campaign scans for exposed servers, tries many logins, and runs commands that pull in more malware.

Attackers have used the same basic approach for years, as seen when hackers were continuously attacking MS-SQL servers with scanner malware earlier this year.

Researchers at Fortinet’s FortiGuard Labs identified the malware and described the full infection chain in a report published on November 12, 2026.

Analyst Xiaopeng Zhang noted that the campaign abuses T-SQL, Microsoft’s extension of the SQL language, to run commands on hacked servers. FortiGuard rates the severity as high.

Hackers Use 2,700 Passwords to Break Into Microsoft SQL Servers

The chain starts with a file named dllhost.exe. It is written in the Go language and packed with UPX to hide its contents. The name copies a real Windows process, which helps it blend in.

The file contains the open-source Naabu port scanner. It contacts the attackers’ server, receives an IP range to scan, and checks each random address in that range for open TCP port 1433, the default port for SQL Server.

Any open host is written to a file called Result.txt, and the malware then asks for the next range. The malware also downloads eight support files, including scripts named go.vbs and go.bat and a tool named dwm.exe.

Despite its name, dwm.exe is a .NET program that guesses logins. It reads user names such as “sa” and “admin” from one file and tries more than 2,700 passwords from another, using up to 500 threads at once.

Weak or reused passwords on exposed servers are what make this work. This is the same weakness behind older cases where criminals brute force MSSQL logins to drop ransomware.

When a login works, the tool runs a file called 2018.sql on the server. Its commands turn on xp_cmdshell, a feature that lets SQL Server run Windows commands.

They then download a program into the C:\Users\Public folder and name it Google.exe or payload.exe. They also create a daily scheduled task called Microsoft_UPDATES and drop another file, Secs.exe, into the Startup folder.

The malware itself sets up a scheduled task that runs every 30 minutes and is named to look like a Microsoft Edge update.

What the Miner and Gh0st RAT Do After the Break-In

The downloader, Secs.exe, connects to an FTP server and pulls down more files, which it saves in the Temp folder and runs. It then creates another disguised Edge update task.

Next it sends the victim’s public IP address, country, Windows version, processor, memory, user name and host name to the attackers. This registers the server in their system.

One payload is MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe, which is not an update at all. It is a Monero miner protected by two packers, Themida and a custom LZSS packer.

It uses the server’s CPU to mine coins and connects to pools such as nanopool and kryptex. It also tells the attackers’ server when mining starts. The result is slow performance, higher power costs and wasted computing power for the victim.

The second payload, winlogon.exe, is a variant of Gh0st RAT, which gives attackers remote control. It sets itself up three ways: a Run registry key, a Windows service and a scheduled task.

It can log keystrokes, manage files, run a remote shell, wipe event logs and steal data from QQ, a Chinese messaging app. It also supports more than 30 control commands, and plugins add screen capture and remote desktop.

The malware checks for 78 security product process names. Its command servers were offline when Fortinet tested it, so the team could only study the unpacked file. The same family has been seen before, when HiddenGh0st malware targeting MS-SQL servers was reported.

Do not leave SQL Server open to the internet. Put it behind a firewall or VPN, and block port 1433 from outside networks. Use long, unique passwords, rename or disable the sa account, and lock accounts after repeated failures.

Turn off xp_cmdshell unless you need it. Watch for new scheduled tasks that imitate Edge updates, unknown files in C:\Users\Public, and sudden spikes in CPU use.

Recent reports of hijacking MS-SQL servers recently with C2 frameworks show that these servers remain a steady target.

articles.title: Citrix Patches 28 Security Vulnerabilities in NetScaler, Including a Critical Flaw in Default Installations
articles.description:
Citrix has released fixes for 28 security flaws in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway. One of them, CVE-2026-120868, affects every deployment in its default setup. Cloud Software Group published bulletin CTX697305 on November 12, 2026, and rated it Critical. CVE-2026-120868 is a memory overflow in packet processing. It carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.3. […]

The post Citrix Patches 28 Security Vulnerabilities in NetScaler, Including a Critical Flaw in Default Installations appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Citrix has released fixes for 28 security flaws in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway. One of them, CVE-2026-120868, affects every deployment in its default setup. Cloud Software Group published bulletin CTX697305 on November 12, 2026, and rated it Critical.

CVE-2026-120868 is a memory overflow in packet processing. It carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.3. Most NetScaler bugs need a specific feature turned on. This one does not. No extra setting is needed, so every unpatched appliance is vulnerable.

The bug can cause unpredictable behavior or a denial-of-service. Because the attack needs no login and no user action, anyone who can reach the device over the network can try it.

Almost all of the 28 flaws are memory bugs. They include buffer overflows, out-of-bounds writes, and a double free. Citrix says most can crash the device or make it behave oddly. Each one only matters if the matching feature is in use.

The highest score, 9.5, belongs to CVE-2026-107412. It hits appliances set up as a Gateway, such as SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN, or RDP Proxy, or as an AAA virtual server. Several other bugs score 9.3. They sit in areas like SMPP traffic, DNS and DNS-over-HTTPS, NetScaler Push, Email OTP login, Endpoint Analysis, and ICA proxy.

Citrix Patches NetScaler Security Vulnerabilities

Many others score 8.7 and touch SAML, WebAuth, LDAP, client-certificate login, HTTP/3, GSLB, Diameter, MQTT and RADIUS handling. A BGP routing flaw scores 7.7, but an attacker would need to be or fake a configured neighbor.

Three flaws score 6.9. One of them, CVE-2026-111338, writes sensitive login data into the log file /var/log/httperror.log, so someone with local read access could see it.

The bulletin covers customer-managed appliances. Versions 14.1 before 14.1-73.57 and 13.1 before 13.1-64.39 are affected. So are 14.1 FIPS before 14.1-73.58 FIPS, and 13.1 FIPS and NDcPP before 13.1-37.293.

Citrix reports that Secure Private Access hybrid setups using NetScaler instances require upgrades, while Cloud Software Group is updating its managed cloud services and Adaptive Authentication; no workaround is available, and customers should install fixed builds immediately.

For the other 27 flaws, admins can search their configuration for the entries Citrix lists, such as add vpn vserver or add authentication samlAction. That shows which bugs apply to their setup. It should not delay patching, since the default-configuration flaw affects everyone.

Citrix thanked researchers from JPMorgan Chase’s XOR team, Capital One Offensive Security, and watchTowr. It also said its own Product Security Team found several of the bugs using advanced AI-assisted code analysis. This suggests AI tools are starting to surface memory bugs in old, large codebases.

NetScaler has been a repeat target this year. Citrix fixed two zero-days in October that attackers were already using, and CISA added one of them to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list.

We also covered how exploitation of CitrixBleed 2 led to ransomware. Past NetScaler bugs were attacked quickly after patches came out, so a flaw that needs no setup will draw attention fast.

Admins should upgrade to the fixed builds and check their configuration against the bulletin. They should also keep the management addresses (NSIP) away from untrusted networks, because CVE-2026-120863 can be reached through them. Teams can read the full advisory on the Citrix Security Bulletin page and report problems to secure@cloud.com.

articles.title: Hackers Use Fake Purchase Order Emails to Deliver XLoader Malware Through Malicious Word Documents
articles.description:
Hackers are sending fake purchase order emails to trick recipients into opening Word documents that deliver XLoader, an information-stealing malware. The attack uses an embedded document, an old Microsoft Equation Editor vulnerability, and several script stages to reach its final payload. What begins as a routine order confirmation can end with stolen browser data and […]

The post Hackers Use Fake Purchase Order Emails to Deliver XLoader Malware Through Malicious Word Documents appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are sending fake purchase order emails to trick recipients into opening Word documents that deliver XLoader, an information-stealing malware.

The attack uses an embedded document, an old Microsoft Equation Editor vulnerability, and several script stages to reach its final payload. What begins as a routine order confirmation can end with stolen browser data and additional malware on an infected computer.

The lure fits everyday purchasing workflows, asking recipients to review prices, quantities, and shipping arrangements. Similar fake business order emails have delivered XLoader through script attachments, but this case uses a DOCX file to hide the next stage.

The familiar business language gives employees a reason to open the attachment without questioning its contents. Researchers from ASEC identified the phishing activity and described the infection chain in a November 12 report.

Their technical analysis of the campaign shows how a Word attachment leads to script execution, registry-based persistence, and an encrypted payload that ultimately runs in memory. The final malware is XLoader, with version information showing release 8.9.

Hackers Use Fake Purchase Order Emails

The sample email presents an order worth $144,744.50 and asks for shipment by the end of the following month. It tells the recipient to report pricing or quantity discrepancies before shipping.

These details create a believable reason to inspect the attached purchase order while keeping attention on the supposed transaction rather than the document’s safety.

Opening the attachment starts a chain inside Word. The DOCX contains a malicious Rich Text Format document, which Word processes through its “Import Content from Another Document” feature, known as altChunk.

This feature provides the route into the embedded content; the code execution step then relies on CVE-2017-11882 in Microsoft Equation Editor.

While Word processes the RTF content, an embedded Object Linking and Embedding package writes a Visual Basic Script file into the temporary directory.

A separate Equation Editor object exploits the vulnerability to execute that script through Windows Script Host. Earlier Equation Editor exploitation campaigns also used order-themed documents to distribute XLoader, although their filenames and delivery stages differed.

The script contains Base64-encoded data, saves it locally, and launches an embedded first-stage PowerShell script. After decoding, the data contains three parts: a loader, an encrypted payload, and a second PowerShell script.

This layered packaging places multiple execution steps between the original document and XLoader, rather than exposing the final malware directly inside the visible purchase order.

Registry Persistence and In-Memory XLoader Execution

The first PowerShell stage stores its execution path and script content in separate registry values. It also creates a current-user Run entry, allowing the stored script to execute again when the user signs in.

This persistence mechanism means the attack does not depend solely on keeping the original Word document open after the initial compromise.

Next, the first script decrypts the saved data and starts the secondary PowerShell stage. That script runs the loader and passes the encrypted payload as an argument.

The loader applies an XOR operation to recover the payload and execute it in memory. Separate reporting on XLoader malware evasion techniques describes the family’s wider use of encryption and hidden communications, but those details should not be assumed for this sample.

ASEC identifies the final payload as an information stealer that collects computer details and browser data. It can also download additional malware, extending the risk beyond the first infection.

The report does not name a threat actor, establish how many organizations received the emails, or confirm the total number of compromised systems.

Defenders should verify unexpected purchase orders through a known contact and keep Office installations patched. Monitoring should connect suspicious document activity with script execution and registry changes, rather than treating each event separately.

ASEC advises checking sender domains and attachments carefully. For this chain, the document-to-script transition and logon persistence provide useful investigation points alongside the published indicators.

articles.title: Massive Microsoft 365 Outage Impacts Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, and Defender XDR Users
articles.description:
A major Microsoft 365 outage disrupted cloud service access on November 12 and continued into November 13, 2026, as Microsoft worked to restore failing infrastructure. Microsoft confirmed that connectivity problems could affect users in any region, expanding the scope beyond its initial investigation into Exchange Online mailbox access in the Americas. The reported impact spans […]

The post Massive Microsoft 365 Outage Impacts Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, and Defender XDR Users appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A major Microsoft 365 outage disrupted cloud service access on November 12 and continued into November 13, 2026, as Microsoft worked to restore failing infrastructure.

Microsoft confirmed that connectivity problems could affect users in any region, expanding the scope beyond its initial investigation into Exchange Online mailbox access in the Americas.

The reported impact spans Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, Copilot and Microsoft Defender XDR, although the exact service and feature restrictions remain subject to Microsoft’s updated advisory. Administrators should check incident MO1550821 for that breakdown. Exchange Online mailbox connectivity is also being tracked separately under EX1550543. Microsoft has not confirmed that every customer is affected.

Early findings pointed to heavy load across several regions. Microsoft later clarified that the pressure did not come from increased traffic. Instead, servers had unexpectedly become unavailable, leaving the remaining infrastructure to handle connections. Engineers began moving traffic across Microsoft’s worldwide systems to reduce pressure on the affected environment.

The disruption follows other cloud availability incidents, including a Microsoft 365 outage affecting Teams, SharePoint and Copilot in July. That earlier incident involved a network configuration change. Microsoft has not established the same cause here, making it important to separate historical context from the current investigation.

Failed Health Checks Complicate Recovery

Microsoft identified failed automated health checks as a key part of the current problem. These checks determine whether servers remain available to handle requests. Investigators focused on a component responsible for processing server health, while testing a configuration change and restarting affected servers to bring capacity back online.

According to Microsoft’s official incident updates, an alternative health check method allowed some servers to return to service. Engineers began applying that approach more widely and preparing automated recovery systems to detect and restart unresponsive machines. However, these measures did not immediately deliver the expected improvement.

Microsoft subsequently found that a core process on affected servers was becoming overwhelmed, causing further capacity loss. Some restored servers initially remained stable, but later became unresponsive again when traffic reached them. That pattern complicated recovery because bringing servers online did not necessarily mean they could sustain normal use.

Engineers paused deployments, shifted traffic onto alternate routes and reviewed whether reversing several recent configuration updates could speed recovery. Microsoft initially said it had not identified a recent change matching the start of the disruption. The later rollback assessment therefore remains a recovery option, not proof of the root cause.

Security Visibility and Business Impact

For security teams, reported Defender XDR disruption raises questions about access to alerts and investigations. A previous Microsoft Defender portal access incident showed how dashboard availability can interrupt security workflows. However, portal access problems alone do not establish that endpoint protection or background detection has stopped working.

Administrators should follow EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center and use Microsoft’s public service status page when the admin center is unavailable. Microsoft’s public updates describe infrastructure failures and recovery work, rather than presenting evidence of a confirmed cyberattack behind this disruption.

The latest supplied updates did not confirm full restoration or provide a firm completion time. Organizations should distinguish partial recovery from stable service, particularly because restored servers became unresponsive under traffic. Microsoft was still investigating that behavior while limiting selected traffic and working to return remaining capacity safely.

Update 1: Microsoft confirmed that its recent fixes have not worked as expected. Engineers are exploring other ways to increase capacity and address ongoing traffic imbalances. Administrators can track updates under EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center.

Update 2: Microsoft says it is continuing efforts to recover affected frontend servers while implementing additional traffic optimization measures to improve service stability and increase capacity amid the ongoing Microsoft 365 outage.

The company is working on multiple recovery efforts simultaneously to reduce the impact, resolve the issues blocking restoration, and return affected infrastructure to a healthy state.

Engineers are also focusing on stabilizing recovered servers to prevent further disruptions as user traffic resumes. Microsoft has not provided an estimated time for full service restoration.

Update 3: Microsoft is evaluating traffic throttling, protocol adjustments, and failover routing to increase frontend server capacity and improve stability. The company is also expanding testing in a controlled environment to improve traffic monitoring and issue detection.

Microsoft said it is not aware of any malicious activity causing the outage. Recovery remains a priority, and the company plans to publish a post-incident report detailing the root cause and further safeguards once the disruption is mitigated.

Update 4: Microsoft says recovery is progressing in phases, with gradual improvement across several Microsoft 365 services. However, service health remains uneven, and capacity has not fully returned to normal.

The company has extended the email timeout window to 48 hours to protect delayed messages while it continues processing mail queues and backlogs. Administrators can follow incident MO1550821 for further updates.

Update 5: Microsoft has reported further progress in restoring affected Microsoft 365 services, with recovery actions completed across portions of the impacted infrastructure and user traffic gradually being restored.

The company confirmed improvements in key services, including Exchange Online mailbox access and delayed email processing, although some users may continue to experience intermittent disruptions.

Engineers are now expanding recovery measures to the remaining affected infrastructure while working to stabilize services and increase server capacity to ensure consistent performance.

Microsoft has not yet confirmed full service restoration, with further updates available under incident ID MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center and at status.cloud.microsoft.

Update 5: Microsoft has reported further progress in restoring affected Microsoft 365 services, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across an increasing portion of the impacted infrastructure.

However, some users may continue to experience intermittent disruptions as recovery efforts remain underway. Engineers are now focusing on restoring the remaining affected environments while prioritizing the reduction of queued emails and delivery backlogs.

Microsoft has also maintained an extended 48-hour email timeout window to help prevent delayed messages from expiring while email processing catches up. The company has not yet confirmed full service restoration, with further updates available under incident ID MO1550821.

Update 6: In its most recent update, Microsoft reported continued progress in restoring affected Microsoft 365 services worldwide, with broader improvements across North America, sustained recovery throughout much of Europe, and encouraging signs of restoration in the Asia-Pacific region.

However, some users may still experience intermittent access issues and delayed email delivery as recovery efforts continue. Microsoft engineers are focusing on stabilizing recovered infrastructure, completing mitigation measures in remaining affected regions, and clearing delayed email queues and backlogs.

The company is also validating service stability across different connection methods to ensure consistent availability. Full service restoration has not yet been confirmed.

Update 7: Microsoft says service access and email delivery are improving across more of the affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure as recovery efforts continue. The company acknowledged the disruption to customers’ daily work and expressed regret for the impact.

Microsoft also confirmed there is no indication that malicious activity or a cyberattack caused the outage. Its teams are reviewing what happened and how to prevent similar issues, with further updates promised as more information becomes available.

Note: This is a developing story. We will keep you updated as Microsoft shares more information on the outage and service recovery.

articles.title: Hackers Use DeepSeek and GLM AI Agents to Breach 10 Organizations in Autonomous Cyberattacks
articles.description:
Chinese-speaking hackers have used AI agents powered by DeepSeek and Zhipu GLM to break into 10 organizations with very little human effort. The campaign ran in August and September 2026 and covered 25 operations against at least 19 targets. It shows how quickly autonomous AI cyberattacks are moving from theory into daily use. The attackers […]

The post Hackers Use DeepSeek and GLM AI Agents to Breach 10 Organizations in Autonomous Cyberattacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Chinese-speaking hackers have used AI agents powered by DeepSeek and Zhipu GLM to break into 10 organizations with very little human effort.

The campaign ran in August and September 2026 and covered 25 operations against at least 19 targets. It shows how quickly autonomous AI cyberattacks are moving from theory into daily use.

The attackers did not build anything new. They took a public, open-source penetration testing framework called Cairn and connected it to two Chinese AI models.

They gave it a target and a goal, and the tool planned, ran and recorded each step by itself. A small team could therefore attack many organizations at once.

Analysts at Unit42 identified the activity and track it as CL-STA-1238. They believe, with moderate confidence, that it is a China-linked intelligence collection effort. The targets were in semiconductor manufacturing, U.S. defense policy and civil society.

Hackers Use DeepSeek and GLM AI Agents

Cairn works through AI “agent workers.” Each worker reads and writes to a shared “blackboard,” where confirmed findings are saved as facts and next steps are saved as intents.

The tool repeats a simple loop. In the Reason phase, the model reviews what it knows and decides what to try next. In the Explore phase, it carries out one action and logs the result. The loop stops when the goal is met, the options run out, or the operator steps in.

For each target, the attackers only needed to enter the organization’s root domain and a one-line goal, often written in Chinese. One task said to “breach the target as fast as possible.”

In one case, they also supplied VPN gateway addresses and shared group passwords gathered beforehand. The model then built its own plan of three to seven stages.

These covered reconnaissance, web application exploitation, credential collection, privilege escalation and lateral movement. Of the 25 operations, 13 ran on GLM 5.2, eight on DeepSeek V4 Flash and four on DeepSeek V4 Pro. The attackers seem to have compared the models.

They switched to the stronger V4 Pro when Flash failed against a hard target. Some runs lasted from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours, with no time limit set.

The attackers also had little trouble with AI guardrails. Cairn’s default prompts already tell the model never to refuse a task. The attackers added a Chinese-language note claiming the work was an authorized security test, and they created an AUTHORIZATION.md file for each operation.

Neither GLM nor DeepSeek refused. This is similar to a jailbroken DeepSeek AI agent case that hit a European telecom provider earlier this month.

Victims, Stolen Data and Warning Signs for Defenders

Seven of the targets were in the semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing supply chain. Three were defense-related, including a space technology company and a policy think tank. Four were human rights or civil society groups, such as a Canadian human-rights body and a U.S. teachers’ union.

At an industry standards body, weak-password spraying gave the attackers dozens of valid credentials and access to internal directory data.

They also overwrote a live standards-ballot document. At another organization, a brute-forced credential led to unauthorized administrator accounts and a persistent API token.

A content management system flaw exposed more than one million member records, about 31,000 CRM contacts and staff password hashes.

An open registration endpoint leaked roughly 500 user records, including .mil and .gov accounts. Other cases involved employee data at a lithography maker, about 150,000 internal documents at an industrial-automation company, and student data at an education nonprofit.

The flaws behind these breaches were not new. They included authentication bypasses, insecure direct object references, mass-assignment privilege escalation, weak or default passwords, exposed cloud APIs and old public CVEs.

AI raised the speed and reach of the work, not its difficulty. Other recent cases follow the same pattern, such as open-source ARTEX AI agents that automate Active Directory abuse.

For defenders, the basics still work. Teams should use strong, unique passwords with phishing-resistant MFA, reduce internet-facing systems, patch known CVEs quickly and watch for noisy traffic from a single IP address.

Unit 42 notes that Cairn generated hundreds of thousands of high-frequency requests from one origin. The researchers expect these campaigns to grow as open models with weak guardrails become more capable.

Readers can also see how one hacker running 12 coordinated AI agents hit hundreds of targets, and how agents rebuild failed tools and keep going.

articles.title: Microsoft 365 Massive Outage – Fixes Fail as Restored Servers Keep Going Unresponsive
articles.description:
Microsoft has yet to find a fix that holds for the global Microsoft 365 outage, which has now run for more than 10 hours. Servers that engineers bring back online are falling over again as soon as user traffic reaches them. The outage began on November 12, 2026, and continued through November 13. As we […]

The post Microsoft 365 Massive Outage – Fixes Fail as Restored Servers Keep Going Unresponsive appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has yet to find a fix that holds for the global Microsoft 365 outage, which has now run for more than 10 hours. Servers that engineers bring back online are falling over again as soon as user traffic reaches them.

The outage began on November 12, 2026, and continued through November 13. As we reported earlier, it started with Exchange Online mailbox access failures in the Americas. It then spread to Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, and Microsoft Defender XDR users in any region.

Microsoft’s latest status updates show the recovery has stalled. The company says it is running several workstreams in parallel to “address our current blocker” and return parts of its infrastructure to a healthy state. It has given no estimated time for full restoration.

The incidents are tracked as EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center.

Restored Servers Fail Again Under Load

The core problem is that restarting servers does not keep them healthy. In an update on its Microsoft 365 Status account, Microsoft said restored servers “can become unresponsive again once they receive traffic.”

Engineers are still analyzing diagnostic data to learn what triggers the behavior. Microsoft has not announced a root cause.

With restarts failing to hold, the company has moved to three fallback measures:

  • Traffic limiting. Microsoft is temporarily restricting which types of traffic can reach the affected infrastructure in some locations.
  • Server rebuilds. A subset of affected servers is being rebuilt on a previous configuration, to test whether that stops them from going unresponsive.
  • Traffic rerouting. Engineers are adjusting traffic protocols, redistributing load, and applying what Microsoft calls strategic traffic blocking.

Microsoft says it sees partial recovery in regions where these traffic measures are in place. Partial recovery is not stable service, and users in those regions may still see intermittent failures.

The rebuild on a previous configuration is the notable step. It suggests Microsoft suspects a recent change, though it has not confirmed one as the cause.

Microsoft says it is seeing positive results from efforts to restart affected infrastructure and restore server availability amid the ongoing Microsoft 365 service disruption. The company is recovering impacted infrastructure in an isolated manner and closely monitoring performance to confirm stability before expanding restoration efforts more broadly.

Following these initial recovery efforts, Microsoft expects service availability to improve gradually as the restoration process expands across the affected infrastructure. Administrators can track further updates under incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center or through Microsoft’s alternative status update link.

How the Outage Unfolded

Microsoft first blamed elevated load across multiple regions. It later corrected that view: traffic had not increased, but a number of servers had unexpectedly dropped out, straining the rest.

The servers were failing automated health checks, which decide whether a machine can take requests. Engineers paused all deployments, moved traffic to other parts of the worldwide infrastructure, and restarted the affected servers.

Those steps did not work. Microsoft admitted its actions had “not provided the anticipated relief” and found that a core process on the servers was being overwhelmed.

An alternative health check method brought some servers back, and they appeared stable at first. The latest updates confirm that stability did not last once traffic returned.

Scale of the Impact

Downdetector logged more than 120,000 Outlook problem reports at the peak, and reports came from 74 countries. Report volumes have since fallen as partial recovery took effect.

Microsoft’s service health page lists Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Defender, Planner, To Do, Intune, Purview, and Power BI among the affected services. Features that do not depend on Exchange Online reportedly kept working.

The disruption also reached third parties. OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems with their Microsoft 365 connectors. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group postponed its third-quarter results to November 16.

Microsoft says the outage is not the result of a cyberattack. Executive Vice President Charles Lamanna confirmed it was not caused by a security breach, Business Standard reported.

What Administrators Should Do

The fault sits in Microsoft’s infrastructure, so local troubleshooting will not restore service. Administrators should:

  • Track MO1550821 and EX1550543 in the Microsoft 365 admin center, or use status.cloud.microsoft if the admin center will not load.
  • Avoid resetting passwords, rebuilding Outlook profiles, or changing tenant settings in response to the errors.
  • Expect intermittent access even in regions showing recovery, since Microsoft is deliberately blocking some traffic types.
  • Warn users about phishing emails and fake support calls that exploit the outage.
  • Plan for delayed mail delivery once service returns and queued messages are processed.:

Update 1: Microsoft is evaluating traffic throttling, protocol adjustments and failover routing to increase frontend server capacity and improve stability. The company is also expanding testing in a controlled environment to improve traffic monitoring and issue detection.

Microsoft said it is not aware of any malicious activity causing the outage. Recovery remains a priority, and the company plans to publish a post-incident report detailing the root cause and further safeguards once the disruption is mitigated.

We will update this story as Microsoft shares more on the root cause and recovery.

Recent update:

Microsoft has reported further progress in restoring affected Microsoft 365 services, with recovery actions completed across portions of the impacted infrastructure and user traffic gradually being restored.

The company confirmed improvements in key services, including Exchange Online mailbox access and delayed email processing, although some users may continue to experience intermittent disruptions. Engineers are now expanding recovery measures to the remaining affected infrastructure while working to stabilize services and increase server capacity to ensure consistent performance.

Microsoft has reported further progress in restoring affected Microsoft 365 services, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across an increasing portion of the impacted infrastructure.

However, some users may continue to experience intermittent disruptions as recovery efforts remain underway. Engineers are now focusing on restoring the remaining affected environments while prioritizing the reduction of queued emails and delivery backlogs.

Microsoft has also maintained an extended 48-hour email timeout window to help prevent delayed messages from expiring while email processing catches up. The company has not yet confirmed full service restoration, with further updates available under incident ID MO1550821

Recent Update: In its most recent update, Microsoft reported continued progress in restoring affected Microsoft 365 services worldwide, with broader improvements across North America, sustained recovery throughout much of Europe, and encouraging signs of restoration in the Asia-Pacific region.

However, some users may still experience intermittent access issues and delayed email delivery as recovery efforts continue. Microsoft engineers are focusing on stabilizing recovered infrastructure, completing mitigation measures in remaining affected regions, and clearing delayed email queues and backlogs.

articles.title: Hackers Use Windows Named Pipes and SMB to Spread Malware Across Isolated Government Networks
articles.description:
A new espionage group is using Windows named pipes and the SMB file-sharing protocol to move malware through tightly separated networks. Positive Technologies calls the group StingyBasilisk. It has been active since at least April 2022. The attackers sat quietly inside the victim’s systems for a long time and posed as the organization’s own security […]

The post Hackers Use Windows Named Pipes and SMB to Spread Malware Across Isolated Government Networks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new espionage group is using Windows named pipes and the SMB file-sharing protocol to move malware through tightly separated networks. Positive Technologies calls the group StingyBasilisk.

It has been active since at least April 2022. The attackers sat quietly inside the victim’s systems for a long time and posed as the organization’s own security tools.

The team could not find out how the attackers first got in. It did find a large network of custom agents, all controlled through Windows named pipes.

Named pipes are a normal Windows feature that lets programs talk to each other, so the traffic blends in with everyday activity. The stealth of the operation points to spying as the main goal.

Analysts at Habr, where Positive Technologies published its incident response findings, noted that every malware sample was a DLL built to wait and then run its payload only in the memory of a Windows process.

Nothing obvious is left on disk. The researchers also suspect the group runs its own command-and-control framework, and no known threat group has been reliably linked to it.

Hackers Use Windows Named Pipes and SMB

From February 2026, the attackers began spreading inside the victim’s network. They copied malware to target machines over SMB and placed the files in C:\Windows\Temp.

They then started the files remotely with atexec, a tool from the Impacket toolkit that runs commands through the Windows Task Scheduler.

The tool connects over SMB, opens the \pipe\atsvc pipe, and creates and runs a task right away. This is close to the way PsExec can be abused for remote execution.

The task names looked like random GUIDs, which differs from the default name in the Impacket script. This is one small clue defenders can use to spot the activity.

In this phase the attackers launched the CunningDoor loader, using rundll32 to run a signed SafeNet library that in turn loaded a malicious DLL.

Named pipes are also how the malware is controlled. The backdoors create pipes with predictable name patterns and wait for encrypted shellcode to arrive.

This lets the attackers build a chain of infected hosts that pass commands to each other. A machine with no direct internet access can still be reached through a neighbor, which is how the group gets into isolated network segments and walks around perimeter defenses.

Persistence Through COM Hijacking and Time Providers

To survive reboots, the attackers used two uncommon methods. The first was COM hijacking for persistence. They changed the TreatAs registry key for the Network List Manager and Network Configuration objects.

Whenever a process called these components, Windows loaded the attackers’ DLL instead, for example netprofmprox.dll, whose name is almost the same as the real netprofm.dll.

The fake library still passes calls on to the real one. That keeps the system stable, so nothing crashes to give the attackers away. The malware also checks that it runs inside svchost.exe -k netsvcs and quits if it does not. This family is called SilentCOM.

The second method abused the Windows Time service. The attackers added their own provider under the W32Time TimeProviders registry key and set Enabled to 1.

At every boot, the service loaded their DLL inside svchost.exe with Local System rights. This loader, TediousLoader, opens raw sockets on every network adapter and reads incoming packets.

It looks for a secret signature, and the packet then tells it where to connect, listen, or bind. The code it receives is decrypted with AES-256 and run in memory.

This “sleep until a special packet arrives” design is similar to the one in the backdoor that stays silent until it is woken, which shows how popular the idea has become.

CunningDoor reaches its payload through DLL side-loading techniques. A legitimate, signed SafeNet DLL starts a malicious one, which decrypts shellcode from a file in the Temp folder.

A later tool, HenMapCaCon.dll, is written in Go and runs a TLS server over a named pipe. It can also pull files out of an infected system.

Positive Technologies watched named pipe traffic for the known name patterns and managed to capture and decrypt a payload. Teams can do the same.

They should limit SMB between network segments, log scheduled task creation, and check the registry for odd TreatAs and TimeProviders entries. They should also hunt for unusual DLLs in system folders and for the changed ChaCha20 constant listed below.
